text:
An Interview with "Apple in China" Author Patrick McGee about Apple's reluctant shift to outsourcing, its stunning success, and how its position relative to its supply chain has shifted over time.

An Interview with "Apple in China" Author Patrick McGee

Thursday, June 12, 2025

Today’s Stratechery Interview is with Apple in China author Patrick McGee . Apple in China is a masterpiece: it’s one of the best books about Apple ever written, one of the best books about China ever written, and absolutely belongs in the canon of essential books about the tech industry. I strongly suggest that everyone reading or listening to this interview buy a copy .

In this interview we merely scratch the surface of “Apple in China”. We discuss McGee’s background, how he was perfectly positioned to write the story of Apple in China, and how he structured the story. That story, to my mind, comes in three parts: the first is early Apple and why they had no choice but to outsource; the second is Apple achieving stunning success while still being ignorant of the forces that were driving their success in China; the third is about Apple’s awakening to their position, and when and where they crossed the line to being a company that did more to build China than any other.

As a reminder, all Stratechery content, including interviews, is available as a podcast; click the link at the top of this email to add Stratechery to your podcast player.

On to the Interview:

An Interview with “Apple in China” author Patrick McGee

This interview is lightly edited for content and clarity.

*Topics:*

Buy This Book ( #buy-this-book ) | Background ( #background ) | The Story of Apple in China ( #story-apple-china ) | Apple’s Reluctant Shift to Outsourcing ( #apples-reluctant-shift ) | Apple’s Clueless Success in China ( #apples-clueless-success ) | Teaching Engineering ( #teaching-engineering ) | Apple Crosses the Line ( #apple-crosses-line ) | Apple’s Culpability in China’s Rise ( #apples-culpability ) | The Tim Cook Legacy ( #tim-cook-legacy )

Buy This Book

*Patrick McGee, welcome to Stratechery.*

*Patrick McGee:* Thank you, my pleasure.

*Let me get the headline out of the way: This is the best book about Apple ever written, one of the best books about China ever written, and one of the best books about tech, period. Congratulations.*

*PM:* Wow, thank you. I mean, I’ve been stunned by your breadth of knowledge and then the depth that you go into so I’ve actually been quite nervous as to what you think about the book, so that means a lot. Thank you.

*It is funny you mentioned that, because I was in a group chat talking about how phenomenal this book was, and I was reflecting on it. I’m like, “I don’t think I learned that much”, then I’m like, “But when it comes to this particular issue, I’m pretty sure I’m like the 99.999 percentile of awareness of it”. And to be clear, I did still learn stuff, but what was so striking was not just what you reported, and the reporting is phenomenal, but I thought the way that you told the story and you put things together, and this is what I want to get to in this interview, about Apple’s position relative to its supply chain and how that shifted over to time, that’s what was so exciting to me, it’s like this is a story that needs to be told, but the way that you told it I thought was fantastic, so I’m very excited to talk more about it.*

*PM:* Yeah, great. That’s my own self-assessment as well, which is that I think I knocked it out of the park on sourcing. The level of detail and whatnot that I was able to get through the last 30 years to me was the biggest attribute, and then the writing is not spectacular, the writing is just a reporter, you can tell I’ve worked for a newspaper, it’s just very matter of fact, but it’s structured in a really good way where you’re left wanting to read the next chapter. The pacing is really good and it’s kind of bite-sized chapters. There are about 42 chapters and they’re roughly 3,000 words each, so I liked how digestible and fast-paced it was.

*We’ll get to the structure in a little bit, but when I start these interviews — like I said, I wanted to get that out of the way, everyone who’s listening needs to go buy it , I saw you’re number seven on the non-fiction chart , we need to bump you up. Look, if you pay for Stratechery, you can pay for this and I’m telling you, it’s totally worth it, I’m telling my listeners.*

Background

*I do always start these interviews asking more about who I’m talking to, what’s your background? Where’d you get started? I think it’s probably particularly pertinent to the topic at hand. So starting from the beginning, where’d you grow up? How’d you get started in journalism? Let’s go from there.*

*PM:* I grew up in Calgary, Alberta, so I’m Canadian. I have two older brothers and my older brothers and my two parents, we all have a degree or two in religion, so that’s actually the sort of family conversation. My dad was an Anglican priest when I was a young kid, and my parents had met at divinity school, and then I think I would fairly say we sort of grew up in a theological library. So lots of questions about various religions and cultures and that sort of thing. So we all have, I mean, this is the argument over the dinner table all the time, right?

*You have anticipated a question we’re going to get to at the end, but this is actually a fantastic framing — sorry, continue.*

*PM:* I’m a reasonably staunch atheist, but I find religion to be a fascinating lens through which to view history or culture or anything else. I’m inclined maybe to mysticism, if anything. Then I have various family members who of course, if my dad was an Anglican priest, would feel differently about the crux of these issues. But I suppose what I’m really pointing at is that we’re a humanities family, reading, writing, thinking in some way, shape or form, that’s what everybody in my family does.

I studied anthropology at university and then sort of morphed into a degree in religion. I maybe wasn’t anticipating doing that, but I spent a lot of time focused on Papua New Guinean religions from a hundred years ago because the birth of anthropology through the likes of James Frazeer and Bronislaw Malinowski was absolutely fascinating to me. Some of my favorite subjects were about the Trobriand Islanders , who according to Malinowski, didn’t understand the connection between the act of sex and procreation. I got all interested in the psychoanalytic take on this, which is that Malinowski misunderstood his own ethnography and that this was the Oedipus complex transmitted in the Papua New Guinean Island. So anyway, I’m going off on a tangent, but I’m just, my history is not computers—

*I already told everyone that you’re a good storyteller, so I am eagerly anticipating to see how we’re circling back. So please continue.*

*PM:* (laughing) Yeah, so I got really involved with Freud, with Wittgenstein. I really studied intellectual history, but through the prism of religion. The problem with that is, it’s fascinating for four years, it’s good for cocktail conversations, I’ve read a lot of interesting books, but it doesn’t have any job prospects so I graduated with honors and stuff and then met immediate crisis as I had no idea what I wanted to do with my life and I wasn’t going straight into graduate school.

So the short version is that I fell into journalism just in my home city, living in the garage of my best friend, and did that for a few months. The magazine unfortunately collapsed, I happened to be in DC at a time visiting my girlfriend, and from there I just sent out 25 letters and I ended up getting an economics reporting job, so I stayed in DC, and this was all one year before Lehman Brothers collapsed, so we’re just beginning to hear terms credit crisis at a time when I didn’t know what a credit crisis was, but it ended up being the perfect time to become a macroeconomics reporter, because by the time the world was dealing with the Lehman troubles, I was already reporting on it for a year.

I sort of had 12 months of getting up to speed reading the Greenspan biography and everything like that, that basically led to becoming a bond reporter and getting a job at the Wall Street Journal, and then I had this reputation at the Wall Street Journal walking in every day and grabbing the pink paper, the Financial Times, and reading that because I preferred it. And somehow that reputation found itself over-

*Made its way to the Financial Times?*

*PM:* Made its way to the FT and they were hiring for a service they were calling Fast FT, they wanted to hire me for New York. I eventually didn’t get the job, but I said, “That’s okay, I’ve been in New York for five years, I think I want to move on anyway”, and they sort of said, “Well, wait, would you move to Hong Kong?”, because the same position was available in Hong Kong. So that was my serendipitous connection to Asia. I’d been to Southeast Asia before and whatnot, but I hadn’t been to Hong Kong so I ended up basically running Fast FT for three years out of Hong Kong, that was just at the time when the Umbrella Revolution took place, that’s like 2013 to 2016.

Then if you do that, Steve Jobs connect the dots backwards thing for your life, my book idea basically comes out of covering Hong Kong and the greater China region for three years, moving to Germany, covering the automotive industry and supply chains for three years, and then going to California to cover Apple for four years. When you couple those things together — China, supply chain, and Apple — you sort of get the origins of the book.

*That’s amazing. I mean, you’re right, it is a classic Steve Jobs looking backwards idea.*

The Story of Apple in China

*I do have to ask, the book is called Apple in China. Were you tempted to title the book, “Designed in California, Made in China?”*

*PM:* Yes! That was actually one of the iterations. I guess the trouble was, you wanted a book where you didn’t need the subtitle to understand what the context was, and the only way to get both entities in the book was to have a kind of boring title.

*Well, you also cover retail and you cover sales and things along those lines, so it’s not just the supply chain.*

*PM:* And it’s not just China. When the New York Times reviewed the book, they were like, “China doesn’t really enter the picture until page 90”, and that’s true, but how would you encapsulate that in the title? You’d have to give some boring textbook eight word title.

*To me, that is one of the things I liked about the book, so we’ll come back to that famous phrase in a moment, but I read the book as being in three parts. I think you actually had five parts or something with those 42 chapters.*

*PM:* Six.

*Six, got it. So my three that I took away was first, why Apple went to China in the first place, and I thought it was so important and valuable that you went back through some of this history. I was just writing about Apple and China stuff just a few months ago , and I went back to that Fremont factory for the Mac and things along those lines, and I think it’s really important to appreciate this fact that they were late in many respects.*

*But then number two, part two, Apple’s combination of staggering success in China, both in terms of sales and manufacturing, all of which happened to a — you very adroitly explained — a very clueless company in many respects.*

*And then third, Apple’s loss of innocence and double down. To me, that’s the arc of this story, and there’s a bit about the end about their current predicament and what they might do next, but is that the structure you were going for? That three-piece story, or have I done my own meta-editing on top of you?*

*PM:* You’ve kind of done your own thing, but I wouldn’t disagree with any word that you said. I mean, by the time I went on book leave in September 2023, I had the contours of the story, and for me it was four parts so now I’m just trying to figure out if I remember those four parts. I think I needed to tell the early history when Apple was building its products itself, and then one early realization I had was that it’s usually a sentence or two in a magazine profile that basically says, “They hired Tim Cook, who closed down Apple factories and moved to China” — that’s a gross oversimplification. So there’s the seven-year experimentation phase where the iMac alone, the translucent iMac —

*This the part I learned the most, by the way.*

*PM:* Yeah, it was being built in six different counties.

*Right, with LG and then the Mexico thing. To me, that was the huge unpack. Obviously I’ve dived a lot into China in the context of diving into early Apple, but that whole intervening period, I’m glad you highlighted that because to me, that was like every page, I’m like, “Wow, that’s interesting, I didn’t know that”. It was really valuable.*

*PM:* I remember having this thought in my head when writing that I wanted an Apple nerd, let’s say, to open the table of contents and be like, “Well, I don’t even know, LG goes global? Why is LG in this book?”. So they built the iMac in Korea and then they built it in Wales and Mexicali, and who knows that history well? So I wanted the reader to be impressed that I’m talking to Welsh technicians who ran the supply chain out of Wales.

*I was impressed. I’m impressed, I think I’ve made clear, I’m impressed!*

Apple’s Reluctant Shift to Outsourcing

*Well, let’s go through this. Tell me about that first part, which ties into this and their initial forays with outsourcing. I thought you did a very good job of describing the financial imperative for outsourcing. It’s marginal work as opposed to tech, where it’s all sort of upfront and it’s like cloud computing — or not even that. It’s more tangible of that physical goods and doing it as a service.*

*PM:* It’s variable cost instead of fixed cost.

*That’s right, that’s what I was going for.*

*PM:* The problem with running your own factory is you are paying for idle workers when you don’t have products being built, whereas manufacturing-as-a-service changes that completely.

*Absolutely. So this bit of just them being the last holdout, and them wanting to build it themselves, talk more about that, because I do think that’s important and sort of a mollifying — What’s the word I’m going for? — the book ends up I think, pretty rough on Apple, and appropriately so, but I don’t think you’re mean. Actually, I thought there were opportunities for you to take shots that you didn’t because some things weren’t clear, like iCloud keys in China. You’re like, “Well, we don’t know for sure”. You talked to some people, they think we do know for sure, but you weren’t taking cheap shots. But if you read this book, it’s very sobering. That’s why I think it’s useful to say, “Look, Apple started out in a very, very different place”.*

*PM:* It’s like the founding ethos of the company in the late 1970s that you build your own products. I mean, that’s what Steve Wozniak was skilled at. He could just take a computer apart, retool it to some degree, and then end up with a faster, more beautifully designed computer, and then Steve Jobs realizes the marketing potential of his friend and then just wants to redo the aesthetics of it or what have you.

That’s sort of the DNA of the company, but it’s not the DNA of the companies that begin to clone the PC, let’s say 10 years later in the mid-1980s. They don’t have the same ethos. Because the IBM PC was, to quote someone involved in it, “Bandaged together with existing parts”, those existing parts began to be created in places like Taiwan and Korea where you had this supply chain where you could just import everything, and you didn’t have to be building it yourself.

So this isn’t a philosophical thing so much as a timing thing. For Apple, you had to be building it yourself because there was no electronic supply chain in the mid-’70s. By the mid-’80s, that’s changed, but it’s changed on behalf of the PC clones and so companies like Space Craft Incorporated , the Foxconn of its day, begin doing the circuit board for the IBM PC because they have this automated method of doing it, and then they begin doing the final assembly as well, and SCI ends up playing this instrumental role, not just for IBM, but the PC clone industry. This sort of gives rise to Selectron, Celestica, Jabil, companies that people probably don’t know but actually they become a M&A dream in the 1990s on Wall Street, because companies you’ve never heard of are merging and merging because there’s all sorts of cutthroat demand or cutthroat pricing techniques that are taking place.

So if you remember the Compaq shock, I think this might be 1992, I don’t believe it’s in the book, but this is when Compaq dramatically cuts prices by 20 or 30% on PCs, and it’s because they’re the first to really go to Asia and exploit the opportunities there of having the final assembly done.

So sometimes people say that Tim Cook is the architect of moving to China, and I don’t think he is. That’s not a knock against him, there is no architect. The architect, if you will, is the suppliers themselves, who by competing for orders, are realizing that the place to go is Asia and then within Asia, the place to go after 2001 essentially, when China enters the WTO, is China.

So you had to tell that story because you needed to understand that Apple really tried to build everything themselves. That is the DNA of the company. Steve Jobs is really controlling, even when he leaves the DNA stays, and it’s only because everybody else has done so well with logistics, manufacturing and efficiency, in all those respects that Apple is near days away from missing payroll.

*And Apple can’t sell enough to fill their factories so that whole variable cost issue versus fixed costs, that’s what was killing the company, quite literally.*

*PM:* Yes, but that’s why it’s so important not to write a polemic, because I’m deeply sympathetic to Apple in this regard. They are the last holdout. Nobody should blame Apple one iota for deindustrializing or hollowing out American manufacturing in the ’80s and ’90s, they’re the one company trying to do it all there, and even when Steve Jobs goes to NeXT and found another company, he says, “My favorite thing about the computer is that it’s not built in Osaka”, he really cares about that. So it’s out of total necessity. The company would not exist if they didn’t adopt a global manufacturing strategy, but the significant thing about that is that is adopted before Steve Jobs comes back and ipso facto before Tim Cook comes back and people don’t understand and I actually give a little bit of credit for Gil Amelio for making that choice.

*Well, part of what makes this book special is that it is, intentionally or not, I think a really fascinating look at some aspects of Apple’s culture. To that end, one of the themes I picked up early on in the book is a certain desire, even a need, for Apple to be the one in charge and them telling others what to do. Even if they don’t know what to do, they need to feel like they are telling the others what to do. Everything has to be a teacher-student relationship, and they are always the teacher, and it’s almost as if suppliers helping them hurt them more than losing massive amounts of money. That just seems to be a continuous theme, particularly in this LG, initial Foxconn era. That’s a theme that comes through very strongly.*

*PM:* Maybe I could tell the story of how Foxconn comes on board, because the line that frankly my wife wrote about this is that Jony Ive and Steve Jobs came up with products that made Apple unique, but the meeting of the minds between Tim Cook and [former Foxconn Chairman and CEO] Terry Gou has made them ubiquitous.

Essentially what happens is that Apple is under such pressure, I mean literally the brink of bankruptcy, to come up with the iMac design and then to produce it at reasonable scale that they don’t know how to manufacture it. It’s LG that basically understands the specs and the production features. Even though Apple has trained them, they haven’t done any of the writing [down of the specifications] or whatever. When the iMac becomes a massive success and it becomes America’s best-selling computer, it’s LG that knows how to build it and LG is refusing Apple’s demands to cut prices because of scale effects.

So Apple, as a secretive project, really unknown even to ID and PD, this is the ops team run by Tim Cook, basically takes a call from Terry Gou who says, “Let me fix this”, and they begin surreptitiously reverse engineering the product so that Foxconn is basically getting up to speed on how to build this thing. What’s interesting is they do such a good job that even though when ID gets involved, they look at it and they say, “Well, it’s been done all wrong, this isn’t to our specifications”, they’re nevertheless impressed with what Foxconn has been able to do, and so they come on as a second supplier to LG and they replicate the triple continent strategy that Apple had.

If you remember in the ’80s and ’90s, Apple made their computers in California, also Colorado, but America is what I’m trying to say, Ireland and Singapore. So when Apple has LG come on to become the first real contract manufacturer who’s going to build their main desktop computer on three continents, LG does it on three continents, and then Foxconn to win the order basically says we will mimic what LG has done, so they end up building in the Czech Republic. Which again, a narrative I don’t think anyone’s really familiar with. And Fullerton, California, which is never a big volume player, but of course you’ve got the proximity to Cupertino.

So it’s actually where a lot of the great lessons are taught between students and master, if you will, Apple and Foxconn. So the proximity to Cupertino is significant, even if the volume is coming out of Fullerton, never are. As you’re building products in three continents like that, the more you’re seeing that China is just winning out every time, the affordable labor, the abundance of labor, the efficiency of the labor and my narrative here on the Czech Republic, it’s a little bit heartbreaking because essentially what happens is that Foxconn realizes that in China you don’t have labor unions, you don’t have a free press that’s writing negative stories about you, etc and so the reason why the Czech Republic doesn’t really work out, although the factory is there for 10 years building Apple products, is that the lower labor standards, the lower environmental rights, etc. of China just allows Foxconn to work more efficiently in China.

*One of the things that was really interesting is that initial wave going into China, they were seeking efficiency and low labor costs, Apple was pursuing something else or found something else. Tell me about that.*

*PM:* Yeah, so I say that when the likes of Dell and HP were moving to China, they were doing so for the reasons you just mentioned, which I might just call margin. When Apple goes there, they’re seeing unconstrained design potential. So you could build an automation unfriendly product knowing that if you had a conveyor belt set up where each person has 10 seconds to fulfill their task, you could basically get anything done. They don’t just see low cost and abundance of labor, they understand the possibilities of creating something that would be extremely difficult to make, but with people being paid 50 cents an hour and having tens of thousands and later hundreds of thousands of people in a factory, they could get it done.

*This is a really important piece of what China gave Apple, because it’s so easy to get anchored on the low cost bit. But if you want to make something that’s cutting edge, by definition, that whole initial wave you’re talking about, someone figures out how to automate PCB boards, so they can just make a bunch of them. Everyone has the same one or they go through these assembly lines, it’s all standardized, it’s all the same, and Apple’s like, not that “We can go there and tap into standardization”, it’s, “We can go there and be more customized than anyone else but do it at scale”. That’s a reality very, very early, you could not get that in America or anyone else, and it’s under-appreciated. If you like Apple for what Apple does where they actually create new things and new ideas and new phones that look different than anything that came before, China was part and parcel of that.*

*PM:* And this is why I think the first 25 years of Apple actually really instructs how the company operates today, because when they were building things on their own, they had that “Control your own destiny through manufacturing” mentality, and so when they moved to outsourcing, they do something that is unlike what anybody else does.

I don’t even think outsourcing is the proper term, it is in the sense that it’s the third party building your product, but they’re taking such control over those factories that they’re doing something nobody else is really doing and this is where you get into their effect being something like a nation builder when we’ll come back to that later because we’re too early in the narrative.

*We will definitely come back to that for sure.*

*PM:* But essentially in order to get it done in Korea or to build the iPods in Taiwan manufacturing design engineers from Apple — and by the way, back then they’re called supply base engineers, this is just a footnote in the book. But basically the people that understand how to build the production processes, they’re flying over to these countries in Asia to train and equip the teams, basically teach engineering one-on-one.

*I knew this very early on. Back when I started making enough money to fly in business class, and I’d be on that United flight to Taipei most frequently, I sat next to someone from Apple every single flight, because this is the old United, the 2-4-2, where you were seatmates with someone so you’re going to have a conversation whether you wanted to or not. And man, I met a lot of Apple people, I can promise you that.*

*PM:* That is hilarious. So yeah, I would talk to people that worked on the Pixel, let’s say, or worked at Motorola in the late 2000s, and that’s what they would say. It would be like you’d be the one Pixel guy and everybody else in first class worked for Apple.

*Yep, totally.*

Apple’s Clueless Success in China

*One of my favorite parts of the book was the story of Apple retail in China.*

*PM:* Yes, that’s my favorite part.

*It kind of seemed like a distraction coming off the LG and the Foxconn stuff, and I’m like, “What’s the point here?”, but I thought it was — to me, this was one of the keys of the book, because what made it so interesting and notable was the extent to which it showed just how clueless Apple was about China. I’m sitting there watching as someone who’s not lived in China, but lived in Taiwan, and there’s some aspects that are similar, there’s some aspects where I know, I personally probably wouldn’t really want to live in China for a lot of the things that are expressed and articulated in this section that is just much more intense and a reality there and it sort of speaks to another cultural observation, which is the Apple bubble and the complete inability to have a theory of mind for anyone but themselves. People listening to this, and you have a bit in here about Steve Jobs getting mad at third party developers earlier in the other parts, but all these cultural things that we see or the people listening see, and things like the App Store, they see things like Apple’s presentations or Apple getting snippy with journalists or whatever it might be — they all come through in the book in these totally unexpected other places.*

*PM:* Yeah, this is my favorite part of the narrative, and partly it’s because of the behind-the-scenes writer thing, which is that I wrote a 70-page book pitch, and we had five publishers bid on it, and then Simon & Schuster won out and it’s been an incredible process since then.

But I, as the author of the 70-page book pitch, knew that I had nothing interesting to say from the period 2007 to 2013. In other words, I knew that 2013 was Apple’s political awakening in China. Obviously I knew that the iPhone came out in 2007. But I thought I was going to have this really dull section in the middle that sort of explains in a boring way how the iPhone was built vis-à-vis a Nokia phone or something like that.

Instead, I discovered this narrative of, it’s called, “Insatiable Demand of the Birth of the iPhone Market in China”, without giving too much away. What happens is in 2010, the iPhone 4 just goes wild. It just becomes the gangbusters, conspicuous symbol that every young person in China wants to have, and supply/demand imbalance is so great that these scalpers, who call themselves “Yellow Cows”, recognize this imbalance and they want to amass tens of thousands of iPhones and go to a second tier city. This is a time when there’s 40 different cities in China have a population greater than 2 million. None of those, aside from Beijing and Shanghai, have an Apple Store and so they’re amassing these products and they’re selling them in these other markets.

Well, how are they amassing them? You can’t buy more than two iPhones per person, so they’re busing in migrants by the literal thousands to snake outside the store for everyone to buy two iPhones each, and then they’re putting them in these suitcases and going to another city to sell them.

That’s already fascinating, and that’s probably a whole chapter of just describing yellow cows and the gray market, but it gets even more fascinating because they’re often mixed up with the triads, these organized crime groups similar to the mafia, and they get greedy. And so with factory connections, they begin hollowing out the phones, selling the memory to markets in Shenzhen, and then replacing it with lookalike memory that doesn’t actually function, but to the human eye at the Genius Bar they can’t tell what’s going on. And then the yellow cows then go to places like Portland where there’s no sales tax, and they’re avoiding the value added tax in China by smuggling in phones from Portland. But then they’re also zapping the processor so that it renders the phone inoperable. But at the same time, it masks the retail origin, it masks the fact that it’s a US-sold iPhone. So they’re buying these phones with fake IDs, they’re paying one month of a 24-month contract, smuggling the phone into China, and then still selling it for $8 or $900. So they’re finding ways, legally and illegally —

*You’re skipping the part where they’re going in and asking for a return, saying, “My phone is defective”.*

*PM:* Yeah, they’re buying the phone, breaking the phone, smuggling it into the country, breaking the phone, taking it to the Genius Bar, and then Apple, unaware of what’s going on, is giving them a brand new phone, and then they’re selling it on in the gray market. So they’re finding ways to make more money per iPhone than Apple, which is just this extraordinary narrative and essentially what happens—

*And it goes on for years! That’s what’s so fascinating about it. The cluelessness is just mind-boggling, and this idea that Apple cannot conceive of people acting in this way and they don’t believe John Ford about what’s going on, and it just goes on and on and on and on. Like I said, it’s so illuminating about not just what was happening in China, but about what Apple is like as a company. You have this idealistic vision that sees the best and sees the possibilities, and they apply that to everything, and it’s not applicable in lots of situations.*

*PM:* And that narrative, you’re not wrong to say, “Wait a minute, this seems different from the rest of the book” and for a long time, I did see it as a detour, except that it ties a nice ribbon on two big narratives. One is the right to repair narrative, which isn’t really in the book, but I explained that the reason why all the parts in an iPhone today are serialized to the motherboard is that all these products were being hollowed out and then replaced by all these parts in China, and that takes Apple eight years to figure out how to basically use these X-ray style machines to get a near atomic level view of the iPhone to figure out which one has been tampered with and which one hasn’t been, because the yellow cows are changing the IMEI number on both the SIM card and the back of the phone in ways that are just totally flummoxing Apple and potentially costing them millions upon millions of dollars.

It’s also pissing off the China teams, by the way, because if you’re having phones that are sold in America, it’s the American teams that are getting the credit, the American teams that are getting the market share or whatever, and the China teams are feeling like we’re not getting the full credit for how well the iPhone is doing in China because the phones are being smuggled in. So there’s all this tension within the Apple sales organization, which is fascinating.

Then the other thing, without going into detail, is I think this solves the riddle of why CCTV and Xi Jinping attack Apple in 2013, and it’s because of these alleged warranty differences. So he really is put in a bind, and I really am sympathetic to the bind that he was put in, but Steve Jobs is such an enormous figure that I don’t think you could just say, “Well, things probably would’ve played out the same”.

No, he reacted so differently from anybody else, and had such a different sense of product, vision and control, and he would see the threat, in my mind, that Beijing was pressuring Apple in such a different way that I can’t help but imagine it would be very different.

I will say I asked someone that knew Steve Jobs for nearly two decades, this question just the other day, and they sat there for a solid 30 seconds thinking about it, and I am not going to do that on a podcast, but that’s the sort of thing it is that sort of question, and this is someone who knew them personally, worked with them personally, and basically said, “I think it would be a big, big test of Steve Jobs’s integrity”, and that’s kind of the best answer they could muster. They recognize what a challenging position it was.

*One of the best parts of the book that we actually didn’t touch on at all is the rise of Xi Jinping and the way that interweaves through all this, there’s another great character in the book, Doug Guthrie, his whole story that is fantastic. And so yes, you already said my conclusion. You think we covered a lot of material in here? This is a big book. It was 300 some pages. How many pages is it?*

*PM:* It’s about 400.

*It is dense and it’s readable and it’s compelling. I absolutely mean it, it’s one of the best tech books ever written. I think it’s the best book about Apple, and I’ve never done this, I’ve had authors on before, I have never said to my audience, “If you care about tech to a sufficient degree to pay for Stratechery, you owe it to yourself to go buy this book”. Phenomenal job, and it’s great to talk to you.*

*PM:* Huge thanks, Ben. I really appreciate that.

title: WBD Split, HBO and Warner, Whither Sports?
subject: WBD Split, HBO and Warner, Whither Sports? (Stratechery Update 6-16-2025)
dek: WarnerBros. Discovery is splitting up, but the real split goes back to Turner Broadcasting. View in browser | Listen in your podcast player STRATECHERY WBD Split, HBO and Warner, Whither Sports? Monday
text:
WarnerBros. Discovery is splitting up, but the real split goes back to Turner Broadcasting.

WBD Split, HBO and Warner, Whither Sports?

Monday, June 16, 2025

On Thursday’s episode of Sharp Tech , Andrew and I discussed Apple’s Retreat at WWDC, and Meta’s investment in Scale AI.

This Thursday is a federal holiday; as a reminder Stratechery follows the stock market holiday schedule ; there will be no Stratechery Interview.

On to the Update:

WBD Split

From the Wall Street Journal :

Warner Bros. Discovery is splitting itself into two stand-alone publicly traded entertainment companies, separating its HBO Max streaming service, movie studio and TV production business from its cable networks. One company will be home to CNN, TNT, TBS and Warner’s dozens of cable channels, as well as its international holdings. That entity, called Global Networks for now, will hold as much as a 20% stake in the second entity, which Warner is referring to as Streaming & Studios. It plans to use earnings from that stake to pay off debt. The move effectively undoes much of Warner Media and Discovery Communications’ 2022 merger, separating Warner’s marquee film and TV from Discovery’s reality and nonfiction fare.

Warner, like other entertainment companies including Disney and Paramount Global, has seen ratings and revenue decline in its once-powerful cable network operation, with consumers ditching traditional pay-television in favor of streaming. Comcast is in the process of spinning off the bulk of its cable network business into a stand-alone company named Versant that is expected to be complete by year’s end. Warner is betting that its parts are worth more than the whole. Traditional media companies are trying to keep up with rivals such as Netflix and Amazon Prime Video that are unburdened by legacy cable businesses.

Warner told investors late last year that it planned to restructure into two operating divisions. It said Monday that the separation will unlock shareholder value and give each company the ability to be more nimble in a rapidly changing media landscape.

I do feel compelled to cover this because, as much as I like celebrating when I get things right, I also need to own my Ls, and I’m taking a big one here. In 2021 and 2022 , I was very optimistic about the idea of combining Warner Bros. and Discovery. My reasons for optimism included:

* Increased bargaining power with MVPD providers
* A streaming package that appealed to the entire household, with a combination of prestige content and top-notch “filler” (my affectionate term for Discovery-style reality shows)
* A better advertising offering that extended across linear TV and streaming

The biggest mistake in my analysis was not properly accounting for the debt which the new Warner Bros. Discovery was taking on, a mistake that was greatly amplified by the significant rise in interest rates that has occurred over the past few years (although WBD’s debt is still fairly cheap and is going down); S&P Global downgraded WBD’s debt to junk status late last month , thanks in large part to declining linear TV revenues.

It’s important to acknowledge, however, that my reasons for optimism were overstated as well. First, there are serious questions about WBD’s MVPD leverage going forward, particularly now that TNT has lost the NBA (more on the sports angle in a moment). Second, there is no evidence that Max’s breadth does anything to mitigate churn, which remains amongst the highest of the streaming services. Third, despite the fact that Discovery had a decent ad product, WBD hasn’t really made anything compelling, and has actually used CNN and sports to push customers out of the ad-supported version and into the higher-priced tier, strongly suggesting their ads just don’t monetize that well.

Basically, nothing seems to have worked here, although at least Max is called HBO again.

HBO and Warner

About that name change; from Variety in May :

Turns out, Warner Bros. Discovery thinks HBO has some pretty good brand equity, after all. This summer, streamer Max will bend the knee and rebrand back to its original name, HBO Max. The change comes just over two years after Warner Bros. Discovery decided to drop HBO from the streamer’s name to become just Max. Note that while HBO and Max have carried separate commercial branding during that time, they’ve competed under one “HBO/Max” label for industry awards. The surprise announcement, made less than two months after Max tweaked its logo to look more like the classic black-and-white HBO color scheme, was revealed at Warner Bros. Discovery’s upfront presentation to ad execs in New York on Wednesday.

In a press release, WBD said “returning the HBO brand into HBO Max will further drive the service forward and amplify the uniqueness that subscribers can expect from the offering. It is also a testament to WBD’s willingness to keep boldly iterating its strategy and approach — leaning heavily on consumer data and insights — to best position itself for success.”

From one perspective, dropping the HBO name never made much sense; my Dithering co-host John Gruber spoke for many when this news dropped :

Everyone should be clear on what to make fun of here. We should not be making fun of the fact that they’re changing the name back to HBO Max. No one likes to admit to mistakes. It’s intensely uncomfortable. And people who are good at politics and PR are good at spinning mistakes as not-mistakes. We should, in fact, congratulate them for admitting to this dumb fucking mistake and re-embracing the “HBO” name.

On the other hand, I actually was always pretty uncomfortable with over-extending the HBO name; I wrote back in 2018 when AT&T was looking to expand Warner Bros. streaming ambitions:

Here it’s easier to argue that the New York Times was directionally correct about changes coming: today HBO is a brand built on differentiation to a much greater extreme than any other TV channel or streaming service. There aren’t that many shows, relatively speaking, but 40 million households or so pay anyways because those shows are must-see.

Compare that to Netflix: certainly the streaming service is investing lots of money in having differentiated content, but the long-term goal, and by extension the ultimate value proposition for consumers, is offering something for everyone all of the time. To be TV, in other words, but freed from the constraints of geography and time; one subscribes to Netflix not to get a particular show, but simply because that is what one does (just as one once subscribed to cable).

Can you see the difference? Just think of the tagline: “It’s not TV, it’s HBO”. That’s not simply a slogan! At least it wasn’t, but it will be if AT&T sees the brand’s ultimate value as a consumer front-end for a de facto Netflix competitor, that is to say, TV.

More broadly, if my interpretation of these comments are correct and AT&T plans to build a streaming service to rival Netflix, well first good luck, and second, that is quite a bit higher level of ambition for the Time Warner acquisition than I anticipated. That’s not necessarily a compliment! The reason I wrote about the possibility of Time Warner content differentiating AT&T wireless service through zero rating is that that was an actual benefit of acquisition that could not necessarily be gained through contract. Building a Netflix competitor, on the other hand, is first and foremost about cash, and it’s not clear why AT&T is better positioned to furnish that cash instead of the market.

OK, maybe I can take the W on this analysis? It holds up pretty well! In the end, the mistake was not so much about combining Warner Bros. and Discovery as it was trying to take on Netflix in the first place; my instincts were right about that, I just wish I had stayed anchored on that point all the way through.

To that end, the return to HBO branding makes even more sense with the news of this split, which isn’t just an unwinding of the Discovery merger: that’s giving up on competing with Netflix as a general purpose something-for-everyone streamer. What this split really is is an undoing of the 1996 acquisition of Turner Broadcasting by Time Warner. Time Warner, before that acquisition, had differentiated content from its studio and a premium cable channel; the new Time Warner is going to have differentiated content from its studio and a premium streaming service.

The real question, however, is if this roll-back should go even further. Time Warner was itself the product of a merger: Time Inc. started in publishing but launched HBO in 1972; Warner was a studio that merged with Time in 1990. Obviously all of Time’s publishing assets are long gone, which leaves just HBO, but is HBO even worth it anymore? It’s not just that the brand equity has been diminished; it’s that feeding a streaming service is a distraction from simply making great content and selling it to the highest bidder. I further complained about the watering down of HBO in 2019 and added:

There are two points to be made about this deal. First, despite the fact that streaming services are supposed to be paying full market rate for shows, even if they made those shows themselves, it is striking that all of the production studios happen to be acquiring their own shows. Warner is acquiring “Friends” and “Big Bang Theory”, NBCUniversal is acquiring “The Office”, and the show that Netflix is acquiring, “Seinfeld”, was produced by Sony, which is largely sitting out the streaming service war.

This, for the record, speaks well of Sony: I remain convinced that at some point most of these streaming services are going to fold as their executives — or their replacements — realize that fixed cost assets are best monetized by selling them to the highest bidder, or to multiple outlets, not by restricting their reach.

This is still correct, and it cuts both ways: Warner is better off selling content to the highest bidder, and HBO is better off bidding for the best content. There’s no reason they have to be under the same roof.

Whither Sports?

From Awful Announcing :

Monday morning, news broke that Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD) would be splitting into two companies: one that houses its TV and movie studio along with its Max (soon to be HBO Max) streaming service and another that houses its legacy assets, including the TNT Sports family of cable networks…

The move obviously has massive implications for sports fans. TNT Sports owns numerous prevalent live sports rights in the United States, and its split from WBD will impact how and where fans can access those games. Similarly to Versant, WBD’s new entity, which is temporarily being called Global Networks, will have to navigate its future without direct access to a broadcast network or a streaming service. However, unlike Versant, which is primarily acquiring the scraps of NBC’s larger live sports portfolio, Global Networks is acquiring the entire enchilada from WBD. That means the:

* NCAA Men’s Basketball Tournament (through 2032)
* MLB (through 2028)
* NHL (through 2028)
* College Football Playoff (through 2028)
* NASCAR (through 2031)
* French Open (through 2034)

For individuals who access TNT properties through a traditional pay-TV bundle, not much will change. The question becomes how these networks will be distributed digitally as more consumers move to streaming and cable goes the way of the dodo. In the interim, TNT Sports properties will continue to stream through Max, per the company’s investor call discussing the move on Monday. But that will be a temporary solution. At some point, TNT Sports will need to find a streaming partner willing to license its content for its platform. And given TNT’s live sports portfolio, that may prove more challenging than it seems.

It’s only been three weeks since I put together this overview of U.S. sports rights in anticipation of nearly every major sporting event being available via streaming, starting this fall, and there’s already a wrench in the plans!

On one hand, it makes total sense to include TNT Sports in the spin-off: sports are essential to maintaining some sort of leverage with MVPDs, which is critical to maintaining the cash flow necessary to cover all that debt; meanwhile, sports just don’t make sense for a streaming service that is retreating to premium, given just how expensive rights are.

What is a bit weird, at least in terms of timing, are those college football playoff rights; from ESPN in late May :

ESPN and TNT Sports have reached a five-year agreement for TNT Sports to sublicense select College Football Playoff games from ESPN starting this season, the networks announced Wednesday. TNT Sports will present two first-round CFP games during the 2024 and 2025 seasons. In addition to the first-round games, TNT Sports will add two quarterfinal games each year, starting with the 2026 season through the 2028 season. TNT will be the primary network televising the sublicensed CFP games, among additional TNT Sports distribution platforms. ESPN will show all other CFP games on its networks, including the national championship game. ESPN will also continue to manage the sponsorship program for the presentation of the CFP.

This deal makes sense from ESPN’s perspective: they get to reap the benefit of having the college football playoffs while sharing the costs (remember, when it comes to streaming, having must-see events is more important than having huge amounts of inventory). And, at the time it happened, it made sense for TNT: these games give them leverage with MVPDs, and provided a reason to subscribe to HBO Max at a time when they didn’t have many other sporting events. That last justification no longer exists, however (although the first one is more important than ever). Indeed, as the Awful Announcing article notes, the most likely outcome is that TNT starts licensing streaming rights to another entity: ESPN is an option, as well as Fox’s upcoming Fox One streaming service.

The larger question is what happens in 2028: will sports leagues want to re-up with TNT Sports if they don’t have a streaming service? Will they want to separate rights? What should concern all of them is similar to the biggest objection to my argument above that Warner and HBO should be separate entities: if Warner simply sells shows, it runs the risk of monopsony with a dwindling pool of buyers; if sports starts to consolidate in terms of streaming then the leagues could eventually face a similar issue, with ESPN as a potential long-term winner.

Regardless, all of this is progress for the industry as a whole: the prior structure of content makers, channels, and distributors made sense when everything went over a wire; now that everything is over the Internet, that entire middle layer doesn’t really have a reason to exist. What will be interesting to watch is just how far content makers — particularly those who give up on streaming directly — go out of their way to prop up distribution end points so that they’re not completely at the mercy of Netflix and, to a lesser extent, ESPN.

text:
Microsoft and AI continue to fight, and WhatsApp adds ads and subscriptions (and I explain why as a creator I'm not interested).

Microsoft-OpenAI Drama Continues, WhatsApp Ads, Channel Subscriptions and the Creator Perspective

Tuesday, June 17, 2025

Jon at Asianometry has another great historical video, this time about Lisp Machines .

On to the Update:

Microsoft-OpenAI Drama Continues

From the Wall Street Journal :

Tensions between OpenAI and Microsoft over the future of their famed AI partnership are flaring up. OpenAI wants to loosen Microsoft’s grip on its AI products and computing resources, and secure the tech giant’s blessing for its conversion into a for-profit company. Microsoft’s approval of the conversion is key to OpenAI’s ability to raise more money and go public. But the negotiations have been so difficult that in recent weeks, OpenAI’s executives have discussed what they view as a nuclear option: accusing Microsoft of anticompetitive behavior during their partnership, people familiar with the matter said. That effort could involve seeking federal regulatory review of the terms of the contract for potential violations of antitrust law, as well as a public campaign, the people said.

Such a move could threaten the companies’ six-year-old relationship, widely seen as one of the most successful partnerships in tech history. For years, Microsoft fueled OpenAI’s rise in exchange for early access to its technology, but the two sides have since turned into competitors, making it more difficult to find common ground…OpenAI and Microsoft are at a standoff over the terms of the startup’s $3 billion acquisition of the coding startup Windsurf, the people said. Microsoft currently has access to all of OpenAI’s IP, according to their agreement. It offers its own AI coding product, GitHub Copilot, that competes with OpenAI. OpenAI doesn’t want Microsoft to have access to Windsurf’s intellectual property.

The companies continue to be at odds over how much of OpenAI Microsoft would own if it converts into a public-benefit corporation. Microsoft is currently asking for a larger stake in the new company than OpenAI is willing to give, people familiar with the matter said. OpenAI has to complete the conversion by the end of the year, or it risks losing $20 billion in funding…The startup is trying to renegotiate elements of that deal alongside its planned conversion. It wants to join with other cloud providers so it can sell its technology to more customers and access additional computing resources. Microsoft, meanwhile, wants access to OpenAI’s technology even after the startup declares its models have achieved humanlike intelligence, which would end the current partnership.

The Information came out with a story a few hours later corroborating much of The Wall Street Journal story, particularly in terms of the points of conflict, with a very telling line:

OpenAI wants Microsoft, the startup’s biggest outside shareholder, to have a roughly 33% stake in the reshaped unit in exchange for foregoing its rights to future profits, according to a person who spoke to OpenAI executives.

The Wall Street Journal doesn’t indicate who its sources are, but there’s little doubt in my mind they too are on the OpenAI side, and I get why: my biggest takeaway from this story is that I have underestimated the amount of leverage that Microsoft has over OpenAI. I most recently wrote about this slow motion train wreck last month and said:

Here’s the big question: what is more valuable to Microsoft in the long run? Those rights to $100 billion in profits, along with the revenue share they now enjoy, or perpetual rights to OpenAI’s models? I think it has to be the latter (to put $100 billion in context, that is $17 billion short of Microsoft’s total operating income last year). Of course OpenAI — and the rest of its investors — almost certainly doesn’t want to give up so valuable an asset, but I’m not sure if they will have a choice; the fact of the matter is that Microsoft put in the money to make OpenAI an entity worth fighting for, and they would do well to give up future profits from OpenAI to secure profits of their own.

I still think that this is broadly correct — and note that the right to make OpenAI models available to other cloud providers is one of the points of contention in this story — but the fact that OpenAI (in my interpretation) seems to be reduced to issuing fantastical threats through the press suggests that the decision about the endpoint of these negotiations is almost entirely up to Microsoft. To that end, I can understand if the company is pushing for more than I suggested; indeed, if anything these threats through the press might make Microsoft want to hold onto more, since they’ll probably have to fight OpenAI again in a few years. I still think, however, that this is all the more reason to give more ground now, in exchange for an iron-clad agreement securing Microsoft’s exclusive Azure access to OpenAI models in perpetuity.

As for the Windsurf angle, my interview with Cursor CEO Michael Truell made clear just how important the data generated by these IDEs are:

*Is that a real sustainable advantage for you going forward, where you can really dominate the space because you have the usage data, it’s not just calling out to an LLM, that got you started, but now you’re training your own models based on people using Cursor. You started out by having the whole context of the code, which is the first thing you need to do to even accomplish this, but now you have your own data to train on.*

*MT:* Yeah, I think it’s a big advantage, and I think these dynamics of high ceiling, you can kind of pick between products and then this kind of third dynamic of distribution then gets your data, which then helps you make the product better. I think all three of those things were shared by search at the end of the 90s and early 2000s, and so in many ways I think that actually, the competitive dynamics of our market mirror search more than normal enterprise software markets.

Anthropic executives have made similar comments about the importance of this data feedback loop in terms of creating Claude Code; to that end, you can see why OpenAI would not want to share this sort of data with Microsoft to use to improve GitHub Copilot, even if their contract mandates that all IP is available to Redmond. And, frankly, I think OpenAI has a point; the spirit of the agreement is about AI models, not products or product usage data, which Microsoft has had plenty of opportunities to harvest on its own (a separate but related question I have is if OpenAI shares ChatGPT usage data with Microsoft? It would seem so?).

Again, it does seem that Microsoft holds all of the cards for now, and relinquishing any of their rights would be a big short to medium term sacrifice. And, along those lines, I’m just an analyst sitting at my computer; I don’t have a fiduciary responsibility to shareholders. I continue to think, however, that Microsoft should be focused on securing long-term rights to capabilities that align with its existing business, which is model access and exclusive rights to sell OpenAI models; let the product stuff go, including Windsurf data.

This is still a bitter pill to swallow for OpenAI: not only would they get more leverage on their training spend if other cloud providers could sell OpenAI models, but they would also have a better chance of monopolizing the market; as it stands existing AWS and GCP users are probably not going to switch to Azure just to get OpenAI models, but will instead use Anthropic or Gemini. The bitterness of that pill, however, is directly correlated to the cynicism/naiveté entailed in setting up the non-profit structure in the first place .

WhatsApp Ads

From the New York Times :

On Monday, WhatsApp said it would start showing ads inside its app for the first time. The promotions will appear only in an area of the app called Updates, which is used by around 1.5 billion people a day. WhatsApp will collect some data on users to target the ads, such as location and the device’s default language, but it will not touch the contents of messages or whom users speak with. The company added that it had no plans to place ads in chats and personal messages…

WhatsApp, which unveiled the changes at the Cannes Lions advertising industry conference, also said it was introducing paid monthly subscriptions for content creators, similar to offerings from competitors like X, YouTube and Twitch. The app will also let users and businesses advertise their “channels,” which are one-way broadcasts that can be sent to large groups of people…

The introduction of ads may call attention to WhatsApp’s previous stumbles with privacy. In 2021, the company proposed changes to its terms of service that some users interpreted as more data sharing. The revisions incited a global backlash. This time, WhatsApp braced for pushback, saying any data sharing with other Meta-owned apps for ad targeting was optional. Users can choose to link their WhatsApp, Instagram and Facebook accounts, so ads on WhatsApp can be based on data collected from those platforms, Ms. Srinivasan said.

WhatsApp has always been a bit of a funny app in that it has always had a tab bar at the bottom that I personally have only ever interacted with by accident; these new ads are going in the “Updates” tab, which is an evolution of “Status”, which has been there from the beginning and is, I think, a hangover from AOL Instant Messaging (I’m not sure who made this graphic — it looks like its from WhatsApp? — but I found it on Reddit ):

I’ll take Meta’s word for it that Updates are used in some markets; it has continued to be a part of the UI for a reason, I suppose (perhaps because it has always been a natural place to put advertising). That, by extension, is certainly a reason to not be bothered by this news: I’m not going to see the ads anyways! Even if I did, however, I wouldn’t begrudge Meta this move: WhatsApp provides me tremendous utility, that utility is connected to WhatsApp being free-to-use (because it has network effects), so of course it makes sense that there would be ads at some point (but I hope that there is eventually a subscribe-for-no-ads option).

What is interesting is that WhatsApp just yesterday pushed me to add my email address for security; maybe this is just a coincidence, and Meta wouldn’t also want to use that email address to identify me, but given that I haven’t linked my WhatsApp account to my other Meta accounts, or registered my WhatsApp phone number with Facebook, the company will probably be reduced to using something like IP addresses to target data, for ads that I probably won’t see (Meta is emphasizing that they don’t sell your data to advertisers, which of course they don’t; it’s too valuable. What is useful is being able to link accounts for targeting purposes).

Again, I don’t begrudge them these attempts, to the extent they are true; indeed, when and if advertising gains a greater presence in the app I would be tempted to link the accounts just to get better ads. And, of course, I appreciate WhatsApp’s end-to-end encryption, which means that Meta couldn’t use message content to target even if they wanted to; in that light, have at my other Meta data.

Channel Subscriptions and the Creator Perspective

What is more interesting to me are the new subscription options; from the WhatsApp blog :

Today we’re introducing some new features for our Updates tab, which is home to both Channels and Status. We’ve worked over the last two years to make this tab the place for you to discover something new on WhatsApp and it’s now used by 1.5 billion people a day. We’re encouraged by the enthusiasm and also want to help admins, organizations, and businesses grow on WhatsApp.

We’re going to do this in three ways:

* *Channel subscriptions:* You’ll be able to support your favorite channel by subscribing to receive exclusive updates for a monthly fee.
* *Promoted Channels:* We’ll help you discover new channels that might be interesting to you when you’re looking through the directory. For the first time, admins have a way to increase their Channel’s visibility.
* *Ads in Status:* You’ll be able to find a new business and easily start a conversation with them about a product or service they’re promoting in Status.

These new features will appear only on the Updates tab, away from your personal chats. This means if you only use WhatsApp to chat with friends and loved ones there is no change to your experience at all.

I had a chat with a WhatsApp executive about the Channels subscriptions and Promoted Channels items in the context of my being a creator, and this was my feedback:

* First, I’m certainly always in favor of new ways to monetize, but more importantly, am interested in new ways to connect to my subscribers.
* Second, what I am not interested in is having new channels to monitor or manage; a critical component of the creator business model is managing scarce resources, which is not just money, but also time.
* Third, what I need most is better ways to acquire and retain customers; what I am not worried about is marginal costs that drive revenue.

What I thought was interesting about this conversation was the initial disconnect we had on point three. Specifically, I personally have no issue paying 30% or whatever fee a platform wants to charge for acquiring customers; I would be happy to pay Apple or YouTube or Meta or whomever else for access to new channels. After all, every customer is incremental zero marginal cost revenue; if I have to pay $3 to get $10 of revenue that’s still $7 I wouldn’t have had otherwise.

What I don’t want to do is have to manage the complexity of individual silos, or only give my subscribers a portion of what they are entitled to; my ideal relationship to a scaled platform is the one I have with Spotify . I’m able to manage my subscribers via Passport, which connects with Spotify on the back-end to unlock Stratechery Plus content on Spotify. Right now there is no cost for this connection, but if Spotify ever wanted to start selling subscriptions on my behalf — and taking a fee, naturally — that would be ok with me too. The key difference from, say, YouTube subscriptions, or this WhatsApp product, is that I still ultimately own the connection with the subscriber, and can give them everything they are entitled to: not just podcasts, but also emails, website access, etc.

This remains one of the core concepts of Passport: of course I sell subscriptions directly using Stripe, but Passport can accept any front-end for payments, whether that be the App Store, WhatsApp, YouTube, etc., just as it can link to any back-end for distribution, from email to SMS to RSS to Spotify. Unfortunately nearly all of those other payment options completely intermediate the customer — I can’t even get an email address. What I need is scalability of my management time and the ability to be multimodal; if I get that, I’m happy to pay fees on incremental revenue.

Anyhow, what that means in terms of this announcement is that I’m not interested in setting up Channel subscriptions; I am seling subscribers more than just WhatsApp updates. If, however, I can tie that into my broader offering, then I’d be happy to pay Meta to help me acquire customers through WhatsApp or any of their other properties.

text:
Everyone wants xAI to exist, but is anyone actually using it? Then, Xbox as it once existed is dead; it's just Windows now.

xAI Raising Money, xAI and Oracle, Xbox = Windows

Wednesday, June 18, 2025

On yesterday’s episode of Sharp Tech , Andrew and I discussed why I’m more optimistic about Cursor than Perplexity, the seemingly deepening partnership between Apple and OpenAI, and our take on Bill Simmons’ and Chuck Klosterman’s normie takes on AI.

As a reminder, tomorrow is a federal holiday; there will be no Update.

On to the Update:

xAI Raising Money

From Bloomberg :

Elon Musk’s artificial intelligence startup xAI is burning through $1 billion a month as the cost of building its advanced AI models races ahead of the limited revenues, according to people briefed on the company’s financials. The rate at which the company is bleeding cash provides a stark illustration of the unprecedented financial demands of the artificial intelligence industry, particularly at xAI, where revenues have been slow to materialize. To cover the gap, Musk’s startup is currently trying to raise $9.3 billion in debt and equity, according to people briefed on the deal terms, who asked not to be identified because the information is private. But even before the money is in the bank, the company has plans to spend more than half of it in just the next three months, the people said.

Over the course of 2025, xAI, which is responsible for the AI-powered chatbot Grok, expects to burn through about $13 billion, as reflected in the company’s levered cash flow, according to details shared with investors. As a result, its prolific fundraising efforts are just barely keeping pace with expenses, the people added. A spokesperson for the company declined to comment. However, Musk said “ Bloomberg is talking nonsense ” in a response to a post on his social media platform X that referenced Bloomberg’s article…

Musk’s entrant in the AI race has struggled to develop revenue streams at the same rate as some of its direct competitors, like OpenAI and Anthropic. While almost none of these companies offer public figures on their finances, Bloomberg has previously reported that OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, is expecting to bring in revenues of $12.7 billion this year. At xAI, revenues are expected to be just $500 million this year, rising to north of $2 billion next year, investors were recently told…

Musk’s team at xAI, which is racing to develop AI that can compete with humans, believes that they have advantages that will eventually allow them to catch up with peers. While some competitors rent chips and server space, xAI is paying for much of the infrastructure itself and getting direct access through X, which previously bought a significant stockpile of the most coveted and high powered computer chips. Musk has said that he expects xAI will continue buying more chips.

I don’t, on one hand, see any reason to take Musk’s word that “Bloomberg is talking nonsense”; it would certainly be helpful from my perspective if xAI were to share evidence of strong revenue growth or high demand. Grok 3 was state-of-the-art when it launched, but Anthropic and OpenAI seem to have quickly caught up in model quality, while my personal opinion is that Grok’s quality has decreased as it has been optimized for cost and scale. I personally — along with the vast majority of consumers — am back to using ChatGPT most of the time, which is a much better product above-and-beyond model quality, while Anthropic continues to dominate most coding workflows. Obviously I’m not the representative customer — although Stratechery’s spending-per-employee on AI is extremely high! — but absent evidence I find the $500 million revenue figure very plausible.

One problem facing xAI is that they don’t have a hyperscaler partner to both share in the costs of training and hosting models, and also to serve as a go-to-market channel for enterprise workloads; OpenAI has Microsoft, Anthropic has Amazon, and Google obviously has itself. xAI frames their ownership of their own infrastructure as a differentiator, but I’m not sure I see why that would be the case, particularly given the fact that GPUs are not long-lived assets relatively speaking (although data centers are); indeed, GPU ownership exacerbates xAI’s revenue challenges, given that the way to make money on those GPU purchases is to make sure they are utilized 100% of the time, which is easier to do the larger the customer base desiring access to them.

xAI and Oracle

Could that mean, however, that the more important news from yesterday is this item from Reuters ?

Oracle said on Tuesday that its cloud computing division is working with Elon Musk’s artificial intelligence firm xAI to offer the startup’s latest AI model to business customers. Grok 3, as the model is called, first came out February and aimed to rival the latest offerings from DeepSeek and OpenAI. Musk made the model available to paying subscribers of his X social media platform, as well as through xAI itself.

Oracle will now offer Grok 3 from its data centers to corporate users who want to use the model but need their data to remain under their existing security protections with Oracle, Karan Batta, senior vice president at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, told Reuters on Monday. Oracle also offers models from Meta, French startup Mistral and Cohere on the service, part of its overall strategy of providing versions of popular models in a way that businesses can integrate into corporate software. “Our goal here is to make sure that we can provide a portfolio of models – we don’t have our own,” Batta said. “That’s the current strategy. We are going to be the one that offers all of them.”

xAI and Oracle actually have had quite the roller-coaster of a relationship. Grok 1 and 2 were both trained on Oracle’s cloud, but xAI did Grok 3 on its own; from The Information last July :

Musk’s xAI and Oracle have ended talks to expand an existing arrangement under which xAI rents specialized Nvidia AI chips from the tech giant. Instead, xAI is buying chips to build a data center on its own, according to several people involved in the talks. XAI had been discussing a multiyear agreement to rent Nvidia chips from Oracle for a planned supercomputer, The Information reported in May, in what could have been a $10 billion deal. But the talks stalled over issues including Musk’s demand that the supercomputer be built faster than Oracle thought possible, and Oracle’s concern that xAI’s preferred location did not have access to an adequate power supply, according to someone involved in the talks.

Musk famously built his new Memphis data center in record time and with off-grid power sources (which have recently been taken down after a new electrical substation came online), and has acquired land for a second Memphis data center ; that, however, is why yesterday’s announcement — the coverage of which focused on making xAI available to Oracle’s corporate customers — was so curious. Note this line from Oracle’s press release ( emphasis mine ):

xAI has selected Oracle to offer xAI’s Grok models via Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) Generative AI service for a wide range of use cases, including content creation, research, and business process automation. *xAI will also leverage the scalability, performance, and cost efficiency of OCI’s leading AI infrastructure to train and run inferencing for its next-generation Grok models.*

Now “train” could have a whole host of meanings; the most likely explanation for that line is that Oracle will do post-training for enterprise specific use cases, which lines up with them taking on enterprise workloads. Still, while Musk ended up being right that he could build a data center faster, economics may end up mattering more than speed in the long run, and Oracle is really the only partner left to dance with.

Then again, Oracle isn’t the only entity that might want xAI to survive and thrive; companies like Cursor or Perplexity, for example, should absolutely want there to be more competition at the model layer. Apple might have been a prospective partner, although it does appear that the company is doubling down on OpenAI. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, meanwhile, conspicuously showed a pre-recorded video with Musk at the Build developer conference last month; Azure offers Grok as an option in a similar manner to this latest Oracle deal. Perhaps the company that could most use xAI, however, is Meta; the fact that xAI now owns X (née Twitter), however, almost certainly makes any sort of tie-up a non-starter. Indeed, the reports that Meta is throwing around all kinds of money to hire AI talent is probably a risk factor for xAI.

Regardless, everyone in the ecosystem should want xAI to exist as a check on the other model providers; the challenge for xAI is getting everyone — or at least more people — to want to actually use it and pay for it.

Xbox = Windows

From The Verge :

Microsoft is confirming today that it’s working on a next-gen Xbox console in partnership with AMD. Xbox president Sarah Bond made the announcement in a minute-long video posted to YouTube , promising to deliver “an Xbox experience not locked to a single store or tied to one device.”

The headline is the AMD partnership, but the real news — at least in my interpretation — is that Xbox as we once understood it is well-and-truly dead. Here’s the video and transcript:

At Xbox, our vision is for you to play the games you want people you want, anywhere you want. That’s why we’re investing in our next generation hardware lineup across console, handheld, PC, cloud, and accessories.

I am thrilled to share we’ve established a strategic multi-year partnership with AMD to co-engineer silicon across a portfolio of devices, including our next generation Xbox consoles, in your living room, and in your hands. Together with AMD, we’re advancing the state of art in gaming silicon to deliver the next generation of graphics innovation to unlock a deeper level of visual quality, an immersive gameplay and player experiences, and hands with the power of AI, all maintaining compatibility with your existing library of Xbox games.

This is all about building you a gaming platform that’s always with you, so you can play the games you want across devices, anywhere you want, delivering you an Xbox experience, not locked to a single store or tied to one device. That’s why we’re working closely with the Windows team to ensure that Windows is the number one platform for gaming. The next generation of Xbox is coming to light and this is just the beginning. We can’t wait to show you and see what’s next.

“Xbox as we once understood it” was basically a direct PlayStation competitor: sure, it had components that were basically the same as a PC, but it was a single defined bill of goods, with a locked down operating system and a single game store; Microsoft sold consoles at a loss, at least at the beginning, and made money by selling both first party games and from licensing revenue on third party games. It’s a good model, as Sony can attest, but that’s the problem: Sony won by recognizing the changing economics of gaming and pivoting to an exclusives model with the PS4 generation.

I wrote about these changing economics at length in 2022’s Consoles and Competition , but briefly: as the costs of asset development dwarfed the cost of the core technology (particularly with the rise of licensable game engines), developers were heavily incentivized to support all platforms, rendering Sony’s investments in hardware differentiation moot; the company responded by acquiring a host of game studios and becoming the default choice for gamers only buying one console, thereby winning the third-party licensing game as well.

In short, Sony is the integrated winner, which perfectly explains this Microsoft announcement: they are going fully modular, supporting a host of hardware, from cloud to handhelds to PCs to a (relatively open) future console; the operating system across those devices will be Windows, and anyone can run on Windows, including competitors like Steam. That right there is the big win: by opening up, future “Xbox’s” will have access to the most games by far, and while Microsoft might make less money on every individual hardware or software sale, they might be able to make it up in volume from Windows licensing; at a minimum this strategy is at least broadly aligned with Windows and Azure and Microsoft’s orientation as a services business, and its nature as a platform.
