An interview with Sierra founder and CEO Bret Taylor about his career in tech and the future of AI.

An Interview with Sierra Founder and CEO Bret Taylor About AI Agents and Tech History Lessons

Thursday, June 26, 2025

This Stratechery interview is another installment of the Stratechery Founder series; as a reminder, one of the challenges in covering startups is the lack of available data. My solution is to go in the opposite direction and interview founders directly, letting them give their subjective overview of their companies, while pressing them on their business model, background, and long-term potential.

Today’s Stratechery Interview is with Sierra founder and CEO Bret Taylor . Taylor has one of the most storied careers in Silicon Valley: after Stanford he worked at Google, was CTO at Facebook, founded Quip, became co-CEO of Salesforce, and most recently founded Sierra, a B2B AI Agent building company. Taylor is also chairman of the board of directors of OpenAI, and previously was the chairman of the board of Twitter.

In this interview we discuss the highlights of Taylor’s career, including a discussion of how Google and Facebook used to be, and why it’s so hard to continue to innovate as you become a large company. Then we discuss the enterprise market and when products can win by being the best, and how they differ from consumer markets. We discuss Sierra, Taylor’s new AI agent startup, and why he believes there is a narrow window to build a significant new company, and whether or not AI like Sierra will lead to job losses. Finally, we discuss why ChatGPT is a generational consumer product, thanks in part to messaging being the right UI paradigm for AI.

As a reminder, all Stratechery content, including interviews, is available as a podcast; click the link at the top of this email to add Stratechery to your podcast player.

On to the Interview:

An Interview with Sierra Founder and CEO Bret Taylor About AI Agents and Tech History Lessons

This interview is lightly edited for content and clarity.

*Topics:*

Background ( #background ) | Google and Facebook ( #google-and-facebook ) | Quip and Best-of-Breed vs Suites ( #quip ) | Salesforce and Consumer vs. Enterprise ( #salesforce ) | Sierra ( #sierra ) | Agents and Business Model Paradigms ( #agents ) | AI, Jobs, and Technological Progress ( #ai-jobs ) | AI and Messaging ( #ai-messaging )

Background

*Bret Taylor, welcome to Stratechery.*

*Bret Taylor:* Thank you for having me.

*It’s an honor to finally have you on, I’ve been looking forward to this conversation for a while. As you know, I like to go back to the beginning of these conversations. So tell me where did you grow up? How’d you get started in tech? Let’s go back to young Bret.*

*BT:* Do you want the short answer or the medium answer?

*Give me the medium answer and I might dive in and ask a couple of follow-ups.*

*BT:* Born here in the Bay Area, Oakland, California, proud Oakland Native, wish we still had some sports teams, but that’s not the case. I ended up in technology, I was in high school when the web came out, we got an AOL subscription, all that, I didn’t really think of it as a career. I ended up on my 16th birthday buying a 1971 VW bus for $700.

*Nice.*

*BT:* Going to the movies with my friends and promptly rear ending a brand new Cadillac — it was parked by the way, I didn’t even have a good reason for it. Left a note on the windshield that, long story short, the guy who owned the car appreciated my honesty, offered me a job at his gas station to pump gas and clean the bathrooms. Every day I would go to that gas station and there was a mechanic next door, and he was complaining about how expensive it was to make a webpage and get it listed on Yahoo directory, which was all the rage back then. I was getting paid $4.25 an hour at the gas station, the job I took in large part because I felt guilty for hitting someone’s car and I asked, “How much will you pay me to make a website?”, he said, “$400”. Doing the math on that $4.25 an hour, that’s a lot of bathroom cleaning.

So I went to Diablo Valley Community College, which had a computer lab, taught myself HTML, made a webpage, got paid $400, promptly quit the gas station job. I felt like I’d done my time with the guy and ended up doing web design for a lot of local businesses, so by the time I ended up at college at Stanford, it was the peak of dot-com bubble, but I had kind of already caught the bug, so I think if you had met me my last year of high school, I might’ve said maybe I want to be a lawyer or something, but by the time I stepped foot at Stanford, I was making webpages and had sort of turned it into a pretty profitable business.

Then going to Stanford in 1998, it was like you were tripping over startups on the way to class so I have a feeling I might’ve caught the bug anyway, but it actually preceded that.

*I think it’s interesting because you didn’t really learn to program program until you got to Stanford, right?*

*BT:* Yeah, exactly. I don’t know, does HTML not count? I guess you’re probably right.

*The reason I find this part of the story interesting is I can relate to it a lot in that I was on the, “I’m going to make webpages for local businesses” bandwagon, didn’t really program until I got to college, and I think we’re very similar in age, and I just think it’s interesting to look back on your career, and it’s like you started with the entrepreneurship part and then tacked on the tech later, whereas you talk to other people like, “Oh yeah, my dad got me a computer when I was six years old and then I learned BASIC”, and then they’re off to the races and it took you a while.*

*BT:* We always had a computer in the house, so I was definitely very technically literate and I wasn’t intimidated by it, but it wasn’t like I had anything to do with it. I didn’t have a Mac, we had a PC, so I didn’t get the HyperCard bug , I love that program. I sort of wonder if I would’ve discovered programming earlier had we had it.

*Same thing I had a hand-me-down x86 PCs.*

*BT:* Exactly, yeah, the people with the cool Macs got to HyperCard and caught the bug early. I feel like I’ve met so many extremely talented engineers where HyperCard was the thing that nerd sniped them into becoming a developer.

Then I got to Stanford and took CS106X, which is their intro class, and I was hooked. I would go home from that class and I would program for fun and I just couldn’t get enough of it, and it was just felt so empowering to me. I remember thinking at one point, “There’s nothing that I can’t do with this that these large companies are doing”, and I just felt so much leverage in the act of creating software and so much empowerment and it was really fun.

I’ll fast forward to the end, you can tell me where you want to double click, but graduated in ’02, finished a Master’s degree, started what could have been a PhD, but did one year to get a Master’s and by the tail end of my Master’s year, I was working full-time at Google, so I actually took vacation from Google to take my finals of my last quarter.

Google and Facebook

*Did Google recruit you just there at Stanford or did you know them? Obviously the timing is right to be a Stanford student interested in computer science and connect with Google.*

*BT:* It was total luck.

So the dot-com bubble burst right in the middle of my college career. So the beginning of college, you go to the computer lab and there would be pizza sponsored by Company X — I never paid for food my entire college, you’d just go to the computer lab and there’s a recruiting team with free food. I joke by the end, like 2002, there was tumbleweed going through because of everything.

So when I left, I had an offer to be a software engineer at VMware and an offer to be an associate product manager at Google, and I ended up choosing Google. Working on a kernel is the most fun thing ever for a geeky infrastructure engineer like me, a systems engineer. But Marissa Mayer , who was a teaching assistant when I was at Stanford, had gone to Google, she was the one who recruited me to the associate product manager program. I sort of followed her and I knew some Stanford folks who had gone, I didn’t actually know what a product manager really meant, and so I took a huge leap of faith on it and followed people rather than the job. I would’ve said I actually knew what the VMware programming job was—

*I was going to say, it’s not like VMware would’ve been a bad company to latch onto, but it’s not like the rocket ship, I mean, rocket ship almost seems to undersell joining Google in 2002.*

*BT:* And who knew? We were still selling the yellow search appliance when I got there, AdWords was invented right around the time, but they were selling banner ads for keywords at the time. People always are like, “How did you choose?”, and I’m like, “Honestly, I just followed people and lucked out a little bit”.

It was helpful that the dot-com bubble burst though, because to some degree, when maybe some new grads were more sophisticated than I was, but it just limited the playing field to the healthiest players. So it was almost like chemotherapy, you kill some healthy cells, but you kill most of the bad cells. So the companies left were the companies that had really viable businesses, so I feel fortunate I didn’t graduate in 1999, I just feel lucky in a lot of ways.

*So tell me about Google and I do have to verify — is it true that you rewrote Google Maps in a weekend?*

*BT:* (laughing) That is mostly true. Do you want that story?

*Sure, give it to me. I know it’s out there, but it’s such a great story.*

*BT:* Yeah, I think it’s out there because of Paul Buchheit who created Gmail, and I ended up starting a company with him, and he told that story once and then it just spread like wildfire.

So we launched Google Maps in February 2005 and it was a bunch of hard won lessons about how to make an interactive web application, and I think it was really the first of its kind.

*It was mind blowing when it came out.*

*BT:* Oh, it totally was. Things like Gmail and Google Suggest had done live updating of the page, but to drag the map and actually have it be an interactive graphical experience was truly groundbreaking. Truly groundbreaking, meaning in the sense we would crash browsers like it was going out of style. Lars Rasmussen and I would walk down to the team, we had a lot of Firefox engineers at Google at the time, and we’d have them load Firefox in the debugger so we could figure out what code path was crashing and then find a way to work around it, so we were really on the bleeding edge because the document object model in the browser was just not designed for what we were abusing it to do.

As a consequence, when you’re really doing true R&D and you actually don’t know which path to go down, first, when we ended up launching, there was a lot of cruft in that code base just because it had all these failed experiments, we had gone off on all these expeditions and did not clean it up. So even unusually at time of launch it had a lot of debt.

Then we ended up wanting to launch support for Safari, which was a relatively new browser at the time. There was no mobile phones yet, Safari is a very important browser now, at the time it was considered long tail for the relatively modest Mac desktop user base, but we’re Google, so all the numbers add up to actually statistically significant numbers, so we had an engineer on our team and it was 2004 so XML was still popular, and so we had used all these features and Internet Explorer to parse and use XML, many of which weren’t supported in Safari.

One of the engineers who was tasked to implement Safari support implemented this homegrown XML system, XSLT transform system , and it was like a lot of impressive engineering, but it meant that loading Google Maps took forever and at the time you still had dialup modems, even high bandwidth internet connections weren’t as fast as they’re today.

*I remember in college I was lusting after T1 or whatever, which is I think 2 megabits or something like that.*

*BT:* It’s a different world nowadays with all the front-end development, they wouldn’t even know what to do. But it was hundreds of kilobytes of JavaScript, which at the time just even parsing it running, it was slow, let alone downloading it, so I had gotten really frustrated with it and in particular we were growing really rapidly. We had launched satellite imagery and the product was growing like a weed and it was just hard to just get the team to focus on this because everything’s on fire all the time.

So as an engineer, I had a model of the system in my head. I knew how we rendered vector graphics for driving directions, which was very hard at the time, I knew how we did tiling for the maps, I knew that we shouldn’t be using XML at all, and I had an idea, JSON, the term hadn’t been coined yet , so I was like, “We should just be evaluating JavaScript rather than using XML”, and I just had this image in my head and I just am the type of person I get really obsessed with things. It was like Friday afternoon and I was like, “I’m just going to do it”. Then it started working and this as someone who makes software, you get kind of addicted to the light at the end of the tunnel and you’re like, “I don’t want to go to bed, I’m going to do this until it’s done”.

*(laughing) In this case it’s not a train, it’s often a train going backwards, “I see the light and it’s receding!”*

*BT:* So when it got to the nearing the end of the weekend and it was clear, the whole thing kind of worked, I was like, “Oh, now I want to impress my colleagues, I’m just going to keep going”, and so then I sent out the demo and it was almost 1/10th the JavaScript bundle size and a lot faster and worked in all browsers and it took a while to polish it up before we ended up fully launching it. But that definitely happened and I think almost every other software engineer I know has this quality who really likes the craft, which is when you end up solving an architectural problem and you see that light at the end of the tunnel you get plugged into the matrix and you just can’t help yourself.

*Here’s the question I have about that, I love to hear the story, but you haven’t been at Google in a long time, but do you think from the outside looking in and remembering all those long weekends and whatnot, is it even possible for anyone, no matter how talented, to do what you did at Google today?*

*BT:* I would guess not. It’s interesting, I read your posts pretty religiously and I think you talk a lot about strategy and platforms and the different moats afforded by them. Culture is really interesting as you grow, and I think one of the — I’ll say some things that might not seem related, but I believe they are — one thing that happens as you grow a company is there’s less space for generalists.

*You just said that how you had all the different views of what was happening in Google Maps in your head and back then to be a PM was actually it afforded you that opportunity as opposed to owning some narrow slice or whatever.*

*BT:* Well, not only that, I mean you mentioned something that’s actually pretty significant — I was a product manager! Nowadays, I don’t even know if product managers would have the privilege of submitting code to the source code repository, but at the time, every culture I feel like is strands of DNA, often the strengths and the weaknesses are very intertwined.

*Oh, completely.*

*BT:* I think Google’s 20% time is fairly maligned in some ways because it has a sort of entitled indulgent element to it, but it was also somewhat true. Paul Buchheit in making the first Gmail prototype, he did it in his spare time, a PM like me could spend the weekend rewriting some code, and the engineers were not only not offended, they were super excited about that dynamic. There was a sense that Google at the time of we have this great infrastructure which was truly, truly unique at the time, like the data center infrastructure, the distributed computing infrastructure, and thanks to the AdWords team, no thanks to me, we had the greatest business model of all time.

Then the other interesting part of Google at the time is that because the dot-com bubble had burst, it just had this incredible density of talent because you sort of had choice.

*All the refugees that were good ended up there.*

*BT:* The entire Bell Labs team was there, all the Greybeards who made Unix had offices near me. I was like, “Oh my God, these people are gods, I get to talk to them”, I shared an office with Peter Norvig .

*The famous Google relation to the dot-com bubbles is they bought up all the dark fiber and so to this day they continue to have a networking advantage that’s downstream from that. But you’re articulating the exact same thing in terms of just talent, because they survived the dot-com bubble, they were there, they were good, they were exciting, they were making money, they accrued all these advantages that have paid off for decades.*

*BT:* It’s amazing. And being there as a 20-something, I went there straight out of college. You go in these rooms and I mentioned, I shared an office with Peter Norvig who wrote my textbook in the last class I took in college and I go in, I’m like, “Hi Peter, sir”, he was incredibly gracious by the way, didn’t mind that this 22-year-old kid was there. So it was just amazing, what a fun time, I’m so grateful that I got to experience that.

But to go back to your question, could it happen today? I don’t think so. What you end up doing with these companies is the really reductive thing is every time something goes wrong, you make a process to fix it. You end up with this layering of processes that ends up making the company ossified, and you end up sort of this frozen version of a once great firm, and that’s the reductive version of what happens to these companies.

But it’s also some of it’s very rational. Larger companies are regulated more, small mistakes can end up having big consequences. I wasn’t at Microsoft after the antitrust trial of the early 2000s , but you hear a lot of ex-Microsofties talk about the before and after and if the stories are true, might’ve motivated Bill [Gates] to leave. I don’t know if that’s true or not, by the way. I think as you grow, you end up not even irrationally adding safeguards, checks and balances, which leads to organizational hierarchies and all these other things. And as a consequence, Google Labs, which was sort of the playground where you launch these things, it’s hard to do.

The other thing that’s really interesting is when the numbers get bigger, it’s harder as well. So just think about it this way, when I was at start at Google, we had much less than a billion in revenue and so you could start a new business there and you could imagine, “Wow, this could really contribute to the future of this company”. What is Google’s revenue now? You probably know off the top of your head.

*$130 billion I’m going to guess.*

*BT:* Yeah, a lot. Well, imagine today launching the equivalent of Google Maps, and you start to think about the natural growth of a technology product, a consumer product, even a great one.

*By the way, it was $350 billion. I was not even close. (laughing)*

*BT:* Oh yeah, you’re totally off.

*Income was $100 billion.*

*BT:* Which is insane, by the way, those margins are insane. So the other interesting thing I would say with larger firms is patience or the lack thereof. You could be as essentially if there’s a new market, growing a new business organically, there’s just a natural inertia. You can’t grow a new business, there’s certain limits to it. Obviously social businesses can grow much, much faster. But growing, say a new advertising business, you need to curate advertisers. You need all these things, if it’s a service like Google Maps, there wasn’t really a viral component to it. When I left Google, MapQuest was still bigger than Maps. I mean obviously anyone with a brain would know that those lines were going to cross, but you had to have the patience and endurance to do that, and I see so many companies launch new products and it doesn’t grow fast enough.

These sort of infamous projects like podcasting platforms that came and went and Google Reader somewhat infamously and who knows whether that was a good business or not, but you end up with these worlds where you can end up looking at a spreadsheet and discounting almost all innovation as not valuable enough, not fast enough and I think it creates this natural sense for these big companies to be too acquisitive, to sort of essentially acquire businesses at scale because it’s easier to understand how it impacts the trajectory of your company.

So I think there’s a lot of things. You end up with process additions, natural hierarchy, which leads to lack of empowerment, rational checks and balances because of regulatory pressures and others, and then this thing where you’re too big for any new organic innovation to have a short-term impact, and it’s why it’s really interesting to look at companies that are very oriented like Google and Apple towards organic innovation. It’s really the level of discipline I think you need as a leader to really follow through on that is extremely, extremely high.

*One more quick Google question. I mean, you’re in the AI space, we’re going to talk about Sierra in a little bit. Google, it strikes me, they continue to have this tremendous infrastructure advantage, they did do the long-term investment. Well, they still acquired DeepMind, but they’ve been nurturing this for a long time. It feels like they can’t make a product to save their lives . I do like what they’ve done with Search , I guess that’s the one team that can still get stuff done. Where do you rank them? Are they the favorites? Are they going to be disrupted? What’s your take?*

*BT:* Favorites as in AI broadly, you mean? I’m the chairman of OpenAI, so I’m a homer on this one. I think OpenAI and ChatGPT, I believe will come to define this wave of large language models.

*You’re preaching to the choir here, as you know.*

*BT:* But I don’t necessarily think exclusively at Google’s expense, I think Google has just a ton of assets as a company, it’s a very impressive company so I never count them out. It was like Intel has their woes now, but I remember Intel sort of swings and misses at 64 bit and eventually found their way. When you have the scale, you don’t need to hit a homer every time you’re up at the plate and so Google has YouTube, Gmail, Search, all these other things, they have a lot of talent as well. So I believe ChatGPT will define this next era of technology, but not everything is zero-sum. That’s not the way these things work and I think Google’s a really talented company.

*Well, after Google you start FriendFeed and then you’re acquired by Meta, that was then called Facebook obviously, become the CTO. Do they have a similar problem? They do have the social component — they do have, Mark Zuckerberg is still there — but is it just an issue where Mark Zuckerberg wants to push this company like they are Facebook in 2010, but it’s Facebook in 2025 and are some of these big company forces sort of inescapable?*

*BT:* Yeah, it’s interesting. It’s such a different company from when I was there, first of all. So I actually, while I am familiar with the company, it’s a very different shape. At the time it was called Facebook and while we had acquired Instagram, we hadn’t yet acquired WhatsApp and certainly not created the virtual reality unit and the AI lab was nascent when I was there. It’s interesting on its face, if you look at the impact of AI on social media, it’s quite a bit more nuanced. One could look at a Google Search box and ChatGPT, and you can see a lot of overlapping use cases. You could say, well, some of that usage has to be cannibalized just because if you’re finding information —

*If you’re asking a question in one place, you’re not asking it in another, yup.*

*BT:* Yeah, I don’t think the same is true of something driving towards engagement and certainly social media will have a huge place in it. I think you could look at early Instagram filters as sort of an example of a generative would be generous, but there’s been this interesting intersection between content creation and social and all of that.

*Isn’t there a time component though? I mean people are spending a tremendous amount of time in ChatGPT.*

*BT:* Absolutely. To some degree, there’s only so much time in the day. So if you’re using one product, you won’t use another. But I think the jobs to be done of a social media platform are slightly different than something like a ChatGPT, that’s my personal take. And obviously there’s some overlap, but it’s interesting because Mark Zuckerberg is one of the most ambitious founders of all time, and so he doesn’t settle for having Instagram and Facebook, he moves into WhatsApp, he starts a virtual reality lab, he invests a lot in Llama. So the interesting about Facebook and Meta is I do think, if you will, the threats of these new technology are very different just because the use cases are different. But his ambitions are much beyond those.

*It’s two great conflicts in tech. We have Google with the classic disruption conflict that is well-documented, but it’s going to be interesting to see play out an incumbent with all the advantages versus this bottoms up, use it not as good at search at some things, but good at other things. Facebook is what you just talked about. It’s can a founder overcome the ossification and bigness of a company and still push it forward? We kind of don’t know the answer to either, it’s going to be interesting to watch.*

*BT:* We don’t, but never count Mark Zuckerberg out. I mean, the guy’s incredible and incredibly ambitious and willing to put his money where his mouth is, which is I think something. I mean it’s why I admire him.

*I won’t ask you about any recruiting pitches you may or may not have gotten over the last…*

*BT:* I’m an OpenAI homer, so I don’t think they would call me.

Quip and Best-of-Breed vs Suites

*I’m curious about Quip . So what was the thesis behind doing Quip? And well, yeah, just start there.*

*BT:* Yeah, sure. And with the benefit of hindsight, somewhat flawed, so I’ll qualify that.

*I’m curious about your hindsight, but tell me what you were thinking at the time.*

*BT:* Yeah, so when I was at Facebook, I was there as CTO during the growth of the smartphone and it was quite disruptive to Facebook. We also benefited a lot from it, but we went through some pretty deep trough of despair to come out the other side.

*It was beautiful for me because I started Stratechery when you were in the trough.*

*BT:* Oh really? Okay, that’s great.

*The two companies I could get on, well actually there was three. Number one, everyone was sure if Apple was going to get disrupted by Android. I’m like, “No, it’s not”. Number two was everyone was down on Facebook, I’m like, “This is a monster, it’s going to be massive.” And number three was just being in general anti-Steve Ballmer and Microsoft because I had worked there and then saying they should push on the cloud, etc. So I do feel it’s my version of you joining Google — much less lucrative! — but by and large I’ve been at the right place at the right time for some of these companies.*

*BT:* Well, thank you for your faith in us. And I was both responsible for what I think was the worst mobile app of all time, which was this HTML5 piece of shit, and the rewrite — so I’ll take blame and credit for the trough and hopefully climbing out of it a little bit too. But it shows it was just like, especially as CTO was accountable for some of this bad decisions, but we also did the big rewrite, which actually really accelerated our growth and some of the early mobile app install ads and things like that, that turned out to be really consequential over time.

But anyway, through that experience, I got humbled a little bit, I learned a lot. I learned a lot about mobile technology, and it was really probably more fun with the benefit of hindsight than it was in the moment. Being in that trough is never fun, but I really came to deeply and intuitively understand the impact of smartphones on the world, and it was interesting because when you run a big consumer service, you’re kind of on the bleeding edge of some of these behaviors and the enterprise lags.

*And it’s hard to know what is a fad and what is actually meaningful and is going to matter for everyone.*

*BT:* Totally. Like Clubhouse comes and goes, but TikTok remains, right. It’s complicated though and it’s very arrogant to say most of us who’ve been in this space for a while, you don’t bat a thousand in your predictions. Maybe you do, I certainly don’t.

*Nope. I was a big Clubhouse guy . That was a humbling moment for me because I didn’t appreciate the extent to which my experience on Clubhouse was different by virtue of being well-known and that wasn’t representative of normal people at all in their experience. So yeah, that a huge miss by me.*

*BT:* We could go on a whole sidetrack on that, but I’ll go back to the Quip, but that’s such an interesting topic, by the way. Actually one of my, I don’t tweet very much, but one of my ones was like, “What’s your worst technology prediction?” — mine was I thought iPads would be more popular than they are, and we talked through it. Anyway, so fun topic, but go back to Quip.

At one point during when we were coming out of the trough of despair had mandated that everyone at the company use Facebook groups rather than email lists and use Facebook Messenger rather than email in an effort to dogfood so we would only message each other on our mobile phones, you just never pulled out your laptop. And the idea was just like, “We’re going to suffer until our product is exceptional”, and it was a really effective, this is one of Mark Zuckerberg’s strengths, right? We’re going to will it to be.

*He did the same thing mandating Android at one point when your Android app was terrible.*

*BT:* Yeah, exactly. So I ended up through that realizing we were a Microsoft Office shop and all these other things, and you end up looking at slides or virtual overhead projectors and Microsoft Word documents even on mobile were on virtual pieces of paper and I came to deeply feel that perhaps the productivity suite, which was the anchor tenet of the PC for very, very long, just kind of developer tools and stuff, the core productivity suite, I said, “Gosh, could this be the moment where the jobs to be done shift? Just because presenting while important, it’s not a really good form factor on mobile, documents on this formatted for printing versus formatted for the screen”. And at the time too, Microsoft refused to make apps for any platform other than Windows phone, this kind of perfect storm.

*That was a good spot for me. It’s so easy to criticize it obviously right .*

*BT:* So we decided to take a big swing knowing that going after the productivity market is a little bit like invading Russia in the winter. But we said if there’s a time where the ossified way we use the software will change is probably right now.

I think with the benefit hindsight, I think we did fairly well. But for every one of us as individuals, and interestingly enough, this is the most mind-blowing part about this trend is, Silicon Valley is disrupting the job of software engineering and so oddly, not only are the people making this technology not immune to it, but I would say software engineering and customer service are probably the two most shovel-ready opportunities for these models. So it’s in the hallways of Silicon Valley we’re talking about, what am I going to do four years from now?

I just think it’s important to both not become a doomer or a pessimist, I think that’s just silly, and I think we should invest in this technology. I think it’ll grow the economy, I think it’ll improve people’s lives, but it’s also important to not be callous or arrogant, and say, “Look, it’s very uncomfortable if you had developed a set of skills in your life and you talked about me rewriting Google Maps in a weekend”. Well, maybe that’s a commodity now. That cool story is going to be talking about the human calculators at NASA before they installed the big IBM computer and so I think both are true at the same time and so I always try to have a ton of empathy about it, but also a ton of optimism.

AI and Messaging

*All right, you said you want to talk consumer. What do you want to tell me about consumer and AI?*

*BT:* Two-and-a-half years ago, when ChatGPT became popular, right after I left Salesforce amusingly, like, “Huh, I wonder what industry I’ll work in”, and then ChatGPT goes and you’re like, “Okay, I’m pretty excited”. I had talked to an investor friend of mine and had predicted that there would be $1 trillion consumer company and 10 $100 billion-plus enterprise companies created as a byproduct of large language models and modern AI. I mean, it might be off by a little bit, there might be two, I think that what’s really exciting about consumer right now is I think ChatGPT is that really important service and it reminds me a little bit of the early days of Google, where search and Google were interchangeable, and ChatGPT is really synonymous with AI for most of the world.

The thing that I really like about it is if you and I were having, and both of us are pretty informed people, three-and-a-half years ago, if we were talking about artificial general intelligence, and not cynically or anything like that, and said, “What form factors would it take?”, my guess is neither of us would have guessed something like ChatGPT, as simple and consumable as it. You’d think about, I don’t know what I would’ve thought about, but it’s hard to imagine now because it is a form factor. The fact that we’ve created something that’s approaching super intelligence and it’s not only broadly available for free to everyone around the world, but it’s accessible as a personal assistant you have a conversation with, I think is one of the most delightful quirks of artificial general intelligence because it’s so much more democratic than I think we probably would’ve predicted it would be if we had talked about it three-and-a-half years ago.

So on the consumer side, I just think ChatGPT is the most important, not only technology, but product in AI, and I think we will look back at it as a very democratizing force to serve OpenAI’s mission, I think very authentically, and I think that’s just super exciting. I just think it’s funny, because I don’t think anyone would’ve predicted it, as evidenced by its really silly name, right? It’s like a research preview that became the most important product of all time, and I think that’s just awesome.

*Oh, you guys bought chat.com, but no, ChatGPT is too good. I mean, I’ve always been a huge advocate of messaging, one of my lucky breaks was I wrote an Article called Messaging is Mobile’s Killer App and literally, the next day Facebook announced they were acquiring WhatsApp and I’m like, “Slipped that one in just in time!”.*

*But I think what’s interesting now that I think back on it is this was a bit where actually the user interface paradigm came first, and AI just slotted so naturally into it, and messaging is obviously so great for — that’s what people are used to, that’s the user interface they know and their experience with. Kind of like how the PC in many respects created the user interface for the web, we were clicking around on the desktop or using HyperCard or whatever it might be before actually web links and the web came along, and maybe it’s like people think about technology comes, then the interface. But it’s the opposite, the interface gets there first and the technology can fit into it.*

*BT:* I love that thesis. And I agree with you and it’s interesting, because like many things, with the benefit of hindsight it’s obvious, but it was totally not obvious before. You watch old movies, even if dystopian ones, like 2001: A Space Odyssey, and you’re just talking to a computer. To some degree, when you imagine science fiction, the technology melts away, the screens melt away and to some degree then you’re like, “Oh, of course, that’s what AI should be”, but it was totally not obvious to anybody.

*Well, it’s so interesting, because messaging is so great, it fits with mobile. Obviously, mobile creates the conditions for messaging. Messaging, the asynchronous nature of it is ideal because you have a lot of conversations going on at the same time and it’s funny because that actually papers over a lot of AI’s deficiencies right now, which is sometimes it’s slow, it takes a while to think about it. But that’s fine, we’re used to leaving a conversation and coming back to it later. Whereas with voice, it needs to be perfect all the time right there, and the tech just isn’t there yet to do it and so that’s why it ended up not being the right interface.*

*BT:* Yeah, fascinating.

*You’re fascinating. It’s great to talk, it’s been a long time coming, but I’m very interested to see what happens next and maybe we’ll talk again when Sierra’s IPOing.*

*BT:* That’d be awesome, I’m looking forward to it.

*Sounds good. Bret Taylor, thanks for coming on to Stratechery.*

*BT:* Thanks for having me.

dek: Meta won another fair use case, even though the judge wanted to rule against LLMs; he'll have a hard time doing so. View in browser | Listen in your podcast player STRATECHERY Training AI is Not
text:
Meta won another fair use case, even though the judge wanted to rule against LLMs; he'll have a hard time doing so.

Training AI is Not Fair Use?, LLMs and Scale, Pushing on a String

Monday, July 7, 2025

Happy July 4th! I had a great summer break, and I hope you all had the same. And, at the same time, I’m happy to be back.

It is, however, summer, which means the usual summer schedule through August. Namely, while there will still be three Updates and/or Articles a week, there will be no Stratechery Interviews; in addition, there will be one extended episode of Sharp Tech a week, along with the usual two episodes of Dithering .

On to the Update:

Training AI is Not Fair Use?

A day after the Anthropic fair use decision that I wrote about just before the break came down, the same federal circuit delivered a strikingly different ruling in reasoning, but not outcome. From Bloomberg Law :

Meta Platforms Inc. escaped a first-of-its-kind copyright lawsuit from a group of authors who alleged the tech giant hoovered up millions of copyrighted books without permission to train its generative AI model called Llama. San Francisco federal Judge Vince Chhabria ruled Wednesday that Meta’s decision to use the books for training is protected under copyright law’s fair use defense, but he cautioned that his opinion is more a reflection on the authors’ failure to litigate the case effectively.

“This ruling does not stand for the proposition that Meta’s use of copyrighted materials to train its language models is lawful,” Chhabria said. “It stands only for the proposition that these plaintiffs made the wrong arguments and failed to develop a record in support of the right one”…The ruling comes two days after a judge in the same court ruled largely in favor of AI competitor Anthropic PBC, which was similarly accused of illegally using books to train its models.

As a quick refresher, here is the Stanford Library’s summary of the fair use test :

The only way to get a definitive answer on whether a particular use is a fair use is to have it resolved in federal court. Judges use four factors to resolve fair use disputes, as discussed in detail below. It’s important to understand that these factors are only guidelines that courts are free to adapt to particular situations on a case‑by‑case basis. In other words, a judge has a great deal of freedom when making a fair use determination, so the outcome in any given case can be hard to predict.

The four factors judges consider are:

* The purpose and character of your use
* The nature of the copyrighted work
* The amount and substantiality of the portion taken, and
* The effect of the use upon the potential market.

Judge William Alsup of the Northern District of California ruled that using copyrighted works to train AI was tranformative (factor one, in favor of fair use), commercial (factor two, against fair use), total but no individual work was necessary or reproducible (factor three, in favor of fair use), and an increase in competition for writing generally, but not for the books in question specifically (factor four, in favor of fair use).

Judge Chhabria, also of the Northern District of California, also found that using copyrighted works to train AI was transformative (factor one, in favor of fair use), commercial (factor two, against fair use), total but no individual work was necessary or reproducible (factor three, in favor of fair use). Where Judge Chhabria differed from Judge Alsup was in his evaluation of factor four.

In this Update I’m going to quote extensively from the case, as it’s an obvious counter to my previous Update entitled “Training AI is Fair Use” ; I’ll get into a bit of analysis, but expect more on this topic soon.

LLMs and Scale

Here is the key section of Judge Chhabria’s opinion about the fourth factor:

The Supreme Court has said that the “only harm” that matters under the fourth factor “is the harm of market substitution.” But indirect substitution is still substitution: If someone bought a romance novel written by an LLM instead of a romance novel written by a human author, the LLM-generated novel is substituting for the human-written one. This is different from the (non-cognizable) harm caused by criticism or commentary, which can harm demand for an original work without serving as a replacement for it.

Relatedly, Meta argues that “legitimate” competition from noninfringing secondary works is not cognizable under the fourth factor. It cites the intermediate copying cases for this proposition. But key to those cases’ reasoning was the fact that the secondary users’ competing products did not benefit from the creative expression in the works they copied. By contrast, as discussed, LLMs are better able to generate text (including competing works) because they are trained on the creative expression in copyrighted books. So this competition is not “legitimate” within the meaning of those cases.

It’s true that, in many copyright cases, this concept of market dilution or indirect substitution is not particularly important. That’s because, in a more typical case, an original work is being compared to a single secondary work. If the secondary work is somewhat similar, but not so similar as to effectively be a copy, it still might have a small indirect effect on the market for the original work. But that likely won’t matter. Recall that the fourth factor looks to whether “conduct of the sort engaged in by the defendant” would have a “substantially adverse impact on the potential market for the original.” The existence of some harm from indirect substitution isn’t dispositive of the fourth factor or the fair use inquiry. Where, for instance, the first factor cuts in favor of the secondary user, the law might tolerate a little bit of competition. In cases involving a single secondary work that’s similar-but-not-too-similar, it’s unlikely that harm from market dilution would be significant enough to matter. Even considering the effect of “widespread conduct of the sort engaged in by the defendant,” creating one indirectly substitutional work at a time could only have so great an effect on the market for the original.

This case is different. This is not a case where an original work is being compared to one secondary work. Nor is this case like the previous fair use cases involving creation of a digital tool. In those cases, like Google Books and Perfect 10, the tool could at most be used to access part or all of the original works. This case, unlike any of those cases, involves a technology that can generate literally millions of secondary works, with a miniscule fraction of the time and creativity used to create the original works it was trained on. No other use — whether it’s the creation of a single secondary work or the creation of other digital tools — has anything near the potential to flood the market with competing works the way that LLM training does. And so the concept of market dilution becomes highly relevant.

In arguing that this sort of harm doesn’t count just because it’s never made a difference in a case before, Meta makes the mistake the Supreme Court instructs parties and courts to avoid: robotically applying concepts from previous cases without stepping back to consider context. Fair use is meant to be a flexible doctrine that takes account of “significant changes in technology.” Courts can’t stick their heads in the sand to an obvious way that a new technology might severely harm the incentive to create, just because the issue has not come up before. Indeed, it seems likely that market dilution will often cause plaintiffs to decisively win the fourth factor — and thus win the fair use question overall — in cases like this.

Judge Chhabria’s argument is in many respects a logical extension of the argument both he and Judge Alsup make about factor three: in that case, both (correctly, in my mind) argue that while LLMs use the entirety of a copyrighted work in their training set, this is not necessarily a violation because the scale of data necessary to train an LLM means that any one work is not critical to the LLM, and besides, both Anthropic and Meta take care to ensure their models do not output exact copies of copyrighted work. In other words, Anthropic and Meta are not necessarily violating the individual copyright for a work because the scale of copyrighted work necessary is so large that the relative contribution of any one work renders the violation immaterial.

Judge Alsup’s dismissal of factor four, however, ignores scale; from his opinion :

Authors contend generically that training LLMs will result in an explosion of works competing with their works — such as by creating alternative summaries of factual events, alternative examples of compelling writing about fictional events, and so on. This order assumes that is so. But Authors’ complaint is no different than it would be if they complained that training school children to write well would result in an explosion of competing works. This is not the kind of competitive or creative displacement that concerns the Copyright Act. The Act seeks to advance original works of authorship, not to protect authors against competition.

Judge Chhabria says this is absurd:

In a recent ruling on this topic, Judge Alsup focused heavily on the transformative nature of generative AI while brushing aside concerns about the harm it can inflict on the market for the works it gets trained on. Such harm would be no different, he reasoned, than the harm caused by using the works for “training schoolchildren to write well,” which could “result in an explosion of competing works.” According to Judge Alsup, this “is not the kind of competitive or creative displacement that concerns the Copyright Act.” But when it comes to market effects, using books to teach children to write is not remotely like using books to create a product that a single individual could employ to generate countless competing works with a miniscule fraction of the time and creativity it would otherwise take. This inapt analogy is not a basis for blowing off the most important factor in the fair use analysis.

As I noted before the break, I’m sympathetic to Judge Chhabria’s argument generally; using human analogies for computers ignores the fact that the speed and comprehensiveness with which computers can undertake human-like actions — like reading a book — makes for a fundamental difference in practical effects. To that end, just as computers can ingest books at far greater scale than humans can, so can they output text at a far greater scale; that, in Judge Chhabria’s mind, means that using copyrighted material to train LLMs fails the fair use test because the end result is an overwhelming amount of competition for copyrighted authors that is not at all analogous to a human reading a lot of books and subsequently writing one of his or her own.

Pushing on a String

And yet, despite the fact that Judge Chhabria spent the first four pages of his opinion making this case — even before he got to the legal analysis — he ultimately ruled in Meta’s favor. Again from his opinion:

Courts can’t decide cases based on what they think will or should happen in other cases. They must decide cases based on the arguments presented and the evidence submitted by the parties. The question, then, is whether these particular thirteen plaintiffs in this particular case have presented enough evidence to win on this factor. Or, to put it more precisely given the procedural posture of this case, whether these plaintiffs have presented enough evidence to raise a genuine dispute of material fact sufficient to give the question of market dilution to a jury. The answer is no.

Judge Chhabria is clearly frustrated with the plaintiffs in this case, practically begging them to come up with even a shred of evidence that LLMs have harmed the plaintiff’s market opportunities.

Where a defendant introduces evidence of a lack of market harm, “and the plaintiff fails to introduce empirical evidence countering such a showing, the fourth factor should be weighed in the defendant’s favor.” That is exactly what happened here. Meta introduced evidence that its copying hasn’t caused market harm. The plaintiffs presented no empirical evidence to the contrary — no evidence that the copying has already caused market harm, and no evidence that the copying is likely to cause market harm in the future. All the plaintiffs presented is speculation, and speculation is insufficient to raise a genuine issue of fact and defeat summary judgment.

Here’s my observation: Judge Chhabria thinks he is criticizing the plaintiffs, but actually that last sentence characterizes his entire opinion. Judge Chhabria goes on and on about the the speculative harms of AI, but ultimately rules for Meta because “speculation is insufficient to raise a genuine issue of fact and defeat summary judgment”; what I would argue is that this isn’t a failure of the plaintiffs to present evidence, but is in fact the flip-side of the scale argument that Judge Chhabria says makes Meta guilty. I’ll let Judge Chhabria make the case for me:

The plaintiffs argue that they didn’t need to present empirical evidence because market harm can be inferred. For this argument, they cite to Hachette, in which the Second Circuit inferred market harm — even though the plaintiffs had not provided “empirical data” showing any and the secondary user presented expert testimony that there was none — because it was “self-evident” that the secondary use would cause such harm if widespread. In Hachette, the secondary user maintained a database that let internet users “download an identical copy of” the plaintiffs’ books for free. The secondary use therefore offered a directly “competing substitute” for the original books.

While it made sense to infer market harm in Hachette, it doesn’t make sense to do so here. First, the Supreme Court has stated that no “inference of market harm . . . is applicable to a case involving something beyond mere duplication for commercial purposes.” In Hachette, the secondary use was basically “mere duplication.” Here, by contrast, Meta’s use is highly transformative and has a purpose well beyond that. Second, unlike in Hachette, Meta’s use does not let users access any significant portion of the plaintiffs’ books, so it isn’t self-evident that Meta’s use would create harm via direct substitution. Nor is it self-evident that Llama will harm the book sale market by enabling users to create a flood of competing books. It’s possible, even likely, that Llama will harm the book sale market. But to conclude that it will requires inferring that Llama (and not just any LLM) can be used to create such books, that it will be used to create such books, that consumers will purchase those books instead of books written by human authors, that consumers will buy those books instead of the plaintiffs’ books in particular, and that Llama is meaningfully better at creating those books because it was trained on copyrighted material. In Hachette, on the other hand, the only necessary inference was that readers might choose to download the plaintiffs’ books for free instead of paying for them — a much shorter (and more obvious) inferential leap.

On this record, then, Meta has defeated the plaintiffs’ half-hearted argument that its copying causes or threatens significant market harm. That conclusion may be in significant tension with reality, but it’s dictated by the choice the plaintiffs made to put forward two flawed theories of market harm while failing to present meaningful evidence on the effect of training LLMs like Llama with their books on the market for those books.

I disagree; that conclusion is dictated by the fact that measuring the market harm of LLMs to an individual author is effectively impossible, for the same reasons that any one copyrighted work are inconsequential to an LLM (i.e. Judge Chhabria’s factor three analysis). These authors may amend their case — Judge Chhabria clearly hopes they will, as he couldn’t be more clear that he wished he could rule in their favor — but they will face the fundamental problem of figuring out how to measure the buying decisions of individuals; actually, it’s worse than that, because the harm Judge Chhabria wants to find is the measurement of buying decisions not made.

In this there is a strong similarity to the challenges faced by those seeking to use traditional antitrust arguments to constrain Aggregators; I refer to it as “pushing on a string”; from 2020’s Anti-Monopoly vs. Antitrust :

So much modern antitrust action against tech companies is like pushing on a string: the reason these companies have power is because so many customers choose to use them, and it is both difficult and probably unwise to try and regulate the individual choices of billions of users. At the same time, as I noted, I am sympathetic to the issue of just how much power these companies have: constraining that power, though, needs new laws that start with Internet assumptions, and anti-monopoly advocates would do well to focus on solutions that, instead of retracting privileges, extend them (a la incorporations in the 1800s).

These aren’t idle words: I have previously laid out ideas for *regulating competition on the Internet *. One thing that is critical is understanding that not all tech companies are the same: Apple and Android are traditional platforms, relatively well-served by traditional antitrust law (except for the fact that their duopoly helps both escape scrutiny together); Google and Facebook, though, are Aggregators, which require a different approach, which I laid out in 2019’s *Where Warren’s Wrong *. These include a focus on acquisitions and anticompetitive contracts, which I was glad to see were also a focus of the committee (although I think the focus on small-scale acquisitions *missed why acquisitions can be a good thing * ).

Judge Chhabria wants to push on a similar string: he can imagine the harms that LLMs cause to copyright holders broadly, and he’s probably right; a finding of copyright infringement, however, requires explicit harm, and it’s not clear at all how that can be measured. To that end, I suspect the eventual prevailing ruling on copyright and AI — which, given the conflict that is already emerging within a single court, seems inevitably headed for the Supreme Court — will ultimately come down in favor of the AI companies; if copyright advocates want a different result they will need to pass new laws (which, for the record, I would oppose, but I’m trying to not let that influence my analysis).

dek: Apple is considering partnering with foundation model providers to replace Siri; the choice of which is profound. View in browser | Listen in your podcast player STRATECHERY Apple + Anthropic?,
text:
Apple is considering partnering with foundation model providers to replace Siri; the choice of which is profound.

Apple + Anthropic?, Apple's Fall, Apple's Options

Wednesday, July 9, 2025

Greatest of All Talk has you covered for NBA free agency; Sharp Tech and Sharp China will be back with new episodes later this week.

On to the Update:

Apple + Anthropic?

From Bloomberg on June 30:

Apple Inc. is considering using artificial intelligence technology from Anthropic PBC or OpenAI to power a new version of Siri, sidelining its own in-house models in a potentially blockbuster move aimed at turning around its flailing AI effort. The iPhone maker has talked with both companies about using their large language models for Siri, according to people familiar with the discussions…If Apple ultimately moves forward, it would represent a monumental reversal. The company currently powers most of its AI features with homegrown technology that it calls Apple Foundation Models and had been planning a new version of its voice assistant that runs on that technology for 2026.

This report came out before the news that I referenced in yesterday’s Article about the head of Apple Foundation Models moving to Meta; that, specifically, and the overall fight for talent generally, may very well force Apple’s hands in the matter. I wrote in the conclusion:

At the same time, to go back to the talent question, I don’t think it’s a surprise that Meta appears to be picking off more researchers from OpenAI than from Anthropic: my suspicion is that to the extent mission is a motivator the more likely an AI researcher is to be enticed by the idea of computers doing everything, instead of merely augmenting humans. And, by extension, the incumbent tool-makers may have no choice but to partner with the true believers.

Microsoft is of course already partnering with OpenAI; the obvious implication is that Apple is going to have to partner as well, whether they want to or not. More from the June 30 Bloomberg report:

The project to evaluate external models was started by Siri chief Mike Rockwell and software engineering head Craig Federighi. They were given oversight of Siri after the duties were removed from the command of John Giannandrea, the company’s AI chief. He was sidelined in the wake of a tepid response to Apple Intelligence and Siri feature delays. Rockwell, who previously launched the Vision Pro headset, assumed the Siri engineering role in March. After taking over, he instructed his new group to assess whether Siri would do a better job handling queries using Apple’s AI models or third-party technology, including Claude, ChatGPT and Alphabet Inc.’s Google Gemini.

After multiple rounds of testing, Rockwell and other executives concluded that Anthropic’s technology is most promising for Siri’s needs, the people said. That led Adrian Perica, the company’s vice president of corporate development, to start discussions with Anthropic about using Claude, the people said.

I do think that Anthropic makes the most sense from Apple’s perspective, but I’m skeptical that the reason Apple started discussions with the company is purely because of the results from their testing; rather, the fundamental issue with OpenAI is what I wrote about earlier this year when tensions with Microsoft started to burst into public. From a January Update about Stargate :

Notice that none of these points of contention have anything to do with the OpenAI board situation; indeed, the more that I think about it, the real problem for the OpenAI-Microsoft relationship dates back to the November before that: November 2022 and the release of ChatGPT. Before then OpenAI was a research lab selling API access on the side; that was a perfectly compatible setup with Microsoft, which wanted the research and also had a built-in customer base for OpenAI’s API (delivered via Azure).

ChatGPT, though, changed everything for OpenAI, and, by extension, made its relationship with Microsoft untenable in the long run. I wrote in March 2023 that OpenAI was The Accidental Consumer Tech Company …This is exactly what we are seeing in this announcement: Oracle and Softbank are there to serve OpenAI, which isn’t a business that Microsoft is particularly interested in.

Apple, more than just about any company ever, isn’t interested in serving another company; indeed, part of Apple’s evaluation is asking the model makers to serve them; back to Bloomberg:

In its discussions with both Anthropic and OpenAI, the iPhone maker requested a custom version of Claude and ChatGPT that could run on Apple’s Private Cloud Compute servers — infrastructure based on high-end Mac chips that the company currently uses to operate its more sophisticated in-house models. Apple believes that running the models on its own chips housed in Apple-controlled cloud servers — rather than relying on third-party infrastructure — will better safeguard user privacy. The company has already internally tested the feasibility of the idea.

This, right off the bat, would seem to make this a non-starter for OpenAI. Having a consumer offering means maximizing the returns to scale, and bifurcating your service between special infrastructure for Apple and the infrastructure you use to serve everyone else seems like a non-starter. This is doubly the case if Apple is asking for a completely independent implementation that is called Siri and doesn’t sync data with ChatGPT proper.

Claude, on the other hand, isn’t going to win the consumer chatbot wars; letting Apple white-label Anthropic models seems much more amenable to Anthropic’s opportunity and ambitions. Anthropic is also experienced at running on different architectures at scale, thanks to the fact they are using Amazon’s Trainium chip (although OpenAI just started using Google’s TPUs for inference).

Apple’s Fall

Still, there isn’t yet a deal; continuing from Bloomberg:

While discussing a potential arrangement, Apple and Anthropic have disagreed over preliminary financial terms, according to the people. The AI startup is seeking a multibillion-dollar annual fee that increases sharply each year. The struggle to reach a deal has left Apple contemplating working with OpenAI or others if it moves forward with the third-party plan, they said.

There are so many interesting facets to this paragraph. Start with the Anthropic angle: the entire reason why Anthropic might be interested in letting Apple white-label their models is because their future is not that of a consumer app; that, though, doesn’t change the fact that Anthropic needs leverage on the money they are spending to be on the cutting edge. To that end, getting a fat royalty check from Apple is a great way to get a higher return on the investments they are making.

Apple, however, is used to companies serving them — and paying for the right to do so. Look no further than Google paying the iPhone maker north of $20 billion a year to be the default search engine in Safari; that’s what Apple thought would happen in AI — and, I must admit, is what I thought might happen a year ago. After the unveiling of Apple Intelligence in 2024 I wrote in an Update that “Apple Aggregates AI” :

Federighi makes the same point I did above: there are lots of things that broad-based models like ChatGPT are good at that Apple isn’t even attempting to take on, and why would they? These models cost an astronomical amount of money to train and inference, and whatever differentiation exists is predicated on factors that Apple doesn’t have a competitive advantage in. What Apple does have is a massive userbase that the model that wants to win will desire access to, so why not trade that access for the ability to leverage whichever model agrees to Apple’s terms?

This gets to the one thing that I think I got wrong in yesterday’s Article: my assumption has been that Apple was going to pay for whatever integration it offered, but now I question whether that is the case or not. OpenAI said in their blog post about the partnership:

The ChatGPT integration, powered by GPT-4o, will come to iOS, iPadOS, and macOS later this year. Users can access it for free without creating an account, and ChatGPT subscribers can connect their accounts and access paid features right from these experiences.

This sounds like a play to acquire users and mindshare, with the potential of upselling those users to a subscription, i.e. the exact same model that OpenAI has on their website and apps. Moreover, if this partnership entails Apple not paying, it also explains why OpenAI is the only option to start: Google, for example, probably wanted to be paid for Gemini, or Anthropic for Claude, and I can imagine (1) Apple holding the line on not paying, particularly if (2) OpenAI is making an aggressive move to build out its consumer business and be a durable brand and winner in the consumer space. In short, my updated current thinking is that both Apple and OpenAI are making the bet that very large language models are becoming increasingly commoditized, which means that Apple doesn’t have to pay to get access to one, and OpenAI sees scale and consumer mindshare as the best route to a sustainable business.

To put it another way, and in Stratechery terms, Apple is positioning itself as an AI Aggregator: the company owns users and, by extension, generative AI demand by virtue of owning its platforms, and it is deepening its moat through Apple Intelligence, which only Apple can do; that demand is then being brought to bear on suppliers who probably have to eat the costs of getting privileged access to Apple’s userbase.

The strategic implications of the Apple Intelligence failure are profound: instead of Apple having a highly differentiated AI offering that it can augment with broad-based models, the company has Genmoji and a Siri offering that is more embarrassing than useful; that means that instead of auctioning off that broad-based model slot to the highest bidder, Apple needs fundamental capabilities to even be competitive, and that means paying up. And, per yesterday’s Article, if Apple isn’t going to pay up for GPUs and AI researchers, then they’re going to have to pay a model company.

Apple’s Options

Which, in the end, is why OpenAI may yet win this contract. The fact that OpenAI’s upside play is as a consumer brand puts them in fundamental conflict with both Microsoft and Apple; recall my illustration from yesterday’s Article:

At the same time, Apple’s userbase is uniquely attractive to OpenAI, particularly if they can get access to that userbase through an interface that is compatible with ChatGPT. That — in contrast to Anthropic — is something that OpenAI would be willing to help fund, which is to say that Apple faces a stark choice:

* Pay top dollar to white-label Anthropic models to create a better Siri
* Pay significantly less — or maybe nothing at all — to simply replace Siri with ChatGPT

So what matters more to Apple? Controlling the user experience and interface, even if you have to pay for it, or giving up control but saving a lot of money? I will say that from this consumer’s perspective I favor the latter: I would very much like ChatGPT to simply replace Siri, but the implication of that is that Apple is committing to being the Samsung to OpenAI’s Android; that seems intolerable to the company. At the same time, Anthropic is only in this for the money, and is Apple willing to pay?

Of course these aren’t the only two options: Apple could soldier along with its homegrown Siri, even though that would almost certainly mean having an inferior product; the company could also risk further antitrust scrutiny and partner with Google — if the Android-maker would have them.

Ultimately, while I as a consumer would prefer they take the ChatGPT option — ChatGPT is for me more important than the iPhone — if I put my business analyst hat on I think they should pay Anthropic. Most consumers aren’t me, and Apple will ultimately be both more comfortable and retain the greatest control over its destiny by — from most users’ perspective — magically delivering a better Siri (powered by Anthropic) than simply giving up and slotting in ChatGPT.

Or, here’s another idea: finally accept that the company that is most aligned with Apple’s business interests is the one Apple’s leadership hates the most: one Mark Zuckerberg would welcome the support for Llama’s development — he’s certainly paying enough! It probably says something about the state of Apple’s leadership that I saved this option for a cursory mention, even if it would likely be the most favorable to the company.
