*DK:* So one parallel idea that I had when I was at CHIPS was, well, we only have supply-side drivers, we could only give you money to build fabs, but what if gave you money to do design porting? If I gave you a fab, say a billion dollars, and the only thing you can use that for is to subsidize design porting from your customer so that they can try you out for free and that was, I thought, splitting the difference between “Here’s supply side money given to you that essentially gives demanders a free trial of you”. I’m not quite sure, that became a bit more complicated to do because then we thought about, “Well, what can we actually use CHIPS money to do?”, and it became a legal question. But again, all that has been thrown out the window now because apparently now we can take the money to even buy a few stakes.

*Are you jealous of it? You had all these ideas and you were constrained by actually following the law. Again, we’re setting that aside for the purposes this discussion, but it’s a bit like, “I’d like to be there now”.*

*DK:* I loved working with Secretary Raimondo and she was excellent. The thing that I’m jealous of is, and this is not a criticism of Secretary Raimondo, is given the scale of the problems that we were talking about, it would’ve been interesting for us to try to break every norm possible to come up with solutions that are just as big, and I’m not sure if that was possible to do.

*If you could have married the expertise that you brought to the table with the willingness to challenge norms that Trump is bringing to the table. Right now I think I share your concern. My experience working with you and working with various people in the Biden administration, which I got calls from people lots of times, very smart people, really wanted to understand and know the issues, but when you looked at the outcomes, frustratingly constrained and I think the flip side of Trump is not constrained. Again, we’re setting aside the issues that come with that, we’re just acknowledging that reality, but concerns about competence and implementation at the core level like, you’re not there anymore. I trust your competence about this, I don’t know the people that are [working on CHIPS now], they’ve never called me. Now, maybe this is biased because I like being called — actually that’s a big pain in the rear end, I don’t like being called, but I always take the calls from the government — so that’s just, it’s like if you have to choose one, the norm breaking or the competence, it’s actually a tougher question than you think, even though anyone reading Stratechery or listening to this interview, their bias is certainly for competence, but sometimes you really do just need to break some norms.*

*DK:* And I would say for the current team that’s there now, I know many of them, they’re actually very good.

*That’s great to hear.*

*DK:* So I wouldn’t actually just straight out assume that this is a bad outcome. I think I’m going to hold judgment until we see what else is coming down the line. Because if I see this as the beginning of something very different, of a different approach to a much bigger problem, then I’m willing to give them a chance. I would love to be part of it in some ways, but no longer there.

But I thought a lot about the, I think I texted you to this, but Tim Geithner , the former Treasury Secretary when the financial crisis was happening, and so he was essentially trying to hold the financial system together before there was going to be another depression in the economy in 2008. He wrote a book about it called Stress Test ) , which I really, really enjoyed.

There was a quote in there that I think is so instructive of his experience, my experience, and what is happening today in the political sphere. He said, “We did save the economy, but we lost the country doing it”, and you should read the book to really think about what that means, why the public lost trust in institutions along the way as the civil servants were trying to save it. You see all the battles that the Treasury Secretary and others had to fight internally among the system to try to save the system, but also having the dual challenge of justifying it to the world and he also says, “When I met Barbara Streisand at a White House state dinner in 2011, she told me, Mr. Secretary, when I see you on TV, I get the feeling you’re not telling us everything”, he says, “I laughed and replied, you have no idea, and I’m going to try to remedy that now”.

So when the book is written about CHIPS, and part of the reason why I wanted to come here and tell some of these stories, is because I think the public does and should know the competence that does go into this decision-making and the problems that it’s trying to solve, because I think at the end of the day, all you’re seeing is announcements saying, “Oh, we’ve decided to give Intel X amount of money and they’re going to build all these fabs”, but there’s all this thinking that goes behind it.

I imagine that’s still happening now, but if we’re going to break norms, I think we should be very clear to the public about why we’re breaking norms and what goals are we trying to achieve and so the answer they’re giving which is, “We want financial upside for the taxpayer”, as the primary driver, in some ways, I don’t quite buy that because there has to be more clever thinking behind this thing.

*They’re not idiots.*

*DK:* They’re not idiots, I don’t think they’re idiots, I think they’re actually very clever. There has to be something going on in the background and discussions that are ongoing about all of this, and so I’m going to give them the benefit of the doubt and say, maybe there’s something to this and if we see a solution, it’s going to have to be out of the norm because we face an enormous challenge.

*I love the connection to the financial crisis. You mentioned you wanted to bring this up before, and I wasn’t quite clear where you were going with it, but in the context in which you brought it up, it makes perfect sense. And this idea of this isn’t just a chip question, it’s a general technological advancement challenge, the “managerial state” sort of idea. Why does direct democracy or the republicanism or whatever it might be, small r on these sort of titles, why is there a challenge and the rise of the bureaucracy and technocracy? Technocrats and all that sort of thing? It’s because the world is incredibly complex and you have this issue.*

*It’s funny, because one of the critiques of the Intel deal is you no longer have market accountability and failing companies deserve to fail. It’s like you call back to the bailout of GM or the bailout of the banks , which to go back to the financial crisis, and it’s so delegitimizing in our mythical understanding of the way our government works that the federal government would save the big banks and let millions of people be underwater on their mortgages and lose everything and all that sort of thing. I don’t know, I don’t even know where I’m going with that, other than it’s interesting where I want to say that chips are different, but it’s also maybe symbolic and emblematic of the overall challenges we face as a society in an increasingly technological age. Why are chips different? Because there’s so much that goes into them. It’s not just written down in a book, it’s a collection of people and learnings and understandings that only can be accumulated via time and that’s not something you can vote into office every four years, or Johnny down the road wants to make changes, he’s going to go to the House of Representatives and stand up and make a speech.*

*That’s why I’m very sympathetic, what Trump did and I am cheating in saying I don’t want to talk about the legal aspects, precisely because they’re probably very much may not be in his favor, and I also really think this needs to happen, so it’s easier for me to just ignore it. But that ties to the financial crisis, it ties to what you’re talking about. This loss of legitimacy in the face of people doing what they believe needed to be done, and we’re not going to solve this particular challenge in this case, other than I just want to compliment you on that analogy, because I think it’s a very profound one that gets at so many issues and challenges we’re facing as a nation, as a human race.*

*DK:* Well, at the very least, I think the lack of trust in institutions that that spurred on from 2008, we’re living the echoes of that now. The willingness to break norms now, I think you could draw a straight line to that as well if the institutions and norms don’t serve us.

*But the whole thing is that we’re both arguing that the norms being broken is necessary and beneficial.*

*DK:* Well, I think norms are there for a purpose for sure. And I like most of those norms. Let’s be very clear. There are many norms that I think that are being broken now by immigration and other things and human decency and how institutions work and how we treat civil servants that are not good, I’m not talking about any of that, let’s just set aside all of that.

What I’m saying is we have an electorate that looks at the system and distrusts it and is totally fine and is voting in people that are willing to break it and in that context, I think we get the Intel thing, which cannot ignore the China-Taiwan risks, because the departure of the analogy that I think we have to draw here is the financial crisis, you have to deal with it right now, the crisis is there, but for now, whatever challenges the China Taiwan invasion or an event or whatever it might be, whether it happens or not, we’re not experiencing that. Our electronics work great, the foundries are working fantastically, if Intel no longer exists tomorrow—

*Nothing changes for most people.*

*DK:* —the average consumer is not going to really feel it right the way that a financial crisis would. But we’re in a situation in which the sun is still shining and we know perhaps that the rain is still going to come and we don’t have a roof, so what do we do in the meantime?

Nvidia and China

I think it’s a really interesting challenge and one other steelman that we can try to do is the H20 and the Nvidia and the 15% export tax and all of that.

*We’ve gone long, I was going to end it by saying we didn’t get to Nvidia, we didn’t get to China, but I promised it at the top, so what is the link here and how does it connect?*

*DK:* So I think we make the mistake of having the US be the only actor that matters and I think China matters too, because they also have an agency.

*I totally agree, this is so core to my belief system. US politics is so wrapped up in the US itself, it treats everyone else in the world as NPCs and a lot of the world is NPCs, but not China, China is a live player.*

*DK:* Yeah, and just as the US government doesn’t speak with one voice, there’s a lot of different voices that have to be unified somehow, China I think is the same way, which is there’s going to be portions of government in China that doesn’t want any Nvidia chips, there’s going to be portions that do want it until China catches up and then there’s going to be parts of industry that absolutely wants Nvidia and may not even like the idea of Huawei being the alternative.

There’s a lot of different voices, but why allow that? I actually understand [Nvidia CEO] Jensen [Huang]’s point, which is you don’t want to create room for them to compete against you, because it’s a formidable technology player that if you give them room, they’re going to create a platform to outcompete you 10 years down the line and if that’s the logic, then it would make total sense for him to go to the White House and say, “Let us sell chips there, sure, we’ll give you 15%, we’ll give you 50%”, because the point isn’t to make money out of China.

*It’s to prevent the rise of a competitor.*

*DK:* Yeah, that’s right. It’s almost like to give it away to them—

*It’s priceless. and this is why people are like, “Oh, we’ll buy Nvidia’s H20 at the price they’re selling them at”, it’s like, “No, they’re selling them at that price as a purely defensive measure”.*

*DK:* Right. At the same time, I will repeat to you what a former high ranking national security official told me. He would say, “China’s going to develop the AI systemm they’re going to develop weapons systems, they’re going to develop weapons system that’s infused with AI, they have every right to do that just as we do, but what I cannot allow them to have is American technologies that will enable them to do that, can not do it”.

So I totally get it from Jensen’s perspective, that from his perspective as the CEO of Nvidia and to his shareholders and to his board, he has to sell to China. No doubt about that. But from a national security perspective, you cannot allow advanced AI systems that are US-based into China for those reasons, and so what I’m observing here in DC is the current outcome is I don’t know if I’ve talked to anyone in the national security circles. I have not, to be very clear, I have not talked to President Trump who is championing this, I’m not sure if I’ve talked to anyone in the national security circles in the executive branch or in Congress that is a fan of this.

So in the long term, I think there’s going to be some tail risk for them, because I’m not sure if he’s convinced the national security circles that this is the way to go and what to do about it and so if the outcome that you want is for the entire world, including China, to be built on a US software stack, then I could see that argument. But if the outcome that you want is as big of a lead between the US and China in terms of AI hardware access, then also doesn’t make sense. So this is a hard one in which I think the language between the industry and the government is not quite cutting it right now in terms of squaring these two things.

*My frustration is the lack of consistency. If you ban Nvidia, you need to also ban semiconductor manufacturing equipment and maybe they should ban semiconductor manufacturing equipment anyway, because I think that’s a much more higher point of leverage in the long run. But to sell China as much semiconductor manufacturing equipment as they want, with the exception of EUV, and also simultaneously ban Nvidia chips, it’s the worst of both worlds, it’s very frustrating to me.*

*DK:* Well, let me push back on that. So if you did allow EUV and let’s say that you give—

*No, I don’t want EUV in China, I think that that’s the single most important thing that’s happened in chip controls.*

*DK:* So then let’s live in a world in which we allow Huawei to have complete access to TSMC. Then the market for H20 would decrease, because Huawei would put out a much better chip with better functionality and so the only way that you could really maintain a market for a degraded chip in China that’s US-based is if you degrade everything else, including foundry access.

This is an argument that I think pretty much every CEO has made to previous administrations, it’s just that this time, it’s carrying weight. You could think of it as an ASML or Applied Materials or SK Hynix or Samsung or any of these companies going to the White House and saying, “We need to be able to sell to China, because if we don’t, it creates a market opening for someone there to replace us and they’re going to oversupply the market and we’re out of the market altogether, this is how they operate”.

China, Taiwan, and Trade-offs

*Yeah, you’re right, you’re forcing me into prioritizing what it is, I think Huawei building at TSMC is the best outcome of them all. In my view, this is the flashpoint, Taiwan is what matters. Obviously, I’m biased,* *I may be less biased than I was previously , but if China is dependent on Taiwan being intact, that is a good situation in my estimation.*

*DK:* So you’re optimizing for maintaining and increasing the dependence on Taiwan from a Chinese perspective?

*Yes.*

*DK:* I think a lot of national security folks would say what we’re optimizing for is a inherent AI leadership of hardware perpetually, and again, this is a case in which it really matters what you’re optimizing.

*This is one where I think I could vociferously argue every single position, because they’re all legitimate. But to me, the great hope in the world is I think there’s a real cultural misunderstanding issue in my estimation. The US mentality is to drive to resolution and so it just bugs, I think, Americans that Taiwan, “Wait, what do you mean it’s not a country?”, “Yes, it’s a country”, “Can we clear this up and move on?”, and the best answer is “No, we can’t and ideally, we never will”, and I think there’s a world in which we do maintain the status quo in a way that is acceptable to China in the long run and I think that a way to get there and ensure it is just as the number one reason there won’t be a war is the economic interdependence of the US and China. The best way for China to not invade Taiwan is to make it too valuable to destroy.*

*DK:* Well, I’m certainly not a China expert or a Taiwan expert, I’m an economist at heart and a strategist in technology, but I think one thing that’s very clear and I think it’s obvious for people like you and me who observe the markets, but I think for most people, we frame the AI competition between US and China as who has the best capability, but it is absolutely 100% fact right now that neither the US or China makes any of the chips that drive their AI. So both countries are 100% dependent on foreign technologies in terms of hardware, the dependence is there in terms of Taiwan, Japan, even Europe and other places for the equipment and things like that.

So I think we’re living through a unique portion of history and I’m not sure how much parallels you could even draw to the Cold War, because at least during the Cold War and the nuclear battles, each country, the US and the Soviets, had more control over their own technologies, their weapons technologies, than before than what it is now with AI hardware. Neither country really controls that stack at the hardware side and both have fundamental weaknesses to try to win.

This ties us full circle, everything we discussed about Intel, we’re talking about fundamental weaknesses in the US system to outcompete Taiwan and TSMC and you could take it from the Chinese side too. You could look at that and say, “Well, the fundamental weaknesses that China has is about the lack of trust and the lack of innovative capacity”, and all of that to be able to do that, and so what I would love is you could come up with different solutions depending on the problem that you’re solving for and so I never approach a problem and say, “No, that’s stupid”, because you’re getting it wrong in that solution.

The positions that you’ve taken about Intel and H20 and others, there are smart people that I know that would vehemently disagree with you about all of those things, but you’re optimizing for specific problems and these people that would disagree with you are also optimizing for different problems.

*That’s right. Both of our arguments can be totally airtight, just we’re pointing it to different directions.*

*DK:* Exactly. So I think it is really important for policymakers to articulate very clearly what the strategy is and what problems they’re prioritizing for, so that the markets could react and bend around that.

*Yeah, this is a really important point. I think this was something that came up — we’re talking about broader societal questions — I think this is something that came up in COVID, where the problem with the tyranny of experts is that there is no right answer to so many of these questions. Everything is a trade-off and the fundamental role of a leader in society, which for us in a democratic system is the politicians, is to balance the trade-offs and to choose the order, the priority stack, what I call it. What is most important? What is second most and what is third most important?*

*The fundamental failure of our politics is not politicians not knowing all the answers, because in a technological age, that’s increasingly impossible. The fundamental failure is the lack of courage and frankly, cowardice to make trade-offs. If you make the trade-offs and you signal what’s most important and what’s not, the experts can come in and fill in the details of how to make that happen, and I think that’s what you’re saying. We need to choose what’s most important. Is it having a completely indigenous stack? Is it controlling the software stack? Is it doing whatever is necessary to prevent war? You have to make a choice, you need to communicate that and then we can let the market work. The market will figure it out after that.*

*DK:* Yeah. There’s a intermediate step and I agree with all that, there’s a intermediate step in making sure that those leaders have a clear understanding of the fundamentals. Fundamentals of how the market worked, how we got here, why we got here and what’s next and allow them to think long term, and what I found frustrating when I was in government was that there was generally a lack of that.

It’s hard to get, because there’s plenty of people that are incentivized to give you information that are biased and I don’t think it’s anything ill-willed, but a company will come to you or an association will come to you and they have their viewpoints for strategic things that they want accomplished, and it’s really hard for you to have a fundamental assessment of what is true and where things are going, so that the leaders can make decisions.

So people have asked me, “Why go to a company like TechInsights after being the architect of CHIPS? Why not go do something else?”. To me, it was really important for me to try to stay in a place where I could try to provide some of that on market assessment, fundamental assessment, so the strategy makers, whether it’s at a company level or government level, to look at this and say, “Okay, here are the pain points and here how things are operating, here’s how the demand works here and supply works and so let’s drive the ship this way”. Trying my best to do that, but it’s hard, it’s not easy.

*Well, the good news is now that you’re a takesman at TechInsights, you get to come here and drop takes on Stratechery. I said after the first time we talked, I have to have you on again. Feel the same way now, this was a great conversation and Dan Kim, look forward to talking to you again in the future.*

*DK:* All right, sounds good and thanks for the invitation again.

text:
Oracle's stock sky-rocketed after reporting massive future performance obligations, mostly from OpenAI. It's a big risk, but Oracle is uniquely prepared to capitalize.

Oracle Pops, From Databases to AI, Oracle and OpenAI

Monday, September 15, 2025

On Thursday’s episode of Sharp Tech , Andrew and I discussed Apple’s iPhone event and the absence of awe, Oracle’s big quarter, plus a host of mailbag questions.

A quick scheduling note: this week’s Stratechery Interview will run on Wednesday instead of Thursday. More generally, now that I am back in America, expect Interview days to move around a bit, with the default being Thursday, but not nearly as rigid of a schedule as I had in Taiwan.

On to the Update:

Oracle Pops

From the Wall Street Journal :

Oracle shares surged by as much as 43% Wednesday after the software company said it won several billion-dollar contracts in its latest quarter. The wins revealed a bigger foothold in the booming artificial-intelligence race than was previously understood. The database-software company has $455 billion in outstanding contract revenue that it expects to collect for the latest quarter that ended in Aug. 31. Those performance obligations were up more than fourfold from the same quarter last year. Oracle signed four multibillion-dollar contracts with three different customers during the quarter, Chief Executive Safra Catz told analysts and investors…

Several more multibillion-dollar customers are expected to sign on in the next few months and push the company’s remaining performance obligations up to more than $500 billion, Catz said. Shares closed up nearly 36% at $328.33, a new all-time high, on a day that marked the largest percentage increase since December 23, 1992, when the stock gained nearly 44%. Through Tuesday’s close, the stock had gained 45% so far this year.

First off, it’s worth remembering that Oracle has a very, shall we say, colorful history when it comes to performance obligations: back in the 1990s Oracle had to restate its revenue after recognizing future performance obligations as revenue, and in the 2010s faced a whistleblower lawsuit about doing the same for its cloud business. Fortunately for everyone involved, Oracle this time is getting credit for unrealized performance obligations specifically, so we should be in the clear.

That just leaves one question: will the performance obligations actually be realized?

From Databases to AI

Before getting to that question, it’s important to understand that Oracle isn’t some random player in AI infrastructure: they actually have a very compelling offering for both business and technical reasons.

Start with the latter: back in 2008 Oracle launched its Exadata computing system. The first version was built by HP and was designed specifically for running large scale databases on premise, with a focus on low latency and deterministic performance characteristics. Then, in 2010, Oracle closed on its deal for Sun Microsystems, and brought production of Exadata in-house with an increased focus on optimizing and engineering the entire stack.

An essential technology for achieving low latency and deterministic performance is RDMA: remote direct memory access. What this means is that one machine can read/write another machine’s memory across the network, which is obviously very useful for large scale database applications (you can trivially replicate transactions, for example).

This focus on databases also meant that Oracle was very focused on networking, in two respects: first, low latency required scalable horizontal networking; Exadata started out using Infiniband, but later shifted to ethernet. Second, achieving deterministic performance required offloading networking functionality from machines onto a separate networking interface controller (NIC); Oracle achieved this with what it calls the “SmartNIC”, which is a software-defined NIC (in contrast to AWS’s Nitro ASIC) that sits underneath a virtual machine and manages networking without impacting the performance of said machine.

Oracle was famously late to the cloud, and started to lose a lot of marketshare in databases to AWS in particular; the company realized that the best route to catch up was to build the best solution for its existing customers. That meant basically offering Exadata in the cloud, complete with SmartNICs, ethernet, and RDMA; existing Oracle customers could simply “lift-and-shift” their existing Oracle installations and get the exact same performance on OCI that they had on premises.

All of this happened before LLMs came along, but critically, it turned out that Oracle was arguably the single best prepared cloud provider for the unique needs of LLMs, particularly training: training LLMs requires massive scalability with low latency and deterministic performance, exactly what Oracle had been focused on building. And, of course, LLMs needed RDMA and networking optimized for it, which was the specific part of the stack that Oracle had been focused on in-house. Oracle, almost completely by accident, and despite — or maybe because? — being late to the cloud, had built the perfect LLM cloud.

Notice, however, what Oracle did not build: there is no Oracle GPU, and there is no Oracle model. Rather, OCI is kind of like the TSMC of AI infrastructure. Morris Chang, TSMC’s founder, told the Computer History Museum how the company became a pure-play foundry:

I paused to try to examine what we have got in Taiwan. And my conclusion was that [we had] very little. We had no strength in research and development, or very little anyway. We had no strength in circuit design, IC product design. We had little strength in sales and marketing, and we had almost no strength in intellectual property. The only possible strength that Taiwan had, and even that was a potential one, not an obvious one, was semiconductor manufacturing, wafer manufacturing. And so what kind of company would you create to fit that strength and avoid all the other weaknesses? The answer was pure-play foundry…In choosing the pure-play foundry mode, I managed to exploit, perhaps, the only strength that Taiwan had, and managed to avoid a lot of the other weaknesses.

TSMC’s neutrality is a massive strength; it’s what enables the company to be the collective action solution to the need for the entire ecosystem to invest in massively expensive foundries. Everyone trusts and works with TSMC to push chip production forward, to the benefit of all; on the flipside, a huge challenge Intel faces with its foundry efforts is that no one trusts them to (1) not prioritize their own products if push comes to shove and (2) not to unfairly benefit from their IP.

Oracle’s LLM neutrality, meanwhile, means that on the model side it is a trustworthy partner. What is more critical, however, is that unlike every other major cloud player, Oracle isn’t developing their own chip; they are all in on Nvidia. Not only does this mean that their network is perfectly optimized for Nvidia, but it also means that they are one of Nvidia’s most prized customers; as long as GPU demand still exceeds supply, Nvidia would, all things considered, prefer to sell to companies that aren’t trying to replace them. This, by extension, means that Oracle has consistently had capacity to sell even as other clouds are further back in line for Nvidia’s latest systems.

Oracle and OpenAI

The biggest and most obvious customer for this capacity is the biggest pure-play AI company: OpenAI. From the Wall Street Journal :

OpenAI signed a contract with Oracle to purchase $300 billion in computing power over roughly five years, people familiar with the matter said, a massive commitment that far outstrips the startup’s current revenue. The deal is one of the largest cloud contracts ever signed, reflecting how spending on AI data centers is hitting new highs despite mounting concerns over a potential bubble. The Oracle contract will require 4.5 gigawatts of power capacity, roughly comparable to the electricity produced by more than two Hoover Dams or the amount consumed by about four million homes…

The OpenAI and Oracle contract, which starts in 2027, is a risky gamble for both companies. OpenAI is a money-losing startup that disclosed in June it was generating roughly $10 billion in annual revenue — less than one-fifth of the $60 billion it will have to pay on average every year. Oracle is concentrating a large chunk of its future revenue on one customer — and will likely have to take on debt to buy the AI chips needed to power the data centers…

Compared with Microsoft, Amazon and Meta, the biggest spenders of the AI age, Oracle has a far greater debt load relative to its cash holdings. The cloud company’s spending to keep up with the AI boom is already outstripping its cash flow, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence. Microsoft has a total debt to equity ratio of 32.7% compared with 427% for Oracle. For the fiscal year that ended in June, Microsoft’s operating cash flow was about $136 billion, with capital expenditures including leases of $88 billion. For Oracle, the operating cash flow for the 12-month period ended in August was $21.5 billion, with $27.4 billion in capital expenditures, S&P data show.

It’s just as well that Oracle’s big increase in future performance obligations was primarily OpenAI, given that ChatGPT is by far the most used AI application; it seems likely that a big reason for the run-up in the stock price was the realization that the easiest way for public investors to invest in OpenAI is to invest in Oracle. Still, there’s no escaping the reality that this is a massive risk: Oracle, annoyingly enough, separates software and cloud revenue, but combines them when it comes to expenses; it’s safe to assume that software margins are covering for the lack thereof in the cloud, and if that OpenAI revenue doesn’t come through the company could be in big trouble.

At the same time, weird as it may seem for a company founded on an IBM side project in the late 1970s to be betting it all on OpenAI specifically, and AI generally, Oracle is arguably the best argument yet for the vigor that comes from founder control. Larry Ellison may be 81, but he’s still Oracle’s CTO, and I don’t think it’s an accident that of the big three tech companies founded in the late 1970s — Apple and Microsoft are the other two — it’s Oracle that is taking the biggest AI risk of all; Apple is on the periphery , and Microsoft bowed out of funding OpenAI’s ambitions (while still keeping the option — and a large chunk of business — they earned from their earlier funding).

It’s also the case — if you’ll forgive a bit of morbidity — that Ellison may not be around if this deal goes sour. He’s not worried about the long-term, quite literally, which is perhaps why Oracle is taking this massive risk. At the same time, it’s a risk that he and Oracle have been preparing for for a long time, and as an observer of the industry, I find it pretty thrilling.

Oracle's AI commitment requires debt, which marks an inflection point in a potential AI bubble; then, Apple finally increases iPhone prices

The Oracle Inflection Point, Apple's Price Increase

Tuesday, September 16, 2025

Jon at Asianometry just visited the Bay Area, and reports that Silicon Valley is Doing Hard Things Again .

To repeat yesterday’s scheduling note: this week’s Stratechery Interview will run on Wednesday instead of Thursday. More generally, now that I am back in America, expect Interview days to move around a bit, with the default being Thursday, but not nearly as rigid of a schedule as I had in Taiwan.

On to the Update:

The Oracle Inflection Point

I wrote about Oracle’s big stock pop yesterday in the context of Oracle’s genuinely compelling tech stack and business positioning; Doug O’Laughlin wrote a bigger picture piece on Fabricated Knowledge that I think is worth highlighting as well. O’Laughlin makes two big points:

First, and in-line with with my notes about Oracle’s technology stack, O’Laughlin notes that Oracle’s success suggests that there is less of a moat in terms of legacy cloud incumbency than you might think:

This is what disruption looks like. I have argued before that the hyperscalers’ old moats, balance sheets, and CPU-centric distribution were less impregnable than they appeared. SemiAnalysis’s ClusterMAX benchmarks confirmed this, and it is now a genuine contender from Oracle. Capital as a moat is not a lasting one.

History suggests that incumbents rarely dominate tangential markets. A focused challenger emerges, captures share, and reshapes the landscape. AWS played that role a decade ago; Oracle may be playing a similar role now. Amazon’s in-house Trainium effort increasingly resembles an “Amazon Basics” strategy, viable but not leading, while Oracle doubles down on the largest GPU-first cloud in the world.

The AWS part in particular very much echoes the concerns I expressed in Paradigm Shifts and the Winner’s Curse ; while AWS (and Apple’s) AI strategies are understandable, both run the risk of falling behind in a world where performance matters most:

Go back to that illustration from The End of the Beginning : Apple and Amazon are betting that AI is just another primitive in continuous computing that happens everywhere.

The most optimistic AI scenarios, however, point to something new:

A better word for “Anywhere” is probably autonomous, but I wanted to stick with the “Where” theme; what I’m talking about, however, is agents: AI doing work without any human involvement at all. The potential productivity gains for companies are obvious: there is a massive price umbrella for inference costs if the end result is that you don’t need to employ a human to do the same work. In this world what matters most is performance, not cost, which means that Amazon’s obsession with costs is missing the point; it’s also a world where the company’s lack of a competitive leading edge model makes it harder for them to compete, particularly when there is another company in the ecosystem — Google — that not only has its own custom chip strategy (TPUs), but also is integrating those chips with its competitive leading edge large language model (Gemini).

The reason I want to highlight O’Laughlin’s article, however, is the second point: while I noted that Oracle is going to have to use debt to finance the infrastructure necessary to serve these purchase obligations, it was only in passing; O’Laughlin argues that is the most important takeaway:

There is no way for Oracle to pay for this with cash flow. They must raise equity or debt to fund their ambitions. Until now, the AI infrastructure boom has been almost entirely self-funded by the cash flows of a select few hyperscalers. Oracle has broken the pattern. It is willing to leverage up to hundreds of billions to seize a share. The stable oligopoly is cracking. I wrote about this earlier , and I think that we are starting to see the markers of a classical bubble.

The implications are profound. Amazon, Microsoft, and Google can no longer treat AI infrastructure as a discretionary investment. They must defend their turf. What had been a disciplined, cash-flow-funded race may now turn into a debt-fuelled arms race. That’s a vibe-shift if I’ve ever seen one.

Welcome to the next and newest phase of the capital cycle. I believe the Oracle quarter achieved something more elusive than just revenue. I believe Oracle has just sparked the elusive animal spirit to life. I believe that for me, Oracle is the quarter that we will remember in history. I am starting to think that the tariff tantrum will be primarily felt in the lagging-edge parts of the market, while the explicit plan is to spend more on AI capex to drive our economy forward.

O’Laughlin makes a critical point: until now the single best riposte to those worried about an AI bubble is that all of this capital expenditure is being funded out of positive free cash flow from the Aggregators; now, however, a debt-fueled player has entered the market:

Let’s sketch out the state of the future from here. I believe that the 2000 comparison is now 100% complete. What we have lacked in this cycle so far is almost no debt-led funding. The Oracle RPO shows what’s possible if you’re willing to flex your balance sheet, and this will kick off an uneasy race.

Compare the spending of the big three with that of Oracle. Oracle is going to go negative free cash flow to win, and it’s likely that incumbents will respond. I believe it’s time for technology incumbents to start spending a lot more, and most have already indicated they will…

I think the simplest way to think about this is through the framework laid out in the book “Boom” by Byrne Hobart . Occasionally, capitalism disregards return on capital once every 20-40 years, to single-mindedly invest in a new technology. What really makes the bubble big is that all the parties are aligned in the same direction for the outcome. I think the stars are aligning, and debt is the real accelerant.

I interviewed Hobart about his book last fall ; these are his words:

Bubbles are this weird financial phenomenon where asset prices move in a way that does not seem justified by economic fundamentals. A lot of money pours into some industry, a lot of stuff gets built, and usually too much of it gets built and a bunch of people lose their shirts and a lot of very smart, sophisticated people are involved with the beginning, a lot of those people are selling at the peak, and a lot of people who are buying at the peak are less smart, less sophisticated, but they’ve been kind of taken in by the vibe and they’re buying at the wrong time and they lose their shirts, and that’s really bad.

As we discussed, this thesis isn’t new; Carlota Perez made a similar argument in Technological Revolutions and Financial Capital . Hobart’s focus, however, isn’t just on the infrastructure that is built, but on the otherwise impossible innovations that occur when everyone buys in all at once:

*What I took away is your book was much more of a sociological exposé, like spiritual almost, and I shouldn’t say almost because you were actually quite explicit about it. It’s like you were seeking — the goal of this book, it feels like — is to call forth the spirit of the bubble as opposed to have some sort of technocratic overview. You give us useful history, but there’s not really charts or microeconomics, it’s an exhortation. Is that what you were going for?*

*BH:* Yes, it is an exhortation. We do want people to pick up a copy and quit their job halfway through reading it or drop out of school and start something crazy. I don’t want to be legally liable if you do something sufficiently crazy, and I think that the spiritual element is something that we did want to talk about in the book, because I think if you — you can apply this totally secular framework to it, and it’s perfectly valid. Of course, if it is a mostly materialist framing of things, then it has a lot more real world data because it’s all reliant on that real world data, but if you have the belief or at least suspicion that all of us are unique and special, and there is something that we are, if not put on this Earth to do, at least there are things that we are able to do that other people wouldn’t do as well, that part of our job is to find those things and do them really well. Bubbles play into that in an interesting way because they tell you it’s time, it’s like you wanted to do this kind of thing…

*Well, and to your point, a lot of these things have so many interlocking parts, all of which need to be built at the same time. FOMO is this coordination function, and I’m just parroting the points in your book, but it’s this coordination function that gets lots of people solving lots of different problems, all of which need to be solved in parallel and that’s, to your point, you can’t build it out serially, it has to be done that way.*

*BH:* Yes, it has to be done in parallel. One way that we talk about it is that industry clusters, they’re really interesting phenomenon where, if you want to work in finance, you do what I did, you get to New York by all means necessary. If you want to be in movies, you go to LA. If you want to be in tech, you go to the Bay Area.

What bubbles do is they create one of those clusters in time rather than in space where this is the time when everyone is doing this thing, and so this is the time to do it. If you know that people are building other elements of the — they’re building parts of the infrastructure that your thing needs to be built on, then it’s actually a less risky thing to build. So Amazon was a less risky business because AOL was mass mailing their disks and telling everyone, “Get on the Internet”, and then AOL became a less risky business because Yahoo is giving you stuff to find on the Internet. eBay and Amazon are giving you stuff to buy on the Internet. Everyone’s creating websites so you have these feedback loops in both directions.

This is what I meant when I talked about Oracle’s investment being “thrilling”; and, for the record (and in response to some feedback I received), I wasn’t being critical of Larry Ellison while noting his age: if you’re not investing to change the world, then ultimately, what is the point?

What remains to be seen is what — beyond the technologies that are created in parallel — is the durable good from the bubble, if it is forming; I discussed this question with Daniel Gross and Nat Friedman in January in the context of Stargate and the imminent arrival of debt financing:

*DG:* By the way, the other lens on the news today is an economic one, which is, put all this stuff aside, it is just the nature of bubbles that after spending a few quarters spending balance sheet money, debt comes into play. That happened at the telco bubble, that happened at the railroad bubble…

I think if you look at telecom as a fraction of institutional grade debt, I think in 1996 it’s like 5%, and then in 1999 it suddenly spikes to 10%, and then just before the bubble bursts, it spikes again I think to like 15%. And so, it’s just like the nature of the way these things work. You spend your balance sheet, you want more capital, you start issuing debt.

And then the main question to think about is basically, does everything go as planned or not? Because if it does, it’s a wonderful trade, because you get to basically dilate time, you pull things forward, and paying a little bit of interest is fine, but if it doesn’t, and there’s a hiccup along the way, the pain is much greater. I think it’s just a natural act of things…

*Well, I think the big concern has to be that, what is the debt going towards? The telco bubble, at the end of the day, it was hilariously stupid economics. The bits were going to go to zero, but at the same time, there is still Internet traffic basically running over the infrastructure that was laid down back then.*

*NF:* That’s right. Yeah, bubbles are good for the country, they’re not good for sophisticated investor.

*Well, they’re good for the country depending on what they’re spent on, right?*

*NF:* Well, of course, yeah.

*So, you have a data center, which is I think a 30-year depreciation, and then the GPUs are I think accounted for in a five-year depreciation, but actually are unusable after about 36 months. So, you already have a problem there in terms of your accounting for the GPUs go and by definition, taking debt out on a 36-month sort of item is probably not ideal, that is rapidly diminishing in value. But if say we had a power build out, well, guess what? We can be using electricity forever.*

*NF:* That’s right.

*I think the critical question and moment right now is, can we direct this bubble spending? And this is almost like the depressing thing about this announcement. I don’t want news about a $500 billion investment in data centers, I want news about a $500 billion investment in power generation, which will retain its value, even if the people who build it go bankrupt in the meantime.*

That discussion was in reference to OpenAI’s Stargate announcement; the company says that its purchase agreement with Oracle is a part of that. What I am watching for is where the power for these Oracle investments comes from; more generally, the best thing the U.S. can do for its future would be to build more power. If AI makes that politically viable it will be an incredible contribution.

Apple’s Price Increase

Before the iPhone event completely fades from memory — if it ever entered it — I did want to close the loop on a long-running Stratechery hobby-horse: Apple finally raised iPhone prices.

The way the company did so is quite clever. Here is a comparison of last year’s lineup and this year’s lineup:

2025 2024 Top-of-the-line Big iPhone iPhone 17 Pro Max $1,199 iPhone 16 Pro Max $1,199 Top-of-the-line iPhone iPhone 17 Pro $1,099 iPhone 16 Pro $999 Big iPhone iPhone Air $999 iPhone 16 Plus $899 Regular iPhone iPhone 17 $799 iPhone 16 $799

Apple increased the allure of the big iPhone, making it both incredibly thin and also with the same chip as the Pro, and then slid it into the $999 price point previously occupied by the iPhone Pro; the iPhone Pro, meanwhile, went up by $100. Apple will argue that isn’t a price increase, because $1,099 was the price of the 256GB model last year, and 256GB is now the base level. At the end of the day, however, there no longer is an option for a $999 iPhone Pro, so I’m counting this as a price increase.

What is notable is that iPhones are still historically cheap in real terms; here is the 2025 version of a table I have been posting for the last several years, showing iPhone prices in 2020 dollars:

2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 2 year old iPhone $499 $477 $441 $422 $411 N/A 1 year old iPhone $599 $572 $530 $507 $493 $568 New iPhone $799 $763 $707 $676 $657 $649 iPhone Pro $999 $954 $883 $846 $822 $892 iPhone Pro Max $1,099 $1,050 $972 $1,015 $904 $973

Two additional notes on this table:

* There is no two-year-old iPhone for sale in the U.S.; rather, there is the iPhone 16e for $599
* The one-year-old iPhone is $699, which is less of a price decrease than previous old iPhones; this is also the first base iPhone that had increased RAM (to support Apple Intelligence)

Overall this supports my assumption when the iPhone 16e was announced that Apple was resetting its lineup for AI, and covering its bases for tariffs and inflation as well. Overall the thesis that Apple is increasingly a services company still holds ; Apple may be retreating to its traditional strengths , but it is doing so as a company very much in tune with the importance of services — and the importance of price accessibility — to its bottom line.

An interview with YouTube CEO Neil Mohan about empowering creators while leaning into AI.

An Interview with YouTube CEO Neil Mohan About Building a Stage for Creators

Wednesday, September 17, 2025

This week’s Stratechery Interview is with YouTube CEO Neal Mohan . Mohan joined Google as part of the DoubleClick acquisition in 2007, and became the Senior Vice President of Display and Video Ads. Then, in 2015, Mohan moved to YouTube to become Chief Product Officer, and succeeded Susan Wojcicki as CEO in 2023.

The occasion for this interview was yesterday’s Made on YouTube 2025 , YouTube’s annual product announcement event; unsurprisingly, this year’s announcements were extremely AI-centric. The announcements included:

* Using Veo 3 to create video backgrounds for shorts, converting raw footage to coherent videos, and speech to song.
* Significant updates to live streaming and podcasting, including the ability to generate relevant video for audio-only podcasts
* New brand collaboration offerings and AI-enabled auto-tagging for product placements

I attended the event, and interviewed Mohan in person. One thing that was very interesting about the event is that many of the features were introduced and demoed not by YouTube executives, but by creators; it was a powerful endorsement of the unique relationship YouTube has with the creator community.

In this interview Mohan and I discuss his background, including his vision for DoubleClick that informed Google’s approach to web advertising for years, how YouTube wants to use AI to enhance creators (and not replace them), YouTube monetization, the difference between a platform and creators, and the company’s attempted takeover of the living room TV.

As a reminder, all Stratechery content, including interviews, is available as a podcast; click the link at the top of this email to add Stratechery to your podcast player.

On to the Interview:

An Interview with YouTube CEO Neil Mohan About Building a Stage for Creators

This interview is lightly edited for content and clarity.

*Topics:*

Background ( #background ) | DoubleClick ( #doubleclick ) | YouTube and AI ( #youtube-ai ) | YouTube, Creators, and Monetization ( #monetization ) | The YouTube Stage ( #youtube-stage ) | YouTube on TV ( #youtube-tv ) | The Everything Service ( #everything )

Background

*Neal Mohan, welcome to Stratechery.*

*Neal Mohan:* Thank you for having me, Ben. Great to be here.

*So we’re in New York City talking shortly after your keynote at the Made On YouTube event. Before I get into that, I wanted to share an interesting anecdote, at least interesting to me.*

*Last night, I told a friend that I was in New York City for something YouTube related. I couldn’t remember the name of the event, so I searched on Google, naturally, for “YouTube event New York City 2025” and various permutations of that, and I actually did not find it, I never messaged him back, I waited until I got here today, “Oh yeah, Made on YouTube”. What struck me about this anecdote is not that YouTube isn’t a big deal, obviously it’s a massive deal, or that this event didn’t matter. It was the opposite in that it seems like there’s almost a total disconnect between YouTube and the online world of creators that you’ve fostered, and traditional media, which Google still draws from for things like news and search results, stuff like that. Do you see that disconnect and what’s it like being on the other side of it?*

*NM:* It’s interesting. When we conceived — this is our fourth year doing Made on YouTube — and when we conceived of it, we really thought of it as a place to showcase our innovation. Hopefully you saw a lot of that today from a product standpoint, but really more through for and through the lens of our creators, the YouTubers. The lens that which we look at Made on YouTube and how the features are received, who knows about it, is really through that creator community.

*Right, it’s like this completely parallel ecosystem that me being more in traditional media is like, “There’s something going on over there”, and you almost fail to appreciate the magnitude and volume.*

*NM:* Yeah, that’s what I was going to say is that yes, it’s this ecosystem, this creator ecosystem, you can say it’s parallel, but happens to be a lot of, as you saw with those creators that are in the audience, have tens and tens of millions of followers.

*You could be parallel and be much larger!*

*NM:* Exactly.

*Well, tell me about your background, I always like to get into this when I talk to someone new. Where’d you grow up? What was your path to technology? Did you have ambitions to be the steward of culture, even if the traditional world was missing what was happening under their noses?*

*NM:* Yeah, I grew up in the Midwest, was I was born in Indiana, my dad was doing his PhD at Purdue, so I was born to grad students in Indiana. I grew up most of my childhood in Michigan, outside of Ann Arbor.

*So, are you a Purdue fan or a Michigan fan?*

*NM:* I’m a Michigan fan, but I love Purdue, I took our three kids there for the first time to see where dad was born, and that was a lot of fun. I’m a Michigan fan.

But I grew up in the Midwest, kind of very typical childhood, this is now we’re talking kind of late ’70s, early ’80s, so lots of Transformers and GI Joes and Little League baseball and that kind of a thing. And right as I was about getting ready for high school, my parents moved back to India and so, that was a culture shock for me.

*Everyone thinks about culture shock in this direction, but you go back and you look like you’re Indian, but you’ve grown up-*

*NM:* Definitely don’t sound that way!

*That’s right.*

*NM:* So that was quite the experience. I had to learn nine grades worth of Hindi, and all that from a language standpoint, but just culturally, it was different. I could understand the language, I couldn’t read it or write it or speak it, and you obviously fast-forward, and some of my best friends are from that time period, it was obviously a transformational time in my life, and then I came back.

*Is there a bit, by the way, where we’re talking about these ecosystem, these creators, you can understand their language? Do you feel like you can speak it or did you have to have a crash course there as well?*

*NM:* You mean like the creator lingo?

*Yes.*

*NM:* Yeah, actually, the common thread that I was going to get to is the fact that you asked about steward of culture or what have you, the common thread actually through my childhood was the way that I actually was able to connect with, whether it’s a new community of friends, or fitting into a completely different place on the other side of the world, was actually through things like media and culture.

If there’s any common thread through my life it really is the fact that I love consuming stories, I love contributing to stories and so whether it’s movies, or books, or sports, or creators in today’s world, that has really been a common thread.

I happen to be lucky enough to combine it with my love of technology. One of the things that I remember fondly about my high school days in India is I had this tiny little software company that I started on my own, and it was basically educational software, I built programs that taught kids, of all things, organic chemistry. So it was really those two things, my love of technology, programming, computers, and then this deep love I’ve always had of media of every form that has been turned out to be, and it wasn’t by anything I planned, a common thread throughout my career.

*So, you came back to the US for college then?*

*NM:* Yeah, I came back to college at Stanford, I studied electrical engineering, and I graduated from Stanford right in the mid-90s. And in that sense, I think actually back to this love of media and technology, it was an incredibly fortuitous time to be coming into my professional career. It was really the dawn of the Internet, dotcom 1.0, every type of company, including media companies, were figuring out what this new medium actually was, and how they were going to take advantage of it, launch a website, all that sort of a thing, and that’s when I started my working life.

*In retrospect, what was the biggest misconception that everyone had way back when?*

*NM:* Oh, I think that there were probably, I’m sure there were many of them. Certainly from my standpoint, a lot of it was that a lot of what people understood to be the case in the media world that existed in television for decades or print for centuries would continue forward in the same way in the digital, in the Internet world, and many things did, like the advertising business model or what have you, but there were many things that were very different. The biggest, of course being the marginal cost of production of content and those types of things.

*And also everyone having access, everyone was like, “Oh, finally we don’t have any geographic limitations “, and then “ Oh no, we don’t have any more geographic limitations “.*

*NM:* Yeah, and again, look, I’m an optimist always, I think on balance that was a great thing for human beings and societies, etc. But of course, it came with other types of considerations if you look back on the last 30 years.

DoubleClick

*I want to ask about DoubleClick . You were there, then you went to business school, then you went back, was that the cycle there?*

*NM:* When I graduated from college in the mid-90s, I went to work for a consulting firm, and one of the things I quickly realized, that was I wanted to jump into one of these startups. It was an incredibly frothy time in terms of new technologies, incredibly exciting time to be in Silicon Valley, and I went to work for one of them, it was a company called NetGravity. It was one of the very first Internet advertising technology companies, they worked with many of the companies of the dotcom 1.0 days, like the GeoCities or Broadcast.com’s of the world and NetGravity and DoubleClick merged , that’s how I ended up at DoubleClick.

And there, I got to build some of the foundational Internet advertising technology that frankly exists to this day at DoubleClick. I had worked there for a few years, was working in New York City, decided to go back to business school, went back to Stanford for my MBA, and I was looking at a number of companies out of business school, and then DoubleClick called me again.

*They were then sort of hitting rough times at that point, right?*

*NM:* Well, the dotcom bubble burst around 2000, 2001, I was at business school and basically what happened was DoubleClick was getting taken private, and so it was essentially a chance to reinvest in the company, focus on what its core mission was, which was building this advertising technology software, and so there was an opportunity really basically to be the second in command at the company, coming out of business school, to be responsible for building all the products, to lead the product management team, etc., and so that’s what I did.

*So, there’s this legendary slide deck you created, I believe the word is it 400 slides long. As a pedant, I must ask, what were the exact number of slides? Was it actually 400, or was it like 402, or 398…?*

*NM:* (laughing) I don’t really remember and I’m sure it had a very large appendix too. But I do remember putting that together, it was, like you said, it was kind of like DoubleClick was the poster child of dotcom 1.0, I remember we had this giant billboard in Silicon Valley, right down the road here, saying, “DoubleClick welcomes you to Silicon Valley”. Then obviously the bottom fell out of that first phase of the Internet economy, and so the company needed a strategy as it was being taken private about what this new DoubleClick was going to look like in the dotcom 2.0 world. And so, that’s what I put together.

*What was the strategy?*

*NM:* It was really around the notion that, just like as you said, access and distribution of all of this amazing content was going to be widely available, to all of us as consumers. It meant that the advertising solutions also needed to be open and broadly available, and that became the basis of how we thought about the DoubleClick business, building solutions that were going to allow publishers, web publishers at the time, do what they needed to do to grow their businesses, but at the same time also enabling easy access, scaled access to brands and advertisers to be able to connect with that inventory.

*Right, without having to do one-to-one deals continuously.*

*NM:* Moving away from the old model of the cliché Madison Avenue type model of, “You go out to lunch and you negotiate a deal and it’s bespoke in this particular fashion because you were friends with the head of ad sales at that particular publisher”. So doing away with that model, and really frankly, democratizing the way advertising worked, which in our thesis, back to this kind of strategy book, would result in higher ROI for publishers, but also better ROI for advertisers.

*You’re not in that space anymore, you are obviously in the advertising space, but as far as the web and where DoubleClick still plays within Google, but looking from afar, or across campus as it were, what do you think the future of display advertising and the web generally is? There’s a lot of consternation in the age of AI, if you were back in that space, what would be your take?*

*NM:* Yeah. I haven’t been responsible for those products coming up on 10 years now.

*We won’t hold you to it!*

*NM:* I think that it’s, at the end of the day, ultimately what this comes down to is just like the many amazing creators that you saw today, there has to be a means to sustain that amazing creativity in content production, and it turns out that if you are doing that at scale, one of the best models to do that is advertising because that’s what makes that creativity, that content accessible in the first place.

*Everyone wants attention. The creators want attention, the advertisers want attention.*

*NM:* But we all as consumers want access to amazing content, and the best way to do that at scale is through an advertising model. That has remained true throughout every iteration of media.

*Did you have to be a real salesman for advertising within Google? To be like, “No, look, advertising is good actually, it’s not a necessary evil, it’s something that is actually broadly beneficial to everyone”?*

*NM:* Well, I have to say, Ben, one of the things that I get excited about, you walk the halls of YouTube, you’re going to hear the term “creator” and “content creator” 100 times a day and the common thread between my role leading YouTube today and what I’m describing in terms of my early career at DoubleClick and at Google is this mission to serve these content creators, whether they’re publishers, whether they’re media companies, whether they’re musicians and artists or creators, and the means to do that is actually not just helping them find audiences, but actually to help them build businesses. The way that you can do that at scale in the media world turns out to be through advertising solutions, that’s what keeps that content freely available to fans like you and me.

YouTube and AI

*You talked a lot about AI in today’s presentation, and emphasized how you saw it as a tool to enable creation, but that creators are still in control. It felt like you were trying to walk a little bit of a tightrope there, so I’ll give you another chance to articulate the message about the balance between creators and AI.*

*NM:* One of the interesting things about leading YouTube is that we’re this organization that — we’re a company that’s deeply rooted in Silicon Valley, right? Most of the people that work for me are software engineers, technologists. As you saw today, we pride ourselves on product innovation and being at the cutting edge of innovation, whether it’s the living room or what have you, mobile podcasts, etc.

But we’re also a company that faces the creative industries every single day, everything that we build is in service of people that are creative people, and I use the term “creator” writ large. YouTubers, artists, musicians, sports leagues, media, Hollywood, etc., and from that vantage point, it is really exceedingly clear that these AI capabilities are just that, they’re capabilities, they’re tools. But the thing that actually draws us to YouTube, what we want to watch are the original storytellers, the creators themselves.

It’s, in my view, not very different than when the drum machine was invented or the synthesizer was invented and I’m old enough to remember when some of those technologies were coming out, people would say, “Well, there goes music, how could you be creative with literally this computer thing that’ll spit out the music that you’re looking for?”. You fast-forward decades forward, and of course that’s not the case. What people are interested in is the music that comes from Dua Lipa, who you saw today, because it’s her, it’s authentic to her, she created it, it’s her voice, it’s her style and if she uses a bunch of tools to do that, that’s kind of besides the point.

That’s the point that I was trying to make about AI. I’m a technologist, it’s amazing what these technologies can do, you saw that through the eyes of these creators, but it really is a tool to serve them.

*What’s the more important AI story? The fact that you can use AI to make YouTube videos or the fact that YouTube videos are maybe the single most valuable source of data for AI?*

*NM:* There’s lots and lots of sources of information on which AI technologies are built. I think the interesting story there is, again, just the use of these amazing — these tools are amazing — literally being able to type in an idea and out of thin air produce an amazing video that perhaps millions of people will watch, that is amazing.

But I really think the true amazing thing is that you take that same tool and you put it in the hands of two different people, you’re going to get two very different results. We have creators, enormous creators, tens of millions of subscribers who produce content once a month or even more rarely, and they have set that expectation with their audience and our algorithm is really just a reflection of that audience expectation, so that’s what I say about that. I also recognize that lots of opportunities stem from the audience that YouTubers create on YouTube so their additional opportunities, whether — including opportunities on other platforms or a book deal-

*It’s because they’re taking their audience with them.*

*NM:* I think what YouTubers tell me is that, “My home is YouTube, my real core audience is YouTube, but I love the fact that YouTube allows me in an unencumbered way to create all of these other opportunities for myself too”. And again, you saw that today, look at how many creators are leading into their own brands, launching new product lines, trying out other forms of media, and I think that’s awesome. We want to keep enabling that.

*Are there any stories that I’m missing? Other than the fact that you still don’t disclose your costs, which drives me up the wall ?*

*NM:* [laughs] It’s 20 years, as I said, of YouTube, so it’s been a time of reflection for me and my team. One of the stories I didn’t mention was when I was at DoubleClick, I think my largest client was this video company above a pizza parlor in San Mateo, California called YouTube, so my history with YouTube actually predates both me and YouTube being part of Google. I just remember going, visiting Chad [Hurley] and Steve [Chen] and their teams and them saying like, “Neal, you’ve got to make sure these DoubleClick servers keep up because look at our growth”, and they showed me these crazy charts.

Back then, you knew that there was really special going on, these human beings were coming and sharing their stories, and these other human beings were watching these stories and you fast-forward 20 years later to today and you see all of this amazing product innovation and AI and what have you, but that core essence of YouTube about that human connection, hasn’t changed one bit. And that’s why I’m excited about the next 20 years too.

*Neal Mohan, thank you for coming on Stratechery.*

*NM:* Thank you for having me.
