text:
We are in an AI Bubble: the big question is if this bubble will worth it for the physical infrastructure and coordinated innovation that result?

The Benefits of Bubbles

Wednesday, November 5, 2025

It’s funny to remember that a decade ago there were enough people convinced we were in a bubble that I felt compelled to write an Article entitled It’s Not 1999 ; that was right then, and it’s obviously right now, when we have a clear counter-example: this is a bubble.

How else to describe a single company — OpenAI — making $1.4 trillion worth of deals (and counting!) with an extremely impressive but commensurately tiny $13 billion of reported revenue? Sure, the actual number may be higher , but that is still two orders of magnitude less than the amount of infrastructure OpenAI has publicly committed to buy over the coming years, and they are not the only big spenders. Over the past week every big tech company (except Apple) has significantly expanded their capital expenditure plans, and there is no sign of anyone slowing down.

This does, understandably, have people wringing their hands. What goes up must come down, which is to say bubbles that inflate eventually pop, with the end result being a recession and lots of bankrupt companies. And, not to spoil the story, that will almost certainly happen to the AI bubble as well. What is important to keep in mind, however, is that that is not the end of the story, at least in the best case. Bubbles have real benefits.

Financial Speculation and Physical Capacity

The definitive book on bubbles has long been Carlota Perez’s Technological Revolutions and Financial Capital . 1 ( #fn1-17491 ) Bubbles were — are — thought to be something negative and to be avoided, particularly at the time Perez published her book. The year was 2002 and much of the world was in a recession coming off the puncturing of the dot-com bubble.

Perez didn’t deny the pain: in fact, she noted that similar crashes marked previous revolutions, including the Industrial Revolution, railways, electricity, and the automobile. In each case the bubbles were not regrettable, but necessary: the speculative mania enabled what Perez called the “Installation Phase”, where necessary but not necessarily financially wise investments laid the groundwork for the “Deployment Period”. What marked the shift to the deployment period was the popping of the bubble; what enabled the deployment period were the money-losing investments.

In the case of the dotcom bubble, the money-losing investments that mattered were not actually the dotcom companies that mark that era in Silicon Valley lore: yes, a lot of people lost money on insane IPOs, but the loss was mostly equity, not debt. Where debt was a problem was in telecom, where a host of companies went bankrupt after a frenzied period of building far more fiber than could ever be justified by current usage, fast though it may have been growing. That fiber, however, became the background of today’s Internet; the fact that it basically existed for free — because the companies who built it went bankrupt — enabled the effectively free nature of the Internet today.

The Conditions for Cognitive Capacity

Late last year Byrne Hobart and Tobias Huber made a new contribution to our understanding of bubbles with their book Boom: Bubbles and the End of Stagnation . While Perez focused on the benefits that came from financial speculation leading to long-term infrastructure, Hobart and Huber identified another important feature of what they called “Inflection Bubbles” — the good kind of bubbles, as opposed to the much more damaging “Mean-reversion Bubbles” like the 2000’s subprime mortgage bubble. First, here is Hobart and Huber’s definition of an inflection bubble:

Inflection-driven bubbles have fewer harmful side effects and more beneficial long-term effects. In an inflection-driven bubble, investors decide that the future will be meaningfully different from the past and trade accordingly. Amazon was not a better Barnes & Noble; it was a store with unlimited shelf space and the data necessary to make personalized recommendations to every reader. Yahoo wasn’t a bigger library; it was a directory and search engine that made online information accessible to anyone. Priceline didn’t want to be a travel agent; it aspired to change the way people bought everything, starting with plane tickets.

If a mean-reversion bubble is about the numbers after the decimal point, an inflection bubble is about orders of magnitude. A website, a PC, a car, a smartphone — these aren’t five percent better than the nearest alternative. On some dimensions, they’re incomparably better. A smartphone is a slightly more convenient tool than a PC for taking a photo and quickly uploading it to the internet, but it’s infinitely better at navigation. A car is not just slightly faster and more reliable than a horse (although in the early days of the automobile industry, it was apparently common for pedestrians to yell “Get a horse!” at passing motorists); cars transformed American cities. Modern-day Los Angeles is inconceivable on horseback. The manure problem alone beggars the imagination.

This is what makes inflection bubbles valuable:

The fundamental utility of inflection bubbles comes from their role as coordinating mechanisms. When one group makes investments predicated on a particular vision of the future, it reduces the risk for others seeking to build parts of that vision. For instance, the existence of internet service providers and search engines made e-commerce sites a better idea; e-commerce sites then encouraged more ad-dependent business models that could profit from directing consumers. Ad-dependent businesses then created more free content, which gave the ISPs a better product to sell. Each sector grew as part of a virtuous circle.

What I love about this formulation from a tech perspective is that it captures the other side of the dotcom era: no, Silicon Valley didn’t produce any lasting infrastructure (unless you count a surplus of Aeron chairs), but what the mania did produce were a huge number of innovations, invented in parallel, that unlocked the following two decades of growth.

First, the dotcom era brought nearly the entire U.S. population online, thanks to that virtuous cycle that Hobart and Huber described in the above excerpt. This not only provided the market for the consumer Internet giants that followed, but also prepared an entire generation of future workers to work on the web , unlocking the SaaS enterprise market.

Second, the intense competition of the dotcom era led to one of my favorite inventions of all time, both because of its impact and because of its provenance.

Microsoft famously saw Netscape, the OpenAI of the dotcom era, as a massive threat; the company responded with Internet Explorer, and a host of legally questionable tactics to spur its adoption. What is forgotten, however, is that Microsoft was at that time actually quite innovative in terms of pushing browser technology forward, driven by the need to beat Netscape, and one of those innovations was XMLHttpRequest . XMLHttpRequest , introduced with Internet Explorer 5 in 1999, allowed Javascript to make asynchronous HTTP requests without reloading the page; previously to change anything on a webpage meant reloading the entire thing. Now, however, you could interact with a page and have it update in place, without a reload.

What makes this invention ironic is that this was the key capability that transformed the browser from a media consumption app to a productive one, and it was the productivity capabilities that began the long breakdown of Microsoft’s application moat. Once work could be done in a browser, it would be done everywhere, not just on Windows; this, in the long run, created the conditions for the smartphone revolution and the end of Windows’ dominance . This was, to be clear, but one of a multitude of new protocols and innovations that made today’s tech stack possible; what is important is how many of them were invented at once thanks to the bubble.

Third, the cost and complexity of serving all of these new use cases drove tremendous innovation on the backend. The Nvidia of the dotcom era was arguably not Cisco, but rather Sun: a huge percentage of venture capital went to buying Sun SPARC/Solaris servers to run these new-fangled companies. Solaris was the most advanced operating system in terms of running large websites, with the most mature TCP/IP stack, multithreading, symmetric multiprocessing, etc. Moreover, the dominance of Solaris meant that it had the largest pool of developers, which meant it was easier to hire if you ran Solaris.

The problem, however, is that SPARC servers were extremely expensive, to the point of being nearly financially impractical for the largest-scale web applications like Hotmail or Yahoo. That’s why the former (in its startups days) ran its front-end on free software (FreeBSD) on commodity x86 hardware from the beginning, and why the latter made the same shift as it exploded in popularity. Both, however, had custom-built back-ends; it was Google, founded in 1998, that built the entire stack on commodity x86 hardware and Linux, unlocking the scalability that was critical to the huge growth in the Internet that followed.

This entire stack was the product of a massive amount of uncoordinated coordination: people came online for better applications that ran on hardware powered by software built by a massive array of companies and individuals; that all of this innovation and invention happened at the same time was because of the bubble.

Oh, and to return to Perez: all of this ran over fiber laid by bankrupt companies. What Perez got right is that bubbles install physical capacity; what Hobart and Huber added is that they also create cognitive capacity, thanks to everyone pulling in the same direction at the exact same time, based not on fiat, but on a shared belief that this time is different.

Is AI Different?

This question — or statement — is usually made optimistically. In this case, the optimistic take would be that AI is already delivering tangible benefits, that those benefits are leading to real demand from companies and consumers, and that all of the money being spent on AI will not be wasted but put to productive use. That may still be the case today — all of the hyperscalers claim that demand for their offerings exceeds supply — but if history is any indication we will eventually overshoot.

There is, however, a pessimistic way to ask that question: will the AI bubble be beneficial like the positive bubbles chronicled by Perez and Hobart and Huber, or is it different? There have been reasons to be worried about both the physical buildout and the cognitive one.

Start with the physical: a huge amount of the money being spent on AI has gone to GPUs, particularly Nvidia, rocketing the fabless design company to a nearly $5 trillion valuation and the title of most valuable company in the world. The problem from a Perez perspective is that all of this spending on chips is, relative to the sort of infrastructure she wrote about — railroads, factories, fiber, etc. — short-lived. Chips break down and get superseded by better ones; most hyperscalers depreciate them over five years, and that may be generous. Whatever the correct number is, chips don’t live on as fully-depreciated assets that can be used cheaply for years, which means that to the extent speculative spending goes towards GPUs is the extent to which this bubble might turn out to be a disappointing one.

Fortunately, however, there are two big areas of investment that promise to have much more long-term utility, even if the bubble pops.

The first is fabs — the places where the chips are made. I’ve been fretting about declining U.S. capacity in this area, and the attendant dependence on Taiwan, the most fraught geopolitical location in the world, for years , and for much of that time it wasn’t clear that anything would be done about it. Fast forward to today, and not only are foundries like TSMC and Samsung building fabs in the U.S., but the U.S. government is now a shareholder in Intel . There is still a long path to foundry independence for the U.S., particularly once you consider the trailing edge as well, but there is no question that the rise of AI has had a tremendous effect in focusing minds and directing investment towards solving a problem that might never have been solved otherwise.

The second is power. Microsoft CFO Amy Hood said on the company’s earnings call :

As you know, we’ve spent the past few years not actually being short GPUs and CPUs per se, we were short the space or the power, is the language we use, to put them in. We spent a lot of time building out that infrastructure. Now, we’re continuing to do that, also using leases. Those are very long-lived assets, as we’ve talked about, 15 to 20 years. And over that period of time, do I have confidence that we’ll need to use all of that? It is very high.

Amazon CEO Andy Jassy made a similar comment on his company’s earnings call :

On the capacity side, we brought in quite a bit of capacity, as I mentioned in my opening comments, 3.8 gigawatts of capacity in the last year with another gigawatt plus coming in the fourth quarter and we expect to double our overall capacity by the end of 2027. So we’re bringing in quite a bit of capacity today, overall in the industry, maybe the bottleneck is power. I think at some point, it may move to chips, but we’re bringing in quite a bit of capacity. And as fast as we’re bringing in right now, we are monetizing it.

As I noted yesterday , this actually surprised me: I assumed that chips were in short supply, and the power shortage was looming, but actually power is already the limiter. This is both disappointing and unsurprising, given how power generation capacity growth has stagnated over the last two decades:

U.S. electricity generation by major energy source

At the same time, this is also encouraging: the fastest way to restart growth — and hopefully at an even higher rate than the fifty years that preceded this stagnation — is to have massive economic incentives to build, combined with massive government incentives to eliminate red tape. AI provides both, and my hope is that the fact we are already hitting the power wall means that growth gets started that much sooner.

It’s hard to think of a more useful and productive example of a Perez-style infrastructure buildout than power. It’s sobering to think about how many things have never been invented because power has never been considered a negligible input from a cost perspective; if AI does nothing more than spur the creation of massive amounts of new power generation it will have done tremendous good for humanity. Indeed, if you really want to push on the bubble benefit point, wiping away the cost of building new power via bankruptcy of speculative investors — particularly if a lot of that power has low marginal fuel costs, like solar or nuclear — could be transformative in terms of what might be invented in the future.

To that end, I’m more optimistic today than I was even a week ago about the AI bubble achieving Perez-style benefits: power generation is exactly the sort of long-term payoff that might only be achievable through the mania and eventual pain of a bubble, and the sooner we start feeling the financial pressure — and the excitement of the opportunity — to build more power, the better.

I’ve been less worried about the cognitive capacity payoff of the AI bubble for a while: while there might have been concern about OpenAI having an insurmountable lead, or before that Google being impregnable, nearly everyone in Silicon Valley is now working on AI, and so is China . Innovations don’t stay secret for long, and the time leading edge models stay in the lead is often measured in weeks, not years. Meanwhile, consumer uptake of AI is faster than any other tech product by far.

What is exciting about the last few weeks, however, is that there is attention being paid to other parts of the stack, beyond LLMs. For example, last week I interviewed Substrate founder James Proud about his attempt to build a new kind of lithography machine as the center of a new American foundry. I don’t know if Proud will succeed, but the likelihood of anyone even trying — and of getting funding — is dramatically higher in the middle of this bubble than it would have been a decade ago.

It was also last week that Extropic announced a completely new kind of chip , one based not on binary 1s and 0s, but on probabilistic entropy measurements, that could completely transform diffusion models. Again, I don’t know if it will succeed, but I love that the effort exists, and is getting funding. And meanwhile, there are massive investments by every hyperscaler and a host of startups to make new chips for AI that promise to be cheaper, faster, more efficient, etc. All of these efforts are getting funding in a way they wouldn’t if we weren’t in a bubble.

Hobart and Huber write in Boom:

Not all bubbles destroy wealth and value. Some can be understood as important catalysts for techno-scientific progress. Most novel technology doesn’t just appear ex nihilo, entering the world fully formed and all at once. Rather, it builds on previous false starts, failures, iterations, and historical path dependencies. Bubbles create opportunities to deploy the capital necessary to fund and speed up such large-scale experimentation — which includes lots of trial and error done in parallel — thereby accelerating the rate of potentially disruptive technologies and breakthroughs.

By generating positive feedback cycles of enthusiasm and investment, bubbles can be net beneficial. Optimism can be a self-fulfilling prophecy. Speculation provides the massive financing needed to fund highly risky and exploratory projects; what appears in the short term to be excessive enthusiasm or just bad investing turns out to be essential for bootstrapping social and technological innovations…A bubble can be a collective delusion, but it can also be an expression of collective vision. That vision becomes a site of coordination for people and capital and for the parallelization of innovation. Instead of happening over time, bursts of progress happen simultaneously across different domains. And with mounting enthusiasm…comes increased risk tolerance and strong network effects. The fear of missing out, or FOMO, attracts even more participants, entrepreneurs, and speculators, further reinforcing this positive feedback loop. Like bubbles, FOMO tends to have a bad reputation, but it’s sometimes a healthy instinct. After all, none of us wants to miss out on a once-in-a-lifetime chance to build the future.

This is why I’m excited to talk about new technologies, the prospect for which I don’t know. The more I don’t know projects there are, the more likely there is to be one that succeeds. And, if you want an investment that pays off not for a few years, and not even for a few decades, but literally forever, then your greatest hope should be invention and innovation.

Stagnation: The Bubble Alternative

Hobart and Huber actually begin their book not by talking about ancient history, but about this century, and stagnation.

The symptoms of technological, economic, and cultural stagnation can be detected everywhere. Some of the evidence is hard to quantify, but it can perhaps best be summarized by a simple thought experiment: Will children born today experience as much change as children born a century ago—a time when cars, electrical appliances, synthetic materials, and telephones were still in their infancy? Futurists and science-fiction authors once prophesied an era of abundant energy due to nuclear fission, the arrival of full automation, the colonization of the solar system, the end of poverty, and the attainment of immortality. In contrast, futurists today ask questions about how soon and how catastrophically civilization will collapse.

There is a science-fiction innovation that has been hovering around the edges of the tech industry for the last decade: virtual and augmented reality. It hasn’t gotten far. Meta has, since it started breaking out Reality Labs financials in Q4 2020, recognized $10.8 billion in revenue against $83.2 billion in costs; the total losses are far higher when you consider that the company bought Oculus VR for $2 billion six years before that breakout. Apple, meanwhile, announced the Vision Pro in 2023, launched it in 2024, and has barely talked about it since — and certainly not on earnings calls.

Both companies would argue that the technology just isn’t there yet, and to the extent AR and VR are compelling, it’s because of the money and time they have spent developing it. I wonder, however, about a counter-factual where AR and VR were developed by a constellation of startups, not big companies: how much more innovation might there have been? Or, perhaps the bigger problem is that there was not — and, given that all of the investment is a line item in large company budgets, could not be — a bubble around AR and VR.

More generally, tech simply wasn’t much fun by the time 2020 rolled around. You had your big five tech companies who had each carved out their share of the market, unassailable in their respective domains, and the startup industry was basically itself another big tech company: Silicon Valley Inc., churning out cookie-cutter SaaS companies with a proven formula and low risk. In fact, it’s the absence of risk that Hobart and Huber identify as the hallmark of stagnation:

Of course, the causes of stagnation are complex. But what these symptoms of stagnation and decline have in common is that they result from a societal aversion to risk, which has been on the rise for the past few decades. Societal risk intolerance expresses itself almost everywhere — in finance, culture, politics, education, science, and technology. Broadly, there seems to be a collective desire to suppress and control all risks and conserve what is at the expense of breaking the terminal horizon of the present and accelerating toward what could be.

This is why Hobart told me in a Stratechery Interview that Boom was ultimately an exhortation:

*What I took away is your book was much more of a sociological exposé, like spiritual almost, and I shouldn’t say almost because you were actually quite explicit about it. It’s like you were seeking — the goal of this book, it feels like — is to call forth the spirit of the bubble as opposed to have some sort of technocratic overview. You give us useful history, but there’s not really charts or microeconomics, it’s an exhortation. Is that what you were going for?*

*Byrne Hobart:* Yes, it is an exhortation. We do want people to pick up a copy and quit their job halfway through reading it or drop out of school and start something crazy. I don’t want to be legally liable if you do something sufficiently crazy, and I think that the spiritual element is something that we did want to talk about in the book, because I think if you — you can apply this totally secular framework to it, and it’s perfectly valid. Of course, if it is a mostly materialist framing of things, then it has a lot more real world data because it’s all reliant on that real world data, but if you have the belief or at least suspicion that all of us are unique and special, and there is something that we are, if not put on this Earth to do, at least there are things that we are able to do that other people wouldn’t do as well, that part of our job is to find those things and do them really well. Bubbles play into that in an interesting way because they tell you it’s time, it’s like you wanted to do this kind of thing.

What is fascinating about the AI bubble is that there is at its core a quasi-spiritual element. There are people working at these labs that believe they are building God; that is how they justify the massive investment in leading edge models that never have the chance to earn back their costs before they are superceded by someone else. That’s why they push for policies that I think are bad for innovation and bad for national security . I don’t like these side effects, to be clear, but I appreciate the importance of the belief and the motivation.

And, I must say, it certainly is fun and compelling in a way that tech was not a few years ago. Bubbles may end badly, but history does not end: there are benefits from bubbles that pay out for decades, and the best we can do now is pray that the mania results in infrastructure and innovation that make this bubble worth it.

*

text:
An interview with Michael Morton about AI-driven e-commerce, and why this is both Amazon's category to lose and a threat — and a big opportunity for Walmart and Shopify.

An Interview with Michael Morton About AI E-Commerce

Thursday, November 6, 2025

This week’s Stratechery interview is with Michael Morton . Morton is a senior research analyst at MoffettNathanson with a focus on e-commerce and marketplaces. Morton has worked on both the buy-side and sale-side of equity analysis, and also worked on the YouTube strategy team prior to joining MoffettNathanson. I previously interviewed Morton in April 2024 .

In this interview we dive deep into LLM’s and their potential impact on e-commerce. First, we discuss the pre-LLM structure of the e-commerce market, and why LLMs are a threat to the pull category (Google and Amazon), but not the push (Meta). Then we dive into Amazon specifically: the company is positioned to dominate LLM-driven commerce, but they have business model reasons to resist. That, by extension, presents an opportunity to challengers, particularly Walmart. This was a fascinating discussion and covers topics I expect to return to regularly.

As a reminder, all Stratechery content, including interviews, is available as a podcast; click the link at the top of this email to add Stratechery to your podcast player.

On to the Interview:

An Interview with Michael Morton About AI E-Commerce

This interview is lightly edited for content and clarity.

*Topics:*

Lessons Learned ( #lessons ) | E-Commerce Push vs. Pull ( #ecommerce-push-pull ) | The AI E-Commerce Experience ( #ai-ecommerce ) | Amazon’s Potential and Ad Conundrum ( #amazon ) | Walmart and ChatGPT ( #walmart ) | Amazon Grocery ( #amazon-grocery )

Shopify and Lessons Learned

*Michael Morton, welcome back to Stratechery.*

*MM:* Ben, thanks for having me. It’s great to be back.

*It’s been a long time since you’ve been on, April 2024 was the date — and by the way, fantastic feedback on that Interview, so it’s on me for not having you back on sooner. But I did at the time feel really bad for you, because you had just published this extremely optimistic note about Shopify. We talked about it on the interview and like two days later, they absolutely went in the tank. However, vindication is yours, Shopify’s up more than 100% since then, so congratulations.*

*MM:* Well, in full disclosure, along that journey, I downgraded the stock from buy to neutral because my seat is challenging, and we’ve talked about this before, where it’s not just getting the—.

*If you’re putting prices on stocks, it’s a lot more difficult.*

*MM:* It’s not just the end destination that you need to get right, you got to get the journey. And there was a period where it looked like they were spending more than we thought they should on sales and marketing and again, in my line of work, we’re a bit paranoid, we’re always looking for a potential problem we might not find and I thought I found a problem in the cohorts that they were bringing on board. Turned out to be categorically wrong and in the investment world, you really only learn from your mistakes.

*What was the lesson you learned?*

*MM:* The two big mistakes I’ve made in the last three years since initiating at MoffettNathanson were downgrading secular winners. I was really optimistic on DoorDash when the stock was in the gutters, it was like a $50 stock, I went on CNBC when I initiated, and then famous short sellers trolled me on Twitter. I don’t know if you’ve ever been dragged on Twitter, but it’s not fun. And then it worked out really well and then around $100, I started getting worried about student loans, and I downgraded the stock and they grew right through it. Now I had to find out a year later when it accelerated on “tough comps”, that I was right.

*The secular forces overcame the short term concern.*

*MM:* Yeah, it’s so big, management is so good there, and fortunately I corrected my mistake quickly on that one. Shopify, similarly. Enormous TAM, world-class management, I had the product call correct, I overthought the financial journey.

Shopify is specifically challenging because it’s such a expensive stock from a multiple perspective that you’re on a razor’s edge. There’s no room, really, to miss and I overthought it and that thing has just gone up and to the right and I’ve never got a chance to correct my mistake.

*Well, I’m giving you credit. I don’t remember the intervening note, I just remember when you were on with me. With Shopify, the growth since then, is that down to your thesis at the time? Or are there broader forces and new things, whether that be adding on to the questions around ChatGPT that have made it even more attractive since then, or you think you had it basically nailed all along?*

*MM:* Yeah, there’s two separate things here. One is the product thesis that we had in 2023, that they had opened the door to enterprise but then even beyond that, when it comes to SMBs and the competitive slate that they were competing with globally, they’ve just completely left them in the dust, I can’t think of any company in my coverage that is so head and shoulders above the competition as Shopify.

I interviewed a candidate years ago when I was at a different firm and he was a former consultant, and he was talking and obsessing over product-led growth, and I’m a markets guy, I walked out of the interview and I was like, “I don’t know about all that consulting speak, product-led growth, markets aren’t going to care about that crap”, and I have since emailed him and told him he was right. Shopify is the perfect example of product-led growth. [Shopify President] Harley [Finkelstein] talked about it yesterday on our callback with the management team after their earnings, they don’t do steak dinners and martinis to win these clients, the product is so darn good that they can onboard everybody, from enterprise to your neighbor starting an e-commerce platform.

So the core thesis of the product’s constant state of improvement and leaving the competition behind is true. Now there’s a potential another leg to the Shopify thesis I think we’ll talk about today, and it’s the changing world of LLMs, conversational commerce, and how that’s going to impact e-commerce.

*Look, you should be the host here, that was a brilliant, “Let’s leave a tidbit on the table, let’s not get off track now, we’ll come back to it”, spot on. Just to tie up the other loose strings from that interview, another big topic we talked about was the question of brands coming back to Amazon, and guess what you can buy on Amazon now? Nike shoes and a whole bunch of other stuff , so I think that I’ve gotten that as another win for you as well.*

*MM:* Nike, Estée Lauder, it’s a long list of people, it’s just math. If you look at this share Amazon is taking and try to think about growing in your category, ex-Amazon, that alone makes it impossible and then when you talk about the difficulties of getting leveraging customer acquisition in a digital world, it makes it impossible to go alone and not use this distribution channel. The world has kind of come around to that, but I also think that there’s a chance-

*Look, you might’ve got the Shopify call wrong, but you weren’t John Donahoe driving Nike into the ground , so it could always be worse.*

*MM:* It could be. And in my seat, you have to be very comfortable making public mistakes, it’s just the way it goes.

*Well, on that point, is there anyone that you could think of that is justified in not being on Amazon? Are we limited on just purely luxury brands? Are there just super highly differentiated products that are niche, that have the cost structure, that it makes sense not to be there? Or is everyone not on there just being dumb?*

*MM:* Yeah, that’s a great question. If I was Hermès-

*Nike’s more akin to a CPG product at this point, right?*

*MM:* Yeah.

*I think anyone in that category that is mass market, totally buy your thesis. But I’m just wondering, is there any limit to this sort of assertion?*

*MM:* I would think ultra high-end luxury is a category where — and this is the type of stuff where I have friends who are into watches, and you have to buy a series of watches, same thing goes with Ferraris and stuff like that, Hermès. Those players drive such brand and signaling value culturally that they’re probably fine, I think they’ll be doing the same thing for decades. But other than that, if it’s a consumable product and you’re trying to buy customers, I think it’s really hard.

*Yeah, the one angle, there is a company that I’m thinking of that sort of eschews Amazon, but what it does is it gives them a tremendous in with other retailers for a product that benefits from touching it and handling it. They’re in high-end stores and favored and featured by those high-end stores, in part because their product isn’t on Amazon, which actually benefits them to a certain degree. But it’s one of those questions where, is it still worth it or not? It’s an open question.*

*MM:* Yeah. If there’s not a replacement good, then you’re probably okay. A tough dynamic is there’s not, and this stuff changes constantly, but Lululemon doesn’t sell authorized pants on Amazon, or their gear on Amazon at scale. There’s always unauthorized people that pop up for these types of platforms, but they’re not doing it.

But then Alo, who’s competing for market share with them for this kind of active wear yoga clothes, they sell on Amazon. So even Lulu who has done an incredible job, if you look at their sales and marketing leverage or store presence, from the outside, I don’t cover it, it’s a well-run company. With Alo on there, yeah, maybe you really love the Lulu pants, but when you just have that purchasing frequency, the Prime membership base, the products aren’t too different where you’re like, “Oh, no, I must have these”.

*Yeah, I’m not sure Lululemon is going to carry the day given their stock performance over the last several years.*

*MM:* Yeah, it’s not good.

*Maybe that sort of makes your point.*

*MM:* Yeah, it’s not good. I was subtly hinting at that.

*(laughing) Yeah, there you go, you made it.*

E-Commerce Push vs. Pull

*Well, you’ve written two remarkable reports, just to shift to LLMs because I think the question of LLMs and how it’s going to impact e-commerce is a fascinating one. There’s so many factors that go into this, so I just kind of want to walk through these reports. But I actually want to start with something you put in report number two, which is you noted that it felt like the e-commerce stack was sort of set, we knew how it all worked. What was that? What was the e-commerce as we knew it? It wasn’t going anywhere. All we’re doing is just seeing Amazon win more and more. Walk me through the structure of the market pre-ChatGPT, and why it felt so static.*

*MM:* Yeah, that’s a great way to level set this and it was the genesis of our prior conversation. These are rounding numbers and there’s consumer surveys on this, but half the time you know what you want, you open the app or you start on amazon.com, you get a bunch of different terminology for it, seek-and-destroy or spear phishing, and you’re going in and, “I need baby wipes”, or “I know that I can get my shoe on there”, or deodorant — you go in, you put it in, you click it. Half of what you see are advertisements—

*Half might be generous on Amazon these days, but yes.*

*MM:* Yeah. So half of them are ads sold on a cost-per-click basis and the other half, you would start on Google, and these are what I would call high consideration purchases, you don’t necessarily know.

*Yeah, you’re already pretty far down the funnel.*

*MM:* You’re like, “Hey, I think I need a rain jacket”, or the example that we’ve used a lot is — and I have flat feet, I try to test the channel and the models and search a little bit to get a little bit more specific than just like “AirPods”, or just something that’s very generic and there’s only a few of them — and if you searched for “Best running shoes for men with flat feet”, you would be presented with the carousel of PLAs, like the product listing ads, at the top. There would be six of them and then below that you’d get an advertisement for Runners World, it’d be a sponsored link and you’d go to Runner’s World and it’d be a review and you’d read the review and the review would say, “Here’s the best shoes for what you’re looking for”, and there’d be a little icon and it would say, “Go buy them at Amazon”.

*Just paying out an affiliate fee.*

*MM:* Yes, paying affiliate fees. So you either start on amazon.com, or you end up on amazon.com, and we’ve written notes that all roads lead to Amazon and that is the legacy kind of, I’ll call it just, incumbent funnel, that was very locked in, pretty set in stone, but now we think it’s changing because that is a bad experience for the high consideration purchases.

*Well, let’s get to that changing, but that is the, you had this push-versus-pull framework and so what was the other half of that?*

*MM:* Yes. So with the recent note, the way I’ve been trying to think about the coming disruption to consumer Internet and to be clear, the thesis isn’t dependent on if ChatGPT wins or if it’s Gemini in everybody’s pocket or Perplexity, I don’t care about the end state.

*Siri’s coming, white label Gemini , get ready.*

*MM:* I don’t care about the end state product, I do think ChatGPT has a huge runway here. I care about looking at the digital economy, and this is oversimplified and you can put the exhibit in the transcript of your email up, probably help people visualize it.

On one side of this, you have what I like to refer to as the push-based economy. That’s where you sat down, you open the app, and whether it’s Meta or you’re in Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, you name it, they’re pushing content at you.

*You’re finding all products you didn’t know existed.*

*MM:* Yes. Lean back, kind of experience.

*Which to my mind, this is the part of digital advertising I’ve always been a massive proponent and defender of , because the problem with search advertising, it’s kind of exploitive. A lot of times all you are is paying for placement for something that would’ve been top of organic search anyway and the fact that all these search engines let other people buy your trademark as a keyword, sort of speaks to the game.*

*On the other hand, when I’m on Instagram, and by the way, I mentioned that one of my realizations of living in America, is I thought Instagram ads were good before, now that it has me pegged as being in America , it’s unbelievable, I want to buy every single thing that I see. I think it’s clear Facebook’s been really amping up and pushing — every other Reel feels like it’s an ad these days — and they’re all awesome, I want all of them, it’s incredible. I hyped it up how good it was, I didn’t appreciate how good it was till I was actually geographically in the US.*

*MM:* It’s really amazing how good the push world has got at showing you the right advertisements, and in my opinion today, I think the introduction of AI augments that world from a lot of different perspectives. Meta knows what to show you and they’re better at showing you things that are going to drive engagement but even behind that, if you want to think about this as like a flow chart and on the left side you have push, at the bottom lifting it all up is the generative AI kind of stack. So more content creation, more video creation.

But the right side of this digital economy is pull and this is when you open an app and you start with a query, and this is the world that annoys you. And trust me, I can really unload on some things about this that bother me but you had a group of marketplaces that are in case studies of aggregation. You’ve coined it , and they took this fragmented supply, whether it’s OTAs, whether it’s brands and manufacturers around the world selling goods via e-commerce, whether it’s restaurants or drivers. Now, I think DoorDash and Uber are more insulated and they aggregate it and they’ve built direct relationships with the consumer and what we talked about earlier, they kind of would find their way there half the time going through Google or half the time going directly to an app. I think the models, again, whether it’s Gemini or ChatGPT—

*We’ll just use, with that caveat, we’ll just use ChatGPT as a stand-in.*

*MM:* ChatGPT. I think ChatGPT is going to wedge itself in there.

So if you’re starting in your pull experience, I just call it an informational pull, and you’re starting your journey with a query. I think ChatGPT is a big risk to your business because ChatGPT takes what historically would be these searches that would show you where things are, and now they’re telling you the knowledge behind it, and in that ecosystem of pull, it is perfectly monetized for what we can call the paradox of choice or this extended funnel. Amazon has talked about consumers clicking 14 products before making a purchase and when you throw ChatGPT in there, and we can talk about why I think the answers are better and the evidence I have behind it, I think that funnel is going to smash down.

The AI E-Commerce Experience

*Let’s talk about this, because this goes back to the first note that I referenced, E-commerce and Search, the Coming AI Impact and you mentioned the thesis here is that AI e-commerce experience is superior and you mentioned you got a lot of pushback on it, about people questioning about shifting consumer behavior. So you’ve mentioned this user experience angle a couple of times, walk me through your thesis and why you think that the user experience is better and why that’s going to actually drive a fundamental shift in consumer behavior.*

*MM:* Yeah, I would love to. And again, in my world, I have to bring data to the table and the joke is like, “If I can’t put it in an exhibit, I can’t write a report about it because nobody will read it”.

What we started to do is we took a couple different products and we ran them through the traditional funnel and we’ll go back to the first example I used, shoes for flat-footed runners. What I did to start the exercise was I did hours and hours of research reading literally podiatry magazine posts, and every single post about the best running shoes for flat feet, I organized them, I ranked them, so what shoes got first and second, and we came out with some clear winners. “Here are the one, two, and three best running shoes for people with flat feet”, so we know what the best answer is.

Now let’s put it in Google search, and what you found was the PLAs at the top, the carousel you’ll see a set of icons that are horrible for getting the right answer.

*So are those pure payment to get there, or is Google actually making determination of what’s the best answer?*

*MM:* Yeah, for the work we did, one of the six was of the top ranked running shoes and when you looked at the models, their slugging percentage was, I would say 60 to 80% of the time, what they showed you out of the five icons were the best running shoe. So if they had five, they’d get one bad one.

Now, that’s a good question people have pushed back, “Well, how can these people be at the top of the feed if they’re paying for it” and this inevitably boils down to a conversion game. Shouldn’t it really only be the best products? And in an ideal state, yes, but this is also an output of which websites have better conversion rates? Who has bigger marketing budgets? Who’s looking to build a brand at this specific time? No one knows a perfect answer for the weightings and outputs of Google Search. Well, there are people, but their emails have @google.com, not our email addresses.

*So why did Google’s results get like this, to the extent that you feel one out of six was a good answer? And you contrast the ChatGPT where four out of six are good answers. Is this a matter of, to your point, they’re measuring things like conversion factors, what actually goes through? Is it some people just paid more? Was this something that they can fix or is it that the money flowing in is too much that they can’t actually recommend four out of six because two, three and four might not pay them very much? What happened?*

So, it’s not like the Amazon Prime labeled all over it, and it’s just multichannel fulfillment, and for a long time, Walmart said, “You can’t use that, if you’re a third party merchant selling on our marketplace, you have to use our fulfillment network, or UPS or FedEx, but you can’t use the…” — basically, you can’t use Amazon multichannel fulfillment, you got to play within these rules.

I think it was in April of 2025, Walmart removed the multichannel fulfillment limitation. So now if you’re a Walmart and you’re plugging in your first party and third party inventory into ChatGPT, the whole thing about Amazon’s mode is that FBA business.

*I just want to make sure I understand this. By multichannel fulfillment, you mean that you can buy on Walmart and it’s delivered by Amazon or Walmart? Or Walmart will deliver for any product?*

*MM:* No. So, you can sell it on a Walmart marketplace. Now one of the Walmart rules is is that it can’t be delivered by a truck with Amazon labeling on it. You’ll see the Amazon Flex workers that drive around in cars with stuff, so who knows exactly? And if everybody is going to follow the rules here. But it’s just interesting because Walmart runs towards this new channel, and, in theory, the third party sellers on Walmart’s marketplace that would be presented in a ChatGPT answer have the ability to use a multichannel fulfillment service that is not Walmart’s and is not their own, and it brings that incredible distribution network to ChatGPT.

*Well, the thing with Walmart is — again, the whole Shopify angle and Etsy angle is super clear. As you mentioned, it completes that cycle from Facebook doing the pull side and now you have the push side for this long tail of products that are amazing. I used the example of this 3D-printed rack bit, that I never would have found otherwise, ChatGPT found it for me on Etsy and it was great, it was fantastic, that guy would have never found me otherwise even if he did advertising.*

*Walmart has the third party sellers, it has the long tail, but it also just has all your CPG goods and brands in general that might be on Shopify, but there’s just a lot of stuff that’s just Walmart-type stuff. A lot of that is Amazon-type stuff and is this in some respects the best thing to happen to Amazon, because it’s going to force them to give in sooner, and thus actually make sure they preserve the dominant position that they theoretically should enjoy?*

*MM:* Yeah, that’s a great point. Walmart joining probably forces Amazon’s hand sooner than they might have wanted to make this choice.

But we’ve also laid out, the data shows if Amazon plugged in tomorrow, they would be the most favored answer. All the competing companies would have the same problem that they did in legacy search and Amazon has offsets to this on-site ads risk, in theory. So if ads are 6%, 7% of GMV from the retail perspective, Amazon can just take up the take rate and the FBA fees to offset it. It won’t be perfectly linear, but they can pull some levers here, because the retailers and the brands will just become more dependent on Amazon.

*Your typical seller is paying Amazon like six different fees, so they can all sort of balance out.*

*MM:* Yes and it’s like, “Okay, fine, we’re going to have a conversational commerce fee of 5% to offset the lost ads”, and what are you going to do as a brand? You’re going to pay it, you’re going to have no choice with that, and maybe it actually turns out to be even a slightly lower fee than you were spending for your on-site ads business. This is not complete doom and gloom, they have levers they can pull.

I think Amazon should take their time in this with ChatGPT, because it’s important to underline that ChatGPT needs Amazon more than Amazon needs ChatGPT.

*Why?*

*MM:* If you’re ChatGPT and you’re trying to present an e-commerce offering to the consumer, you can’t do it without 50% of the market. Amazon’s half the e-commerce market, they have the world’s inventory and the world’s distribution network.

*Walmart makes it pretty big, Walmart’s catalog is pretty good, it’s much better than people realize. Walmart’s e-commerce experience is good, their tech stack is really good. I’ve been a Walmart bull for several years now. Why can’t that just replace it?*

*MM:* Oh, no one should sleep on Bentonville, they’re killers, so I don’t disagree with you about that at all. This is why that headline, I think, was very meaningful, because Amazon could have sat on the side — this is the prisoner’s dilemma playing out right in front of our eyes, it’s like who’s going to blink first? And for Walmart, you have more upside of going first.

For Amazon, it does present more risk and I think Amazon does have the luxury though, they can watch, they can let the product get a little bit better, they can see what the adoption looks like, because they know, all the data that I’ve put in all my reports, they have it internally, I’m sure that when they do turn it on, they’re going to steamroll everybody.

Amazon Grocery

*So I did want to get to one non-LLM point, I wrote about it this week, the most viral Article, I think, ever — well, there’s two. One was actually my first year when Microsoft bought Nokia, I was in Taiwan, so I had a time zone advantage, I wrote an Article saying , “This deal makes no sense”, my first real viral hit. The second one was Amazon buys Whole Foods , I think it was on a Thursday, and I immediately had my take and I’m like, “I’m going to sit on it”, and it went through the weekendand everyone wrote their theories, I come out on a Monday with my Article explaining it, bam, like a million views in a day or whatever it was.*

*My theory was, look, Amazon is struggling in grocery, they’ve been trying to crack this for ages, it’s obviously a critical commerce channel, because you go to the grocery store frequently and there’s other stuff you can buy when you’re there. The problem is you’re dealing with perishable goods and it’s just fundamentally different than everything else, it doesn’t fit in this paradigm. How do you develop a system so you’re not losing stuff through spoilage? You have this whole thing. And my point was well, basically, you’re buying a guaranteed customer that’s quite large, so if you remake the chain and one of your customers is Whole Foods, they can consume the excess so that you can get over your spoilage problems, and you can leverage the same network as a series of primitives to do everything else.*

*Great thesis, really fit in with the series I’ve been doing on Amazon, no evidence it has actually come to pass at all, I can’t see any evidence that Whole Foods is actually really — you could get a Whole Foods segment on Amazon.com searching, it’s always a huge delivery fee, it takes forever, it’s not great, so big L for me. What Amazon has announced now is the exact opposite and seems kind of obvious, which is we spent all this time and money building out same-day delivery, same-day delivery fundamentally kind of solves the perishable problem, you just deliver it very quickly, and it’s like we had to go the opposite direction. Number one, what’s your take on this? And number two, is it going to work? Did they finally figure it out?*

*MM:* Yeah. Grocery is the most fascinating category for Amazon.

*Yeah, it’s the white whale.*

*MM:* And e-commerce holistically, it’s the only retail category that Amazon has not just run everyone over, and it’s because it’s the only retail category where the people they are competing with have like a 100-year head start, Walmart 60-year head start, they built 4,000 stores.

I wasn’t always an Internet analyst, I covered a lot of different sectors, and there are these businesses where you have regional monopolies, compressed air companies, because once you start trying to ship it too far, the economics break down because it’s heavy, cement manufacturers, same thing. Grocery is kind of similar, it goes bad, it’s expensive to keep it cold, you need it close to the consumer for it to make economic sense. Doing it in big specialized fulfillment centers far away from the consumers does not necessarily work and there’s not a lot of evidence of that, and the margins are razor-thin.

Now, we’ve published this chart, where on the Y-axis, it’s e-commerce penetration, and then size, and you can see the smaller industries are all really high penetrated, and then way over to the right is grocery and what I’ll call consumerables, since it’s this $2 trillion category, with a low penetration rate. And then we’ve done a similar chart, where you show EBIT margins and penetration rates and it’s really similar, apparel and all these other industries, super penetrated, really high EBIT margins. And then, way over to the side, you have grocery, low penetration, really low margins.

So they have tried everything, and to the company’s credit, they’ve been really transparent. If you look back to the beginning, in 1999, I think it was, Amazon made an investment in a company called homegrocer.com , some $50 million investment. They’ve been trying grocery for a long time, it is just incredibly difficult, and they’ve tried a lot of different iterations, Whole Foods isn’t big enough footprint to make it work at scale.

So what we’ve seen with this most recent iteration is, very quietly, they put refrigerators — I’m oversimplifying, making this sound funny just for enjoyment purposes — quietly, they put refrigerators in their whole same-day fulfillment network in a thousand cities, and they’re going to 2,000 cities. Now, this is a better offering than they’ve had historically.

What we have written though is there is some big limitations to this, because what you want to do, there’s a couple of different types of grocery purchasing decisions. Instacart has its own issues, we think it’s subscale that’s a problem, when you’re competing against Amazon, Walmart, DoorDash and Uber, that’s a really big issue. But Instacart got high-single-digit millions of people’s full grocery basket, then you end up with like plus-hundred-dollar baskets, because it’s a marketplace and it’s giving you the whole offering that a grocer presents, which is 30,000 to 50,000 SKUs and the reason to get the whole basket is because people all have their own different needs. My son is allergic to eggs, I’m lactose intolerant, you need the long tail to fill a full request of a family for their weekly grocery.

This Amazon offering that they’ve put out today has a couple of thousand SKUs, it’s pretty good, you can get organic stuff that you need, it’s a very good top-off order. And Amazon talked about, I was at Groceryshop, it’s a a conference in Las Vegas, a couple of weeks ago, and went to a breakfast, the grocery person was talking, the average grocery user right now buys 14 times a month from them, the traditional US consumer went to the grocery store six times, this is incredible for purchasing frequency. You’re going to take away the reason that people have to go to the grocery store and what I’ve written about in the past, I actually think you put an exhibit in one of your notes about it , was how they’re eating CVS and Walgreens’ front-of-store alive. When they rolled out same-day — for some reason, toothpaste and shampoo always runs out when it’s completely empty and you’re like, “Oh no, I need this now”, well same-day has removed that emergency.

*They changed the mental calculus, where even if it’s a day, it’s like, “Okay, I will just go to Walgreens”, and at some point you realize if they say they’re going to deliver in six hours, the likelihood of you not going in six hours and then regretting not just ordering it when you needed it, it flips in your head, it’s like, “Just order it”.*

*MM:* And what you’ve seen with CVS and Walgreens is they’re closing stores, front-of-store sales are declining. They’re taking the same path to the graveyard that everybody else who was eaten alive by Amazon has for the last 20 years. Grocery is still this nut that is impossible for Amazon to crack.

*Basically, the issue is they don’t have infinite shelf space for grocery, that’s the challenge.*

*MM:* Yeah, I think this is the best product they’ve put out, but it’s incomplete. When I do it, where I live, I get offerings from — if I try to build a basket, I’ll get some stuff that they’re trying to deliver with Amazon Fresh and some stuff with same-day, and they make it look like it’s in the same basket, and then you go to checkout and you have different delivery times.

*Yep, it’s a very unpleasant experience.*

*MM:* No one wants that on a perishable. But the messaging from the company is this is — so there was this debate in the marketplace, is this inning nine? They’ve tried and tried again, and this is what they’re left with, and this is going to be their grocery offering, it’s going to be a top-up order, midweek, I need this type thing, or is this inning one of a new strategy, we’re going to, again, in over-simplistic terms, keep building bigger refrigerators in the same-day network, to where they build a Walmart on the corner of your town, just with no windows and you don’t realize it? If they’re telling the truth, I think this is a whole new ball game for them and this is the strategy that they’re going to take.

*Well, I think the issue is the fact that we talked so positively about Walmart earlier, the reason why Walmart could eventually come back and get there is ultimately because of grocery, and that is the advantage they’ve had, the one that they’ve built out the best, and it is just a fundamental advantage. Walmart started out assuming, “Oh, we have lots of stores, we have lots of logistics, we’re good at logistics, we could be good at e-commerce”, and they had to realize, “No, actually, that didn’t work”. They had to step back, completely rebuild e-commerce, but then incorporate the stores into it in a new way.*

*That’s probably why Amazon, I think there’s a very logical endpoint, which is, “We just have a small amount of SKUs and it’s really good and we’ll top you off, and consumer preferences will change and by the way, those give us more leverage over brands, because if we have a low number of SKUs, they have to pay to be a part of that”. Who’s going to be the yogurt of choice? But they won’t, they will keep pushing just because they know this is their weak spot for someone else to challenge them.*

*MM:* This is a collision course.

*Walmart being on ChatGPT is a manifestation of Amazon’s grocery weakness.*

*MM:* They don’t have a choice, this is where the Walmart and Amazon trains are barreling towards one another, and whenever I do my marketing trips and I’m talking to long-term investors, a lot of times, there’s the Walmart analyst sitting in the room because the Amazon guy is here, we’ve got to think about what Amazon and Walmart are doing, and people are like, “You should cover Walmart too”, and Amazon has to get this right, because like you said, Walmart has a killer grocery product, they’re delivering stuff in under an hour, under 30 minutes, this is their hook into the consumer, and Amazon simply has to be there with this offering or they’re going to be — and if you look at this, so we’ve built these baskets where we price-compare across all the grocers, we go through six of the biggest cities, suburban cities in the US, we go target all the different grocers, we’ve done it for a couple of years, and historically, Walmart, for the perishables, far and away the cheapest, no one can compete with that, and Amazon was in the middle of the road. So the second this announcement came out, we went on, built the exact basket we’ve been building, and it was priced perfectly with Walmart.

*That’s what Amazon is doing.*

*MM:* Yes, Instacart and DoorDash went down a lot the day that this news came out, and I’m looking at it, I’m like, “This looks like a clear shot at Walmart”, they’re going for Walmart prices and Walmart use cases, and the battle is only just really picking up.

*By the way, just as a point of conclusion, this is the other reason for Walmart to do the ChatGPT deal, the early adopters, probably less likely to be Walmart shoppers. This could be purely market expansionary for them in a major way. It really is, I think, a wind in their sails.*

*MM:* It’s their MO, they love finding things that are new use cases for not your typical Walmart shopper, like when they moved into the home furnishing category. If you do expert calls with former Walmart employees, they’ll tell you, “Well, there’s 30,000 furniture manufacturers, and we don’t need to keep the inventory in the store, and if someone’s looking for a coffee table or a desk, that might not be a typical Walmart consumer, this is our way to build a relationship with them”.

So totally, yeah. The average ChatGPT user right now, which in the US, over 25, is over 60 million and if you want to put this in perspective, that is more than there are Walmart app users and 60% of Amazon US users over 25 on the app. So in three years, ChatGPT has built more than half of the direct relationships that Amazon has built in 25 years, and more than Walmart, and they’ve been doing it for 60.

*Well, the other thing about Walmart is people in tech always think about Walmart doesn’t accept Apple Pay, and it’s because they don’t need to.*

*MM:* They don’t have to.

*The people are in Walmart, and Walmart gets to dictate what to do. So why would Walmart pay ChatGPT? They’re very good at thinking through and categorizing, where do we have an advantage, where are we in control and where are we not, and tuning their business accordingly.*

*MM:* People are going to have a lot of different type of leverage in their conversation with ChatGPT. So Shopify and their couple of hundred billion dollars of GMV, and Walmart hundreds of billions of dollars of GMV, and Amazon hundreds of billions. But Etsy, with like 10, and some of the smaller players, they’re going to be more at the mercy, and ChatGPT is going to know, “Hey, this is incremental demand for you”. So totally, yeah. Walmart doesn’t need to take Apple Pay, and they’re going to be able to play hard ball with ChatGPT, and so is Amazon.

*Very good. Michael Morton, fascinating conversation. Great to catch up. Let’s do it again sooner next time.*

*MM:* Ben, thank you, as always, a real pleasure.
