text:
An interview with MoffettNathanson's Michael Nathanson about Netflix's acquisition of Warner Bros. and the Hollywood end game.

An Emergency Interview with Michael Nathanson About Netflix's Acquisition of Warner Bros.

Tuesday, December 9, 2025

Today’s emergency Stratechery Interview is with Michael Nathanson, long-time Wall Street analyst and co-founder of MoffettNathanson . MoffettNathanson, which was founded in 2013, is a subscription-based research group primarily serving Wall Street, and Nathanson specializes in media and tech, with a specific focus on digital advertising. I previously interviewed Nathanson in March 2025 , December 2023 , January 2023 , and June 2022 .

This interview was recorded on Sunday evening, before I wrote Netflix and the Hollywood End Game ; Nathanson and I have debated Netflix for years (although Nathanson no longer covers the stock), and I wanted to discuss the acquisition of Warner Bros. with him while I formulated what I wanted to write. That conversation is below.

In this interview we discuss what Netflix has done right to date, and why they are motivated to pay for a library. We review why Hollywood failed in the streaming wars, and the overall logic of the deal, and whether the deal will be derailed by regulatory concerns. At the end we do sneak in a little discussion of AI; Nathanson has been very bullish about Google since before it was consensus.

As I noted, this was an emergency interview that was recorded before Paramount announced their hostile bid for Warner Bros. (which Nathanson expected). In addition, there is a previously scheduled interview on the calendar for this Thursday as well.

As a reminder, all Stratechery content, including interviews, is available as a podcast; click the link at the top of this email to add Stratechery to your podcast player.

On to the Interview:

An Emergency Interview with Michael Nathanson About Netflix’s Acquisition of Warner Bros.

This interview is lightly edited for content and clarity.

*Topics:*

Netflix’s Execution ( #execution ) | Netflix’s Motivation ( #netflix-motivation ) | Why Hollywood Failed ( #hollywood-failed ) | The Logic of the Deal ( #logic-deal ) | The Streaming Market ( #streaming-market ) | Regulatory Questions ( #regulatory-questions ) | Google and AI ( #google-ai )

Netflix’s Execution

*Michael Nathanson, welcome back to Stratechery.*

*MN:* Thanks, Ben. Nice to be here.

*This is the fifth time you’ve come on to Stratechery, but it’s the first time that is an episode of the emergency variety. I decided that I needed your help in unpacking the Netflix-Warner Bros. deal . You said we had to do it because it was the culmination of so many of our conversations.*

*MN:* Yes.

*It might be a direct quote, it sounds like it’s a direct quote. Well, I went back to our old conversations and this is what you had to say, this is our conversation number one in the summer of 2022 . First you said that you were skeptical about the relationship between money spent on content and time spent on customers and I thought I had you nailed — look, Netflix is spending money on content right now. But point number two was you said there was real value in libraries. Point number three, you said you were skeptical about how well content travels which I’m not sure is pertinent here, maybe it is, maybe it’s not.*

*MN:* It is.

*How are you feeling about those takes a few years later in light of this deal?*

*MN:* I feel pretty good about those takes, man. It’s funny, at that point in 2022, Netflix was spending a ton of money on content. And if you go back, they hit the brakes, right, Ben? They hit the brakes on content spend.

*Yup. It’s been very level since.*

*MN:* Yeah, they started to get more library content. Basically, there was a writer’s strike , an actor strike and, all of a sudden, people started licensing them library content again and everything just took off for them. Margins exploded, engagement exploded, they added the ad tier, they clamped down password sharing, they played their hand perfectly from 2022 on, really perfectly.

*I was going to ask you, you’re not the Netflix stock analyst anymore.*

*MN:* No, no.

*Robert Fishman is so this is more of a celebratory tour, not stock analysis.*

*MN:* How about that? I got the stock wrong more than anything else.

*Well, I was going to say back then, you were on this stock. That conversation was fairly bearish about Netflix and their stock is up 5x since then.*

*MN:* I know, it’s freaking terrible for me. Luckily, I have other ideas.

*What did you get wrong about the company or how they surprised you? You just listed a bunch of things they did well but is there an overarching theme there?*

*MN:* I think what they did really well was they pivoted to a lower priced ad tier that didn’t cannibalize their existing subscriber base, they cut back on password sharing without angering their customer base and they’re able to basically deliver margins through just price increases and great cost control. They hit every button perfectly, it was a flawless execution of these critical elements. And very few companies pull that off, Ben, as you know, from observing all these companies. The ad tier, to me, was the biggest hit of all.

*Is there a bit here where one of your conclusions, you just dropped a piece a couple of minutes before this interview, I think in preparation for this interview.*

*MN:* Yup, yes.

*One of your lessons is, “Don’t look at what Netflix says, look at what they do and what they do is act like a media company”. Is it possible though that maybe the thing is they actually were more of a tech company than you thought? And what I mean by that is you look at business after business that people are skeptical about because they have huge losses and the reality is, those costs, at least in theory, do flatten out at some point because you have leverage on those costs with your massive customer base, you can steady state at $13 billion a year or whatever it might be?* *And maybe the story is as simple as that, they were able to steady state and keep the business going and, inevitably, margins exploded and that was that.*

*MN:* Yeah. For those that don’t watch us, I was vigorously nodding my head. I picked up coverage of the large cap Internet names in 2015, 2016 and I wish I had started on Internet and then done media, because the lesson in Internet is simply that. I learned enough from my mistakes at Netflix to not downgrade Meta at $80 a share in the third quarter of 2022. We defended Alphabet when people were railing about the ChatGPT fear. I think you’re totally right, I think they won because their platform was better and they understood how to use technology to build a better mousetrap and their competitors only knew how to make better content, they did not know how to leverage technology. You’re right, Ben, and that’s why, in the beginning, when you and I would have those debates, and I think it happened way before 2022, what I missed in the debate-

*Right. Our debates, it took us a long time to start recording them but we’ve been arguing about Netflix for years and years.*

*MN:* Exactly. And I’m like, “No, you have to spend more on content, you have to burn more on content”, and they didn’t partly it’s because they’ve leveraged licensed content really well. But you’re right, I think not coming at it from a tech vantage point was my biggest mistake in covering this stock and I wish I could have gone back and looked at the way we look at technology now. And that’s the lesson I learned more than anything else.

*(laughing) I wasn’t trying to make you feel bad right up front.*

*MN:* No, it’s cool. Look, you know what? I’m fortunate that our clients still want to talk to me even when I get things wrong so that’s life.

Netflix’s Motivation

*Well, you just wrote, to go back to the piece I mentioned that you just wrote, it’s entitled A Tale As Old As Time. What did you mean by that title?*

*MN:* Ah, tale as old as time. That, over my career, I’ve seen many cases, many mergers just like this. It was the birth of Time Warner was essentially this deal. It was Time Inc., owner of HBO, buying Warner Bros. for their library and their production capabilities, that was the beginning of Time Warner. Then you have Paramount, Showtime, you’ve had Turner Time Warner. We’ve seen this over and over again, people have to consolidate to get more access to libraries and production capabilities.

*Which of those is more important, the libraries or the production capabilities?*

*MN:* Libraries, because you and I would agree that Netflix was able to build this massive machine never having a library. They found production capabilities but they didn’t have a library and yet they built this amazing company.

But I think, and you had written this a couple weeks ago , that chart that they put in their investor relations earnings call that showed the flat lining of growth around a couple countries at Netflix, to me, not covering the name, I was always focused on slowing engagement growth as a problem and I think they’ll never acknowledge it because they never tell you these things. But I think, at the end of the day, slowing engagement growth is why they needed to get Warner’s and HBO’s libraries.

*Expand on that because I think this is probably the critical point. Because, at the end of the day, I think the ultimate bull case for Netflix is they don’t have to buy anyone, everyone just sells to them.*

*MN:* Right.

*Why did they need to buy in the end?*

*MN:* Because I think their fear was, if Paramount had gotten hold of Warner, Paramount would pull their content and Warner’s content from Netflix. If you look at, not one show from Warner drives Netflix engagement but, in total, they have Big Bang Theory when they had it, they have some CW shows, they have Friends around the world, different places, there’s enough stuff from Warner that helps drive the flywheel and losing that would’ve driven slowed down engagement and I think they’ve realized that.

And also, the idea of Pay-One movies and films, they’ve not had a great track record at their own original films, they just haven’t. And maybe they can go back to the old HBO model of Pay-One meaning the movies appear in theater for a limited amount of weeks then they go onto HBO and they drive value in terms of consumer value. I think they’ve realized that they needed to add more elements from Warner to drive their flywheel and they needed to keep it out of Paramount’s hands because, [Paramount Skydance CEO David] Ellison, at his heart is a technology, he’s a technologist, he really is. I think people underestimate the knowledge he has from a technology side. Obviously, his dad [Oracle CEO Larry Ellison] is legendary but I think David Ellison sees himself as a technology person and I think if I’m Netflix, I didn’t want that guy with his bank roll to get these assets.

*Okay. I want to come back to Paramount and David Ellison in a little bit, but this is where I think I was with you a bit, I was raking you over the coals, hanging you out to dry. But one of the things I always posited about why music was different than the video industry is because the power of the library and for most people, the vast majority of listening is to library content. The moment a album is released, it’s immediately part of the library and that was why the labels, ultimately, despite the fact they were the poster children for the disruption from the Internet via Napster and whatnot, ended up coming out, all things considered, I think, pretty well and still exert a fair amount of power over the Spotify’s and Apple’s of the world as it were. I think I underestimated the extent, to your point, that video library content matters and I think I wrote a mea culpa at one point about, okay, I underestimated Friends or just things like that.*

*MN:* Suits.

*Suits, yeah .*

*MN:* That they were having Suits. This was the biggest show in 2023, it was an 11-year-old show that cracked Netflix top 10 of all time.

*I’m curious about this because I think the Friends thing is it’s this cultural staple that people will just watch again and again and again and again and simply having that provides a massive amount of churn prevention and whatever it might be for a service. Suits though is the counter case and the optimistic case for this deal because Netflix made it back into a thing.*

*MN:* Yes.

*Suits was never Friends.*

*MN:* No, it wasn’t, you’re right. But Ben, isn’t that, financial math aside, you have to be optimistic that what they get on their hands from Warner will have real shelf life on Netflix’s platform, they’re going to drive engagement by getting all this content.

*Yup. I’m just thinking now they could drive entire — one of the things is what are they doing with Bill Simmons and Spotify and the podcast thing . Well, I suddenly now have a wishlist for a Sopranos re-release focused podcast, the whole thing around it. Let’s relive that one, that was a good one.*

*MN:* That was a good one. You know what? There are shows in HBO that Netflix’s core audience have never seen. Even Game of Thrones, it was the biggest show in the world but it wasn’t as big as Netflix’s shows. You can imagine Game of Thrones coming back on the home screen, Game of Thrones month or something.

*Yeah, because that’s the thing. All these shows that have huge cultural cachet, actually, the audiences are very small.*

*MN:* They’re not that big, they’re great. The thing is HBO, pound for pound, makes the best content and it blows me away. Even Succession, which is one of my favorite shows, it never was that big of a show. For people like me, it was the show but it was a coastal elite show, it wasn’t a worldwide smash for all it was.

Why Hollywood Failed

*You mentioned this combination of bringing HBO to Time Warner’s content being one of the original OG media merger deals that you were referring to. Why couldn’t that work for streaming? Why was HBO such a successful play before but not after?*

*MN:* Yes, that’s a great question and that’s an indictment on the people who ran Time Warner and HBO beforehand. The problem they had was they had existing distribution agreements with cable operators, cell operators and they had pricing terms that were pretty high, call it $10, $12 a month wholesale, they could not easily pull their content from those cable operators and offer a lower tier Netflix light package to go over the top. They needed to basically work distributor by distributor, year over year, pull back and change the licenses to their contracts.

They were making so much money and they optimized for profitability at HBO that the idea of going backwards and they also — you know what, Ben? They sold their shows internationally. So, they would make shows in the US and they would license into Sky in the UK, they would sell it for a dollar, two bucks a month in Asia Pacific, they never had a global footprint and they didn’t want to go global because they were, again, maximizing profitability.

And again, to your point about technologists and media companies, technologists don’t give a shit about short-term profitability, they’re like, “Let’s build the best consumer product possible”. But HBO was 25 years in at that point, they were maybe even 30 years in, they just didn’t have it inside themselves to rip up the model and the playbook. And in 2013, I think Netflix warned them they were coming at them but, “So what, okay, that’s fine, we’re not doing anything about our business”, and it was too late.

By 2016 when they sold themselves, it was just too late, they had let the opportunity slip and they sold themselves to AT&T which was not a good partner for that asset. I like Jason Kilar who ran it, I don’t know if he’d ever been in your podcast, he had the right vision but they didn’t have the balance sheet to take this on at that point.

*I think you’re a little hard on these people. That’s disruption, you can’t give up the profits that you have. The ironic thing is they felt like they needed to have a lower price for going over the top, they probably just got over the top for more money, maybe they could have went the way to higher prices all along and that might’ve helped solve the problem. But I think it speaks to the fact that just because a business model seems adjacent doesn’t mean it’s the same and, actually, it’s very, very difficult to move over from column A to column B.*

*MN:* Yeah. Well, it’s funny, Ben, I think — I’m a very transparent person. One of the things I got most wrong from a media analyst standpoint was I didn’t think Netflix would scale outside the US as well as it did because, covering media before Netflix, the only international businesses we ever saw out of the US companies were in the UK or Australia. They didn’t really build businesses outside of English language secondary markets.

So I think if you’re [Former Time Warner CEO] Jeff Bewkes, [Former HBO CEO] Richard Plepler, anyone in media saying, “Okay, great, we’re going to have to go through France and Germany and Thailand and South Korea”, that’s not going to work, it hasn’t worked for us ever. So I think I give Netflix a ton of credit for actually finding opportunities in these markets that appeared to be disinterested in US content. And that was, I think, if you look at this from a classic media standpoint, that was something that we didn’t estimate properly in the business model.

*I completely agree, I think that that’s a good point. And I think it’s fairly understandable, I think you should stop being so mean to yourself and everybody else.*

The Logic of the Deal

*Well, to go back to this overall, I think if you zoom out, you were talking about the logic of the deal, I agree it’s fairly obvious. I think there’s a natural state of affairs for general entertainment that there’s only one or a limited number of points of distribution. That used to be the cable bundle, the cable bundle came about for accidental geographic reasons , but it was a very logical way to organize content. Of course, everyone then blew it up, but the results were never going to be stable. You had all these entertainment companies who seemed to have no idea that content was not king, sustainable customer acquisition and retention was, and given that consolidation was inevitable, well, of course it’s going to end up at Netflix. Where else could it end up?*

*MN:* Right, exactly. But the funny thing is, Ben, when you go back to other businesses in the development cycle, there’s usually content acquisitions in the beginning of a new platform distribution model. Turner was building out TBS and TNT, he merged with Warner Bros , he bought MGM . Usually you don’t see this acquisition from the leader to buy a library that’s late in their build out, they’ve won already, but the fact is they’re going to keep on winning by getting these assets under their control. The gap between them, well, it’s just going to widen going forward.

*I think as someone who’s posited a Theory about this sort of virtuous cycle that results when you have the largest audience, you have the best customer acquisition strategy, your churn is mitigated. You get advantages in acquiring supply, which makes your offering that much more attractive, and you get a virtuous cycle going on. I think a lot of listeners going at me for years about whether Netflix is or is not an Aggregator, I guess you could argue they’re paying $80 billion, it’s not like they’re getting it for free.*

*MN:* Exactly. Yeah. They’re not YouTube in that sense, right?

*Right. But they also have $80 billion with an unsecured bridge loan apparently , to make the purchase.*

*MN:* Exactly. Yeah, it’s crazy. So you were hitting on the things I wrote, my hot takes, the other thing is it’s basically, when I look at the world, so the media guys clearly lost, Netflix clearly won, but I think these fairy tales don’t always come true. Look at Fox/Disney . That seemed like the same idea six, seven years ago and this way, I think you’ve learned as a media analyst now that you’ve become, there’s these relationships inside these industries that are not as normalized as you think. There’s egos and there’s agreements and it’s not that easy to get directors to want to work with you if they don’t think you’re going to put their movies in your theater or the back end’s going to disappear on a TV production company that’s not going to want to make shows for you, that’s going to take some time.

*Isn’t it all risk for Netflix that no one trusts them that they’re going to have theatrical releases or that they’re going to pay back ends?*

*MN:* Yeah, I know. And that’s to me what I’ve learned again, Robert Fishman, if he was on this podcast, we go back to our Disney/Fox model from the merger seven years ago, very little of what we assumed in that model actually played out. Fox was subsumed by Disney and all the Fox businesses that we thought we would model in terms of profit streams, we can’t find them anymore. It’s just been put into Disney and Disney Plus and Hulu and I think we’ll look back three or four years from now and say, “Wow, things didn’t work out as these Wall Street analysts predicted”, because relationships are very, very fluid in terms of how things get done.

*So is there a story here where this deal actually kind of goes sideways? We’ll get to the regulatory questions in a little bit, but assuming it goes through, actually Netflix does get a good library, but HBO’s not HBO anymore because it’s owned by Netflix quite literally.*

*MN:* Yeah, exactly. The guys who make the shows HBO could be picked off by another company. Casey Bloys , who runs HBO, consistently high hit rate, that’s a person that I would target to try to hire. The people who are on Warner Bros. TV, I’d try to hire them too. I’d make sure that the best directors are under my contract at Universal and not at Warner, I think that the industry itself is going to now go on attack mode and try to save what it can out of the status quo. If I was a competitor, I would pluck off whoever I can to come join me before this thing gets going.

*So how does this not become ultimately — how does Netflix get its full worth from this? Because the Warner Bros. revenue model includes selling stuff to TV, it includes theatrical releases. If they’re going to stick with their model and trim all this down, or is this to your point that you think they might adopt some aspect of these model? Isn’t their revenue destruction implicit in Netflix specifically buying this asset?*

*MN:* Yes. And let me ask you a question, Ben. Walt Disney’s cashflow in 2019, 2018 before it bought Fox, what year did Disney’s cashflow get back to where it was pre-Fox, pre-COVID? So 2018, call it $10 billion of cashflow. What year did it get back to where it was pre COVID, pre-Fox, pre-streaming?

*It hasn’t?*

*MN:* 2025. It took seven years.

*Oh, I see. I was almost there.*

*MN:* You almost did. But I guess my point is that they’ll slow down their cost of content spend, they’ll raise prices, but that the content opportunity longer term will be interesting to watch because I think people will look to go someplace else as time goes on.

*You mean by the directors and then the content creators.*

*MN:* Yeah. The talent’s going to find — if I’m an agent, the agents have historically been very distrustful of Netflix, and they’ll try to find someplace else to go to get a back end.

*So what’s the other place to go?*

*MN:* Universal and what happens with Paramount or Sony. Sony always looks in this world as a hero because they avoided all this carnage and kept themselves very pure, I love that story.

*My personal heroes, I know. I’ve been in Sony’s corner all along .*

*MN:* I know.

*Why do you think Warner Bros. chose Netflix instead of Paramount? Is this the moment of sanity in the industry we’ve all been waiting for? I mean, it kind of feels like Paramount is the last of the insane or do they still have company?*

*MN:* Yeah, Robert covers Paramount, but I would say to you, Paramount on their own scares me. They don’t have the girth to compete here, I think they went with Netflix because they thought it was a much better outcome in the long run for their company, and they didn’t trust these guys at Paramount to actually come in with the cash. I don’t know.

But the question I have, and I asked Robert, we’ll talk about this in our — it doesn’t feel like this is the end of the story. If I’m Paramount, why wouldn’t I come back? I would feel you’ve got to come back and just outbid Netflix because what’s their story? What’s their hand look like without this asset?

*Well, I don’t understand Paramount generally. I guess this is the question about David Ellison and what they’re doing. It feels like a rich tech kid with a lot of money who wants to build a media company, but they seem like the weakest of the streamers or I’m not sure what they actually have going on that gives them — yes, they and Peacock and whoever else and Time Warner should probably all be together, but is there any justification here for their sudden prominence in the industry other than you have a guy that’s willing to spend money?*

*MN:* I think you have CBS, you’ve got the top network in the country, you’ve got access to live sports that sports hand’s pretty good. Paramount Plus, even though people may not realize it, that Taylor Sheridan content has done really well for them .

*They just lost him .*

*MN:* They lost Taylor. I know, exactly. But I think you take CBS and sports and you go from there, their studio needs a lot of help. So under the Redstones, they’ve under-invested in studio, he’s going to try to fix that. If you want to be mean, I really ripped the Redstone family up too for terrible strategy for 20 years. But you know what? The people I’ve talked to about David Ellison really think he understands content creation and technology and he has a vision for what this industry needs to do and he’s got money behind him that’s smart money.

The Streaming Market

*Well, let’s think about the regulatory question. What is Netflix’s market?*

*MN:* Paid premium streaming. I don’t think you could say it’s YouTube, do you? Or it’s got to be paid premium streaming, it has to be. I would not say it’s all time spent in media, that would not be the right way to think about it.

*Why not?*

*MN:* Because at the end of the day, their combination of premium content, content library, better delivery system will lead to separation between them and everyone else. And this field’s got to accelerate their ability to take price in the market and I just think you’ve got free over here and free is becoming more and more short form or just AI-delivered and because it’s free, I don’t think it competes. Well, I’m backing up. I’m rethinking this as I answer the question because you are going to be, “Michael, they compete with a free product, what’s the big deal?”.

*Here’s the problem. There is one scarce resource in the world, that resource is customer attention . I mean, there’s a reason why Netflix doesn’t talk about any other streamers, they talk about YouTube.*

*MN:* YouTube and sleep.

*Yes. And I guess I could, okay fine — if you want to, now, I think it’s actually legitimate to say they compete with TikTok, but if you want to not go so far and say, okay, they compete for TV, it’s hard not to see how linear TV, YouTube, and these other services are in their market limiting it to the definition of their business model. That’s tactics, that’s not a strategy.*

*MN:* No, you’re right, and I’m walking back, you should be happy, I should have done this in 2015. I’m walking back my hot take, and I agree with you, Ben, that the right way to think about it is you’re competing with all these businesses around the world serving video and you’ve chosen a model that’s actually going to be harder to defend because you’re charging money for content that’s becoming better and better free. The quality of free content’s only getting better, the delivery system’s only getting better, personalization is getting better, good luck trying to run that into the future against these guys.

*Well, so isn’t that the bit where actually Hollywood should be hailing and cheering for Netflix as their champion because at least someone’s charging for content?*

*MN:* Yes, I think that’s right. But they just worry about the number of buyers, they just worry about the number of buyers in any auction. They just lost. Warner, to their credit was always seen as the independent, it really was Sony before Sony, they were the arms dealer to the world, and they still attracted a ton of great content because of that.

*Yeah. This is the part I’m having a hard time parsing, where I wanted to talk to you because I think if you look at the overall arc of entertainment, the impact of the Internet, which is really this story, it’s the dramatic expansion of the plane of competition, in this view, this is an obvious move, it makes sense for everyone, it’s probably good for consumers, it’s good for Netflix, it’s good for Hollywood, it’s good for all of them. The problem is no one thinks that, for one, they don’t think that for a lot of very good reasons. And I think my concern for Netflix is this feels too soon. The end game is them owning and controlling everything, but I don’t know that everyone is aware we’re in the end game.*

*MN:* Right, right. I agree with you. But this may push the end game closer. This may make the end game one or two years away.

*Right. Well, yeah, this is sort of kicking it off. It’s going to be a question of how much of a reaction there is. The truth is, say talent doesn’t want to go to Netflix. Where are they going to go? Disney?*

*MN:* Exactly. No, they’re not going to do it because Disney is not going to, they’re going to be very disciplined at Disney, so you’re going to go to Universal or Paramount or Sony and then the problem is you’ll have under-scaled streaming assets, so no one’s going to see my content if I put it on Peacock. It’s like it won’t be renewed because there’s no audience there in years two and three, so it’s a problem.

*What’s going to happen to Peacock?*

*MN:* Peacock and Paramount have to figure this out. You need consolidation, I agree with you, I always thought it’d be three, there’d be some combination of Warner, Paramount and Peacock. Now you need a combination of two, right? You do.

*Well, how many streamers do you think there are by the end of this? Paid premium streamers as it were?*

*MN:* Four, I think. Does Amazon Prime count?

*Yes.*

*MN:* Yeah. So Amazon Prime, Disney, which Disney will be an amalgamation of all their Disney products into one — I’ve always said I don’t want three Disney apps, I want one place.

*Which they’re finally getting to?*

*MN:* Yeah. Netflix, of course, and then whoever comes emerging out of this, the next deal, if there was a next deal, Paramount or Peacock, and that’s where we are. We have four, we have four broadcast networks.

*This is another way to get to your article. Shouldn’t the fourth have been Hulu?*

*MN:* Oh my gosh. Well, I thought you didn’t want to be mean!

Can I go back for a second? Disney outbid Comcast for Fox and gain control of Hulu — remember it was two-thirds Disney, one-third Comcast. At that point, [Comcast CEO] Brian Roberts should have gone and made peace with Bob Iger and said, “Look, Bob, I know we’ve not been great together, but we need to basically come together and make Hulu global and keep Hulu straight, get a strong outset”. Instead, he pulled his content, he launched Peacock, and Hulu is a little bit weaker for it, and Peacock is not stronger for being on their own. Yeah, it’s a story, Ben, of it’s hard for these guys to work together and build assets in committee, that’s another take we’ve realized over the decade, these things don’t work in committee, they just don’t.

*Yep. Well, this is where Brian Roberts and Bob Iger were actually the best possible people for each other. When Brian Roberts was running a distribution company and Bob Iger was running a content company. Once they got into each other’s business, then all the problems started.*

*MN:* Yeah, exactly. That’s totally right, it didn’t have to be this way.

*The problem is that old structure, that old structure entailed them arguing all the time because they were arguing over rates, arguing over all these agreements, but that was actually the best possible thing for them because it held them both in their place and they could maximize that.*

*MN:* Exactly. This goes back a long time, but Jeff Bewkes, to his credit, wanted to build something called TV Everywhere, which was the idea that if you want to watch Friends on demand, you can go to your Xfinity box and watch it on demand or go to Time Warner Cable, but they couldn’t get all the rights together and they couldn’t get their cable operators to work with them. And they had an idea to build an on-demand product 15 years ago, but they just couldn’t get the industry to work together on it. That was the attempt to try to stop Netflix from finding value in on demand licenses.

*Well, this is the miracle of cable is cable is downstream of remote cities who couldn’t get a broadcast putting up poles, you literally had community access TV, they could get access to TV via community project. And obviously, Comcast most famously rolled all these up. Time Warner Cable rolled these all up, etc., Charter sort of, etc., etc. I always thought this has been very instructive where the only way they got to one of the most amazing businesses of all time was literally by having no other choice, and that was actually a precursor of being pessimistic for all these companies in the Internet era because the Internet gives you infinite choice and that was actually the worst possible thing for all these companies.*

*MN:* Yes, for the other half of their business. For the video side, not good. The data, it’s a good thing, but there is leveraged the video and data. So it was half-and-half.

*Yeah, that’s not the kind of company they are, and the problem is there’s one other thing that can force you into the structure you should be in, which is money and you don’t have enough of it and that’s sort of where we’re ending up at.*

*MN:* Yeah. No, it’s interesting. I mean, you should have Craig [Moffett] on to talk about Comcast because I don’t want to opine on his company, but I’ll say this, they had every advantage. They’re in the most homes, they owned NBC, they had a piece in Hulu, they owned Sky. They had an ability to actually make a real impact more broadly, and it feels like they haven’t done that.

*I think that’s the other lesson, is there’s lots of things that look like advantages that actually really aren’t, they’re just sort of nice to have. If they’re not aligned with the core of the company, then it’s sort of moot.*

*MN:* Yeah. The other take is, you know what, it’s your point about technologies. You need a founder, you need a committed vision, you need just something about technology companies and they just understand what they’re driving towards and they get it done in a way that media companies are not structured to do it. To your point, maybe it’s just too many agreements, maybe it’s too many status quo arrangements.

*Well, I think Sony has played their hand right, why have they figured it out?*

*MN:* They figured it out because they were smart, because I think they realized they couldn’t be the seventh streaming company in the business, they also don’t have networks to defend. Having a network to defend, cable networks, you were kind of forced into, “Now what am I going to do? I’m losing subscribers, what am I going to do?”, “Well, I’m going to build a streaming business, I’m going to undercut my pricing to find subscribers”, and the whole thing started falling apart.

*I think that’s actually a really important insight, is they could see the market rationally because they didn’t have something to lose.*

*MN:* Exactly. And then let’s give Fox credit for selling the studio and everything else to Disney and it’s sticking with sports and news and becoming a live broadcast company. They’ve had a great success doing it, and that’s been something that we always called out, they were smart the entire time.

*So did you ever watch KPop Demon Hunters , by the way?*

*MN:* I did not, I apologize, you should know my age.

*I thought you were going to watch in the plane, or something!*

*MN:* You should know my age and my kids’ ages, we’re post-KPop in my home, unfortunately.

*I mean, the Netflix — you haven’t watched the movie, so you’re not biased by the movie, there is the great ongoing debate, would KPop Demon Hunters be a success with or without Netflix? Had it just gone to theaters first like a normal release?*

*MN:* You know I agree with you, that’s your take, I agree with you 100%, it never would’ve been what it was without Netflix, it would’ve come and gone on a hot weekend, that’s what would’ve happened.

*Do you think that influenced Netflix’s thinking for this deal?*

*MN:* Without a doubt. Don’t you think? We can take a show you barely heard of and make it into a success after three weeks on the charts — yeah, I totally think so. But also Ben, we don’t have to spend as much money as we once had to spend to compete, the cost to compete is coming down and will come down as time goes on, margins will go up higher and higher because of their cost of content being controlled right now.

*Well, I mentioned before the name of this game is customer acquisition and churn mitigation and that is the number one lesson that I think Hollywood did not know, did not understand, it’s something that tech knows intimately, it’s Facebook and Google. You know it now sort of from the other side and yeah, to this point, even if they do lose talent, even if they do have trouble because people don’t trust them as far as theatrical distribution or backend, their ability, the way to overcome that is to prove again and again that you think you made something great. Do you want it to be KPop Demon Hunters, or do you want it to be whatever riff raff just ran on Peacock last week?*

*MN:* (laughing) It’s true. Right, exactly. And by the way, there’ll be a second and third. Don’t you want to be part of the second and third version of that? Don’t you want to be known for the guy who made that show? I agree with you completely. Again, I have my doubts about what people have in their models on the acquisition side for Warner, but I don’t have any doubt that this is classic media that’s going to result in a better outcome for Netflix, the platform. It really will.

*I think the other takeaway for Netflix from KPop Demon Hunters is the market’s view is I can’t believe Sony gave all this to — or a lot of people in the industry’s views , I can’t believe Sony gave all this to Netflix. Netflix’s view is, “I can’t believe we don’t own it all”.*

*MN:* Yeah, exactly.

*“Because we are responsible, we did this”, I think that’s their great regret with Formula One . It’s like, “We made this sport and we actually didn’t own the upside”.*

*MN:* I agree. Another hot take is, I was surprised that Apple, a name that you talk about a lot, didn’t show up. I’m like, “Where are we going? Where are we going guys?” — you’ve got, I think, 2% of streaming viewing share. They have great content, but they don’t have an audience, so they miss their opportunity here, they really did.

*They’re seeking to gather up all the talent that’s fleeing Warner Brothers, give them carte blanche?*

*MN:* Yeah but to your point, if your churn is 5x what Netflix’s is, and you can’t raise prices and you don’t have a customer acquisition funnel, it’s great you’ve got great content, which they do, but no one’s got to know about it, that’s the challenge. But I kind of feel like, and going back to your reading of my work or comments three or four years ago, that second point about libraries, I think people don’t realize in Silicon Valley the value of owning recurring libraries. I really don’t.

*Well, tell me more.*

*MN:* Because I think people always think we need the iPhone 17 Air, we need to keep innovating. And look, sometimes people just want to come home from a hard day at work, put on Friends or Seinfeld, sit back with a beer and laugh and watch something they’ve watched 30 times. I just think that no one is running the old version of Windows, we don’t do that, we just want the newest latest thing.

*Well, I think YouTube, this is sort of the way back in the day, we talked about Netflix competing with HBO, now it’s like Netflix competing with YouTube and this is probably a critical point. YouTube is so predicated on the new and the thing you talk to YouTube creators and the reason they burn out is they just have to keep producing new content and they feel like if they take even a week off that their numbers start to go down and those numbers are tied to ads being shown, which is how they make their money. And it is a rat wheel, hamster wheel, whatever it might be.*

*MN:* It’s not good.

*Yeah, this is Netflix, library is the opposite, this is the perhaps savior of professional content, which is it ideally retains its value. And this was a point that, again, was Netflix going to actually have — that was one of the theories for Netflix is their marginal cost, as the marginal cost to acquire customers increases. The way you do that is the marginal value of your library is increasing at the same time, but is this sort of just straight up buying of increase in the value of the library outpace all the Netflix Originals since they started?*

*MN:* I think it does, Ben, I do. With Stranger Things getting off the air later this month, that’s the one example of a true franchise, multi-year franchise, but it’s coming to an end. Think what they get in DC Comics or Harry Potter or all the Warner TV shows, I think they knew in their hearts of hearts, and again, they’ll never tell us because whatever Netflix tells us, you ignore, you wait for their actions to actually show you the ultimate truth, but have to believe they’re worried about engagement longer term, I have to believe that, and this shores it up.

Because to your point, finding the next great show, this is always my worry back in 2015 to 2020 that it’s much harder to create hits than you think, a lot of it is randomness, you need more shots on goal. But here you’ve reduced your shots on goal need because you’ve got a chunk of content that’s just going to keep you happy half the time and now my need to fill the other half is going to be lessened.

*And to the extent we resuscitate or make things popular, we’re going to internalize the upside instead of pulling up Suits and we have to pay 5x the price down the road.*

*MN:* Yeah. We’ve got to pay Meghan Markle and new Suits comes out and we built Suits into a big thing and now it’s available on Peacock for new Suits.

*Yep. I think that is sort of the logic of why buy — that’s always the question in M&A. Why buy if you could just make a deal? Well, if you are uniquely capable of increasing the value of the asset, then you need to own the asset.*

*MN:* And if you think to your “Why now?”, if you think Paramount with Ellison and this asset becomes a challenger in a way they weren’t before, you do this. You go on aggressively and take it out of their hands.

Regulatory Questions

*Is this going to be challenged by the DOJ? I’m not holding you to it.*

*MN:* Yeah. One of the things Craig and I have learned, the whole firm has learned, the past year is that it’s such a transactional government that it’s just really hard to diagnose this. It was weird, what, six, seven years ago that Trump’s DOJ challenged AT&T/Time Warner, it took two years to go through court, that was a terrible decision, but they did it.

Will it be challenged? I think everything is a negotiation. I would not be surprised if it should be challenged because it’s a transaction here and Ellison is going to want to not give up. I think he’s going to keep going. We have a very dim view of the current state of US regulatory, I think I don’t want to put you on the spot, but as Wall Street analysts, we throw up our hands here.

*Well, it’s the uncertainty, none of us like uncertainty. That’s very frustrating.*

*MN:* Yeah. And precedent, right? It’s a new precedent every day. It’s wild if you would’ve told me just to pivot for one second that the tech bros would be the most favored nation status in this Trump administration, I didn’t see that coming, it took a whole inauguration to prove it.

*Look man, when are you going to learn? Don’t bet against us!*

*MN:* (laughing) Exactly. Data centers and AI regulation going away, it’s pretty amazing, it really is.

*Well, to that point, how much of the calculation in Netflix’s thought process is worst case scenario, this gets challenged, we go to court, it’s a two, three-year process, we lose, $5 billion is a small price to pay to basically make sure no one gets this and also that it dies on the vine?*

*MN:* I’d say that’s 10% maybe at most. I think they said, “Look, we should buy this, it makes sense for us, keep it out of Ellison’s hands, let’s go”. I think they think, if I’m reading the Bloomberg story that came out tonight , Sarandos and Trump have spent time together, I think they think it’s rubber-stamped approved. I think they went into it thinking, “Oh yeah, this is going to be done deal because Ted and Trump have hung out together”.

*Who knows, to your point, it’s hard to say.*

*MN:* Exactly. Who the heck knows?

*Would that be worth $5 billion to them?*

*MN:* Nah, to have this get weaker and weaker?

*Well, also for no one else to own it.*

*MN:* No one else. I mean, basically block it forever?

*Well, block it for the next three, four years by the time which everyone else might be out of business.*

*MN:* Yeah. But truth be told, core company’s going to get worse, licensed content will only continue to be a thing, they’re going to keep on licensing content, core company’s going to keep weakening. Subscriber growth will slow at all these non-Netflix businesses. Yeah, it’s probably a good way to just get what you want another way, which is we’re going to get more and more content licensed to us.

*Should Hollywood be concerned that Netflix is going to actually reduce the amount of licensing they do after this deal?*

*MN:* Yes, I think Hollywood’s going to be concerned, there’s only two companies left, I’ve done a lot of work in this. The only two companies left that don’t license their content to third parties is Apple and Netflix. There was a time like four years ago that we debated, “Would everyone just internalize their content and not offer second or third windows?”, that was a debate. Now that debate’s over, the only two people who’ve not done that are Apple and Netflix. So I think people are going to say, “Look, you’ve shown us by history that you don’t have third party, you don’t do backend deals with third party windows, that’s a problem for our profitability going forward”, it really is.

*But are they also worried that Netflix is just going to spend less to license their content?*

*MN:* Oh, without a doubt. Yeah, totally. If you were able to get agents and managers and the best talent in a room and a bar to talk honestly with them, they would tell you how much they hate this deal, they really would. They hate this deal.

*How are you feeling about Disney these days?*

*MN:* It’s Robert’s company, I’m looking forward to seeing who comes in next to run Disney, I really am looking forward to seeing who comes next.

*Are you looking forward to seeing the next predecessor to Bob Iger?*

*MN:* Yeah, I am. I’m looking forward to seeing — Disney’s parks business has just been incredible at how well they run that business, it’s amazing. Well, this is our whole point about live. Going further, there’s a report that Warner wants to build a DC theme park. So if you imagine under Netflix’s control, maybe they start building more theme parks, competing with Universal, who knows? The idea of live, in person, Ben, when we talk about a lot, you and I, I just think that value is going sky-high, and that’s what Disney’s done a great job on.

*Well, is this why you think Netflix is getting into live?*

*MN:* Yeah, without a doubt. The Netflix House in Philadelphia , yeah, they have a Broadway show. They need to reach consumers in the flesh, touch consumers personally.

*Do you think that they will actually get more seriously into theatrical after this deal?*

*MN:* No. I think they’ll do it for two years, they’ll have a couple windows, “Hey, we’re doing a three-week run of a movie”. No, they’re paying lip service to that, and they will not say that. They’ll be like, “We want to support the people at Warner. I want to keep windows alive and we love theaters and we think they’re important”, and then they won’t do that as time goes on.

*Why? Aren’t Windows good? You can make more money on your content more often.*

*MN:* Well, trust me, again, the idiot Nathanson’s been writing about this for a decade about film windows are actually a good thing.

*Right. But you put that in your article is that Netflix does change. They don’t tell you they’re going to change, but they do change, they have sports rights now.*

*MN:* Yeah, exactly, they have advertising.

*They said, “We build, we don’t buy”, they just announced $80 billion purchase. Why not? It’s bigger opportunity to make money. You preserve your talent relationships, it’s free marketing for your streaming service. To your point about the Warner Bros./HBO strategy back in the day. I’m not so sure, I think it’s possible they actually do, again, they might be serious about this.*

*MN:* Why not? By the way, my tale is old as time, you know what that’s from? That line?

*I feel like I should know this.*

*MN:* Oh, come on. Beauty and the Beast!

*Oh, yes.*

*MN:* The Disney Beauty and the Beast. I think Disney has the right strategy, so do Warner, you need to support film windows, they make movies more valuable to consumers in streaming land, they build buzz, they build awareness. KPop is the anomaly, we get that, but that’s not normal.

*Yeah. I think they might do theaters.*

*MN:* Really?

*Yeah.*

*MN:* Well, they’re doing sports, they’re doing advertising.

*Exactly.*

*MN:* Who knows? They’re making original content now at Netflix, that’s amazing.

*There you go.*

*MN:* They said they never would.

*They don’t even do DVD’s anymore, I don’t know if you’ve heard about that.*

*MN:* Exactly. Exactly.

Google and AI

*Has Google won ? Is OpenAI dead ? You are the Google guy now.*

*MN:* Oh, man. I love reading your stuff every morning on Google. I mean, we were bullish over the summer. Again, what we didn’t appreciate, we appreciated, but didn’t have the evidence of their chip opportunity, their ability to basically take all the investments that they’ve made in infrastructure, you see it paying off and I think that’s been the last leg of the stock is a realization that these guys have a massive opportunity on the infrastructure side.

So the harder stock — Google is easy, Alphabet’s easy — Meta is now the one that feels like they need some work to do. They need some explaining to do over at Meta on the cost side. It feels like the market’s really turned on Meta and I know you’ve been writing about that as well , the risks that maybe Meta faces. That’s been a really interesting flip of pro-Google, anti-Meta in the past couple months.

*So first off, they clearly played the card over the summer that I think I called them out on, which is they’ve been stuffing ads in Instagram, unbelievable. But number two, what about this news that they might be making big cuts to the Metaverse ? That was always the hand they could play.*

*MN:* Exactly. And that’s why, again, the lesson learned, Ben, we didn’t downgrade the stock. Even after their last quarterly commentary about costs, they can have a year ahead of them where the margins contract by 400 basis points. If you do the math, their costs are going to grow 30% or so, which is crazy against revenues of 24, 25 — they need to cut costs, they have to cut costs if they want their stock to go up. And Zuckerberg’s a capitalist at the end of the day, that’s what we’ve learned over and over again, so I’m waiting to hear more about costs going forward, I really am.

*Right. So you think that not only is this news valid about these Metaverse cuts, it’s inevitable?*

*MN:* It’s the tip of the spear, they need to do more, they really do. I know how much you love the Orion glasses , but when am I going to get those in my living room, Ben? Years away.

*I’ve been critical of their whole Metaverse thing since 2013. So there’s a bit where you just have to accept that this is where the stuff’s going to be built. But yeah, I’ll write about it.*

*MN:* For the losses at Reality Labs, he could have bought Time Warner, he could have outbid Netflix for Warner Bros if it wasn’t for all the Reality Lab losses he put up. Think about that.

*(laughing) Yeah, I think I might still rather have Reality Labs, but it’s a close call. Well, yeah, we’ll see. Google — do you think they’re going to win the consumer market? That’s sort of the big question. The oddity of the AI market right now is every company seems misaligned to their most present market opportunity, I don’t know that enterprises are going to want — they’re going to be allergic to a world where they’re totally reliant on Google and consumers don’t care about that. Consumers are fine with the all in, integrated, does-it-all choice, and often that’s what wins. And there’s Gmail, there’s Chrome, there’s Search, the OG. Google’s not first, but they’re sort of irrepressible.*

*MN:* They got Maps. I think they have Maps over there, they have a good mapping product, exactly. It’s so funny, I keep reading your stuff. I’m like, I know you had Michael Morton on , why are we not getting ads at ChatGPT a year ago? What is up with their allergy to ads? And I want to be on this show with you when the ad launch happens, I don’t know when that’s going to be, but it seems insane that they’re not more pro ads given their business models.

*Well, the problem is the ads are going to suck and you need to introduce the ads that suck when you have a clear lead. So by the time you have your challenge-*

*MN:* Yeah, exactly.

*Yeah. I’m so tortured about them because I guess my defense is, yes, they had the big lead, they had the huge consumer market, but if you don’t have the business model, what’s it worth?*

*MN:* Yes.

*And maybe I should have been even — I expressed that last week, but maybe I should have been even clearer — look, if I’m not sure Google’s going to win, they’re almost certainly going to win. You have Netflix, I have Google.*

*MN:* I want to remind you about that going forward too.

*Fair enough, all right.*

*MN:* Thank you.

*Well, this is a good sort of capstone for you and me, for you specifically.*

*MN:* I know.

*What’s next? What are the next dominoes that you’re looking for?*

*MN:* Well, Mike Morton kind of teased them, it’s the open web, it’s on-site advertising, it’s kind of the open Internet as we know it. E-commerce, how it all fits together. So our next couple years can be focused on the downstream impact of LLM search on the open Internet, what does it mean? We’ve lived through disruption our entire careers, I’m looking forward to seeing what happens here, it feels like it’s coming.

*Are independent content producers going to be okay?*

*MN:* I hope so, Ben. We’re both doing okay, so that’s good. And that’s why we wanted to be on with you because I’m like, you know what? Honest conversation is valuable, and I really do think it’s valuable to have these conversations.

*All right. Well, I’m going to congratulate you on this deal, I feel like you’re the real winner here. So Michael Nathanson, congratulations on the Netflix deal and it is good talking to you.*

*MN:* God bless you, Ben. Thank you so much. Congrats on the Packers , by the way.

*Great win, great stuff. The Bears Still Suck! *

text:
The Trump administration has effectively unwound the Biden era chip controls by selling the H200 to China; I agree with the decision, which is a return to longstanding U.S. policy.

Trump Allows H200 Sales to China, The Sliding Scale, A Good Decision

Wednesday, December 10, 2025

On Thursday’s episode of Sharp Tech we discussed my angst about OpenAI and the looming Google threat, as well as Apple executive changes, Trainium 3, and Substack.

Then, on this week’s episode of Sharp China , Bill and Andrew discussed President Trump’s plan to let Nvidia sell H200 chips to China.

On to the Update:

Trump Allows H200 Sales to China

From Bloomberg :

President Donald Trump granted Nvidia Corp. permission to ship its H200 artificial intelligence chip to China in exchange for a 25% surcharge, a move that lets the world’s most valuable company potentially regain billions of dollars in lost business from a key global market. The decision was announced by Trump in a post on his Truth Social network, capping weeks of deliberations with advisers about whether to allow H200 exports to China. Trump said he informed Chinese President Xi Jinping about the move and that Xi had responded favorably. He added that shipments would only go to “approved customers,” and that chipmakers such as Intel Corp. and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. would also be eligible.

The move represents a victory for Nvidia in its push to get Trump and Congress to relax export controls that have kept the company from selling its AI chips to the world’s largest semiconductor arena. Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang has forged a close relationship with Trump since the November 2024 election and has used those ties to make his case that restrictions only boost Chinese domestic champions like Huawei Technologies Co.

At first glance, this seems in line with the Trump administration’s earlier reversal of its initial ban on the sale of H20 chips . That, however, was actually restoring the status quo the Trump administration inherited from the Biden administration.

To fully understand this decision, you actually have to go back to 2022 and the initial Biden chip ban. The key parameter the initial ban focused on was memory bandwidth; from a November 2022 Update (quoting an October 2022 Update ):

I don’t think it is a coincidence that the rules specify 600 Gb/s given the fact that Nvidia’s A100 chip has 600 Gb/s interconnects. I explained why this matters in a Daily Update :

Nvidia’s data center chips, like the current top-of-the-line A100 and upcoming H100, have the same architecture as its gaming chips (Ampere in the case of the A100 and 3000 line of gaming chips; Ada Lovelace in the case of the H100 and 4000 line of gaming chips); the biggest difference (beyond clock speed and the allocation of cores amongst shaders, tensors, etc.) is memory: data center chips not only have more of it, they also have much higher speed memory buses, both in terms of on-board memory and also interconnects for working with other chips. This, by extension, gets at the difference between training and inference: while inference (i.e. the application of machine learning models) can run on single GPUs, training (i.e. the creation of those models) is done on fleets of them; the training of AI models specifically appears to have been the primary target of the Biden administration.

As I further explained in that Update, maximizing compute is increasingly a matter of system design, not just chips; this is particularly important in terms of AI training, which is an “embarrassingly parallel” task: the speed of processing increases basically linearly with the amount of processors available, but the trick is keeping all of those processors busy, which is where the memory bandwidth comes in. In other words, the A800 chip, which is limited to 400 Gb/s interconnects, will operate as fast as the A100, but it will more likely be sitting idle more often because the interconnect is saturated moving data around.

The A800 I’m referring to was Nvidia’s response to the chip ban: the company quickly came out with a variation of the A100 chip that had lower chip-to-chip bandwidth, thus fitting into that particular iteration of export controls. The H20, then was the successor to the A800, but in the meantime, the Biden administration had released a new set of rules that not only restricted memory bandwidth but also placed limits on actual computational performance. In other words, the H20 was, relative to the H200, a worse chip than the A800 was relative to the A100.

The reason to retrace this history is that what the Trump administration is doing is basically unwinding the Biden chip controls almost completely. Of course the H200 can be used for inference; more critically, it was, until the release of the GB200, the go-to chip for training, thanks not only to its performance, but also because of the way tens of thousands of chips could be linked together in a coherent manner to handle the massive amount of data necessary to train large models.

Note that I say “almost completely”; before the Biden chip ban Chinese companies could buy the exact same chips as American companies. Today, however, American companies are buying GB200 chips, which are a significant leap forward from H200s; the implication of this policy is that China is allowed to be on the same technology curve as the U.S., but a generation (or two) behind.

The Sliding Scale

This, I would note, is not that extraordinary; it’s actually a return to the way the U.S. managed technological exports for decades, under what was known as the “Sliding Scale”. This paragraph from a Clinton administration fact sheet about Export Controls on Computers explains the concept succinctly:

Today’s announcement is President Clinton’s third revision to U.S. export control parameters since 1993. Today’s announcement reflects this Administration’s efforts to ensure effective controls on militarily sensitive technology while taking into account the increased availability of commodity products, such as servers and workstations, of which millions are manufactured and sold worldwide every year.

When controls were last revised in 1995, we knew computer technology would continue to advance rapidly — and that we would need to update control levels periodically. Accordingly, for the past year, the Administration has conducted a review of our computer export controls that took into account (1) the rapid advance of computing technology since 1995, (2) our security, nonproliferation and other national security interests, and (3) the need for a policy that would remain effective for at least six months.

The Administration’s computer export controls are designed to permit the government to calibrate control levels and licensing conditions depending upon the national security or proliferation risk posed at a specific destination, and to enhance U.S. national security and preserve the technological lead of the U.S. computer industrial base by ensuring controls on computer exports are effective and do not unnecessarily impede legitimate computer exports.

This fact sheet is one of many running across multiple administrations; the overarching goal has traditionally been to preserve U.S. dominance on the leading edge without creating the conditions for that dominance to be superceded by alternatives created elsewhere, which is not only a national security threat, but also reduces the competitiveness of U.S. firms by denying them the revenue that fuels R&D.

The best evidence that this framework is at play was this story from Bloomberg :

President Donald Trump decided to let Nvidia Corp. sell its H200 artificial intelligence chips to China after concluding the move carried a lower security risk because the company’s Chinese archrival, Huawei Technologies Co., already offers AI systems with comparable performance, according to a person familiar with the deliberations.

Administration officials who weighed whether to clear Nvidia’s H200 had considered multiple possible scenarios, factoring in the views of national security hawks in Washington, said the person. Options ranged from exporting zero AI chips to China to allowing exports of everything to flood the Chinese market and overwhelm Huawei. Ultimately the policy backed by Trump called for clearing H200s to China while holding back the latest Nvidia chips for American customers, the person said.

The move would give the US an 18-month advantage over China in terms of what AI chips customers in each market receive, with American buyers retaining exclusive access to the latest products, the person said. White House officials concluded that pushing the H200 into China would prod Chinese AI developers into building on the US tech ecosystem rather than turning to offerings from Huawei or other local chipmakers…

Underpinning the move was an assessment that Huawei can compete far more closely with Nvidia than the US has acknowledged. White House officials focused on a Huawei AI platform known as CloudMatrix 384 that relies on the company’s newer Ascend chips, the person said. Officials found that CloudMatrix 384 performed as well as a similar Nvidia system known as NVL72 that uses the US company’s most advanced Blackwell-design chips, according to the person, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive matters. Adding a sense of urgency, the person said, was a conclusion by US officials that Huawei would be capable in 2026 of producing a few million of its Ascend 910C accelerators, a chip designed specifically to compete with Nvidia’s product line. That compares with a US estimate, given in June, that the Shenzhen-based company would be able to make just 200,000 of the Ascend line this year.

I wrote about the CloudMatrix 384 in this Update — the same Update where I criticized the Trump administration for banning the H20 — and concluded:

The reality is that right now we are in the messy middle: we’re not actually stopping Huawei from building a system that is capable of doing large language model training (albeit inefficiently), but we are hurting the fortunes of a U.S. AI champion and limiting their long-term competitiveness. And, of course, we are incentivizing everyone in China, from the government to private enterprise, to ultimately remove the point of leverage that we can’t even wield properly.

We aren’t in the messy middle anymore! More generally, what this move signals is an overall decision to not treat AI like it’s something special — the Biden administration was, I thought, overly influenced by the doomer wing of AI — but rather like the latest iteration of American-developed technology.

A Good Decision

My position on this decision will not surprise long-time readers: I think it’s a good one.

First, as I laid out in AI Promise and Chip Precariousness , I think that the vast majority of discussions about the national security implications of AI are too narrow. Ban proponents limit their consideration to AI itself and its military applications, and imagine a world where the U.S. develops extraordinary capabilities that maintain and/or restore our military dominance generally, and over China specifically.

However, there are three big problems with this point of view.

* First, I think that one country having a massive military advantage results in an unstable equilibrium; to reach back to the Cold War and nuclear as an obvious analogy, mutually assured destruction actually ended up being much more stable.
* Second, while the U.S. did have such an enviable position after the dissolution of the Soviet Union, that technological advantage was married to a production advantage; today, however, it is China that has the production advantage, which I think would make the situation even more unstable.
* Third, U.S. AI capabilities are dependent on fabs in Taiwan, which are trivial for China to destroy , at massive cost to the entire world, particularly the United States.

If there were an alternate universe where the U.S. (1) had a clear technological edge in warfare and (2) had the best production capacity and (3) made the components that undergirded that edge in the United States, then that would be one thing — it would be the situation in the world circa 1990. But that simply isn’t the case, which I think should force considerably more modesty on those who dream of AI being a long-term military differentiator.

Second, I continue to think it is worth it and — despite the protestations of the Chinese government — possible to maintain the U.S.’s relative advantage and ecosystem dominance. Even if we grant that the CloudMatrix 384 has comparable performance to an Nvidia NVL72 server — which I’m not completely prepared to do, but will for purposes of this point — performance isn’t all that matters. Ecosystems are far more than just chips: they are software, and developers, and libraries, and APIs, all of which are dependent on the voluntary choices of the most talented people in the world to use. You can pass a law and pay out a subsidy to build a chip; you can’t use the same blunt tools to align the talent necessary to overcome the massive multi-faceted moat that Nvidia has built around their chips. This is a point that I think that people in technology get intuitively, and which completely escapes most people in Washington, who view everything as a commodity; the talent to actually build AI is anything but.

That, by extension, is why I don’t see the Trump administration’s offering as some sort of unilateral giveaway; rather, they are calling the Chinese government’s bluff. That’s how I read this story in the Financial Times :

Beijing is set to limit access to Nvidia’s advanced H200 chips despite Donald Trump’s decision to allow the export of the technology to China as it pushes to achieve self-sufficiency in semiconductor production. According to two people with knowledge of the matter, regulators in Beijing have been discussing ways to permit limited access to the H200, Nvidia’s second-best generation of artificial intelligence chips. Buyers would probably be required to go through an approval process, the people said, submitting requests to purchase the chips and explaining why domestic providers were unable to meet their needs. The people added that no final decision had been made yet.

China has limited access to H20 chips, and you could spin this news as the country successfully holding the line until they got the real deal — and doing so successfully; note that the story doesn’t say the H200 will be banned on the China side. That, however, is why the H200 offer is an effective counteroffer: the real ecosystem payoff is in training, and there’s no question that the best Chinese talent is going to want to work with the H200, not the Huawei alternative. To that end, the choice facing China is continued progress on AI, or a multi-year pause and stringent import controls, which I’m skeptical will be effective. It was one thing to align the necessary ingredients for an indigenous AI ecosystem when the U.S. was doing you the favor of not selling you chips; it’s another thing entirely to make fetch happen on your own from the top down.
