text:
An interview with Ryan Jones about Flighty, my favorite iOS app, and how the App Store has evolved over the last 15 years.

An Interview with Ryan Jones About Flighty and Building Apps in 2025

Thursday, December 11, 2025

Today’s (normally scheduled) Stratechery Interview is with Flighty founder and CEO Ryan Jones . Jones builds my favorite iOS app: Flighty . The holidays are coming, and a lot of you will be traveling with winter conditions looming: the app you need is Flighty, which tracks your flights, gives updates before the airlines, and tracks your history.

More broadly, Jones is an App Store veteran. His first app, Weather Line , came out in the middle of the initial App Store boom, and shot to the top of the charts. He has a unique vantage point into how the App Store has evolved, and appreciates its strengths while critiquing its weaknesses.

In this interview, we discuss Jones’ background, his experience with Weather Line, and how App Store capabilities directly impact the viability of an app. Then we cover Flighty and its evolution, from data display to prediction, and the potential for a social network for flying and why Apple and AI are threats. The App Store and the app market are one of the oldest focus areas for Stratechery, long before it was cool, and I enjoyed getting Jones’ point of view on what it takes to succeed not just today, but how that compares to the last fifteen years.

As a reminder, all Stratechery content, including interviews, is available as a podcast; click the link at the top of this email to add Stratechery to your podcast player.

On to the Interview:

An Interview with Ryan Jones About Flighty and Building Apps in 2025

This interview is edited for content and clarity.

*Topics:*

Background ( #background ) | Weather Line ( #weather-line ) | Flighty ( #flighty ) | Subscriptions and Predictions ( #subscriptions-predictions ) | Social Flying ( #social-flying ) | Growing an App in 2025 ( #apps-2025 ) | The App Store ( #app-store ) | Competition and Future Opportunities ( #competition-future )

Background

*Ryan Jones, welcome to Stratechery.*

*RJ:* Hey, thanks for having me.

*Usually by the end of the year, things start to slow down a little, people are getting ready to travel. Good timing to have you, for reasons that we will get into. I wasn’t anticipating Netflix buying Warner Bros. this week , so Stratechery listeners get two interviews this week.*

*Anyhow, a few weeks ago on Sharp Tech , I said there were two apps that made it impossible for me to switch from iOS. Fantastical was one , and Flighty was the other. We’re here to talk about Flighty and what it’s like to build an app in 2025. Before we get there, I do want to learn more about you. I know you took a very circuitous route to being here today, so take me back to the beginning. Where did you grow up?*

*RJ:* Oh, man, I have a path. I grew up outside of Houston, Texas, so everything in my world was oil industry. My parents both worked for Exxon, and everyone in the neighborhood and all the kids, moms, and everything at school was all oil all the time.

*Was that what you thought you would do? You just would grow up working in the oil industry?*

*RJ:* Pretty much. I thought my choices were oil or construction. I looked around and was like, “What are the two biggest, boldest things around here?” — it was oil and building huge skyscrapers and stuff. I’ve always been super inquisitive and engineering-minded, good at math, that kind of stuff. Everybody all along was like, “You’re going to be an engineer”, so I went and got a mechanical engineering degree.

I ended up coming back to Texas, working in the oil industry for about four or five years, and this was right when fracking was going crazy and gas was like $10 an MCF .

*Why’d you decide to go back to Texas? Was that just family? That was where you grew up, so that was the thing you were always going to do?*

*RJ:* It was probably the thing I was always going to do, and I knew I didn’t want to do the big banking thing. I actually wanted to do, you’ll appreciate this, I wanted to do an MBA. I felt like I lacked that business side of hardcore education, I’d always been interested in it and paid attention to it, and I’d always wanted to be an entrepreneur eventually, but I didn’t feel like I got the level of economics and management and business operations that I needed. I actually wrote the Dean of the Engineering School of Duke a strongly-worded letter a couple years after of, “I feel well prepared to calculate what would happen if a spring was oscillating on an airplane wing, but I missed a little bit of the other stuff here, guys, come on”.

*Did you get a response?*

*RJ:* No.

*(laughing) You’re here in Texas, you’re working for the oil industry. Suddenly you pop up working at Apple. What was that transition? What happened there?*

*RJ:* The great thing about the oil industry is they give you a ton of responsibility early. Everything there is expensive, so you’re dealing with big budgets immediately, and they’re incredibly good at cultivating the next — they’re always talking about, “You’re the next generation, you’re the next generation”. It’s got a little bit of that Southern vibe of, “Let’s all just help each other, you’re the next generation”. I’m sure that there was infighting and whatever, corporate backstabbing, but yeah, I’m sure that there was, but to my eyes, it was way less than I’d expected.

I got a ton of responsibility early, and then having to — also during this fracking boom, and gas made it even more elevated. What happened was they send everyone to the field for a year when you get hired. They’re like, “You go learn what actually happens on the ground, you can’t manage from here if you haven’t actually done those things”, I lived in the middle of East Texas for a year, did a ton of fracking, some drilling rigs, all the stuff you see in the movies, if you will. Because of the boom, basically on day one what they want you to do, what you’re supposed to do, is ride around in a truck with another guy for a month and then figure out what you want to do after that. They were basically, I showed up and they said, “There’s a frack job starting tomorrow, go run it”.

Which a frack job is, whatever, a million dollars a day being spent and 250 guys on the ground and $100 million worth of equipment, just a massive operation, I somehow got thrown into that right away and had no idea what I was doing, an insane amount of responsibility. Like a young guy, I would always work nights. I would work nights, being the leader of 50, 60, 40-year-old guys who had tons of expertise and they looked to me to answer questions. I just learned really fast to be like, “Well, what would you do, what do you think”, and yadda-yadda. After a little while, I got decent at it, but it was a ton of — I really learned quick to manage and to deal with high-risk/reward situations. Fracking is, to do a very short version of it, you’re pumping water and sand into the ground, and it takes around three minutes to get through the pipe and into the rock formation, and so you’re monitoring the pressure at the surface. You are making all of your decisions three minutes in advance, based on the pressure at the surface, about what you think is going to happen downhole three minutes later. If you get it wrong, bad things happen. You basically have to make a very expensive and potentially dangerous decision every 30 seconds, to keep going or not. I learned to deal with a lot of big decision-making with a lot on the line really early.

The other thing that was happening, so this was 2007, 2008, a little thing called the iPhone, at the exact same time this was happening. In between frack jobs, I would get on Twitter, read about, “Oh, my gosh, the software doesn’t just fall from the sky, there are humans out in California who write software and make these things”. It was just a total — I don’t want to say total, but it was, let’s just say, a total, “Oh, my gosh, people actually make software, someone actually has to do that”, it had never really crossed my mind before.

*This was very late. It wasn’t, “I got a computer when I was in sixth grade and typed out BASIC programs”, it was a very come-late-to-the-industry moment.*

*RJ:* 100%, yeah. I guess I can draw the line in hindsight, I was very engineering oriented and I liked to take things apart, figure out how things work, do things on my own. Then I minored in architecture, so I definitely have always had a little bit of taste or aesthetic to things. I don’t like just build it just to build it, I like it to look great and all those things and work great in the end, you’re absolutely right.

It just was like, “Wow, these things”. Following Paul Haddad and Loren Brichter and these people who made these original Tweetie iPhone apps that were just — it never crossed my mind that that was possible.

*I can definitely relate. I grew up in small-town Wisconsin, and I was interested in technology, I was the only one around me that was, but it never occurred to me to go work in tech, it wasn’t even in the realm of possibility, that was something that happened out in San Francisco and California. Yeah, I totally know the perspective that you’re talking about, one that I think is very foreign to a lot of our listeners, so you and I may be commiserating between the two of us here, but it’s very hard to explain if you didn’t grow up just completely out of that world.*

*RJ:* Yeah, you feel like you’re watching it from afar. Diggnation was a big part of me learning about tech, just anything that I could do to get involved in that world or try to understand what was going on on the ground.

*You’re working for the oil company, the iPhone is interesting — there’s a few twists and turns, I feel like that are coming in this story.*

*RJ:* That’s right. The good news about the oil industry was all the responsibility, and it’s a great industry to work in, they educate you, and they work what’s called a 9/80, which is kind of a funny variant of this 996 thing that you hear in Silicon Valley now. They work nine days every two weeks for 80 hours total, which is a very dumb way of explaining you get every other Friday off. There’s just a lot of really cool cultural stuff, and they don’t — I gave that example to say you don’t grind your ass off.

Anyway, so it was hard to leave to one extent, but I had the distinct feeling that I’m going to look up 10 years from now and think what would’ve happened, I had to try, I couldn’t bear the thought of looking up and just staying in oil and never having tried starting something in tech. At that time, it was all apps.

Weather Line

*So is this when* *Weather Line got off the ground?*

*RJ:* You got it. Yeah, it was all apps. Weather apps were somehow kind of a battleground, if you believe it. This is very, very early. Things started slow, a little bit like they are with the AI stuff now, it was crawl, walk, run. I’ve tried multiple times in my life to code, not my thing, can’t do it, so I found a partner just remotely on Twitter, online, and built Weather Line.

The goal that I had set for myself was if I can get this app into the Top 100 in the App Store — which you’ll remember back in the day, it was like everyone’s watching the top charts — if I can get into the Top 100 in the App Store, that means I have an idea what I’m talking about. That means I can be a product guy, if you will, that’s the thing that I thought I would fit best into in Silicon Valley.

*Just to back up, Weather Line was actually an awesome app. The description’s in the title, you showed the weather as a line, so you could see the graph of temperature, of precipitation, of all those sorts of things. John Gruber , I was just actually looking this up, had a very effusive endorsement of Weather Line , I’m looking at this back in 2013. But was that just sort of the take — “There’s a bunch of weather lines out there and they all are difficult to read, I just want to see where it’s going”?*

*RJ:* The idea was can I get it in the Top 100, and we launched and it hit No. 17 in the App Store, and Gruber was a big help there.

*Just for context, this is 2011, is that right? Or 2013, somewhere around then?*

*RJ:* That’s right.

*What does No. 17 in the App Store mean? What sort of numbers are we talking about?*

*RJ:* Oh, I mean, that’s like Instagram, but these were huge apps, I should look up a screenshot.

*Millions of downloads?*

*RJ:* I don’t know about millions. Hundreds of thousands.

*Hundreds of thousands, yeah.*

*RJ:* Yeah, per day.

*Yeah, that’s a lot. It’s so interesting, because I do want to compare and contrast when we’re going to get to Flighty in a little bit, but that was, to your point, app mania. That was the thing to do, people were downloading apps left and right. Was this a thing where you just launched it and it took off? What were the drivers of getting to those kinds of numbers, hundreds of thousands a day?*

*RJ:* This is kind of where part of my life about Twitter being massive comes in. As someone who was away from the core of the scene, I was talking to people, trying to learn about things on Twitter, and basically was very good at covering the iPhone from a normal person point of view, a very, very lame version of Stratechery. I was talking about what is the strategy that they’re executing, what will they probably do next year, what’s going to change with iOS, and somehow got a following from that. Small, but lots of really cool people, like [Marc] Andreessen and Gruber and you and M.G. Siegler , lots of, I thought, really cool people that started listening to what I was saying about iPhone stuff.

I really subscribed to the, “If you want something, just provide value to the other person and just see what happens, let it go”, my success rate of cold emailing people and saying, “Hey, I want to work for you”, or whatever is low, but if I do some work that I know you’re probably already doing and say, “Hey, I did this thing for you”, it’s worked very well for me in my career. I would send a note to people and say, “Here’s a 20-second video, it’s the most accurate data in the world”. At that time, it was the Dark Sky, Dark Sky had just come out, so it was a 60-minute rain prediction thing, and we had this unique take that shows everything you need to know about your weather in one view. People really loved it and gravitated towards it, so it just took off, literally organic.

*This is what we’re going to get to with Flighty, is data, finding good data sources. I mean, it’s almost like drilling for oil, if I could make an analogy. Is there an analogy there? What’s unique about that? How is it that that actually is the core of what you’ve — to be clear, you have two massive hits now, so you’ve repeated it. Why are they both about data?*

*RJ:* I think it just goes back to being super inquisitive, and just digging and digging and digging until I get to the bottom of something. I didn’t understand why no one was doing that visual representation on weather with that data, I got to the bottom of the Internet and I didn’t have an answer, so I did it. Same with Flighty. I didn’t understand why no one was doing a great flight tracking app. Every time I was taking a flight, I was digging around for where’s the most accurate data, what’s going on with the plane, all these things that I’m sure we’ll talk about. I eventually got to the bottom of the Internet and I had no answer. Just as an entrepreneur, it ate away at me enough where I said, finally, “I have to do this, the opportunity seems so big, I don’t understand it. If I’m wrong, I need to find out why nobody else cares about this”.

*Back in 2011, 2013, Apple did not yet support subscriptions . What was the business model for Weather Line?*

*RJ:* It oscillated between $3 and $5 upfront, which was terrible.

*Right* , *because weather data is an ongoing expense, right?*

*RJ:* That’s right, it was really tough, it wasn’t a huge financial success. That’s how I accidentally ended up at Apple. I was in Austin, we were living in Houston at the time and I was in Austin and a big fan of Apple, and just looked up if there was any people in the alumni network who worked at Apple. A guy immediately replied, “Dude, we’re not hiring right now”, I was like, “No, you don’t understand, I finally left the oil industry, I have an app that people know of, I don’t want to get a job, I just want to come meet people”. Met with him, hung out, he a month later said, “Hey, will you apply for this job?”, I said, “No”, then he kept pestering me, and then I just got curious.

*I mean, this sounds like a real lesson. You had to go in and not want to get a job, is how you managed to get a job.*

*RJ:* It honestly is a recurring thing in my life, of I just kind of put myself out there, meet people, offer help and value when I can, I’m not very good at saying, “Hey, I want to come work with you”, and then just banging down the door until I get it done. I’m more of a spread helpfulness everywhere and watch what happens kind of person.

*Apple in Austin, especially back then, was mostly all operations stuff, right?*

*RJ:* That’s right. It was the year before they moved all the operations there, so at that time it was iPhone, iPad, and then while I was there, Watch was launched. I ended up staying for two years because I legitimately enjoyed it, worked on iPhone and iPad and Mac operations and then during that time, Weather Line, you’re not allowed to update it, you can’t have an app, which drove me nuts because you’re allowed to be a musician.

*Oh, as an Apple employee.*

*RJ:* Yeah. You’re allowed to be a musician and have something on iTunes back at the day, or you’re allowed to do basically anything, but you cannot have an app in the App Store. And so I couldn’t really update it, I kind of just had to let it go as it was and then I decided to switch jobs, and subscriptions happened is literally the truth, so that gave me the opening to do Weather Line 2 and to move it into subscriptions, to do the whole thing. Back 10 years ago, everyone was super panicking anytime one of their apps moved from paid upfront to a subscription, but that made it viable that I could work on it and make a living off of it more or less.

*Got it. So Weather Line was acquired , you have not disclosed who acquired it, there’s rumors out there about big companies that launch an app shortly thereafter that looks a lot like yours, but people can go figure that out for themselves. But was this ultimately a happy ending or was it, “I’ll push this as far as I can”? What’s the mood on the end story here?*

*RJ:* Very happy ending. I was happy to get out of the weather game and it was kind of an unsolicited buyer who, like you said, had a strong need for it. So they were willing to pay more than I’d ever dreamed and I was happy to do it and to consult for them thereafter to make sure it was a good, clean takeover.

Flighty

*So I think even before it was acquired though, you started Flighty, right? Do I have the timeline right?*

*RJ:* You got it, you nailed it. Yeah.

*Give me the Flighty origin story.*

*RJ:* Okay.

*Yeah, I have them all turned on, so I sometimes wake up to 25 Flighty alerts, but I love it so it’s good. This is fully customizable, for those in the audience, don’t worry, you can have far fewer alerts.*

*RJ:* But the way we think about the funnel, we have a very generous free plan. I think there’s no ads to this day. We don’t do anything creepy with privacy, it’s actually fully anonymous, I have no idea who’s who in the app, you don’t have your name in there anywhere. Well, you can enter your name, but we don’t use it, you don’t have to have it anywhere.

And then we, throughout the experience, have places that say, “Hey, there’s a delay for your flight to Chicago, and if you want to see the exact reason, you can upgrade to Pro to see it”, or, “Hey, if you’re entering all of your past flights, you can enter the past year for free, but if you want to go further than that, it is part of the Pro experience”, or, “Hey, we can import your flights from the calendar, we’ll import the most recent year, but if you want more, it’s Pro”. So we have a very, when I say old school, I mean we believe in the service, we believe in the product, we let you try it as much as we can, and then when you get to the point where it’s like, “All right, you’re either a user or you’re not”, we ask for you to pay at that point.

So we have a lot of free users who use the app a ton, and I think it’s been huge in terms of word of mouth. It’s great for those people to be able to use the app for an unlimited number of flights for years and years and years, and it’s okay if they don’t ever use the Pro version. Word of mouth is how we grow and we really value the product experience, so it’s been a perfect balance for us.

*A lot of consumer apps ultimately decide, “I’m going to have to go enterprise”, that’s where people actually pay. I’ve pushed you for ages, I want family management, I want to be able to put flights in for other people. Is this something that you might have to go now that you’re feature complete, you’re doing the app prediction stuff, but do you feel the edges of the consumer market or do you still think there’s a long way to go?*

*RJ:* It’s a great question. I would love to do a deep dive on how do I figure out what’s the TAM? How do I figure out if we’re reaching the end of that road? I don’t know. Each time I think, “Oh man, everyone in the world must know about Flighty”, we meet someone who has no idea. To answer your question, we haven’t said this yet but we’re a tiny team. We started with three, and today we’re seven.

*It’s like the best possible App Store sort of story, a small team can make this amazing app that’s used by everyone in the industry and make a great living from it, it’s amazing.*

*RJ:* Yeah, thank you for saying that. We feel super fortunate, and I don’t have to worry about marketing, it’s great.

The App Store

*So are you on Team Apple when everyone’s complaining about the App Store?*

*RJ:* You know me, man, I can’t keep my mouth shut. I try to say exactly what I would say in private in public on Twitter, of like, “Okay, this is going too far and this is not”, and be pretty clear about it.

*Do you think people forget about this? They forget actually how amazing the App Store is and are a little bit too focused on all the things that they perceive is unfair, but those things only exist because the App Store was created in the first place.*

*RJ:* I absolutely think that. It frustrates me to no end when people are saying it should be 0%, it’s just so absolutist and it has no recognition of the value that the App Store fee is bringing. I think the fair number is way higher than most other app developers, most other app developers will say 7%, 10%. I think the fair number is in the 15 to 20% range, they’re doing a crazy amount of stuff with refunds and fraud and making sure the credit cards are up-to-date. All of that stuff, people have no idea how difficult it is, so I would say I’m a little on both people’s side. I think 30% is pretty high in today’s day and age.

*But it’s like 10% high. It’s not like 20% high.*

*RJ:* Exactly.

*Or 10 basis points I should say or 100, whatever, you know what I’m talking about.*

*RJ:* And while we’re on my complaints, one that maybe you need to do a breakdown in this, people always talk about the 30% versus 15%. And so for people who don’t know, the first million, you get at 15%, but that’s only the first if you stay under a million, it should just be first million every year, but let’s set that aside.

*So you’re punished by going over a million, unless you get to a significantly higher number.*

*RJ:* Correct. And the second year of an individual user’s subscription, you pay a lower fee, you pay 15%. So everyone always gives those caveats when they talk about, “The App Store has a 30% fee, but it’s also like 15%”, and the perception that people get then is like, “Oh, okay, it’s probably in the 20, 21, 22-ish percent range”, actually, if you do the actual math and you math it out as they say, the only way to get 50% of your users on 15% and 50% of users on 30% is if you’re declining, you can’t be adding any new users, so any app who’s flat or has growth is 27, 28, 29%. There’s very, very few apps that pay in the teens, and it’s probably because they’re either A) tiny, or B) dying. And it drives me nuts that people give them the little bit of the benefit of the doubt of, “Oh, it’s either 15 or 30”, by and large, it’s like 28, 29.

*So as someone who recognizes the benefits of the App Store, has had critiques, if you were made czar the App Store tomorrow, what would you change? Setting aside regulations, setting aside all the sorts of things, you’re in control of everything — I go back to Weather Line, your business straggled along because there were not subscriptions, the business model part was missing, and this is the part I’ve always been frustrated with Apple is you want to take all this control, but if that comes with responsibility, and part of your responsibility is making it viable for developers to actually have businesses. I was on that for ages and ages and ages, and they never did do — I always wanted them to do upgrade pricing, which we never got, at least we got subscriptions. But you’re the czar to the App Store, how do you make this — again, as someone who acknowledges that there’s a lot of good things about it — how do you make it better?*

*RJ:* Let me find my note, that’s a great question, I actually have a note somewhere. Man, I feel like I have so much to say on this topic, I don’t know if I’ll get to it all.

*Well, this is one of the reasons I want to talk to you. I love Flighty, but I haven’t talked about the App Store in a long time and it’s still not even close to perfect, but it’s become such a fraught topic because everyone’s so focused on the bad parts and there is still this middle ground of things Apple could do better. And coming from a point of, “We appreciate what you’ve done, but it’s 2025, let’s go”.*

*RJ:* I’m with you 100%. It feels like there’s a little bit of old thinking that’s kind of in a rut and it needs a little fresh take, especially from the point of view of we’re getting to the point where we have 5, 10, I don’t even know, 20 different versions of what the rules are all over the world, and it’s a little bit like, “All right, let’s take a clean pass at this”.

One of the things that drives me nuts, and this is probably not what you would expect me to say, but the rules are broken often and they’re there for a good reason, and the reason that they’re broken often is that there’s no punishment.

*Notifications is a big one. It is infuriating to get notifications from an app where you need notifications like an Uber or a DoorDash or something like that, I can’t turn the notifications off. To get an advertisement and that is infuriating, but then Apple sends advertising notifications, that is a classic tragedy of the commons example where it would actually be nice to have an App Store regulating this and not only are they not regulating it, they’re violating it themselves.*

*RJ:* I agree a hundred percent and I was having a conversation with someone on Twitter again the other day about this of — I think we’re a great example of an App Store kind of poster child in a lot of respects.

*Yeah, seven people, super successful.*

*RJ:* To a certain degree, I have to play the game that’s on the field, I can’t just pretend like it’s 2010 over here with how we’re behaving. If you think about it actually from a point of view of like a society—

*What does that mean? What’s something you have to do because it’s just the way it’s done?*

*RJ:* Our pricing page, everybody does the, “What’s the annual price versus the monthly price?”, and the rules very clearly say you’re supposed to list it a certain way and everybody kind of gets as close to that line as you can and what’s considered a marketing push notification, people get as close to that line as you can. And I wish it wasn’t allowed because I wish my competitors wouldn’t do it and then therefore I couldn’t do it.

But at a certain point — I think we compete in a classy and fair way, we don’t go over the top with all these things, but at a certain point we have to play the game on the field. But if you think about it from a society point of view, imagine if there were laws and rules, but when you broke them, someone just told you like, “Hey, dude, you broke that rule, try again”, it doesn’t work like that. You have to have some sort of—

*Consequences.*

*RJ:* Consequence is exactly the word I was looking for. The consequence is the actual deterrent, the fear of the actual consequence happening and there’s ways that they could do this where it’s like de-ranked in search or your features are taken down. You don’t have to kick an app out of the App Store Uber style for doing these things, but if there’s no actual punishment or consequence, without doing it explicitly, you’re kind of incentivizing people to push the rules.

*Because your competitor will do it.*

*RJ:* Correct, and so it’s an arms race.

*It’s funny because it’s really tough because I completely agree with you. Can Apple actually provide value to the App Store, please, if you’re going to control everything? But then that runs smack into the, “They have so much control”, “It’s unfair”, “Dictator of the world”, antitrust, etc., which I guess is sort of a takeaway in its own right.*

*RJ:* Yeah, to me, maybe I’m too simplistic, but it’s a very simple, as soon as the story went from iPhone growth to Services growth, this is what we all feared, and I think they’ve done a pretty decent job of restraining themselves. It could be a lot worse, but I wish it was dialed back a decent amount.

Another thing that drives developers nuts is refunds, they are very strict with allowing refunds, and a lot of times I want them to give a refund, I’m like, “Please give this user a refund”, but I don’t have any say in that. We have one little API we can communicate with where we can give them, I think, 200 characters of text and other than that, I have no say in it.

*Interesting. Usually, because you would think the problem would be someone uses it for a week and then asked for a refund, it’s very unfair, but actually you have the opposite problem.*

*RJ:* That’s right. Or people literally just don’t mean to download or they don’t mean to subscribe and they do, or they bought the family plan instead of the whatever plan, I don’t know the actual rules, no one really does, but you have around 14 days to ask for a refund and they’ll basically say yes, but there’s caveats to that. If they see a user that’s asking for a ton of refunds all the time, they don’t grant them as much. So there’s a lot of value they can bring to the ecosystem because they have that point of view, but they just kind of haven’t gone to the point where I can say, “I really want this person to have a refund unless there’s something you see on your end”, that’s one that drives us nuts.

I’ve actually had to Apple Pay users, because we have a really high lifetime price, we have a $300 lifetime plan for people that hate subscriptions or want to pay once with their business credit card or stuff like that, so when that purchase goes wrong, people are like, “Dude, this is not a $5 thing, you just charged me $300 and I’m not getting the value I thought I was going to get or it doesn’t work the way I thought it worked”, anything, and I’ve had to just Apple Pay people $250, it’s crazy.

*Wow, that’s amazing. Well, anything else on the list? You’re czar, you make refunds easier, you actually enforce the rules. All things considered, that’s not that many things. I really agree on the consequences one because that has really metastasized into just a horrible user experience in many respects, but is there anything else big picture? How can this be a better economy?*

*RJ:* I think I have the same view as most people about the anti-steering, that was insane. It seems like that’s getting fixed to a certain degree, I do wish that they would enable our external payments to be even easier and people like you and me know this, but not everyone may know that they’ve actually, in certain economy, in certain countries, in certain situations, you can do it a lot more now, but the numbers are turning out that it’s not that clear cut of a win. So it’s to their point that, “Hey, look, we’re providing almost 30% of value”, I think the numbers are a little lower than that where developers are able to basically do all the things that Apple provides and the funnel works out the way such that they’re getting, let’s say, whatever, 22, 25% is what they’re ending up paying. So Apple’s point is getting proven, they are providing that amount of value, but right now there’s no kind of outlet for people to find that out on their own, and so everyone’s just super aggravated.

Competition and Future Opportunities

*Would you ever do an Android app?*

*RJ:* That’s a great question, we think about it all the time, and I think this is one of the benefits of being a small team. We really have to do what do we think is the next best thing for our user base at any given time and we meet up every quarter, we all do a little dog fooding and we fly somewhere and the three of us, the original team, we meet up and strategize for what we want to do the next quarter, or we look further out than that.

And we always talk about Android. It’s always mentioned, and there’s always stuff that is higher value, higher upside for us and higher upside for the users that’s at the top of the list for the iOS.

*It feels like Android is not a viable enterprise for a small team, that’s a commitment for a larger company.*

*RJ:* That’s right. The way that we would have to do it if we did it would be get a small team, one or two people that more or less followed right behind us with iOS, so we wouldn’t be able to plan it and execute it simultaneously, we’d have to continue with what we’re doing today, and then once it works well on iOS, have a couple people apply it to Android.

I, of course, didn’t say this, but I heard recently at a conference, people say numbers like 50% of their effort goes to Android and 20% of the revenue comes from Android, and 50% of the effort goes to Android and 70 to 80% of the problems come from Android. So I think people who aren’t in the weeds may not realize the extent to which those markets are very different. A good example would be we probably also just aren’t a natural fit for Android, we’re $60 a year premium subscription, and it’s pretty commonly known-

*You don’t see a lot of Android phones in the front of the plane, put it that way.*

*RJ:* That’s another thing. And it’s pretty commonly accepted that you have to be more of a free model if you go to Androids, so it’s a little bit antithetical to who we are.

*Yeah. One of the things you always talk about is one of your biggest customer bases continues to be pilots and flight attendants and things like that. Is that still the case?*

*RJ:* Yeah, it is. It’s probably 25 to 30% of our users. We don’t have an amazing read on it because we’re super high on privacy, but based on all the indicators we have, customer support and places where you can tell us what you do, I think it’s 25 to 30%. And it’s actually a great word of mouth mechanism for us. If a crew member knows something about the plane that’s going to happen before the other crew members, you can bet your ass they’re going to tell the pilot and other crew members. And it spreads like wildfire through the crew, and then the crew will mention it at the front of the plane, like you said, and the people at the front of the plane will say, “Wait, how did you know that?”, and then it just spreads that way.

We have a lot of really cool stories too about someone sitting in 1B who mentions, “Oh shoot, we just got delayed”, and the crew and the pilot hear the comment and say, “No, we’re not”, and then five minutes later like, “How the heck did you know that?”. We’ve had a couple scenarios where a plane gets diverted and the person on the plane got the diverted alert and mentioned it in front of a crew member who had no idea yet, so there’s been some very cool things that come out of having the fastest thing.

*I’ve shown the app for crew members before, for sure, this is definitely something that’s happened.*

*Who’s your biggest threat? Is it Apple?* *They’re building in some of these features as far as flight tracking. Is it the airline apps themselves? Who do you worry about, if anyone?*

*RJ:* Am I allowed to turn this question around on you? I would love to know what you think it is.

*Oh, I’d say it’s Apple. They’ll give a bare, basic, sufficient, they show my flights. The problem with the airlines is you have to download the airline app, and presume you’re flying multiple airlines. I guess the question I would have, I think I know the answer, but which airline has the best app?*

*RJ:* I think United’s is pretty good.

*Yeah. United’s is miles ahead of everyone. I made a claim a while ago that United is actually the best airline in the world—*

*RJ:* That’s one of those things you’re not allowed to say out loud, you can’t say that out loud.

*Because their tech stack is so much better than everybody else. Delta’s getting better but it’s still not even close, and the Asian airlines are a total disaster.*

*RJ:* I agree with you 100%, but if you say it out loud, people go ballistic, as you know.

*What’s next for you? You had a list of 10 apps. Are you going to do another one or are you a Flighty lifer?*

*RJ:* Close friends ask me that. Every once in a while, they’ll say, “What’s the next app?” — Flighty is the next app, it’s taken over, the potential and the product market fit is beyond what I had dreamed of, and I love working on it every day.

*Do you fear AI, that my AI is just going to tell me in my ear, “Hey, your flight’s delayed”, and I don’t need to look at a well-designed app anymore?*

*RJ:* It’s definitely something I think about, it’s at the top of the list of the fears, I do also believe in our ability to be the people that can execute on that, we have a ton of data. One of the reasons we’ve succeeded to the degree we have, I think, is we’re small and we all live this problem all day, every day, and we’re super focused on it, no other companies are doing that. So I think if anyone figures out how to apply that in the right way, there’s no reason why it can’t be us first, but it’s definitely a sea change that we are aware of and keeping tabs on. But I don’t think natural word of mouth growth with no marketing will happen forever, I’m not drawing a straight line through all of our metrics.

*That’ll be the next department is an actual marketing department.*

*RJ:* Yeah, so we’ll see when you can see things start to bend, the curves start to bend, and that’ll be an interesting time. But right now, it’s not a hold onto the rocket ship in terms of Silicon Valley exponential, but in terms of a bootstrap world, we’re doing everything we can to just keep shipping great features.

*Do you think anyone could build an app like Flighty today?*

*RJ:* Is your question more competition or could someone actually do it?

*No. Like, someone, “I want to be like Ryan, this is very inspiring, I want to build an app”.*

*RJ:* Oh, I don’t know, I don’t know, man. CalAI is this small team who’s had a huge breakout success story, it’s more or less you take a picture of a plate of food and it tells you how many calories it is. And I mean, they’re making, if the numbers they say are true, $40 million, big, big annual numbers for an app and that’s a 18-month-old app.

So to answer your question, the AI stuff is a complete unlock. Just like what’s happening at Facebook and OpenAI and Perplexity and all these huge AI companies, how do we actually apply that thing? That 100% is happening at the app level. There’s just things you’ve never thought of and things we’re all thinking of as toys that can be whole products and verticalized and specialized, so I think someone could do it. I hate to say it like this, but 90% chance if it’s not an AI-native, AI-first thing, you’re in an uphill battle. That’s the sea change that has unlocked avenues that weren’t possible before. When I started, it was subscriptions allowed you to monetize premium flyers, and I think AI has just changed the abilities, that’s the sea change that’s right now.

*Ryan Jones, maker of my favorite app, thanks for coming out Stratechery.*

*RJ:* Thanks for having me, Ben.

text:
Disney made a deal with OpenAI, which both speaks to the durability of Disney's assets and to OpenAI's competition with Google.

Disney and OpenAI, Totems in an AI World, Google Versus the World

Monday, December 15, 2025

On Thursday’s episode of Sharp Tech , Andrew and I discussed Netflix’s acquisition of Warner Bros.

This is the last week of Updates for 2025; expect two Updates, including today, an Interview, and the annual Year in Review. After that Stratechery and most Stratechery Plus properties will be off for two weeks, and return on Monday, January 5.

On to the Update:

Disney and OpenAI

From the Wall Street Journal :

Disney is making a $1 billion investment in OpenAI and will allow the AI platform to use its characters and properties to generate short, user-prompted social videos. Disney’s three-year licensing deal will let users generate videos using Sora, OpenAI’s short-form AI video platform, of more than 200 Disney, Marvel, Star Wars and Pixar characters. A curated selection of these short videos will be available to stream on Disney+…

Disney and OpenAI announced their deal a day after Disney sent a cease-and-desist letter to Google accusing the tech giant of “infringing Disney’s copyrights on a massive scale,” demonstrating the carrot-and-stick approach it is taking to artificial intelligence. Alphabet’s Google is the biggest tech company to incur Disney’s wrath for allegedly using copyright material to train its AI systems and allowing its tools to output material that violates copyrights. The Disney letter includes dozens of images and screenshots of videos created with Google’s Gemini, Nano Banana and Veo apps featuring Disney-owned characters like Darth Vader, Homer Simpson and Spider-Man.

OpenAI will compensate Disney to use its characters in Sora, according to a person with knowledge of the matter. The companies didn’t disclose financial terms of the arrangement. In addition to its $1 billion investment, Disney is getting warrants to buy more stock in OpenAI at its current $500 billion valuation.

This is an interesting deal, in part because Sora 1 sent such tremors through Hollywood; now the biggest Hollywood Studio (just ahead of Warner Bros.) is licensing its assets for the Sora app. What changed?

Perhaps the correct answer is to look at what didn’t: what makes Disney unique is its massive stable of copyrighted characters, thanks to its long history of animation and purchase of Pixar, Star Wars, Marvel, and 21st Century Fox. One big advantage of owning these franchises is that their value is independent of individual actors; this helps ensure that Disney retains a greater share of the profits generated by their copyrighted characters, because there isn’t a human who can hold them hostage. Or, to put it another way, Disney is, more than any other Hollywood Studio, the most tech-like in its economics: it has tremendously valuable assets that it can leverage again and again at zero marginal cost.

You see the implications of that in this deal; from The Hollywood Reporter :

As for what consumers can expect with the Sora deal, Iger said that the deal encompasses some 200 characters, as well as props (like lightsabers) and worlds from Disney IP. Notably it will not include the voices of characters. Sora users will also be able to insert themselves into scenes. The deal is partially exclusive, meaning that Disney characters will be exclusive to Sora for a window (Iger suggested it is around a year)…

“We are not including name and likeness, nor are we including character voices. So in reality, this does not in any way represent a threat to the creators at all,” Iger continued. “In fact, the opposite. I think it honors them and respects them, in part because there’s a license fee associated with it. The other thing it does is it enables us to be comfortable that OpenAI is putting guardrails essentially around how these are used.”

That is certainly one interpretation of the deal; another is that the deal is in fact a demonstration that Disney’s model is, as I noted above, predicated on not having a dependency on individual humans. And, contra Iger’s assertion, this does represent a threat to creators, because the only scarce resource is time and attention: to the extent this initiative is successful is the extent to which consumers are spending more time with Disney’s assets than they are consuming the work of actual humans.

Totems in an AI World

One of the theses I have had about AI has been a self-serving one: I believe that content like Stratechery’s will become more valuable in an AI-dominated world, not less. Moreover, I think this thesis holds even if Gemini or ChatGPT becomes better at analysis than I am. The reason for this belief is the fact that LLM-derived AI is the ultimate manifestation of the individualization of content. I don’t know if this is true, but it seems likely that LLMs have already generated more text than all of humanity ever has; the reason I cannot know is the same reason why it hasn’t left a mark: AI content is generated individually for each individual user of AI.

This Update, on the other hand, is being read by tens of thousands of people, and they are all reading the exact same thing as everybody else. This is from one perspective a bad thing: wouldn’t it be great to have my content perfectly customized for your interest? I think the more compelling angle, however, is that because my content is the same for everyone it provides a useful totem pole for discussion and community. If you and your co-worker are both subscribers, you have something to talk about, confident that you are starting from the same Update; you don’t get that from AI.

The corollary here is that I can see Disney’s brands becoming more valuable in an AI world as well, and Sora is a perfect example. One thing that OpenAI got right with the initial launch was the concept of cameos, where you can put your likeness into videos, and make that likeness available to others; cameos were a totem that made the videos you generated fundamentally more interesting to people you knew (or who knew the person in the cameo), giving you a reason to watch. Indeed, if you remember back to the first week of Sora, the chief totem was OpenAI CEO Sam Altman — anyone who had access to Sora at the beginning was almost certainly intensely interested in AI, so one of the central figures in AI was an obvious person to anchor videos on.

The problem with cameos, however, is that not everyone enabled them — I never did — and that the universality of such totems was fundamentally limited to your network, if you even had one (or one that logged into Sora regularly). What actually has seemed to happen is that Sora has been intensely interesting to people who are interested in creating videos, and not very interesting to those who wish to consume them — the 90-9-1 axiom I wrote about when Sora launched seems to have held up, at least in broad strokes. Social networks are nice, but there is a reason Meta chased TikTok past them.

In this view, then, Disney’s assets are potential totems. Everyone knows who Mickey Mouse is; ergo, using Mickey Mouse for some absurd AI video is, by default, more interesting than using some random animal, or a person who most people don’t recognize. Granted, it is still AI slop, and maybe most people will never be as interested in that as they are in actual humans, but it is AI slop that at least has the possibility of spreading broadly. And, if it does, Disney has not put the framework in place to profit.

Google Versus the World

The other thing that interests me about this deal is that it is a further manifestation of a theme that has become very clear over the last couple of months: it really is Google versus the world. To go back to the chatbot and chip wars , Google is trying to win at every level of the stack, from products to models to chips. It’s OpenAI and Nvidia, meanwhile, who are the champions of a much more modular approach.

This deal fits in that framework. Google — at least according to Disney — is very much following its approach to the web, which is to focus on maximum scalability and avoid the mess of business deals and access rules and whatnot. Google Search wouldn’t be as dominant as it is if Google had had to make deals with everyone it wanted to index; similarly, it’s easy to imagine Google adopting the policy that it’s not making deals for anything unless it absolutely has to. That’s the best way to bring its infrastructure to bear; deals are simply grist in the flywheel.

That, by extension, is an opportunity for OpenAI. The “startup” doesn’t have anything close to the infrastructure Google has; ergo, it is very much in OpenAI’s interest to continue to set the precedent that deals are a part of doing business. After all, deals are an area where OpenAI isn’t structurally disadvantaged.

More generally, I’ll repeat an observation I made after Gemini 3 launched: one of the weirdest things about analyzing the current moment is how the three biggest AI labs seem stuck in lanes that don’t entirely fit them. Google is the consumer giant, delivering at scale, but ChatGPT was first to the consumer space; ChatGPT is the subscription-based productivity tool, but its biggest asset is a massive user base that is best supported through advertising; Anthropic, meanwhile, has the biggest enterprise business, but also has the model that is actually the most consumer friendly (but barely used by consumers at all).

To that end, I think Disney in particular is playing this well. Google’s preference is surely to move to a YouTube-like model where copyrighted material isn’t banned but simply shifts the monetization payout; this is a solution that scales. Disney, though, wants more, and OpenAI is motivated to give it to them, particularly if it makes it that much more difficult for Google to scale seamlessly.
