text:
Thick clients were the dominant form of device throughout the PC and mobile era; in an AI world, however, thin clients make much more sense.

Thin Is In

Tuesday, February 17, 2026

There was, in the early days of computing, no debate about thick clients versus thin:

When a computer was the size of a room, there were no clients: you scheduled time or submitted jobs, and got back the results when it was your turn. A few years later, however, thin clients in the form of a monitor and keyboard arrived:

There is no computer in this image; rather, this is a terminal connected to a mainframe. That’s why it’s called a “thin” client: it’s just an interface, with all of the computing happening elsewhere (i.e. in another room). By the 1980s, however, “thick” clients were the dominant form of computing, in the form of the PC. All of your I/O and compute were packaged together: you typed on a keyboard connected to a PC, which output to the monitor in front of you.

A decade later, and Sun Microsystems in particular tried to push the idea of a “network computer”:

Adrian Cockcroft, CC-SA 4.0

This was a device that didn’t really have a local operating system; you ran Java applications and Java applets from a browser that were downloaded as they were used from a central server. Sun’s pitch was that network computers would be much cheaper and easier to administer, but PCs were dropping in price so quickly that the value proposition rapidly disappeared, and Windows so dominant that it was already the only platform that network administrators wanted to deal with. Thick clients won, and won decisively.

If you wanted to make a case for thin clients, you could argue that mobile devices are a hybrid; after all, the rise of mobile benefited from and drove the rise of the cloud: nearly every app on a phone connects to a server somewhere. Ultimately, however, mobile devices are themselves thick clients: they are very capable computers in their own right, that certainly benefit from being connected to a server, but are useful without it. Critically, the server component is just data: the actual interface is entirely local.

You can make the same argument about SaaS apps: on one hand, yes, they operate in the cloud and are usually accessed via a browser; on the other hand, the modern browser is basically an operating system in its own right, and the innovations that made SaaS apps possible were the fact that interactive web apps could be downloaded and run locally. Granted, this isn’t far off from Sun’s vision (although the language ended up being JavaScript, not Java), but you still need a lot of local compute to make these apps work.

AI vs. UI

The thick-versus-thin debate felt, for many years, like a relic; that’s how decisive was the thick client victory. One of the things that is fascinating about AI, however, is that the thin client concept is not just back, it’s dominant.

The clearest example of this is the interface that most people use to interact with AI: chat. There is no UI that matters other than a text field and a submit button; when you click that button the text is sent to a data center, where all of the computation happens, and an answer is sent back to you. The quality of the answer or of the experience as a whole is largely independent of the device you are using: it could be a browser on a PC, an app on a high-end smartphone, or the cheapest Android device you can find. The device could be a car, or glasses, or just an earpiece. The local compute that matters is not processing power, but rather connectivity.

This interaction paradigm actually looks a lot like the interaction paradigm for mainframe computers: type text into a terminal, send it to the computer, and get a response back. Unlike mainframe terminals, however, the user doesn’t need to know a deterministic set of commands; you just say what you want in plain language and the computer understands. There is no pressure for local compute capability to drive a user interface that makes the computer easier to use, because a more complex user interface would artificially constrain the AI’s capabilities.

Nicolas Bustamante, in an X Article about the prospects for vertical software in an AI world , explained why this is threatening:

When the interface is a natural language conversation, years of muscle memory become worthless. The switching cost that justified $25K per seat per year dissolves. For many vertical software companies, the interface was most of the value. The underlying data was licensed, public, or semi-commoditized. What justified premium pricing was the workflow built on top of that data. That’s over.

Bustamante’s post is about much more than chat interfaces, but I think the user interface point is profound: it’s less that AI user interfaces are different, and more that, for many use cases, they basically don’t exist.

This is even clearer when you consider the next big wave of AI: agents. The point of an agent is not to use the computer for you; it’s to accomplish a specific task. Everything between the request and the result, at least in theory, should be invisible to the user. This is the concept of a thin client taken to the absolute extreme: it’s not just that you don’t need any local compute to get an answer from a chatbot; you don’t need any local compute to accomplish real work. The AI on the server does it all.

Of course most agentic workflows that work tread a golden path, but stumble with more complex situations or edge cases. That, though, is changing rapidly, as models become better and the capabilities of the chips running them increase, particularly in terms of memory. When it comes to inference, memory isn’t just important for holding the model weights, but also retaining context about the task at hand.

To date most of the memory that matters has been high-bandwidth memory attached to the GPUs, but future architectures will offload context to flash storage . At the same time, managing agents is best suited to CPUs , which themselves need large amounts of DRAM. In short, both the amount of compute we have, and the capability of that compute, still isn’t good enough; once it crosses that threshold, though, demand will only get that much stronger.

This combination of factors will only accentuate the dominance of the thin client paradigm:

* First, if compute isn’t yet good enough, then workloads will flow to wherever compute is the best, which is going to be in large data centers.
* Second, if larger models and more context makes for better results, then workloads will flow to wherever there is the most memory available.
* Third, the expense of furnishing this level of compute means that it will be far more economical to share the cost of that compute amongst millions of users; guaranteeing high utilization and maximizing leverage on your up-front costs.

Yes, you can run large language models locally, but you are limited in the size of the model, the size of the context window, and speed. Meanwhile, the superior models with superior context windows and faster speeds don’t require a trip to the computer lab; just connect to the Internet from anywhere. Note that this reality applies even to incredible new local tools like OpenClaw: OpenClaw is an orchestration layer that runs locally, but the actual AI inference is, by default and in practice for most users, done by models in the cloud.

To put it another way, to be competitive, local inference would need some combination of smaller-yet-sufficiently-capable models, a breakthrough in context management, and critically, lots and lots of memory. It’s that last one that might be the biggest problem of all.

The Memory Crowd-Out

From Bloomberg :

A growing procession of tech industry leaders including Elon Musk and Tim Cook are warning about a global crisis in the making: A shortage of memory chips is beginning to hammer profits, derail corporate plans and inflate price tags on everything from laptops and smartphones to automobiles and data centers — and the crunch is only going to get worse…

Sony Group Corp. is now considering pushing back the debut of its next PlayStation console to 2028 or even 2029, according to people familiar with the company’s thinking. That would be a major upset to a carefully orchestrated strategy to sustain user engagement between hardware generations. Close rival Nintendo Co., which contributed to the surplus demand in 2025 after its new Switch 2 console drove storage card purchases, is also contemplating raising the price of that device in 2026, people familiar with its plans said. Sony and Nintendo representatives didn’t respond to requests for comment.

A manager at a laptop maker said Samsung Electronics has recently begun reviewing its memory supply contracts every quarter or so, versus generally on an annual basis. Chinese smartphone makers including Xiaomi Corp., Oppo and Shenzhen Transsion Holdings Co. are trimming shipment targets for 2026, with Oppo cutting its forecast by as much as 20%, Chinese media outlet Jiemian reported. The companies did not respond to requests for comment.

The memory shortage has been looming for a while, and is arguably the place where consumers will truly feel the impact of AI; I wrote in January in the context of Nvidia’s keynote at CES:

CES stands for “Consumer Electronics Show”, and while Nvidia’s gaming GPUs received some updates, they weren’t a part of [Nvidia CEO Jensen] Huang’s keynote, which was focused on that Vera Rubin AI system and self-driving cars. In other words, there wasn’t really anything for the consumer, despite the location, because AI took center stage. This is fine as far as Nvidia goes: both the Vera Rubin announcement and its new Alpamayo self-driving system are big deals. It is, however, symbolic of the impact AI is having on technology broadly, and that impact is set to impact consumer electronics in a major way. Specifically, not only is all of the energy and investment in the tech sector going towards AI, but so is the supply chain.

A big story over the last few months has been the dramatically escalating cost of memory as the major memory manufacturers shift their focus to high-bandwidth memory for AI chips in particular. What that means is that everything else is going to get a lot more expensive: memory is one of the most expensive components in nearly everything tech-related, and given the competitive and commoditized nature of the industry those costs will almost certainly be passed on to the end users.

This AI crowd-out dynamic arguably started with the hyperscalers, who diverted ever increasing parts of their budget to GPUs in place of CPU purchases, but now it’s coming for everything from grid power to turbines and now to components, and it’s only going to increase and become more impactful to end users. In other words, Nvidia may not have talked about consumer electronics at the Consumer Electronics Show, but they are having the biggest impact on the industry by far.

The downsides of this crowd-out effect are obvious; I pity anyone trying to build their own PC, for example, but soon their pain will be everyone’s pain as prices inevitably rise on everything that needs RAM.

At the same time, I think the reported PlayStation delay is telling: apparently the PS5 is “good enough” for Sony to wait for more memory capacity to come online, and they’re probably right! Thick clients — of which consoles like the PS5 are the ultimate example — have long since reached the point of diminishing returns when it comes to hardware improvements. I think you could make the same case for PCs and phones as well: what we already have is already more than sufficient for almost any task we want to do.

Moreover, the plateau in thick client capability is happening at the same time that the need for any capability at all is disappearing, thanks to these entirely new AI workflows that happen in the cloud. Yes, it sucks that AI is making memory scarce and personal computers of all kinds — from PCs to phones to consoles — more expensive; it’s also making them less important than ever.

Of course thick clients could make a comeback, particularly since local inference is “free” (i.e. the user pays for their own electricity). As I noted above, however, I’m skeptical about local inference in the near term for performance reasons, and the memory crunch is going to make it uneconomical for the foreseeable future. And, by the time local inference is a viable alternative, path dependency downstream of these few years may have already led to many workflows moving to this new paradigm.

It will, to be clear, be a transition: UI isn’t just about how to use a computer, it also, as Benedict Evans noted on a recent Interview , embeds critical aspects of how a business works. Open-ended text prompts in particular are a terrible replacement for a well-considered UI button that both prompts the right action and ensures the right thing happens. That’s why it’s the agent space that will be the one to watch: what workflows will transition from UI to AI, and thus from a thick client architecture to a thin one? Current workflows are TBD; future workflows seem inevitable.

text:
Shopify is poised to be one of the biggest winners from AI; it would behoove investors to actually understand the businesses they are selling.

Shopify Earnings, Shopify's AI Advantages

Wednesday, February 18, 2026

Happy Chinese New Year! Monday, February 23, I will be taking a vacation day; there will be no Update. There will be a Stratechery Interview tomorrow, and I’ll be back on Tuesday.

On to the Update:

Shopify Earnings

From Bloomberg :

Shopify Inc.’s adjusted earnings missed analyst forecasts despite stronger-than-expected revenues. The shares fell. Shopify earned 48 cents per share on an adjusted diluted basis, short of the 51 cents expected by analysts in a Bloomberg survey. US-listed shares, which had rallied this week ahead of the report, dropped 13% to $110.37 as of 11:56 a.m. in New York, the most intraday since April 2025. The e-commerce firm’s revenue grew 31% to $3.7 billion during the quarter, topping the nearly $3.6 billion predicted in a Bloomberg survey. Shopify’s roughly $124 billion of gross merchandise volume, a measure of how much business is flowing through the online platform, also beat expectations.

Ah yes, Shopify is a software company, so they’re doomed. Totally reasonable reaction! I’m being sarcastic, of course; Shopify is extremely well-positioned to be a big winner from AI. What was striking about the earnings call is how apparently non-obvious this was.

Shopify’s AI Advantages

There are a host of reasons that Shopify is set to benefit from AI, many of which are generalizable; here are some examples just from the earnings call:

Exclusive Data and a Way to Leverage It

From President Harley Finkelstein’s prepared remarks:

The AI era has now reached commerce, and you’re about to see what that looks like at scale. You’re seeing the start of this new normal. And when Tobi said we would be the ones creating it, he was not exaggerating. Shopify was built for this moment. No one, and I mean no one is better positioned to lead in this new era. We’ve spent decades building the infrastructure that allows every type of merchant to thrive. We have trillions of data points from billions of transactions across millions of merchants. Simply put, we believe we have a more diverse commerce data set than almost anyone else on the Internet. And of course, data is what AI is fueled by. This is an enormous advantage, and it’s also a real responsibility, and it’s not one we take lightly.

The data point should be self-evident; what is exciting is that Shopify has built out the ad-buying network I called for four years ago , which is where that data can really pay off. Finkelstein again:

Let’s talk about Shop Campaigns, our advertising product, which is really starting to gain traction. In 2025, Shop Campaigns revenue doubled and merchant adoption tripled, metrics we will look to build on in 2026. Shop Campaigns is a merchant-first high-intent network native approach. We’re giving merchants big platform reach without the risk. They only pay when a customer converts, no sales, no spend. And we’ve now added X, Snapchat, Bing to join Google, Instagram and Facebook, so our merchants can advertise with zero risk across 8 channels, including the Shop App and Shopify storefronts.

Shop Campaigns isn’t necessarily the right choice for the sophisticated merchant who can manage their own campaigns on Google or Instagram; what it is is something that is easy to get started with for the long tail. This is beneficial in its own right, but speaks to something important about the vibe code scare: convenience, ease-of-use, and eliminating risk are selling points; vibe coding your own storefront is the opposite of all of these things!

Shopify has also continued its work to make the Shop App a discovery surface in its own right (with advertising, of course), and has added a third leg to its customer acquisition stool:

And finally, the Shopify Product Network. The Product Network is an opt-in app that uses Shopify’s data network to automatically surface relevant clearly branded products from other Shopify stores on a merchant site widening selection with extra inventory or operations. Merchants can choose where recommends show up, whether that’s collect pages, product detail pages, search results, cart or the post purchase page. And if the shopper buys the product, the host merchant earns a commission while connecting another merchant with a new customer.

This is a brand new offering — it just launched in December — but it’s a great idea that has the potential to not just be beneficial to participating merchants, but also make Shopify that much stickier. And, the best way to do that will be to leverage all of that unique data.

AI-Driven Market Expansion

Back to Finkelstein’s prepared remarks:

Since January 2025, orders coming to Shopify stores from AI search are up 15x. Now that’s on a small base, but that’s still a really big jump in 12 months. And this matters. For our merchants, it matters because it powers the long tail of commerce, servicing smaller merchants to the right buyers who might otherwise have never discovered them. This is merit-based discovery at scale. For buyers, it matters because it’s like having a personal shopper in your pocket, someone who really understands them, their taste, their preference, their size. This used to be a luxury, but now it’s available to everyone, 24/7. And for Shopify, it matters because we believe it can bend the curve of e-commerce penetration by stripping out friction, pulling late adopters in and moving more everyday purchases online. That’s the tide we’re building for, and we’re ready to turn that macro tailwind into share gains for our merchants.

Note that last sentence about stripping out friction, making the same point I did above. More generally, however, I’ve already made the case that AI-denominated commerce will benefit the long tail, which is to say it will benefit Shopify:

There are certainly some AI queries that are basically search queries, but many commerce related queries come higher up in the funnel: you have a vague idea of what you want, or know the problem you are trying to solve, and what you are looking for is help in refining that vagueness into a concrete product that you can purchase. Sometimes the answer is a popular product, but what is compelling about AI as a commerce driver is that it has the capability of finding products in the long tail that you might never have found normally but which the AI, with its vast corpus of knowledge, can surface for you. These kinds of products can certainly be found on Amazon or Walmart, thanks in particular to their large third-party merchant platforms, but the chief home for the long tail is Shopify (for companies) and Etsy (for individual sellers).

This isn’t the only market expansion, however: Shopify doesn’t just benefit from its ads getting better because of AI, but is also one of the biggest winners from Google and Meta getting better at advertising as well.

Interaction with the Physical World

Finkelstein again:

Here’s the thing. Commerce is complex, it’s dynamic, and it’s also easy to get wrong. It’s so much more than just a transaction. It’s a leather goods brand like Parker Clay offering monogramming. It’s a furniture brand like Burrow offering white glove delivery or a nutrition brand like ButcherBox offering subscriptions. It is critical that shopping in an AI conversation is at least as good as shopping at the merchant’s online store. And no one, and I mean no one understands this like Shopify because we’ve spent 2 decades mastering this complexity. So this is a lot more of this new surface area for us. This is a transitional moment in Shopify’s history. We are now designing the new normal, just like Tobi predicted a decade ago, and it will fundamentally change our position in the world.

The impact of AI is going to be felt most acutely in the digital world; the ultimate example is programming, which is purely digital. That impact, however, will be blunted the moment some part of the workflow touches anything in the physical world, and the vast majority of Shopify’s merchants are selling physical goods, with all of the complexity that entails.

High-Risk Workflows

This was the weirdest part of the call: multiple analysts asked semi-panicked questions about whether or not Shopify was threatened by agentic shopping, to the point where Finkelstein felt compelled to step back and explain exactly how an agentic purchase would work.

I just want to sort of go back because I suspect I’ll get more questions on this around Agentic and Checkout. So I said this earlier, but I’m going to repeat this. LLMs do not bypass Shopify’s Checkout. Checkout is really 2 parts. Think of it this way. You have a front end that’s the user interface that buyers interact with and the back end that processing everything server to server. So if you think about a Shopify store today, Shopify runs both the front end and the back end. And under UCP, Shopify still powers the overall experience, but the merchant gets to keep their own checkout system on the back end.

Now with something like ChatGPT, for example, OpenAI will run the front end, which is sort of the screens and the forms that the buyer uses. But Shopify still runs the back end. And so things like order processing and payments through Shopify Payments, that all runs through Shopify’s infrastructure, which one of the reasons that we’re so excited by this is because we get to help merchants sell across a new surface area, but we get to simplify the complexity through the Shopify, the retail operating system that we’ve built here.

And again, the idea that we can help them find and access new customers in a new surface area that, we think, is an incredible thing, and we’re going to make that really simple for them. The key, though, is that it’s really done well. And just going back to the UCP point for a second. UCP is the protocol that covers the full commerce journey end-to-end. And it goes from discovery to checkout to fulfillment, even to returns. And so commerce is complex and it’s easy to get wrong. And one of the reasons that we wanted to create the standard with Google is because we want to make sure that it’s done in the right way to give the merchant experience, the consumer the experience that the merchant really wants to do. And we think UCP does a really great job of that.

Just because an agent finds the item you want doesn’t negate the fact the item still needs to be purchased, and no one is going to want to vibe code a payments flow (more on this in a moment).

One thing I did want to call out is that Finkelstein spent a lot of time talking about the Universal Commerce Protocol the company co-developed with Google; he was also asked explicitly about the comparison with OpenAI’s Agentic Commerce Protocol, which Shopify also supports. What was notable about his answer is that he didn’t talk about OpenAI’s protocol at all; clearly Shopify supports it because they support everything, but all of their weight is behind the Universal Commerce Protocol. That makes sense for the reasons I explained last month : UCP really is universal, while ACP is specific to OpenAI.

Pre-existing Business Model

This is closely tied to the previous item:

Yes. So I think I covered it, but I’ll just repeat it. I mean for Shopify merchants, the economics are the same as if the transaction happened on the online store when it comes to Agentic. Specifically on something like ChatGPT, which requires Shopify Payments, monetization is through payments. It’s the same as if it occurred in the online store. And in terms of some of the other applications as well, if you’re a Shopify merchant, it will default using Shopify Payments. So that is how monetization occurs.

Shopify, like Spotify , already has the right business model for this new world: they monetize the high-risk workflow that isn’t going away, which means they are already set up to monetize agentic purchases.

Horizontal Coverage

Finally, Shopify isn’t a single-purpose tool; from CFO Jeff Hoffmeister’s prepared remarks:

Shopify powers entire businesses, not just websites, delivering reliable operations across checkout, payments, taxes, shipping, identity, fraud prevention and more. Our single platform spans online, point-of-sale, social, marketplaces, B2B, cross-border and now AI-driven interfaces unified by one inventory and customer record. This reduces complexity and expands selling opportunities for merchants.

As AI advances, Shopify becomes even more essential. AI transforms interfaces and accelerates the pace of change, but it doesn’t alter the underlying architecture of commerce. Commerce will always require speed, reliability and trust at a global scale. When I say scale, consider the billions of transactions that we facilitate. But it’s not just about the volume. It’s the comprehensive commerce experience we support. When an AI agent surfaces a product in any interface, merchants still need a reliable, secure and compliant path to purchase and post purchase. They still need our ecosystem of buyers, developers and partners. We help merchants be everything everywhere all at once, representing over 14% of U.S. e-commerce today and rapidly growing percentages in many geographies across the globe, we have an unparalleled view of commerce. Simply, we are the experts at commerce. AI will be a force multiplier. It will help us achieve our goals of democratizing entrepreneurship, inspiring more merchants, driving more transactions and creating more commerce channels.

There are three advantages for being the entire infrastructure of an e-commerce business. First, it will be very difficult for any existing business to replace Shopify. Second, Shopify is the best choice when getting started because it provides everything you need. Third, Shopify is actually the best placed entity to offer AI tools to merchants because it operates over the entire business, which means they have the entire context and data necessary to make AI truly useful.

The SaaS panic has been pretty amazing to watch. I have to admit, though, it’s kind of getting annoying, and this was the earnings call that pushed me over the edge! We got our AI bubble mania, I just didn’t expect it to be pointed entirely and indiscriminately downward. There will be losers from AI, but there will also be winners, and Shopify is very much poised to be the latter.

text:
An interview with Matthew Ball about the state of the video gaming industry in 2026, and why everything is a fight for attention.

An Interview with Matthew Ball About Gaming and the Fight for Attention

Thursday, February 19, 2026

This week’s Stratechery Interview is with Matthew Ball . Ball is the Managing Partner of Epyllion, an investment, investment advisory, and strategic advisory firm, as well as a Senior Advisor to KKR, Venture Partner at Makers Fund, Co-Founder of the Roundhill Ball Metaverse ETF, and an Occasional Contributor to The Economist. Ball’s 2022 book, The Metaverse, was an international bestseller. Ball was previously the global Head of Strategy for Amazon Studios, a Senior Advisor to McKinsey, Director at The Chernin Group’s Otter Media, and an Executive at Accenture. His writing is on his eponymous website .

Ball is a regular Stratechery Interview subject: we previously spoke in March 2020 and February 2023 about the entertainment industry, August 2021 and June 2022 about the Metaverse, and then, in February 2024 and January 2025 about the state of the video game industry.

Today’s interview continues on that latest theme. Ball just released a 164-slide presentation about The State of Video Gaming in 2026 , and what I appreciate about these presentations is that they are not simple year-over-year updates: each edition has a different focus, so that it reads more like a new chapter in a book than like a revised edition.

This year the big focus is on the fight for attention — a fight that video games are losing to a whole host of alternatives, particularly amongst young men. We discuss where video game growth is actually coming from, how consoles are harvesting their position as Aggregators but failing to grow the market, and why Roblox is crushing everyone. We then get into price discovery for app store fees, the impact of rising memory prices, why EA went private, the impact of AI, and whether the Metaverse is still — or ever was — a thing.

As a reminder, all Stratechery content, including interviews, is available as a podcast; click the link at the top of this email to add Stratechery to your podcast player.

On to the Interview:

An Interview with Matthew Ball About Gaming and the Fight for Attention

This interview is lightly edited for clarity.

*Topics:*

Video Games and the Fight for Attention ( #video-games-attention ) | Consoles and Stunted Aggregation ( #consoles-stunted-aggregation ) | Roblox and Advertising ( #roblox-advertising ) | The Market for Young Men ( #market-young-men ) | The Escape From App Store Fees ( #escape-app-store ) | Memory and Rising Prices ( #memory-prices ) | EA and Sports Rights ( #ea-sports-rights ) | AI and the Metaverse ( #ai-metaverse )

Video Games and the Fight for Attention

*Matthew Ball, welcome back to Stratechery.*

*MB:* Glad to be here.

*So, we’re here on the occasion, as we have been every year for the last few years, the annual release of your State of Gaming presentation. We’ll have a link in the show notes, but stepping back, before we get to the presentation itself, what’s your motivation for doing this every year? Just so I guess in general for you, what’s your focus on these days and how does this presentation fit into that?*

*MB:* It is usually about trying to answer some question that is surfaced in last year’s report and/or the dialogue that surrounds it. I actually only started three years ago, I didn’t anticipate doing it on an annual basis, but three years ago is when the industry first started to feel like there was something strange. The one challenge here is I can be on TikTok and Twitter and Polymarket while watching television, but I can’t actually have both hands on controller in a live multiplayer match while multitasking. Gaming is actually one of the few things that drives you all the way in, to the exclusion of others, and therefore if any of them happens to trigger your brain in a distracting way, which could just be you just lost 100 bucks, it could just mean you won 1,000 bucks, or it can be the OnlyFans star that you subscribe just told you a new pay-per-view video is available. Guess what? A lot of those people are gone, and they can multitask in other ways, but not that.

The other thing that I think is separate here is a lot of ink is spilled over online sports betting, which I think is unequivocally a pandemic in the United States, but to put this in perspective, online sports betting had roughly net losses in the United States of $17 billion last year across 35 states, I think. iGaming, which is real money gaming, mostly slots, but some poker, some craps and blackjack, was $11 billion. 11’s a lot less than 17, but it’s only legal in seven-

*It’s still a lot!*

*MB:* It’s only legal in seven states, Ben, and one of them is Rhode Island.

*Wow.*

*MB:* And one of the real problems that has happened in gaming is the casino genre, among others, it’s drawing on everything, happens to be one of the most valuable genres globally. It’s number two in the United States, sometimes number one and the legalization of iGaming has just taken the best whale customers from the non-real money gaming, and then it’s, by the way, these products look the same. They’re sometimes horizontally integrated. The same company that operates non-real money gaming has licenses for Wizard of Oz and Gene Wilder and Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, they just say, “Ben, come over here, man”, and now you can do the same thing but you will get money, is just a much, much better suck on attention.

So we’re getting hit on multiple different avenues here on distraction and focus, but also for certain categories, the dopamine hit is just a lot more powerful. And even if you pull 1% of users out, if they’re your most valuable whales, you’re hit.

*It’s the most valuable users, yep.*

The Escape From App Store Fees

*Platform fees, always an ongoing discussion with gaming. You had a pretty stunning stat: platform fees are 150% of non-China profits. There’s been a tentative pulling of the teeth, loosening of some of these sorts of things, of being able to have people on DTC platforms as opposed to being on the App Store. I think one of the questions here was the assumption that the conversion of the App Store flow is going to be so much better that it’s worth some amount of premium, but one of my takeaways from here is that doesn’t seem to be the case. Going DTC and avoiding those platform fees is in fact worth the drop in conversion or is worth sort of all the hassle of doing it. You had this bit about the Epic’s Game Store only charges 12% — even there, people are rolling their own because 12% is still too high. Is that the right takeaway?*

*MB:* I actually think that the success of DTC has now become underrated.

*Yeah, this is actually the part I was legitimately surprised about, so I completely agree.*

*MB:* So it’s actually helpful because it’s a reason to believe, again, so much of this report is around the headline numbers are misleading. But to that effect, when you take a look at mobile, I pull up five companies that publicly report, they have $4.4 billion in annual booking, so over the last 10 quarters, their revenue has declined by 0.9% on a gross basis, but their net revenue is up 4.4%, and that is just a transfer.

I don’t care how much Apple’s getting, I’m more happy that the publishers are taking some of that. That is despite the fact that part of the reason gross is down is because they are discounting so you move flow and despite that fact, they’re getting arbitrage. And then on top of that, that delta between 0.9 down and 4.4 is a blend of cohorts, they’re investing for a return that will take quarters to years.

*That’s right.*

*MB:* So actually, if we’re seeing 0.9 to 4.4 now-

*The LTV shift is much larger than the actual revenue.*

*MB:* Correct, exactly. And we see a number of companies that are now driving 10, 20, 30% over to DTC. Now, Ben, there’s a caveat here, which is the companies that report happen to be more likely in the casino genre, which means they have exaggerated whale economics and they have an easier mechanic to induce DTC.

*Right, they have huge margin to play with to pull them over and the people they pull over are worth a ton.*

*MB:* Yes. And they tend to be older, and so we can simultaneously say there’s a lot of success while also identifying this as an easier cohort. However, everyone’s familiarity with alternative and web shop and DTC payments is going up. Legal regulations are reducing the friction from those channels, and everyone is learning best practices. Then you have more and more companies like Epic, which, to your point, say, “You can pay 12%”, or just like Valorant runs its own payment service.

I actually think that this has become sneakily powerful. And when you talk to some of these gamemakers and listen to their earnings calls, they will again tell you, “Yes, we might be 10% DTC, but our new games are as much as 70% DTC because we launched them with our loyalty members, we launched them from the get-go with massive incentives, and therefore no one really even onboarded to IAP”. That’s awesome.

*Yep. Because once they’re on, especially with the subscription sort of thing, you’re just going to be there indefinitely, it’s too hard to get people to change, but from the beginning, that makes sense.*

*I see enough in here to say definitively, the numbers, like you go back to the court cases , there’s always the problem, it’s like, “What’s the alternative?”, “What should the number be?”, there wasn’t data to sort of support that. Now there’s more and more data that definitely says 30% is way too high, which we knew intuitively, but now it’s very clear.*

*Do you have any sense, and this is where the Epic example I think is interesting to me, what a number — again, this totally varies by games, there’s casino games, there’s other sorts of games that it’s different — but what is the value that’s provided with an integrated, super seamless in-app purchase experience compared to having the people go to a website, create an account, add their credit card, all those sorts of things? Just what’s your sense of what the value difference there is?*

*MB:* I’m going to evade for a second before I give you the answer.

*(laughing) I know, and I was trying to cover all the caveats so you couldn’t.*

*MB:* But I’ll tell you because it is actually a reason to understand the problems of payments in a different light. First, I mentioned earlier, again, we can only identify half of the independent ecosystem, and so we don’t know, the other half may be more or less profitable. But if you say that the half with identifiable operating income is representative of the whole, then we’re looking at about $20 billion in OI [operating income] and the platform fees of seeing the consoles. The platform fees of Steam, Google Play, iOS, and the consoles are about $34 billion, so you’re looking at about 150% of total operating income sitting there. It also happens that that $34 billion, if we assume that that is some form of arb, exceeds the total consumer spend of the third and fourth markets combined or basically five through eighteen combined, just to contextualize how large that opportunity is.

When you ask what does it look like? It looks like the rate is in the low 10s, but the most important thing is when you take a look at how DTC is being deployed, it is being deployed like Subway deploys coupons. You get percentages back from the more that you buy, you get exclusive items that come through, you get referral bonuses. All of the things that we think of as growth hacking and of customer rewards and of just generally building a long-term relationship with a customer, that just taking a look at Google will give you 18% instead of 30% or 12% instead of 30% misses the fact that what you can’t do are those complex offer systems that roll forward value and every single person who’s run a business knows that those are essential to your Pareto rule.

*Yeah, you need more levers that you need to pull.*

*MB:* Correct.

*And I think what it sounds like you’re going to end up with is you start out with the caveat that, “Oh, this huge shift is happening with these whales”, but actually you’re going to see, I think probably moving down the curve, just high LTV customers in general are going to get pulled off. It’s going to be like they’re doing the base layer of transactions, like Amazon building out the fulfillment network, and we’ll throw off excess delivery to UPS and FedEx or whatever it might be, that will be the App Store. It’s just sort of like the excess monetization layer for folks that it’s not worth necessarily investing our time in, but all the efforts are going to be in capturing first the 1% of whales, then five, then 10, then 20, then 30. That sounds like that’s going to be a major growth focus going forward.*

*MB:* Yeah. And then the answer would be that the platform intermediaries, especially the App Store and Google Play, are actually being paid a fair rate because for the customers who don’t truly value the product like a five-year, 10-year high ARPU customer-

*They’re worth 30%.*

*MB:* They’re worth 30% because actually, you are the difference between monetizing and not. And by the way, that is how most of the world actually operates, when you’re talking about retail or movie distribution.

*That’s right. You pay huge margins to get it on the shelf because that’s like the customer that couldn’t be bothered to research you or go online to get it, they’re just in the store grabbing something. And that shelf is doing a lot of work for you, so they’re going to take their fair share.*

*MB:* Totally.

*Yeah, that makes sense.*

Memory and Rising Prices

*What impact do you think the memory market’s going to have on gaming? There’s already reports about the PlayStation 6 being delayed. Is this going to accentuate the push to lower end devices ? Do we even need a PlayStation 6? Or have we just sort of, it’s actually okay this is happening because we’ve saturated the quality level for these goods anyway?*

*MB:* Anytime that we’re talking about a increasingly insular no-growth ecosystem, you talked about that on the subscription services fees, but consoles, though by inflation adjusted terms are still broadly cheaper than they’ve been in decades, it’s still a real impediment to ask a family to buy a $449 Switch 2 or $500 PlayStation. None of that’s going to help.

I would make the argument that DRAM has actually had a more severe impact than many people are talking about, and therefore, if you believe it’s going to get worse, it’s going to get much worse.

*How has it had a severe impact so far? With PC gaming in particular?*

*MB:* Actually across the ecosystem. Let’s take a look at Nintendo, Nintendo has said very clearly they’re trying to stave off a price hike and I would make the argument they have already made a price hike. Wii Sports was bundled with the Wii for years, after only three or four months, Nintendo canceled the SKU where Mario Kart Tour was available with the Nintendo Switch for $50 more as a bundle. Now, instead of getting $500 or paying $500 for Mario Kart plus the Switch, you have to get the Switch for $450 and then 80 bucks for Mario Kart. The Switch has not gotten more expensive, but there’s a 90% plus attach rate.

*The actual de facto playing experience.*

*MB:* Correct.

*Yeah, their controller prices have been jacked up.*

*MB:* Controller prices have gone up. And then Nintendo does something, which is basically BYO memory. They keep the price down by asking Ben to buy SD cards for his kids.

*And the great thing is they make it so easy to transfer to new ones. Oh, wait, no they don’t. It’s an unbelievable pain in the rear end.*

*MB:* And Switches are widely shared devices. You have three kids, they share it, but as a result, you may need three different pieces of memory, and those card prices have largely doubled at the higher capacities. And so that’s not all Nintendo, but the whole point is the effective cost of loading a Christmas tree for your kids has gone up.

Sony seems likely, as I mentioned earlier, to increase the price of PlayStation Network in exchange for keeping the PlayStation price down. And Valve, in addition to delaying its new VR headset and its Steam Machine living room device, started by delisting their cheapest Steam Deck handheld, now they’ve delisted all three devices, so you are at minimum unable in the United States to get these. And if they come back, they will probably be more costly. And again, we’re relatively early here.

Now, there’s the galaxy-brain argument, which is what happens when we have freed up hardware and accessories expenditure? Will that shift more people to the PC ecosystem with less of a hurdle in? Will that mean that someone who used to spend $500 on a Switch is now going to spend $200 more on games they already have access to? Who knows? But I think that if we say that the systems have already been pretty severely hit and we’re pretty darn early, it’s going to be rough. This is not what the industry needed.

*Is the Xbox dead ?*

*MB:* As a console platform, the center of attention for Xbox seems to, or for Microsoft seems elsewhere.

*It’s just going to be the world’s biggest game publisher? That’s basically how this is just all going to end up as?*

*MB:* Yeah, I mean, look, the console industry has not been good business for very long. You take a look at Sony, it has 125 million MAUs, they’re the category leader in HD, but their margins are in the mid-to-low teens. It’s terrifying to say you’re the category winner in a third-party living room-locked platform with 100 million MAUs.

*Right. You’re a category winner where you would probably delay your next console knowing that it’s not going to hurt you, and yet you still have terrible margins.*

*MB:* Yeah, and some of this is weird accounting and all the rest of it. But again, we kind of get to this macro theme, which is how sustainable is this market when you say a quarter of PlayStation time roughly is playing Fortnite, the next 15% is Call of Duty, they are cross-platform, your entire business model is on taking a rake on those titles — and for most people we can say that a quarter of PlayStation is Fortnite, but in effect, what it really means is that for a quarter of users, the PlayStation is a Fortnite device, it’s just an access gateway. So all of that really raises this question of, again, where is aggregation in the future, where is value, how sustainable, and how much can you turn the lever on pay-gating access before more and more of that value goes into where the network graph looks?

EA and Sports Rights

*Can you explain the EA take-private deal ? I think you actually had a case for this that was probably more compelling than most, but I’ll let you explain.*

*MB:* Well, I’m not going to say that the price is right or wrong, nor do I have any inside information. My argument was that EA has been very forthright in recent years that they believe in and are attempting to converge live sports and traditional sports fandom into interactive product vertically and horizontally and technologically integrated.

It’s often forgotten that the official name of La Liga right now is La Liga EA Sports. And so when you take into consideration the features and products that they are attempting to build, what they are saying publicly, the amount that they spend on sports licenses and branding, and the fact that by most estimates two-thirds of cash flow and as much as 80% of engagement is their three sports franchises, first and foremost, it seems likely that the long-term goal was to acquire sports rights.

You match that into a business model or a valuation many consider inscrutable and situate that within a buyer that has very clear cultural, athletic, and hybrid fandom aspirations, and then say, “What is a 10-year roadmap, and how does going private enable it?”, I think that the plan is to buy up live sports rights. Would I be surprised if the Saudi League, at least outside of many markets globally, is distributed through EA Sports in five years? That would not surprise me at all. When you’re already paying tier-one leagues to rename themselves after your product, why wouldn’t you buy the co-streaming rights? That doesn’t necessarily mean it’s a good idea, it doesn’t necessarily mean it’s going to pan out, but I suspect that it’s core to that thesis.

*Is this ultimately like a customer acquisition bit, like we’re already paying so much for these leagues? I mean, I get in theory the idea. It just sounds very highly implausible to me.*

*MB:* Well, I mean, look, the implausibility is the tough part.

*I guess it’s interesting for someone to see renting sports rights as a more attractive market than the one that they’re in currently.*

*MB:* Well, first and foremost, there are not many people who can afford these rights globally, or in many markets. We see that — it’s Amazon, it’s Netflix, it’s Apple, it’s sometimes domestic providers, but it’s increasingly the domain of very large, well-capitalized tech companies and those with global cultural ambitions. That fits the Saudi model at large very well. Then on top of that, if you say that we see fundamental convergence in monetization and fandom, ESPN is moving into sports betting more and more every year.

*Right. Is that the long-term play is EA is just a sports betting platform?*

*MB:* I think the answer is — and again, this is where I would make this argument like I’m not really making a conjecture, I’m actually just reading what they’re specifically saying — is they would say that EA Sports is the sports platform. You want to watch, you want to play, you want to bet, you want to simulate, you want to do fantasy, you can do it better here. And because we can amass enough of that engagement defensively, we can then absorb the categories that today are undifferentiated UA [user acquisition] margin battles where FanDuel and DraftKings fight each other to death, Penn National and MGM fight each other to death to acquire the better; we can house it here and get a little bit of leverage, yes, with the leagues, yes, with direct competitors, but also with the fan. I can buy that vision.

AI and the Metaverse

*What’s your current take on AI, I guess the most recent AI impact on gaming? Google releases Project Genie , poor Unity just gets obliterated in the aftermath, I think the CEO is — who I interviewed last year , which I really enjoyed, I thought he was very interesting — is out there, I think, making the reasonable argument, “This is actually going to help, asset generation is actually the huge barrier”, etc., I’m not sure if the market is buying that. What is Matthew Ball buying these days?*

*MB:* This is one of those great examples where it’s like a large Hadron Collider where you’re like — you can come up with all of these different angles, but they’re all going to mash together in a semi-unpredictable way.

Is asset generation a real impediment? No question. Is personalization an opportunity to improve monetization and engagement, stop the loss of player? Of course it is. But if one of the primary problems that you identified is that we have a massive influx of competition, well, we’re going to have way more games. If we’re talking about a central thesis of gaming’s five-year relative loss in the attention economy is the emergence of novel, interactive substitutes, then yes, we can debate whether or not the fidelity and the persistence and the memory of many of these experiences is game-grade.

*It’s attention-grabbing-grade, and that’s all that matters.*

*MB:* Exactly. I’ll tell you, are 12 and 13-year-old boys and girls going to stand up a Genie instance and just explore a weird, immersive environment for fun? Of course they are. I spent five minutes in this fun Genie prompt that someone made, which was a ’90s blockbuster, you and I have not been in a blockbuster for 20 years.

*Right. I want to do that one.*

*MB:* Yeah, everyone I tell is like, “I’ll do that”.

*You had a bit in here about Friday nights. You want a real Friday night experience, that’s what you need to do.*

*MB:* And look, is that scalable? Am I going to do that all the time? No, but it’s a good example of a new thing that we will do.

But first and foremost is, when I talk to most operators, the question isn’t, “Are you going to do Genie as a game engine?” per se, we know that a game engine where the calculations and determinism is essential, there’s no faster, cheaper, or more reliable way to do it than an existing game engine structure, but there are many instances in which it’s too expensive to get those calculations or determinism doesn’t matter, or more importantly, where what will be the end state is teaching these generative AI systems to use UE [Unreal Engine] or Unity or Godot the way that Claude does Python, and then understand, I’m looking over a fence in a shooter game or whichever type of game, and the reproducibility, the accuracy, the pixel precision, the determinism of the physics are not essential.

*It’s a classic disruption thing. It’s a new paradigm that is totally inferior on the metrics that the old paradigm cared about, but that misses the point because that’s not what the market actually is.*

*MB:* Totally. Are there other margins? Yes. Do I think people are going to stand up a Claude instance to do a generative AI model to substitute for Flappy Bird instead of just using a Unity seat and running that locally? No, I don’t think so. That makes no sense.

*Flappy Bird, there’s a blast from the past, play Flappy Bird in your Blockbuster instance. Is the metaverse dead? Last question*

*MB:* I always make this point where I actually think this all starts with Roblox. Roblox files their S-1 in October of 2020. And prior to that, the metaverse had been mentioned 13 times in 30 years in an SEC filing, Roblox uses it 16 times. And they said, “We believe we are in a category described as the metaverse”. Right now there’s about a half billion people who use Roblox every month, it is so popular that in the third quarter, Roblox had 83% of the engagement hours of Netflix globally, and it’s growing up to 70% year over year versus Netflix. That would be one, which is actually the cultural significance. Time, spend, creation, capability is all going asymptotic.

The second thing is the metaverse is kind of adversely affected by two contradictory consequences of terminology. One is it is irreparably associated with VR, which does not sufficiently characterize the metaverse, but people force them together, and second is people absolutely and firmly exclude it from general world models. But when you take a look at [Nvidia CEO] Jensen [Huang] in 2021 or [Microsoft CEO] Satya [Nadella], they say specifically — Jensen says half of the world economy will run through the metaverse. His point was industrial, ubiquitous, persistent, interconnected simulations upon which infrastructure, autonomous vehicles, and robotics will run.

Now, when you say this in 2025, people are like, “God, you’re trying to climb onto the AI hype cycle”, and some of that is compensatory from various actors, but when you actually take a look at how this was originally described before the word became NFTs, crypto, and VR headsets, that was the classical characterization. That is more relevant than ever, it’s why everyone is now focused on general world models. It’s why when you take a look at the video game category, massive licensing fees are happening right now for video game footage and quotidian video game footage because people are now understanding that to simulate the world taking a look at regular, high-fidelity physics interactions of people are likely to be some of the best ways to do that.

So, no, do I think it’s dead spiritually, culturally in terms of player engagement? No. Do I think the term is pretty darn buried? Yeah. So it goes, that’s language.

*So it goes. Matthew Ball, good to talk to you again. Fascinating as always, and look forward — I hope there’s one next year, this was a great one.*

*MB:* Thanks, Ben.

text:
Another AI doomer article has gone viral, and like many in the genre, it lacks an appreciation for dynamism and markets. Then, why DoorDash is going to be fine.

Another Viral AI Doomer Article, The Fundamental Error, DoorDash's AI Advantages

Tuesday, February 24, 2026

Well, I mostly had a good day off; it was a shame to have my weekend vacation interrupted by another absurd piece of AI doomerism. Is this going to be a weekly occurrence?

Meanwhile, on last week’s Sharp Tech , we went deep on memory: the industry’s history, why it’s different than logic, how AI is impacting consumer electronics, and more.

On to the Update:

Another Viral AI Doomer Article

From Bloomberg :

The artificial intelligence “scare trade” erupted again on Monday as growing concerns about the disruptive power of AI dragged down shares of delivery, payments and software companies, and sent International Business Machines Corp. to its worst plunge in 25 years.

It began after a bearish report was published over the weekend by a little known firm called Citrini Research. The report, released on social media Sunday, outlined the potential risks to various segments of the global economy, using hypothetical scenarios set in the future, specifically calling out food delivery services and credit card companies as ones facing trouble.

Then AI startup Anthropic said in a blog post Monday that Claude Code tool can help with modernizing COBOL, a dated programming language that’s mainly run on IBM computers. And finally came a warning from Nassim Taleb: investors should brace for escalating volatility and even bankruptcies in the software sector as the AI rally enters a fragile phase.

IBM shares closed down 13%, the biggest one-day drop since 2000. DoorDash Inc., American Express Co., KKR & Co Inc. and Blackstone Inc. all slumped by at least 6%. Shares of other companies name-checked in the article, including Uber Technologies Inc., Mastercard Inc., Visa Inc., Capital One Financial Corp. and Apollo Global Management Inc. all fell by 4% or more.

“The sole intent of this piece is modeling a scenario that’s been relatively underexplored,” a preface to the article, which was published Sunday, said. “Hopefully, reading this leaves you more prepared for potential left tail risks as AI makes the economy increasingly weird.”

It’s difficult to even know where to start with the Citrini article , which spun a compelling narrative that, under the slightest bit of scrutiny, failed to make any sort of economic sense; there were a host of rebuttals on X — I thought this one from Kira was the best point-by-point takedown.

I did want to mention one of the scenarios that stood out to me:

Even places we thought insulated by the value of human relationships proved fragile. Real estate, where buyers had tolerated 5-6% commissions for decades because of information asymmetry between agent and consumer, crumbled once AI agents equipped with MLS access and decades of transaction data could replicate the knowledge base instantly. A sell-side piece from March 2027 titled it “agent on agent violence”. The median buy-side commission in major metros had compressed from 2.5-3% to under 1%, and a growing share of transactions were closing with no human agent on the buy side at all.

The real estate example makes the exact opposite point that the author thinks it does. The truth is that the Internet already completely obsoleted real estate agents in terms of information flow: you can go online right now and get a listing of every house for sale, with pictures, its full history, etc. There is no information asymmetry, but rather information abundance; the fact that real estate agents still exist despite that shift is actually one of the more compelling arguments that humans will be remarkably resourceful in terms of giving themselves jobs to do even in arenas where they ought to be pointless!

Furthermore, to the extent there has been any sort of compression in commissions, it’s due to the courts making it illegal to tie MLS listings to commission rates; that’s a regulatory change, not an ease-of-writing-software change, which again, makes the point that there is a lot more that goes into the economy than software and compute.

The Fundamental Error

There’s a broader issue with the Article, however, and it’s one that I’m familiar with from another domain. This is the Article’s core assertion:

Over the past fifty years, the U.S. economy built a giant rent-extraction layer on top of human limitations: things take time, patience runs out, brand familiarity substitutes for diligence, and most people are willing to accept a bad price to avoid more clicks. Trillions of dollars of enterprise value depended on those constraints persisting. It started out simple enough. Agents removed friction.

There were a number of examples listed, including the real estate one, which, to be fair, is a rent-extraction layer! It’s the last one, however, that had me scratching my head:

DoorDash was the poster child.

Coding agents had collapsed the barrier to entry for launching a delivery app. A competent developer could deploy a functional competitor in weeks, and dozens did, enticing drivers away from DoorDash and Uber Eats by passing 90-95% of the delivery fee through to the driver. Multi-app dashboards let gig workers track incoming jobs from twenty or thirty platforms at once, eliminating the lock-in that the incumbents depended on. The market fragmented overnight and margins compressed to nearly nothing.

Agents accelerated both sides of the destruction. They enabled the competitors and then they used them. The DoorDash moat was literally “you’re hungry, you’re lazy, this is the app on your home screen.” An agent doesn’t have a home screen. It checks DoorDash, Uber Eats, the restaurant’s own site, and twenty new vibe-coded alternatives so it can pick the lowest fee and fastest delivery every time.

Habitual app loyalty, the entire basis of the business model, simply didn’t exist for a machine.

Set aside, for now, the question of agents and Aggregation; that’s a post that is definitely in my mental queue. What is notable about this assertion is the total denial of any positive reason for DoorDash to exist and to be so successful. There is no awareness that DoorDash provided a massive consumer benefit (restaurant food at home) from scratch, that DoorDash massively increased the addressable market for restaurants (or created an entirely new category of ghost kitchens), or that DoorDash provided brand new jobs for millions of drivers. Instead, the Article just sort of takes it as a given that DoorDash exists, and that it is a rent extractor preying on weak-willed humans and their habits.

This is the exact sort of view taken by some of the most frustrating anti-monopoly activists: all large successful tech companies exist not because they created a market with virtuous cycles, solving all kinds of thorny problems along the way, but rather because the government didn’t regulate hard enough, or something. There is no acknowledgment that people use these platforms because they want to use them, because they solve real problems that aren’t obvious to outsiders (like fraud or refunds), and that everyone on all sides of these platforms are acting in their own self interest. Instead, it’s simply taken as a given that the platform in question is exploitive, and that their profit margins are not a result of earned scale but rather unearned monopoly.

This view — both in the Citrini Article and from the anti-monopolists — is grounded in a fundamental lack of belief in dynamism, human choice, and markets. DoorDash didn’t always exist: it was built, and it wins through the affirmative choice of all three sides of the market it serves (customers, restaurants, and drivers). Does the company have varying degrees of power over different sides of that market based on its dominance of the other sides? Absolutely, but that power flows from delivering value, not from extracting it.

What is lethal about this lack of belief (in dynamism, human choice, and markets), is that it inevitably leads to misplaced prognostication about the future. If the fundamental assumption underlying the analysis is that things are as they are, then one can only envision breaking them; however, if you can see how things developed and changed, then you can have the humility to appreciate how things might develop and change in the future, even in the face of something as potentially disruptive as AI. This Article contains no such appreciation, and certainly — particularly if you have read the authors on X the past few days — no such humility.

In fact, the world is not static: it is dynamic, and we are where we are because of choices made by humans, and the fact that markets actual function. I don’t know what the future will bring, but I do know it will not only be different from today, but definitely different from a linear projection of AI capabilities mapped onto an ossified and simplistic model of the world that bears little resemblance to not just the incredible depth and texture of reality, but also the remarkable adaptability of humanity and the power of markets.

DoorDash’s AI Advantages

OK fine, while I’m here, the DoorDash example is just unbearably dumb. Just consider the list of factors I jotted down last Wednesday that make Shopify an AI winner:

* *Exclusive Data and a Way to Leverage It:* DoorDash not only has the most restaurant data, but also exclusive data in terms of customer order history, delivery routing, etc. All of this can be leveraged to not only make a better product but also in advertising.
* *AI-Driven Market Expansion:* I suspect that one of the qualities that will emerge about AI behavior is that it will take the path of least resistance; that’s why the number one recommended retailer for most AI e-commerce queries is Amazon, even though Amazon doesn’t have any special arrangements with chatbots. Similarly, the most obvious endpoint for food recommendations is going to be DoorDash, not to mention the fact that DoorDash can build its own agents.
* *Interaction with the Physical World:* This is obviously a big one: food delivery actually involves the real world, on all three sides of the market; that means that the difficulty in vibe-coding agents that replace DoorDash is basically cubed.
* *High-Risk Workflows:* Buying food means payments; more generally, money needs to flow to all three sides of the market. This is a benefit for the already trusted intermediary.
* *Pre-Existing Business Model:* DoorDash monetizes as a percentage of the transaction, which is to say they are in the transaction, which is happening whether initiated by an agent or a human. That’s good!
* *Horizontal Coverage:* This one is perhaps less meaningful to DoorDash than it is to Shopify, which covers all parts of a merchant’s business; that’s fine, though, because it is more than made up for by network effects.

DoorDash’s network effects are incredibly powerful, because of the three-sided nature of its market. That is, obviously, much more difficult to displace than a two-sided market, which is harder to displace than internalized network effects like, say, a Google Search (which isn’t exactly easy to displace!). More customers means more orders which means more restaurants which means more drivers, all in a virtuous cycle. Moreover, the payoff of network effects isn’t simply platform stickiness: it’s also structural cost advantages. DoorDash can pay drivers less if they make it up in volume; they can charge restaurants more if they make it up in volume; they can charge users more because they have the best selection and delivery speeds — or, if they need to, they can charge less!

So yes, DoorDash is the poster child, specifically, the poster child for why this Article was absurd, and for how out of control Wall Street is with its AI scare trades (oh, and by the way, almost all of this applies to the credit card companies as well).
