text:
Xbox has a new head, who isn't a gamer; I suspect Microsoft is doing what it should have done a decade ago: get out of the console business.

Xbox Replaces Head of Gaming, Xbox History, Whither Xbox

Wednesday, February 25, 2026

Andrew is on vacation this week; there will be no Sharp Tech.

Over on Asianometry , Jon dives deep into Chip Fabs in Space , and rules it “Technically Possible, Completely Impractical”.

On to the Update:

Xbox Replaces Head of Gaming

From the Wall Street Journal :

Phil Spencer, Microsoft’s executive vice president and chief executive of gaming, is set to retire from the company after 38 years, a run during which he built the company up as a videogames powerhouse only to see it lose ground in recent years. Microsoft has promoted Asha Sharma, president of its CoreAI Product unit, to succeed Spencer as head of Microsoft Gaming, effective immediately, according to the company. Spencer, 58 years old, made the decision to retire last year, Chief Executive Satya Nadella told staff in an email viewed by The Wall Street Journal. He will stay with the company for the next several months through the transition.

There are conflicting reports as to whether Spencer’s decision was truly voluntary; meanwhile, there is a lot of drama around this report in The Verge about why Xbox President Sarah Bond wasn’t promoted to the top role:

Instead of picking Bond for the role, Microsoft promoted Asha Sharma, a former Microsoft AI executive, to the top of Xbox. The decision to overlook Bond might have surprised many Xbox fans, but for the more than a dozen current and former Microsoft employees I’ve been speaking to, it’s felt inevitable in recent months…

The pivot away from console, led by Bond, under Spencer’s direction, hasn’t gone well for Xbox. Microsoft’s Xbox hardware revenue has declined for three financial years in a row, and it looks like those declining revenues are going to continue throughout fiscal 2026. With Spencer’s retirement official, Microsoft is hitting the reset button on Bond’s Xbox strategy instead of embracing it further. Microsoft Gaming CEO Asha Sharma is now promising “the return of Xbox,” in a clear message to employees that the strategy over the past few years has not been working. “I want to return to the renegade spirit that built Xbox in the first place,” says Sharma.

Xbox employees I’ve been speaking to have been concerned about the Sharma appointment, particularly because of her previous role as an AI executive at Microsoft. There is also concern about her lack of industry experience in entertainment and gaming. Sharma has been clear she’s not a gamer and has spent the weekend responding to people on X and even taking game recommendations. Some Xbox employees worry she’ll force AI into everything Xbox does, but Sharma was clearly ready for that reaction. “As monetization and AI evolve and influence this future, we will not chase short-term efficiency or flood our ecosystem with soulless AI slop,” said Sharma in her memo. “Games are and always will be art, crafted by humans, and created with the most innovative technology provided by us.”

Bond defenders have pointed out — correctly — that the “Xbox Everywhere” strategy predated Bond, and I’m sympathetic to claims that this article seemed to be throwing her under the bus. And, to be clear, it does appear that strategy hasn’t succeeded. The person who deserves blame, however, is not Bond, or even Spencer: the ultimate person responsible for the current state of Xbox is Satya Nadella, and before him, Bill Gates and Steve Ballmer.

Xbox History

I have been a mostly consistent critic of the Xbox program, not for Xbox reasons, but for Microsoft reasons. From 2014’s It’s Time to Kill Surface :

It is by focusing on the console world that one arrives at the conclusion that the Xbox, all things considered, is a success and something Microsoft can hang its hat on. In fact, that’s exactly what nearly all Microsoft employees, from executives to rank-and-file, do whenever questioned if Microsoft is innovative. “Look at the Xbox! Look at Kinect!” is their refrain.

The problem is that winning at consoles is a small goal, one wholly different from the reason Xbox was created in the first place. For many years now Microsoft has been focused on “Three Screens and a Cloud,” the idea that they as a platform provider ought to have a presence on your desk, in your pocket, and in your living room, all tied together by the cloud. While that specific formulation arrived somewhere around 2009, that vein of thinking was central to Xbox’s creation; the console aspects were meant to be a trojan horse, giving people a reason-to-buy the Xbox (and not a Playstation); the more computer-type aspects would then be added over time until an Xbox was to living rooms what PCs were to every desk in every office and every home (running Microsoft software).

It was this original goal that contributed to the current Xbox One disaster; Microsoft’s newest console is not only underpowered relative to the PS4, it’s also $100 more expensive (due to the mandatory Kinect), and launched with a terrible wave of publicity surrounding its always-on nature. The Kinect and connectedness were both included to help the Xbox One fulfill its goal of being the primary box in your entertainment system, controlling not just games but also live TV with your voice. Unfortunately, it doesn’t work that well for entertainment, even as it has hurt Microsoft’s ability to compete for console buyers. Thus, Microsoft has spent the last year walking back many of the main features of the console, including its DRM system, its connectedness, and, last week, offering the console without the supposedly essential Kinect to make it $100 cheaper. Now it’s the same price as a PS4, but still less powerful and with the same dark cloud.

Here’s the bigger problem though: even if the Xbox One worked perfectly as an entertainment center, it would still cost $499. For those not good at math, that’s $400 more than an AppleTV, and completely unapproachable for anyone who does not care about gaming. In short, it is not enough to consider how the Xbox is doing relative to consoles; the Xbox must be evaluated based on how it is aligning with and contributing to Microsoft’s overall strategy, and in that light, it is an unmitigated disaster.

This is the Gates and Ballmer angle: Gates’ Xbox strategy was fundamentally flawed; Ballmer’s mistake was in not killing the platform when that flaw was clear. I understand why Ballmer didn’t, however: when I was at Microsoft from 2011–2013 it wasn’t just the Xbox division, but the entire company that held onto Xbox as the sole piece of evidence that the company could be cool and interesting to consumers; it had value as a morale booster, above and beyond the console business.

That meant it fell on Nadella to figure out what to do with the division that served no strategic purpose as merely a console. What is notable is that Nadella’s first big gaming move — buying Minecraft — not only didn’t have anything to do with Xbox, it actually seemed counter to the console concept. From a 2014 Article :

Minecraft, though, isn’t just a great financial decision; it’s a good strategic one as well that fits very nicely with Microsoft’s new vision as outlined by Satya Nadella :

At our core, Microsoft is the productivity and platform company for the mobile-first and cloud-first world. We will reinvent productivity to empower every person and every organization on the planet to do more and achieve more.

At first glance, this statement seems to reference products like Office and Azure, but it also works very well for Minecraft. Minecraft is more than just a game: it’s a community, with a huge cloud component, developers, and, at its very essence, it’s about making things. What could be more productive than that?

Moreover, like Office and Azure, Minecraft is truly cross-platform. It’s the best-selling paid-download game on both iOS and Android, and it also has a very popular PS3 version and a newly-released PS4 version, with a PS Vita port on the way. Xbox head Phil Spencer took care to note that this would remain the case:

Minecraft adds diversity to our game portfolio and helps us reach new gamers across multiple platforms. Gaming is the top activity across devices and we see great potential to continue to grow the Minecraft community and nurture the franchise. That is why we plan to continue to make Minecraft available across platforms – including iOS, Android and PlayStation, in addition to Xbox and PC.

Here’s the thing, though: how much better would this acquisition look if Microsoft didn’t own Xbox at all?

Keep that thought in mind; I — and, I suspect Microsoft — will come back to it shortly. What was important over the last decade, however, is the idea that Microsoft’s strategy under Nadella would be about software and services , which meant if Xbox were going to stick around, it had to fit in that paradigm; that’s where “Xbox Anywhere” came from. I wrote about the shift in this 2021 Update :

Right there is the key terminology shift: you don’t buy an Xbox; rather, you become a member of Xbox. It follows, then, that the definition of an Xbox exclusive is no longer about needing a particular type of hardware, but rather a particular membership. The device is a commodity — at least in theory…

What makes Microsoft unique is that the Xbox was a failure: the original strategic goal was to own the living room, not to simply be a games console, and part of the recent press blitz is the revelation that Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella agreed: when he took over he wondered why the company shouldn’t just get out of the console business altogether. Xbox only made sense if it aligned with where Microsoft was going as a company, which was away from device-centric exclusivity and towards over-arching subscription-based services.

The end result is that Microsoft is uniquely positioned to pursue the cloud gaming opportunity: on one hand, they have genuine video game experience, including the ability to actually produce AAA games, but at the same time they aren’t beholden to the old business model. Quite the opposite, in fact: Xbox is very motivated to get to the new business model sooner rather than later.

And even then it’s really hard. Microsoft still had to invest billions of dollars in the latest generation of consoles, even as it was inevitable that the company would be outsold by Sony; Microsoft still had to invest billions of dollars in buying Zenimax, a price that understates the cost given that making valuable IP exclusive would be short-term value destructive; and, of course, Microsoft actually has to make all of this stuff work across not just its own consoles and PCs (not there yet!) but also across mobile devices and TVs.

I still like the strategy. Sony is going to win this generation, but looking 10 years out it seems likely that Xbox is going to be the default gaming service for some number of exclusives and cross-platform titles, with Sony slowly-but-surely reduced to a Nintendo-type position in the market: you’ll buy it for the exclusives, and perhaps hardware that is superior in specific ways, but it will be more of a second console, not your primary gaming device.

There is a part of me that regrets this last Update: I would be feeling pretty good right now if I could declare an unreserved “I told you so”; at the same time, my optimism about this new strategy was about the long-term — which hasn’t arrived yet — and that’s the biggest thing that has changed for Microsoft.

Whither Xbox

If some of these excerpts look familiar, it’s because I used a few of them in early 2024 when Xbox first announced that some of its games would be published on PlayStation; my take then was that the future of Xbox was as a game publisher and services provider, not as a console maker.

At that point, Microsoft seemed remarkably well-placed in AI: ChatGPT was dominant, and Microsoft had exclusive access to OpenAI models, putting Azure well ahead in the enterprise space. Fast forward two years and ChatGPT is still the biggest consumer AI service by a lot, and Microsoft still has exclusive access to OpenAI models, but those days are numbered; Azure, meanwhile, missed its numbers last quarter as Microsoft focused on its own products. I thought that was the right decision , but the broader takeaway is that Microsoft needs to devote all of its resources, from capex spending to engineering to executive attention, to winning in AI.

Given that, my reaction to this news was immediate and I thought obvious: Spencer was out because Xbox the console was out; a non-gaming executive was being brought in to lead the retreat to being the world’s largest gaming publisher, one that might eventually be spun off. Xbox Game Pass, meanwhile, would eventually be sunset, giving a direct path to recouping the cost of all of those acquisitions via the acquired publishers’ original business model: actually selling games for full price. After all, gaming isn’t growing, so Game Pass wasn’t going to make up for subsidizing whales through volume.

This interview with Sharma and new Chief Content Officer Matt Booty did give me some pause; Sharma said:

Xbox players have thousands of dollars invested, in money and time too — it’s incredibly important for me to understand that and protect that…I am committed to ‘returning to Xbox,’ and that starts with console, that starts with hardware. You will hear more about that soon, we’ll have some announcements coming up. You will see us collectively investing here. We also know that there are a lot of players who aren’t on console or our hardware, and I want to deliver great games to them too. I need to learn more about what that can look like, what decisions were made, what we need to do going forward, and I want a little bit of time and space to do that.

Booty added:

Our studio system is fully built around being first-party. We’re not built to just be a publisher…It is core to our partnership with the Microsoft platform, being involved in early hardware decisions — all the work we’ve done to get games like Gears of War running great on new devices like the Xbox Ally, and so on. It is embedded within our structure, we’re not backing away from that. We’re committed to being a first-party games publisher in partnership with our first-party platform team.

That sounds like a commitment to a console at first glance, but on a second read I think my initial instinct was right. Note that Sharma explicitly calls out players not on an Xbox console; similarly, Booty’s hardware example is the Xbox handheld made by Asus , a third party, not a first-party hardware platform. This was framed in that article as a commitment to a console, but I don’t think it necessarily reads that way at all.

More importantly, however, a commitment to a future console simply doesn’t make sense for Microsoft. The original Xbox strategy stopped making sense a long time ago; the reboot didn’t work, or, if you want to be generous, hasn’t worked yet. Most importantly, Microsoft’s priorities are now elsewhere, and that means that Xbox the console isn’t going to get any more runway. The brand will live on in publishing, and there might be future consoles from 3rd-party OEMs; I am extremely skeptical, however, that Microsoft will make a 1st-party console ever again.

text:
An interview with long-time (retired) VC Bill Gurley about his new book about building a career you love, Uber, and the modern state of VC.

An Interview with Bill Gurley About Runnin' Down a Dream

Thursday, February 26, 2026

This week’s Stratechery Interview is with Bill Gurley . Gurley was a longtime general partner at Benchmark, where he led investments in a host of successful companies, including GrubHub, Nextdoor, OpenTable, Zillow, and, most famously and controversially, Uber. Gurley also maintained a widely-read blog, Above the Crowd , that was a significant influence on Stratechery. Gurley retired from active investing in 2020, and recently wrote a book entitled Runnin’ Down a Dream , which went on sale this week.

Runnin’ Down a Dream is not a memoir, but rather a guide to finding and building a career you love. In this interview we discuss the book, and use it as a lens to examine Gurley’s career, which ran from Compaq Computer to Wall Street to Benchmark. Topics include how the modern educational system is driving kids to burnout, why group chats are more important than you think, and how writing helped Gurley break through. Then, we discuss the Uber conflict between Gurley and founder Travis Kalanick, the changing nature of VC in the era of mega-funds, why the AI model companies are getting into products, and whether or not software is dead.

As a reminder, all Stratechery content, including interviews, is available as a podcast; click the link at the top of this email to add Stratechery to your podcast player.

On to the Interview:

An Interview with Bill Gurley About Runnin’ Down a Dream

This interview is lightly edited for clarity.

*Topics:*

Runnin’ Down a Dream ( #book ) | Principles and Background ( #principles-background ) | Above the Crowd ( #above-the-crowd ) | The Power of the Group Chat ( #group-chat ) | The Uber Dilemma ( #uber ) | The VC Barbell ( #vc )

Runnin’ Down a Dream

*Bill Gurley, welcome to Stratechery.*

*Bill Gurley:* Hey, thanks for having me on, Ben. It’s good to see you.

*Well, I have seen you before, most recently I saw you last fall at a basketball game, I thought you would be attending Florida–Texas today, but I hear you’re a working stiff now, having to do book promotion.*

*BG:* Yeah, I’m selling books 24-7, man. Part of it is I made it this far, this book took me about six years to turn into a book from the presentation , and I invested a lot of time. I don’t think I’ll ever do another one, so I have this internal motivator that’s saying, “You got to give it your all”, so I’m leaving it on the field.

*Well, you’re here for three reasons, which you hinted at. First you have retired as an active partner at Benchmark, which means you’re no longer covered by my somewhat permeable but fairly firm rule about not interviewing active VCs.*

*BG:* Fair enough.

*Second, you’ve published a new book, Runnin’ Down A Dream , just went on sale this week, we’ll have a link in the show notes, that’s going to be the primary topic that we talk about. And finally, I know you still have a lot of takes and opinions about tech. You’ve gotten into the podcasting game recently and boy oh boy is it an interesting and challenging time to have takes and opinions about tech.*

*BG:* Unbelievable time. Unbelievable time.

*So with that as a framework, I always start these interviews with new subjects by talking about their background. And I assumed before I started reading the book that that would basically be the same thing, but it turns out you didn’t really get to yourself in the book until the epilogue, and even then it was shorter than I wanted. So let’s start with this specific angle on the book. What was your goal in writing it and why didn’t you want it to be about your own career and journey?*

*BG:* When I set out to write a book, a lot of, especially in the publishing industry, the agents and the publishers wanted me to write about myself or to write about Uber, or to write about venture capital or investing or tech. And of course with my blog posts over the years on Above the Crowd , I’ve mostly only written about those subjects. And I think even some of the people in the publishing industry, “What do you mean you’re not writing about those things?”, “How could you have the authority to write on something else?”, and it just so happens there’s been this passion project that started as a potential blog post.

When I was reading biographies a decade ago, I just really got into reading biographies, and I saw this through line that I felt was a methodology for achieving success in a career that was different than the philosophies that other people had taught, and I gave it as a video presentation at my alma mater six years ago. A few people noticed, a few important people, like James Clear, who wrote Atomic Habits , which I’ve come to realize is maybe the best-selling personal development book of all time, and that gave me the confidence we could go do this. I hired a co-writer and co-researcher, and we ended up speaking to many of the great writers in this type of category: Adam Grant, Angela Duckworth, Daniel Pink, and James himself. We ended up studying a lot of the academic research, we did some new research of our own, and so there was a lot of intentionality that went into it.

The subject is “Runnin’ Down a Dream””, it’s a book that’s meant to inspire, give the permission to go chase something you love, give you the motivation to go do it and give you the methodology to go do it. It’s really about unlocking human potential. A few people saw that early video and have shared with me stories of how that video transformed their career, literally pivots into new directions and more fulfillment and I was telling someone, I’ve always been a closet American Idol fan, which some people are surprised by. But I love the rags to riches story that comes from something like that and I hope I can help lots and lots of people do that.

One last thing on this, somewhere in the past few years, I read this book, From Strength to Strength from Arthur Brooks, it’s a book really about you’ve reached the end of your career or your working career, “What are you going to do now?”, and it was very motivational to me. I think this book, I think I already proved this based on how well the book’s doing in the past few days, has the potential to touch more, well, way more lives than if I’d written a book about how to be a better VC. So maybe I have the same rule that you do.

*Right, avoid the VC. Obviously from my perspective, my audience’s perspective, that’s the first thing they go to. But you mentioned you think you have a different take, and I’m going to go through the principles that you listed in here. But at a high level, how would you characterize what is different about that take and why is it not out there from your perspective?*

*BG:* I think part of it is that unfortunately the US academic system has evolved to a place that I think creates more stress and determinism than it does provide a place for people to develop curiosity, and I’m not the first person to say that. I think in The Coddling of the American Mind , there’s a chapter by Jonathan Haidt called The Decline of Play, and he talks about the resume arms race. The colleges in the US, everyone knows this, but they haven’t increased enrollment, yet the number of people that want to go to them has gone up and so they’ve all become really hard to get into, which puts even more stress on the children. It used to be that they wouldn’t let you pick a major until the end of your sophomore year and now they insist that you apply to a major before you ever visit the school.

It’s a real transformation about how people used to think about the journey, right? It is just so much more systematic and then the parents get caught up in this, and I think in a very well-intentioned way, they want their kid to be successful, but you start packing their school days to fill the resume. So kids today, and once again, I’m not the first person to say this, are over-scheduled. They’re scheduled like you and I were at the peak of our careers, they wake up and they’ve got lacrosse practice and chess lessons and Spanish lessons, it’s a lot. And anyway, I think they get to the end of that and they’re burnt out and they also feel a lot of sunk costs so they don’t explore a lot of possibilities.

I think that’s part of what has just put, there’s a Gallup survey that shows that 53% of people say they’re not engaged at work in the US, and that’s not ideal, obviously. Now add on that the anxiety of AI.

*Yeah, I was just going to say, now this technology is looming, that it threatens to blow up the entire system.*

*BG:* This wonderful person from Australia wrote this great review of my book, and he hinted at those are the people that are most likely, the people that don’t live a fascinated approach to their career are the ones that are probably most susceptible to the dislocation, and we could get into that more. But anyway, what people will find with my book is a much more, it’s like a how-to manual for a bespoke custom crafting of your career, which is not something a university could really do anyway, they can’t help everyone one by one.

We’re both friends with Mr. Sam Hinkie , who is profiled in the book and when Sam read Moneyball by Michael Lewis, he was a consultant at Bain and he made a decision to go after that, and there’s this great thing in his story where he got accepted into Harvard and Stanford, so everybody doesn’t get that choice, but he visited Harvard before he said which one he said yes to and said, “I want to go be this sports analytics executive”, which didn’t really exist, and they didn’t have a specialty in that, they didn’t have a curriculum in that, he felt like they gave him the hand. But he went to Stanford and they said, “That’s awesome”, they were encouraging of it, they thought of five people they would introduce him to, and I want to help people like that. Someone that comes in with this deterministic mindset to go do something maybe that other people would tell you not to do. The books divided into profiles and principles, and there’s like nine profiles.

*We’re going to go through all them, I have a list of almost all of them.*

*BG:* I want to say one thing on this and I’ll stop. Almost all of them are in fields that your parents would tell you not to chase and that’s very intentional. There’s no VCs, there’s no doctors, there’s no lawyers, there’s nothing like that.

*Or if they’re consultants, they’re ex-consultants.*

*BG:* Exactly.

*Well, to this point, when you think about there’s a certain bit like, “Okay, I wrote a book, I want it to sell, I’m doing podcast after podcasts, I’m going to miss a college game with my buddies that I have courtside seats to to promote this book”, so there’s a competitive aspect, “I want a lot of people to read this”, but if you think about the addressable market and you go back to your career as a VC, markets can be way larger than you expect. You mentioned Uber on one of your all-time blog post taking down the New York University finance professor who sized the opportunity by the taxi market — no, it’s market-expansionary. Is there a bit where your book is actually market-shrinking where you want a lot of people to read it, but actually the real success of this book will be measured by if there’s three people, or four people, who ended up doing extraordinary things like the people in this book because they got off the conveyor belt and did something special?*

*BG:* Look, I don’t think it’s for everybody and especially when you wade into the AI and employment space, some people come at me and go, “Well, you’re going to solve all of the employment dislocation from AI”, and that’s certainly not the calling that caused me to write this. But if people are out there that have this little inkling, this little spark that they love this other thing, but they’re doing this one thing, I want to talk to them.

And you’re right, I think the book will be measured more by the number of people that shift. But what I have found — the video’s been out there for six years — I’ve met people that watched that and found their way to a different place. There’s a gentleman who was a school teacher who saw that, and always wanted a career in football and never had given him self a chance to think he could. Today he has a podcast, he has an application you can download to organize and study offensive plays and he’s well known in the football diaspora by people that cover football, and he called me the other day when the book was coming out to thank me for the video. But this guy’s alive, he’s really alive and doing what he loves.

So yeah, the more people I can do that for, it will be quite fulfilling for me. It’ll make me happy and joyful if I help people find something that is more fulfilling for them.

*One more question before we get to the principles and profiles. All these people are amazing and they’re talented and you mentioned Sam, he was weighing offers between Harvard and Stanford. Is there a baseline level of talent or capability or whatever that is necessary to follow through on these principles you’re laying out?*

*BG:* I think what’s necessary is determination and so you need dogmatic determination and the best way I found to find that is people that do what they love, that stuff comes for free. Because they’re so fascinated by the topic that they read about stuff on their own and they consider it pleasurable. I suspect, I’m just going to go out on one guess here, when Clawdbot happened , Ben Thompson had to go read about it, just had to know about it.

*The example is when I was in Taiwan as an English teacher and I grew up very small town, blue collar, never even occurred to me to work in tech, which I think is a mindset — it’s very hard for people on the coast to even grasp or wrap their minds around. So I’m in Taiwan working as an English teacher, and my wife’s like, “All you do is read about tech and talk about tech all the time, why do you not work in tech?”, and I’m like, “That’s a good question, I should probably go do that” — and what do I do today for a living? I read about and talk about tech.*

*BG:* And smile while you’re doing it, which I think is an important thing. And I don’t go back to the Harvard/Stanford question. *BG:* That’s powerful.

The VC Barbell

*One big change, and this aligned with your career, over the last few years is the shift in VC to massive funds investing everywhere from seed to growth stages. Benchmark, however held during your tenure in particular, held onto a more traditional model, smaller fund sizes. Is that still viable?*

*BG:* I don’t know. Candid question, the industrialization of venture capital is a real thing and the largest funds are now raising fund sizes and assets under management that rival Apollo and the PE funds, and they are doing things by encouraging companies to stay private forever that dramatically change the landscape of venture capital and maybe permanently, I don’t know. But to suggest that that’s not real would be crazy.

I do think that once you start behaving in that way and start writing checks at $500 million or $1 billion and having to raise money and manage money of that size your fidelity to care about the $5 million seed or Series A, it gets hard. I don’t think your best people in your organization can be aware of what that means because there’s all these other priorities and obligations now. So I think it’ll still be possible to compete primarily in the early stage and be successful, but you’re going to have to find a way to deal with the reality.

There is a crazy thing happening right now where the majority of rounds that are done in venture capital are proactive. So any successful company, these mega funds are demanding you take money. It’s almost like you have multiple [Softbank founder and CEO] Masa’s out there, and I lived this Masa thing in Uber/Lyft. I lived companies being overfunded intentionally and the things that causes from a company evolution standpoint and understanding unit economics, I think it’s mostly bad for the evolution of these companies. They’re forced to become real grown-ups and kings before — it reminds me of Game of Thrones where the 14-year-old has told they’re king, that’s what’s happening in almost every one of these fields. It’s not just Uber/Lyft now, it’s almost every successful venture company.

*The Uber/Lyft is a precursor of what’s going to happen.*

*BG:* Yeah, and $2 billion a year is not the biggest burn rate anymore, I thought that was crazy. Now, they’re bigger than that, so the field has definitely changed.

*I was going to ask about how much of a problem it is about fewer companies going public and you have this acquisition being frozen and this weird acquihire thing. You mentioned though that these large funds are almost predicated on keeping companies private, which one is it?*

*BG:* Oh, I think they’ve discovered a very clever — first of all, one thing your audience would fully understand and obviously, you would as well, part of what’s happened is there are things that we talk about. We use network effects, increasing returns, power laws, we use these words now and we see these Mag 7, and so part of what’s happened is everyone’s become educated at power laws and so if these large funds think this is one of those companies, they’re willing to pay a really, really high price relative to history because they’ve seen that that would still work out over time.

Now, there’s a question. If everyone believes in power laws, could that get priced into the market? Of course it could, and maybe that’s what we’re about to watch. But the amount of money they’re forcing into these companies creates a burn rate and an aggressiveness of growing the company that I don’t think is healthy. I really don’t, but it is where we are.

*Do any of these apply to the AI model companies?*

*BG:* Yes! And look, you don’t get to choose to be pragmatic like, “Oh, your competitor is going to raise $2 billion”, well, “You’re only going to hire five salespeople? No one’s going to know who you are!”, so sport of kings.

*Yeah. Are these AI model companies, do they have power laws? Are they going to be profitable or are like, what’s your prognosis?*

*BG:* You write about this more than I do. I think both OpenAI and Anthropic, most likely because of the success of the open source models with developers realized that just being a mid-layer model company who was risky, and you’ve seen this shift in Anthropic more than you see it OpenAI, but I think they both decided they had to connect directly with customers. And Anthropic’s last 12 months has been a real exercise in that even competing with some of their best customers.

*Well, that’s the question. Does AI mean VC is back, or does the fact that the model companies realize they have to go into the application layer mean that it’s going to be rough sledding?*

*BG:* We’re going to see, I think there’s going to be a lot of interesting experiments. I love to highlight something you know is true, which is in the beginning of the Internet, everyone started on Sun and Oracle and five years later, they were all on Linux and MySQL and I do think the optimization — in a period of a new breakthrough, everyone wants the best product. No one’s focused on unit economics, everyone’s focused on market share, but one day, and maybe you have to have a crash before this even happens, but I know some of it’s already happening. People start thinking about optimization and Benchmark’s an investor in Fireworks and Cerebras, we’re seeing people move towards optimization and then they experiment and try different things.

One of the companies, Anthropic’s obviously now targeting that, was a customer, is Cursor, and I can assure you Cursor’s playing around with other models because of what Anthropic’s doing to them. And so, you end up in the optimization phase doing things differently than you did, and I don’t think we know yet, I think we’re going to watch it play out.

*Is software dead ?*

*BG:* I doubt it. I think it’s really unlikely, and someone highlighted all the companies Anthropic’s actually paying seat licenses for, the notion that you would build your own ledger for financials is really stupid because the auditors have to come in and touch the thing and there needs to be systematic equivalents with other companies and there’d be no reason for everyone to be on their own bespoke version of that. It would make the auditor’s job ridiculously hard and so, I don’t think so.

*Is there a bit though where SaaS was so easy and so cookie cutter that — you mentioned you focused on the art of VC being an artisan.*

*BG:* Yeah.

*Did the whole industry almost lose that because it got so cookie cutter for an era and now that’s being blown up? Even if no one is ripping out these systems they’re maybe not worth the multiples that they had.*

*BG:* Look, that gets back into some classic learning you’d get if you studied the history of finance and Warren Buffett and this kind of thing. Like stocks, I’ve always believed this, most people in Silicon Valley don’t, are best valued using this kind of cashflow models, not PEs or these kind of things. If you do that, you recognize that if a company has a-

*Terminal values matter!*

*BG:* Yeah, it’s all in the terminal value. And so if all of a sudden, someone, whether it’s an Uber’s case with autonomous or with SaaS, if they think you might not be around in 20 or 30 years, you can see some aggressive multiple compression, really aggressive, and that’s what we’ve seen.

I do think that if you believe SaaS is going to be okay, you shouldn’t be out on Twitter saying that you’re upset or that people got it wrong. You should be raising money and buying stocks, be fearful when others are greedy and greedy when others are fearful.

*Is this actually one of the biggest PE opportunities of all time?*

*BG:* It might be.

*Because all the PEs that were doing SaaS before they bought too high, but now, you can walk in and buy all these companies at a fraction of what they were.*

*BG:* I love that idea and I think you want to look at pricing models.

*If you come in, by the way, how do you fix the stock-based compensation problem? You lay off a bunch of people, that’s going to fix the problem.*

*BG:* I love how you’re thinking. Man, I’m sure there’s PE people that are hearing this and they’re like, “That’s exactly what I’ve been saying internally”. That’s very clever, I think that’s right. I was going to make one point, there are clearly systems that are more wiped out by AI than others, depending on the exact set thing that you do, but you can apply that analysis and AI will help you do that analysis, which is funny.

*For sure, I actually think it’s a massive opportunity. I just don’t know for sure, if I want to be the guy going in and lay a bunch of people off.*

*Is Above the Crowd dead? You did post about your book, but the last post before that was in 2022.*

*BG:* Yeah, probably, but mainly just because, well, here’s where I would say, let’s go see. I do find the ability to use video and podcasting way more efficient to share ideas.

*For sure. Writing’s hard, believe me, I feel the pain.*

*BG:* Yeah. I don’t spend as much time preparing them maybe as I should, but I do find it more efficient and I’ve told a few people this, but after I birth this book and get it moving on its way, I’m going to go do a policy institute, it’s going to be called P3. It has a very specific objective function. But as part of that, I want to synthesize ideas and convey them, use that tool that I’ve learned over the years.

*You sure we’re not going to get a memoir? I’d still read the memoir.*

*BG:* Ah, no, the epilogue’s pretty good. You didn’t like the epilogue in the book?

*The entire VC part was one paragraph. I need more!*

*BG:* (laughing) It’s all good, man.

*You can come here and do a podcast about it.*

*BG:* Fair enough.

*Bill Gurley, it’s great to talk to you.*

*BG:* Good to see you, sir. Thank you.

*Congratulations on writing a book! I’m a blog writer, never written a book, so maybe I’ll have to wait until I retire and I can do the same as you.*

*BG:* I had some help and we took a very long time. I think about it like people say, “Why was Hootie & the Blowfish first album so good?” — they toured the southeast playing frat houses for 10 fucking years! They played those songs forever, and I think writing a second book would be really hard.

*Yeah. Second albums are tough too.*

*BG:* (laughing) Yeah.

*Thank you very much.*

text:
Anthropic is in a standoff with the Department of War; while the company's concerns are legitimate, it position is intolerable and misaligned with reality.

Anthropic and Alignment

Monday, March 2, 2026

*Just because you do not take an interest in politics doesn’t mean politics won’t take an interest in you.
* ― Pericles

This is not an Article about the campaign being waged by the U.S. against Iran, but it’s a useful — and timely — analogy. There is a never-ending debate that can be had about the concept of International Law and who might be violating it. Some will argue that the U.S. is in violation for the attacks; others will note that Iran has been serially violating International Law with both its overt actions and its support of terror networks for my entire life.

What is important to note is that the entire debate is ultimately pointless: the very concept of “international law” is fake, not because pertinent statutes and agreements don’t exist, but because their effectiveness is ultimately rooted in their enforceability. That, by extension, means there must be an entity to enact such enforcement, with the capability to match, and such an entity does not exist.

Yes, there is the United Nations, but said body only operates by the agreement of its members, and their willingness to subjugate themselves to not only its edicts, but to also put forward the capabilities to enforce its mandates. In other words, the only agents that matter are nation states themselves, and the relative power of those nation states is not a function of lawyers and judges but rather their ability to project force and coerce others.

To put it another way, if, after this weekend, you want to hold onto the concept of International Law, then realize the debate has been resolved: Iran was in violation, because their military just had their clock cleaned by the U.S., which means the U.S. decides who is right and who is wrong.

Anthropic vs. The Department of War

While most of the U.S. and certainly the rest of the world were preoccupied with the happenings in Iran, another fervent debate has been ongoing in tech. Once again one of the parties is the United States itself, but the other entity in question is a private company, Anthropic. From the Wall Street Journal :

The federal government will stop working with Anthropic and designate the artificial intelligence company a supply-chain risk, a dramatic escalation of the government’s clash with the company over how its technology can be used by the Pentagon. While Anthropic’s relationship with the administration hit a new low, rival OpenAI said late Friday that it reached an agreement with the Defense Department to have its models used in classified settings, until recently a status only held by Anthropic. Friday’s quick-fire developments between the Pentagon and two Silicon Valley darlings are poised to shape the future of how the federal government and, particularly the Pentagon, uses cutting-edge AI tools.

Anthropic staked out its position earlier in the week in a Statement from Dario Amadei on [its] discussions with the Department of War :

In a narrow set of cases, we believe AI can undermine, rather than defend, democratic values. Some uses are also simply outside the bounds of what today’s technology can safely and reliably do. Two such use cases have never been included in our contracts with the Department of War, and we believe they should not be included now:

* *Mass domestic surveillance.* We support the use of AI for lawful foreign intelligence and counterintelligence missions. But using these systems for mass domestic surveillance is incompatible with democratic values. AI-driven mass surveillance presents serious, novel risks to our fundamental liberties. To the extent that such surveillance is currently legal, this is only because the law has not yet caught up with the rapidly growing capabilities of AI. For example, under current law, the government can purchase detailed records of Americans’ movements, web browsing, and associations from public sources without obtaining a warrant, a practice the Intelligence Community has acknowledged raises privacy concerns and that has generated bipartisan opposition in Congress. Powerful AI makes it possible to assemble this scattered, individually innocuous data into a comprehensive picture of any person’s life—automatically and at massive scale.
* *Fully autonomous weapons.* Partially autonomous weapons, like those used today in Ukraine, are vital to the defense of democracy. Even fully autonomous weapons (those that take humans out of the loop entirely and automate selecting and engaging targets) may prove critical for our national defense. But today, frontier AI systems are simply not reliable enough to power fully autonomous weapons. We will not knowingly provide a product that puts America’s warfighters and civilians at risk. We have offered to work directly with the Department of War on R&D to improve the reliability of these systems, but they have not accepted this offer. In addition, without proper oversight, fully autonomous weapons cannot be relied upon to exercise the critical judgment that our highly trained, professional troops exhibit every day. They need to be deployed with proper guardrails, which don’t exist today.

To our knowledge, these two exceptions have not been a barrier to accelerating the adoption and use of our models within our armed forces to date.

The Department of War has stated they will only contract with AI companies who accede to “any lawful use” and remove safeguards in the cases mentioned above. They have threatened to remove us from their systems if we maintain these safeguards; they have also threatened to designate us a “supply chain risk” — a label reserved for US adversaries, never before applied to an American company — and to invoke the Defense Production Act to force the safeguards’ removal. These latter two threats are inherently contradictory: one labels us a security risk; the other labels Claude as essential to national security.

Regardless, these threats do not change our position: we cannot in good conscience accede to their request.

I actually didn’t realize before this episode that the National Security Agency (NSA) is a part of the Department of War; that certainly provides useful context around the surveillance point. And, as we saw a decade ago with the Snowden revelations, the NSA can be both aggressive and creative in its interpretations of what is legal in terms of surveillance. One might have hoped that telecom companies in particular might have taken a stand like Anthropic did.

At the same time, what is the standard by which it should be decided what is allowed and not allowed if not laws, which are passed by an elected Congress? Anthropic’s position is that Amodei — who I am using as a stand-in for Anthropic’s management and its board — ought to decide what its models are used for, despite the fact that Amodei is not elected and not accountable to the public.

And, on the second point, who decides when and in what way American military capabilities are used? That is the responsibility of the Department of War, which ultimately answers to the President, who also is elected. Once again, however, Anthropic’s position is that an unaccountable Amodei can unilaterally restrict what its models are used for.

It’s worth noting that there are reports that Anthropic’s concerns may be broader than just fully autonomous weapons; from Semafor :

Anthropic is one of the few “frontier” large language models available for classified use by the US government because it is available through Amazon’s Top Secret Cloud and through Palantir’s Artificial Intelligence Platform, which is how its Claude chatbot ended up appearing on the screens of officials who were monitoring the seizure of then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro…

Soon after the Maduro raid, during a regular check-in that Palantir holds with Anthropic, an Anthropic official discussed the operation with a Palantir senior executive, who gathered from the exchange that the AI startup disapproved of its technology being used for that purpose. The Palantir executive was alarmed by the implication of Anthropic’s inquiry that the company might resist the use of its technology in a US military operation, and reported the conversation back to the Pentagon, a senior Defense Department official said.

Anthropic denied it objected to whatever involvement Claude may have had in the Maduro raid, but the Semafor story resonates given the trend in some tech circles to resist any involvement in military operations. And, to that end, one could argue that this stand-off is ending as it should: Anthropic and its models will be removed from the Department of War tech stack, and an alternative will take their place.

North Korea and Nuclear Weapons

Amodei has been outspoken about other aspects of AI and national security; from Bloomberg in January :

Anthropic Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei said selling advanced artificial intelligence chips to China is a blunder with “incredible national security implications” as the US moves to allow Nvidia Corp. to sell its H200 processors to Beijing. “It would be a big mistake to ship these chips,” Amodei said in an interview with Bloomberg Editor-in-Chief John Micklethwait at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland. “I think this is crazy. It’s a bit like selling nuclear weapons to North Korea.”

This rather raises the stakes of a messy procurement decision: consider the implications if we take Amodei’s analogy literally.

Start with Iran: beyond the fact that Iran has been responsible for the deaths of thousands of Americans throughout the Middle East and beyond, one of the arguments for the U.S. intervention is that Iran continues to pursue nuclear weapons capabilities. It’s North Korea that shows why: North Korea doesn’t need to buy nuclear weapons, because they already have them, and it certainly makes any sort of potential military action against them considerably more complicated. Nuclear weapons make you an effective lawyer in the (nonexistent 1 ( #fn1-18410 ) ) court of international law!

In short, nuclear weapons meaningfully tilt the balance of power; to the extent that AI is of equivalent importance is the extent to which the United States has far more interest in not only what Anthropic lets it do with its models, but also what Anthropic is allowed to do period.

This, I think, gives important context to the designation of Anthropic as a supply chain risk. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth said on X :

In conjunction with the President’s directive for the Federal Government to cease all use of Anthropic’s technology, I am directing the Department of War to designate Anthropic a Supply-Chain Risk to National Security. Effective immediately, no contractor, supplier, or partner that does business with the United States military may conduct any commercial activity with Anthropic.

This would decimate Anthropic: at a bare minimum the company relies on cloud hosting from AWS, Microsoft, and Google, all of which have contracts with the Department of War; I imagine the same applies to Nvidia. Fortunately for the company, Hegseth’s declaration does seem out of step with the law , which limits Hegseth’s authority to work covered by U.S. government contracts; in other words, AWS could still serve Anthropic models, as long as it doesn’t use Anthropic models for any of its services offered to the U.S. government.

Regardless, this is an extreme measure that has been met with near universal dismay, even amongst people who are sympathetic to the idea that a private company should not have veto power over the U.S. military. Why would the U.S. government want to kneecap one of its AI champions?

In fact, Amodei already answered the question: if nuclear weapons were developed by a private company, and that private company sought to dictate terms to the U.S. military, the U.S. would absolutely be incentivized to destroy that company. The reason goes back to the question of international law, North Korea, and the rest:

* International law is ultimately a function of power; might makes right.
* There are some categories of capabilities — like nuclear weapons — that are sufficiently powerful to fundamentally affect the U.S.’s freedom of action; we can bomb Iran, but we can’t North Korea.
* To the extent that AI is on the level of nuclear weapons — or beyond — is the extent that Amodei and Anthropic are building a power base that potentially rivals the U.S. military.

Anthropic talks a lot about alignment; this insistence on controlling the U.S. military, however, is fundamentally misaligned with reality. Current AI models are obviously not yet so powerful that they rival the U.S. military; if that is the trajectory, however — and no one has been more vocal in arguing for that trajectory than Amodei — then it seems to me the choice facing the U.S. is actually quite binary:

* Option 1 is that Anthropic accepts a subservient position relative to the U.S. government, and does not seek to retain ultimate decision-making power about how its models are used, instead leaving that to Congress and the President.
* Option 2 is that the U.S. government either destroys Anthropic or removes Amodei.

Note that I’m not making the (very good) argument put forward by Anduril founder Palmer Luckey about the importance of democratic oversight; Luckey wrote on X :

This gets to the core of the issue more than any debate about specific terms. Do you believe in democracy? Should our military be regulated by our elected leaders, or corporate executives?…

The fact that this is a debate over AI does not change the underlying calculus. The same problems apply to definitions and use of ethically fraught but important capabilities like surveillance systems or autonomous weapons. It is easy to say “But they will have cutouts to operate with autonomous systems for defensive use!”, but you immediately get into the same issues and more — what is autonomous? What is defensive? What about defending an asset during an offensive action, or parking a carrier group off the coast of a nation that considers us to be offensive?

At the end of the day, you have to believe that the American experiment is still ongoing, that people have the right to elect and unelect the authorities making these decisions, that our imperfect constitutional republic is still good enough to run a country without outsourcing the real levers of power to billionaires and corpos and their shadow advisors. I still believe. And that is why “bro just agree the AI won’t be involved in autonomous weapons or mass surveillance why can’t you agree it is so simple please bro” is an untenable position that the United States cannot possibly accept.

Again, I think this is a good argument; the one I am putting forward, however, is much more basic and brutal, and doesn’t have anything to do with belief or not in the American experiment (although I’m with Luckey in that regard): it simply isn’t tolerable for the U.S. to allow for the development of an independent power structure — which is exactly what AI has the potential to undergird — that is expressly seeking to assert independence from U.S. control.

Complex Systems

I don’t, for the record, want Anthropic to be destroyed, and I want them to be a U.S. AI champion. I also, for the record, don’t trust Amodei’s judgment in terms of either national security or AI security.

In terms of national security, I already commented on Amodei’s Davos comments on X :

Last year I laid out in AI Promise and Chip Precariousness why I believed a systemic view of the U.S.-China rivalry entailed some painful tradeoffs when it came to chips and China:

The important takeaway that is relevant to this Article is that Taiwan is the flashpoint in both scenarios. A pivot to Asia is about gearing up to defend Taiwan from a potential Chinese invasion or embargo; a retrenchment to the Americas is about potentially granting — or acknowledging — China as the hegemon of Asia, which would inevitably lead to Taiwan’s envelopment by China.

This is, needless to say, a discussion where I tread gingerly, not least because I have lived in Taipei off and on for over two decades. And, of course, there is the moral component entailed in Taiwan being a vibrant democracy with a population that has no interest in reunification with China. To that end, the status quo has been simultaneously absurd and yet surprisingly sustainable: Taiwan is an independent country in nearly every respect, with its own border, military, currency, passports, and — pertinent to tech — economy, increasingly dominated by TSMC; at the same time, Taiwan has not declared independence, and the official position of the United States is to acknowledge that China believes Taiwan is theirs, without endorsing either that position or Taiwanese independence.

Chinese and Taiwanese do, in my experience, handle this sort of ambiguity much more easily than do Americans; still, gray zones only go so far. What has been just as important are realist factors like military strength (once in favor of Taiwan, now decidedly in favor of China), economic ties (extremely deep between Taiwan and China, and China and the U.S.), and war-waging credibility. Here the Ukraine conflict and the resultant China-Russia relationship looms large, thanks to the sharing of military technology and overland supply chains for oil and food that have resulted, even as the U.S. has depleted itself. That, by extension, gets at another changing factor: the hollowing out of American manufacturing under Pax Americana has been directly correlated with China’s dominance of the business of making things, the most essential war-fighting capability.

Still, there is — or rather was — a critical factor that might give China pause: the importance of TSMC. Chips undergird every aspect of the modern economy; the rise of AI, and the promise of the massive gains that might result, only make this need even more pressing. And, as long as China needs TSMC chips, they have a powerful incentive to leave Taiwan alone.

The key thing to consider is the opposite scenario: cutting China off from advanced chips doesn’t just reduce the likelihood that Chinese companies are dependent on a U.S.-based ecosystem, it also reduces the cost of destroying TSMC. More than that, if AI becomes as capable as Amodei says it will — the equivalent, or more, of nuclear weapons — then it actually becomes game theory optimal for China to do exactly that: if China can’t have AI, then it is, at least under current circumstances, relatively easy to make sure that nobody does.

Amodei is, as the quote above notes, cognizant of China as a threat generally; it concerns me that he consistently fails to acknowledge that the implication of his recommended course of action in terms of chip controls is to risk destroying AI for everybody.

Then again, Amodei isn’t really a fan of AI for everybody: he and Anthropic have been vocal opponents of open source models, and were major drivers of what I considered a very misguided Biden executive order about AI . Like the Taiwan situation, I think these positions evince a failure to think systematically:

* First, were there only closed AI systems, then unimaginable power would be vested in the owners of those systems; it seems that Amodei thinks that power should be wielded by him (at a minimum, I would prefer that be wielded by the U.S. government).
* Second, the idea that AI safety can only be guaranteed by a limited number of responsible stewards ignores the massive incentives that exist to build other models. This was clear years ago when only a few companies were working on AI models, and has been proven out by what has happened in reality so far.
* Third, in a world of AI proliferation, the best defense against AI will be AI; this means that more AI is actually safer than limited AI, which means open source is ultimately safer.

There is certainly room for disagreement on these points; what concerns me about Amodei and Anthropic in particular is the consistent pattern of being singularly focused on being the one winner with all of the power, with limited consideration of how everyone else may react to that situation. Or, to be more blunt, the reality that other people exist and they have guns and missiles and yes, nuclear weapons. Might still makes right, and I personally would rather not hand over the future of humanity to a person and a company that seems to consistently forget that fact.

Who to Entrust

I do think this post on X from Ramez Naam is the most optimistic way to frame the debate this weekend:

I do have tremendous discomfort about AI’s surveillance capabilities in particular; there are a lot of safeguards we thought we had that were actually mostly due to the friction entailed in overcoming them. AI, even more than computers and the Internet, is a friction solvent, and I completely understand why Anthropic’s pushback on this specific point resonates broadly.

The way to address this new reality, however, is with new laws and through strengthening accountable oversight; cheering or even demanding that an unelected executive decide how and where such powerful capabilities can be used is the road an even more despotic future.

Our adversaries, meanwhile, will certainly be developing autonomous fighting capabilities (and yes, I admit my chip prescriptions make this more likely much sooner — tradeoffs are hard!); the U.S. will need to move in this direction if we are to remain the ultimate source of international law. And, by the U.S., I mean a democratically elected President and Congress, not a San Francisco executive. I don’t want that, and, more pertinently, the ones with guns aren’t going to tolerate it. Anthropic needs to align itself with that reality.

*

Yes, The Hague exists; its subject to all of the same limitations as the United Nations ↩︎ ( #rf1-18410 )

text:
Why government is not the primary customer for tech companies, and is Netflix relieved that they were outbid for Warner Bros.?

Technological Scale and Government Control, Paramount Outbids Netflix for Warner Bros.

Tuesday, March 3, 2026

I jumped on TBPN to discuss the situation between Anthropic and the U.S. government.

On to the Update:

Technological Scale and Government Control

If there was one thing I wish I had changed about yesterday’s Article Anthropic and Alignment , it would have been to add what I thought was an obvious caveat: my goal was not to endorse what happened between the U.S. government and Anthropic, but rather to analyze. I felt so much of the discussion over the weekend was getting mired in the weeds about what exactly Anthropic objected to, or what OpenAI agreed to, that a much more fundamental point — one I’ve been concerned about for a long time now — was getting lost.

Specifically, if AI is going to be as powerful as its advocates say it’s going to be, then it is going to attract the attention of government; moreover, that government is not only going to seek to control AI, but if it can’t, it’s going to seek to destroy it. This isn’t a normative statement about whether this is good or bad (and, as many folks who were confused by my take accurately noted, of course I think that government interference in private companies is usually bad): it’s an analysis that it is. It certainly isn’t very fun to be called a fascist or a bootlicker or what have you for making this point, but I don’t regret it, because I don’t think I’m making a prediction: I think it’s the way to make sense of what happened last week, and if people start taking this reality seriously I think we will end up in a better place.

There is one extra historical point I wanted to make about the nuclear analogy. The American government famously developed the atomic bomb under the auspices of the Manhattan Project; in other words, nuclear power started under government control, and for that reason there has never been any question as to whether or not government has control. This wasn’t an oddity: who else, other than the government, was going to spend an (inflation-adjusted) $36 billion for a military weapon in the 1940s?

Where things changed was with chips and Bob Noyce. While much of Fairchild Semiconductor’s early work was for the military — the only buyers in the earliest days — Noyce increasingly turned down design commissions from the military in the later years of Fairchild and when he left to found Intel. Part of it was that accepting R&D money from the government meant the government got your IP; part of it was that Noyce was convinced that the government market would be dwarfed in size by the civilian market, and, given the nearly zero marginal cost nature of chips, pursuing the latter would not only be far more profitable, but would actually drive far more demand in the long run, thanks to the lower prices that would come from scale, and ultimately result in much more innovation in both computers and chips themselves.

That’s exactly what happened: by the late 1960s the civilian market was buying more chips than the government, and the lion’s share of those chips were from Fairchild; fast forward to the 1980s and the military embarked on a massive modernization program that was predicated on leveraging civilian technology — which was far ahead of the military’s technology — to make an entirely new generation of weapons. For chips, volume and demand mattered far more than the military’s need; that need was actually best met by buying off-the-shelf.

AI has this dynamic on steroids: the cost of training these models is so large that the amount of investment only makes sense if the market is massive, which is why these models are being developed by private companies on clouds owned by private companies using chips made by other private companies. The military — which was the only customer and thus only funder of nuclear weapons in the 1940s — is just another customer of many, which is actually a good thing: by using privately-developed AI the military gets access to much more capable and rapidly advancing AI than they would if they funded it themselves.

The rub, of course, was yesterday’s Article: AI has the potential to be so powerful that, even though the government didn’t fund its development and isn’t the largest customer, it will still demand control of it, or, at a minimum, to have unfettered access to it. This is a lot more complicated than the nuclear question, where government control and ownership was a given; the sort of actions taken by the government over the last week fly in the face of the concept of private decision making and property rights. Unfortunately, those rights are not set in stone: they are ultimately enforced by someone, and the someone who is doing the enforcement is the one doing the violating. That’s not great, but it’s happening and/or will happen, and it’s important to come to grips with that reality — and I don’t think trying to describe that is at all equivalent to endorsing it.

Paramount Outbids Netflix for Warner Bros.

From the Wall Street Journal :

Paramount Skydance emerged victorious in the bidding war for Warner Bros. Discovery after Netflix said it wouldn’t match the David Ellison-led company’s latest offer for the iconic Hollywood property. Netflix pulled the plug on its deal soon after the Warner board of directors said it determined Paramount’s $31-per-share offer for the entire company was superior to Netflix’s bid for Warner’s movie and television studios and HBO Max streaming service. Paramount is now poised to take control of the entertainment company, home to properties and brands including HBO, Superman and Harry Potter.

“We’ve always been disciplined, and at the price required to match Paramount Skydance’s latest offer, the deal is no longer financially attractive, so we are declining to match,” Netflix co-Chief Executives Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters said. “This transaction was always a ‘nice to have’ at the right price, not a ‘must have’ at any price,” the pair said.

Pending regulatory approval, Paramount will own not only Warner Bros. and HBO, but also many popular cable networks including CNN, TNT, TBS and Food Network. The deal would represent a ground shift for the entertainment industry, which is trying to adapt to seismic shifts in audience habits and technology.

Sarandos told Lucas Shaw in an interview on Bloomberg that Netflix wasn’t concerned about regulatory issues or stock market skepticism of Netflix’s planned acquisition; this was simply a matter of the price being too high.

It’s hard to take that entirely at face value; Netflix has been in the spotlight in Washington like never before as a company, and it’s pretty telling that the stock jumped so significantly upon news that Netflix lost the deal. I don’t buy the narrative that this was all a play to make Paramount pay more than they might have otherwise, but at the same time, I can imagine that there was some amount of relief that accompanied stepping away from this acquisition.

The folks that should be considerably more worried is the rest of Hollywood; Paramount is promising $6 billion in synergies by the end of 2029, which is a fancy M&A word for a massive amount of layoffs. That is certainly ambitious, but it’s also worth pointing out that there will in fact be more synergies than normal because this is very much a horizontal acquisition: Paramount and Warner Bros. are in all the same businesses.

That, by extension, raises the antitrust question. Netflix’s proposed acquisition certainly had some horizontal components — particularly the fact that the leading paid streaming service (excluding YouTube, which you can of course subscribe to) was acquiring a competitor — but it was also fairly vertical in nature: Netflix was a distributor buying a supplier. Per the previous point, however, Warner Bros. and Paramount not only have rival streaming services, but also both have linear cable networks, studios, theatrical arms, etc. This is very much consolidation, not vertical integration, which means it should raise considerably more antitrust scrutiny.

That noted, my initial thought is that the acquisition should be allowed to move forward; consolidation is the natural response in an industry in secular decline. To put it another way, the same caveats that applied to Netflix apply to Paramount and Warner Bros.: the actual competitive space is time and attention broadly, and the biggest threats to both actually stem from the fact that anyone on earth can be a creator.

And frankly, the biggest evidence that this is the real source of pressure was the fact that Netflix attempted this deal in the first place; Netflix has the structural advantage in terms of buying professionally-produced content, but the company felt the need to pull forward the end game because, I suspect, it worried about just how much attention there might be left to win whenever it arrives. Now, though, it will have to wait for nature — and Paramount’s debt load — to run its course. To quote from the end of Sarandos’ interview with Shaw:

*If you feel like this is a rare asset, that also means that an asset like this may not come up again anytime soon, right?*

*TS:* Possibly. Or if you look at the history of Warner Bros….

Maybe the real win will be Netflix saving on integration costs by being able to incorporate both Paramount and Warner Bros. at the same time some time in the next decade.
