text:
An Interview with Eric Seufert about building models for generative AI, why Meta's foundational models are so important, and why understanding advertising leads to optimism about humanity's future.

An Interview with Eric Seufert About Models and Ads, and AI’s Upside for Humanity

Thursday, May 28, 2026

This week’s Stratechery Interview is with Eric Seufert . Seufert is, in my opinion, the world’s pre-eminent digital advertising analyst, and Stratechery’s most frequent interview subject . Seufert writes full-time at MobileDevMemo , and is well-worth the subscription. Seufert is also, as of today, the owner of a Master’s degree in Applied Computation at Harvard.

Today’s interview starts with an overview of Seufert’s master’s thesis, which described how companies can build models to measure the effectiveness of creative (thus unlocking the value of generative AI) using ad platform black boxes. We then move on to why chat checkout failed, how Google has shifted search to AI, and the rapid evolution of ChatGPT ads. We discuss Meta in two parts: first, why CEO Mark Zuckerberg is failing the company by not advocating for ads, and how the company is using foundational models to transform ad targeting. We also touch on Apple, Amazon, and AppLovin, and close with a fascinating thesis: is being pro-advertising correlated with being optimistic about AI and its impact on humanity?

As a reminder, all Stratechery content, including interviews, is available as a podcast; click the link at the top of this email to add Stratechery to your podcast player.

On to the Interview:

An Interview with Eric Seufert About Models and Ads, and AI’s Massive Upside

This interview is lightly edited for clarity.

*Topics:*

DeCANT ( #decant ) | Meta’s Communication Problem ( #meta-coms ) | The Agent Checkout Flop ( #agent-checkout-flop ) | Google’s Successful Gambit ( #google-gambit ) | ChatGPT Ads ( #chatgpt-ads ) | Apple, Amazon, and AppLovin ( apple-amazon-applovin ) | The Prosperous Society ( prosperous-society )

DeCANT

*Eric Seufert, welcome back to Stratechery.*

*Eric Seufert:* Good to see you, Ben. Thanks for having me.

*Well, this is a big congratulations, I believe about the time this is being posted, as people are listening to this, you are walking across the stage in Cambridge to get your Master’s in Applied Computation at Harvard. Congratulations!*

*ES:* Thank you very much, that’s right, Thursday the 28th.

*I’m not sure how much you’ve talked about what you’ve been doing exactly, but as part of your Master’s, you just wrote a thesis which you just posted about on Mobile Dev Memo, we’ll have a link — I think it’s super interesting, I’m very excited to talk about this. So what you did is you developed something that you’re calling DeCANT, a Deep Creative Attention-based Network for pre-Testing. Explain, because this actually touches on — it’s funny, now that I’ve read at least the summary of your thesis, I go back through your archive and I’m like, “Oh, he’s been pre-writing bits about this for a while now”, because it called back to certain ones, particularly around generative AI and the testing problem and all those sorts of things. So this is your stage, you already defended it, you’ve had practice, now you have to defend it to the Stratechery audience, give us your thesis.*

*ES:* Well, maybe a more discerning audience, that’s a little bit intimidating — thank you. Maybe I could just maybe describe some of the background, I haven’t talked about this at all, this is just something I’ve been doing in my personal life.

*I know! It’s very exciting that we’re going to be the first outlet for this. I thought your summary article was great, it was one of those ones I immediately got what you were talking about right away, yet also felt very awed by the complexity of what it was going to go into it, so it was a good summary. So anyhow, I’ll stop interrupting, give me the lowdown.*

*ES:* Three years ago, I think like a lot of people, I kind awoke to this idea that we’re standing at the precipice of this inflection point, not just in digital advertising, but I think in technology broadly and society broadly, and I got nervous that I just wouldn’t be able to operate at the frontier to provide commentary without better understanding machine learning, particularly in the digital advertising space. I just thought it was going to become more and more important to deeply understand these fundamentals, so I applied to go to graduate school and the idea kind of snowballed. I actually looked at like classes at a local community college and then I was like, “Well why don’t I just throw a Hail Mary here and apply to some more prestigious—”

*(laughing) Went to school in Boston, as it were.*

*ES:* Just outside of Boston and yeah, I got in and we ended up having to defer a year because my wife got pregnant and school would have started on the due date of my son, so we deferred a year, and then packed up moved across the country and it was just a really fantastic experience — but it was nice to go into it with some domain expertise too, to understand what I wanted to apply it to. I think it made it a lot more concrete and a lot more actionable, but I don’t think I would recommend this for anybody who is in my particular set of circumstances with remote work and my wife works remotely, and my wife is like a saint and allowing me to do this kind of stuff and young kids and all that, but it works for me.

So what I wrote about was we’re sitting in a stage of the digital advertising market where essentially all of the big platforms are converging to this total end-to-end automation paradigm.

*The black boxes.*

*ES:* The black boxes. But if you kind of dive into a lot of the recommendation system research, which is essentially like the same as ad serving, it’s all the retrieval and ranking methodologies that are applied for selecting ad candidates, it’s the same as it’s used for selecting content candidates in just normal recommendation systems.

*It’s always been weird, it happened for historical reasons, that these were two different tech trees, but it’s been clear for actually a long time that if you’re recommending an ad, you can recommend content and “What’s the actual difference?”.*

*ES:* Right, it’s just the objective function that’s chosen. One is, “I want to optimize for this conversion”, and then the other is, “I want to optimize for some sort of engagement metric”, but essentially you’re using the same technologies, the same methodologies, and so if you dig in all that, it’s gotten supremely sophisticated.

But all of this sits behind this event horizon past which light cannot escape, with the light being your visibility into what the ad platform is doing. It’s totally opaque, and it’s gotten to the point where like you essentially have one lever of control, maybe two. The one lever of control is the creative and then the other lever of control is whatever your objective is that you tell the ad platform. And I say “maybe one”, because you might not have creative.

*That’s right, because generative AI’s coming along and it’s the most obvious application of just make the creative for you and it’s seemed like it’s been the case for a while, that if you’re an advertiser, “Just embrace the void”, has been the answer and that’s part of what makes this interesting. It’s kind of like a, “Maybe not, maybe that’s not the only way”.*

*ES:* I think it is, that’s ultimately the point of this DeCANT’s methodology. But yeah, what are you going to do? Are you going to fight the ocean?

*Right.*

*ES:* This is the direction of travel, you are a single advertiser, you control some amount of budget — this is where things are heading. It’s obviously better for the platforms, it is probably better for you, so whether you like it or not, whether you would agree with it or not, whether you think things could be done in a superior way or not, it’s kind of irrelevant, this is where things are headed, and it’s obviously working out for the platforms, I’m sure we’ll talk about earnings in a second.

So if you accept that, and if you say, “Look, I have no control over this”, and also, “I understand that the cost of creative production is going to zero”, whether the creative production is handled by the ad platform itself, or whether I’m still creating my creatives, if I’m just using third-party tools to do that, it’s trending towards zero.

Now, there are a lot of reasons to believe that many advertisers will reject having the platforms make their creatives for them. For one reason, there’s brand conflicts. For another reason, you’re going to work with more than one platform and you want to have consistency across them. There are many advertisers that won’t just surrender everything to the platform, they’ll still keep control of the creative production.

So if you do that and if you say, “Look, I can’t control what happens beyond that event horizon, light can’t escape, I have no idea what’s happening behind the scenes, his is a total black box”, then you could just treat the platform essentially as this end-to-end system. Essentially, it’s a teacher model, and you could train a student model through behavioral distillation and just say, “When I submit my creative to you, and I apply it in this context” — the context being the country it’s being run in, which you can control for, the language parameters that you’ve set there, the date that you’re deploying the creative, and that’s kind of it, “If I have this context-conditioned creative, can I predict what the ROAS is going to be and distill off of all this information that I’ve gathered from the platform with my own historical performance?” — so that was the premise of the paper of the thesis. And it turns out that, what I empirically showed support for was that, well, this type of deep neural network can do that better than a tree-based method, which I used XGBoost as the best performing baseline, which is kind of like the canonical go-to when comparing performance of a deep network versus a more traditional ML method and so that’s what it showed. And I think there’s like a lot of cool applications for this, it could sit in between.

*Just making sure I understand it, my summary of this, and I think you made a very important distinction — there’s one world where you just give Meta a price and they generate the ad, they do literally everything, and they deliver on the price and you know they’re getting better margins on it, but there’s nothing you can do about it because you’re still getting the best performance by doing that, that’s sort of like the default end state in one area.*

*But your bit about, “You want control of your creative, at the end of the day, your brand is your brand, that’s the most important thing”, but then number two, your point about you want to have consistency across platforms, which is this is where a lot of these sorts of total internalization efforts do fall down because at the end of the day, you’re the entity working across platforms. Meta doesn’t care about YouTube, YouTube doesn’t care about Snap, or whatever it might be. So you want to have control, but, and I think this was in your paper, so I’m going to add it to you, just doing it yourself, testing all your creative, costs a lot of money and is very wasteful, so that’s the benefit of basically utilizing them as a teacher to train your own model. You can have a good idea before you run it with real dollars and sense what’s going to perform and what’s not, which lets you squeeze out a bit of that margin and efficiency that they’re completely internalizing and maximize your return on the platform.*

*ES:* Well, I think it’s a little bit more than some incidental amount of money. A lot of advertisers use 10% as a rough benchmark for testing budget, now that’s 10% with no ROAS accountability, so now imagine clawing a lot of that back because I’m pre-testing, I’m pre-testing with the model that’s been distilled on their model, it’s a lot.

*10% is a lot if you’re talking about these ads, yeah, that’s a great point.*

*ES:* But the thing is, think about from the platform’s perspective, they might not like this methodology because, “Hey, wait a second”, all that testing budget was like free money that they were being handed because it doesn’t perform, but they don’t care, this is just the cost of doing business, right? So that 10%, they wasn’t accountable for ROAS, that got absorbed into just COGS or whatever line item bucket. But now, if they’re actually looking at that as cost savings, well, that’s going to be taken away from us. So I could see where the platforms might be a little bit hostile to this idea.

*But is there anything they could do about it? That’s sort of the brilliance of this model that I see which is it’s embracing the black box nature of what the platforms are doing and, to your point, it’s going to have to be retrained fairly frequently but you argue that’s not going to cost very much. This is why I’m excited about it, it seems like something that’s a pretty genuine innovation that is going to, if anything, get better over time. Am I wrong to be so optimistic?*

*ES:* I don’t want to oversell the model per se, but I think the application and the implementation is novel.

*It’s the concept though. It’s using the network’s ad server as a teacher for your own models, because they’ve reduced so many variables that actually it’s just like an objective function.*

*ES:* Exactly, and the idea of pre-testing, right? So just to test against some sort of model that should mimic what the broader system does.

*Exactly.*

*ES:* But I think there’s another piece here too — if I’m talking about this to a room of brand marketers, I say, “Hey, good news, this allows you to take control of creative production and control your brand messaging everywhere”, they get really happy. If I talk to the hardcore DTC performance marketers, I say, “Good news, make everything, build everything, you can just shoot the fire hose at this thing and it’s not going to blow up your testing account, it’s not going to blow up your testing budget, but you should be making everything, you should be exploring the entire surface area of all possible messaging and pixel combinations that could represent your product — shoot the fire hose, blast everything at it because the cost of producing creative is essentially zero”. Now, you don’t want to hand that over to Meta or to whoever and I don’t want to single out Meta because it’s Meta, Reddit, Google, Pinterest, TikTok.

Meta’s Communication Problem

*Right. Meta’s the stand-in for everyone because they’re also the best at it, so we get to use them.*

*ES:* It’s because of [Meta CEO Mark] Zuckerberg’s quote on your podcast .

*Which was?*

*ES:* “Just give us your credit card, we’ll take care of creative, we’ll take care of measurement, we’ll take care of everything else”.

*That’s right. Yeah, that’s been the bull thesis for a long time.*

*ES:* It’s been the bull thesis when you talk to the DTC guys, it’s not the bull thesis when you talk to the brand guys, and I think that’s part of the issue here.

*Right.*

*ES:* It’s like Mark Zuckerberg, I respect him very deeply as an executive, especially in terms of someone who just accomplishes things very ruthlessly, he’s not a great communicator.

*Nope, about ads in particular .*

*ES:* Exactly. And he does a really bad job, I think, of communicating the vision for the ads platform, if he even deigns to, because a lot of times he just blows that off.

*I had a whole thing about this , this has been one of my theses for a while, is the entire industry has been hurt and Meta in particular has been hurt by the fact Mark does not go to bat for ads. I’m a much bigger public advocate for Meta’s ads, which I think are a societal good, it makes entirely new industries possible, new niches, make customers aware of them. In a way that I see search being more of a skim that’s a little icky and I’m like, “Why am I out here making this case far more vociferously and effectively than you are who likes to pretend that ads don’t exist?”, it drives me crazy!*

*ES:* Let me just pitch a bit of a thought experiment to the audience, I don’t want to put you on the spot, so this is for the audience not for you, although I think you probably know the answer. What’s the name of Meta’s COO?

*Boz [Andrew Bosworth] , right? Oh he’s CTO…who is the COO? That’s a good question, I don’t even know.*

*ES:* Javier Olivan .

*That’s right, I did know that, but yes I did not know it off the top of my head.*

*ES:* But you knew Boz, you know Zuck, you probably know [Meta CFO] Susan Li , but who is the last COO you knew about? It was Sheryl [Sandberg] . You heard her on every earnings call — that’s the issue. Sheryl was the champion for the advertiser, she talked about it on every single earnings call, 10 million advertisers.

*She’d always come in with her five anecdotes of advertisers that are doing awesome, it’s a great point. Google does that, they always have like — and you kind of roll your eyes as you go through it, but there’s a repetition to that of, “Look at this real-world result that is positive”, that is totally missing, it’s a great observation.*

*ES:* So just to go back to the point about the platforms, I think also the platforms would be happy if if the advertisers are happy and they’re making more money and if they’re deploying better creatives that scale better and they’re not actually — there’s not a lot of dead weight loss on creatives that don’t work then, they’re probably going to be spending more money and so probably this is win-win for everybody, just this kind of approach.

*And also if the advertisers are spending all the money to generate the creative, saving their compute resources, I guess at a minimum.*

*ES:* Right, yeah.

*Number one, I think it’s great paper, number two, I’m very interested to see what the implications of this are because I think it’s very compelling, it applies broadly.*

The Agent Checkout Flop

*But there is a second big reason to have you on the podcast, I need to pull up the wheelbarrow to give you a massive heap of Being Right Points. From day one, you expressed strong skepticism about ChatGPT’s checkout product, I think we argued about it a bit the last time you were on. Fast forward, I’m not sure if that product even exists anymore, or at least it’s very deprioritized, Walmart expressed a lot of dissatisfaction with their participation , which I took Walmart’s participation as a positive . You were absolutely, completely, 100% right; where do you want to start your victory lap?*

*ES:* I wrote a piece that got me more hostile feedback than any other piece I’ve ever written — including some of the more critical ones I wrote about Apple, which attracted a lot of negative feedback — called Agentic Commerce Is a Mirage .

Look, that was a clickbaity title, that wasn’t the point I was making in the piece, the point I was making in the piece is that third-party independent agentic commerce is just not viable. It doesn’t align with the interests of the platforms, it’s probably not the best way for those companies, the chatbots, to make money. Advertising is superior and that it just, maybe it was an entry point to bootstrap data , but it wasn’t going to go anywhere, that’s not how people want to buy things, they need to have the platforms, it’s not how they want to sell them, they’re not going to cooperate if it’s going to cost them ad revenue, it’s not going to be conducive to doing all the RecSys [Recommender System] stuff that gets people to expand their cart when they check out and for all those reasons, Instant Checkout didn’t work.

*Right. And to your point, this isn’t just like agents buying things, this is also like buying things from within a chatbot experience.*

*ES:* So the fully automated agent buying on your behalf, I think, is non-viable and I just think that’s not going to work ever. But I think the third-party independent agent of commerce where they’re just recommending stuff for you and then you click through and they get an affiliate fee or actually they facilitate the checkout in the chatbot and they get an affiliate fee — I just thought, first of all, that’s just suboptimal relative to advertising, you get more economics in advertising and also it’s more win-win if you use advertising versus the platforms are obviously—

*It’s very adversarial, yeah.*

*ES:* Amazon held out, you needed Amazon’s participation if this was going to go anywhere, they haven’t, they still haven’t, they’ve been excluding more chatbots if you look at their robots.txt .

But I do think agentic commerce, when it’s bolted into the platform experience, is a viable solution and I think it is working really well. Rufus is working really well, Walmart’s agent commerce tool Sparky is working really well, and so I think there’s, I wouldn’t even say that that’s a future state, I think it’s happening now, I think it’s had success now.

*And so the issue isn’t necessarily the interface, it’s the fact of these conflicting incentives where if you’re on Amazon and using Rufus, Amazon still gets all the data benefits, the advertising surface area, all the sorts of things and everything’s up to date. There’s no integration issues, the cart is consistent, all these sorts of things.*

*The big issue was, yes, ChatGPT can surface you a product you didn’t know about, but every other part of that experience — I think this is like, the more I thought about why you were right, there’s always those stories that you hear about like the impact of millisecond delays in conversions. If you think about that, if that’s a talking point on a site where you’re already there to buy, almost definitionally any sort of integration, just the fall, this is what Walmart was talking about , they’re like, “Our conversions through this are terrible, it’s better to get fewer people clicking through to our site where we could actually make sure they finish the purchase”, which I think is like is the perfect articulation of the point you were making.*

*ES:* Right, and the AOV [Average Order Value] was lower, people were buying one thing at a time. You go to Walmart, you put a thing in the cart, you get a recommendation for five other things you put some more of those in the cart, the average order value goes up.

And the other thing though, I think the bigger more fundamental thing was that the economics were just suboptimal to advertising, the economics just didn’t work as well as advertising.

*What do you mean? What do you mean like an affiliate fee versus versus an ad?*

*ES:* The affiliate fee versus ads, because the ads you submit your true value as a bid, there’s just more value to be had there. If I’m just getting an affiliate fee that’s like an arbitrarily chosen percentage off of the top line and then ultimately you’re going to end up preferencing this low cost stuff and so that could degrade the user experience, but also you’re just going to make less money.

Having a bid allows everybody to say, “This is what it’s worth to me to get that impression”, and so you’re going to get the higher value stuff — it’s modified by the conversion rate, but you’re going to usually tend to get more higher value things that get selected for versus just the affiliate fee, which is a fixed percentage is going to tend to have lower valued stuff because it’s a higher conversion rate.

*You’ve doubled down on your argument that AI advertising — this is somewhat related — should not look like search advertising. You explicitly wrote last month, Search Is the Wrong Mental Model for Chatbot Advertising , and I’ve largely agreed with you and made the case myself. One area, though, where I’ve gotten pushback from people is the questions about the mental state of consumers. It’s like, to what extent can AI actually be like an Instagram experience where what’s actually the difference at the end of the day between the content and the ads? People are on AI to do work, to be productive, display advertising is not going to work there. What’s your pushback?*

*ES:* I think anywhere you’re applying attention is a good candidate for display advertising.

*Right, and there’s a vast umbrella and conversion capability underneath Instagram that is still very profitable.*

*ES:* And also I would point you to mobile gaming, mobile gaming is very much a lean in activity, it’s not a passive lean back consume Instagram videos activity, and you know ads work pretty well in mobile games.

*Great analogy, yep.*

*ES:* So does a lot of streaming too, maybe less so now, I think a lot of these streaming shows are designed for lean back passivity, but I just watched the new Jack Ryan movie , I could not make heads or tails of that narrative, it was really poorly written, and they did the thing that Matt Damon was talking about where they restated the plot in the dialogue like six times.

*(laughing) And it’s not just that you weren’t paying attention, it’s also that the plot didn’t make any sense, so maybe they were just making it worse.*

*ES:* It was just a nonsensical plot, but that’s an aside.

So my sense is like, if an ad break is an ad break, and they do capture your attention, that’s actually one of the arguments that AppLovin makes with its advertising product, which is why they think it’s more attractive than social, because it’s an actual ad break, you get a pause in the gameplay, and you’re forced to watch some minimum number of seconds before you can move on, that’s a really compelling idea. And again, if you tie this, if you anchor the ad to the context of the conversation, there’s going to be some very large percentage of conversations that are not monetizable at all.

*Right. Which is the case with search, by the way.*

*ES:* Exactly. They said 80%, historically we’re not monetizable at all and so you get so much more monetizability if you’re actually just tethering this to whatever the person is doing elsewhere on the Internet.

Google’s Successful Gambit

*Has Google actually — is this an argument they’ve been dramatically under-monetizing Search? Because all these non-monetizable search results should have Facebook-style display advertising next to them, because why not?*

*ES:* Yeah, maybe. I think what happened with Search — I mean first of all, search is fantastically profitable, it’s probably like one of the best business model innovations of all time, and it grew 19% last quarter on a huge base, so I’m not trying to denigrate the performance of Search.

But I think Google Search may have been a victim of the MAYA principle, like an industrial design, Most Advanced Yet Accessible. And so if you change it too much, then it’s not Google Search anymore and people don’t recognize it and they know how to use it, so you could change it incrementally and that’s what they did through what I’ve called Google’s Gambit and this like pretty protracted evolution of that experience.

*I’ll let you finish, but I had Google’s Gambit further down the interview, I’d love for you to walk me through that as well.*

*ES:* The premise of Google’s Gambit was essentially that they were taking this big bet — keep in mind I started writing this series like 18 months ago, so when they introduce AI Overviews — they’re taking this big bet, “If consumers are getting accustomed to a chat-like interface, we have to adapt to that, but if we adapt too fast, then people will say this is a totally new experience, I might as well just go to ChatGPT” — this is disorienting, you can’t just overnight flick the switch and have Google as Google AI mode, so you’ve got to take this in incremental steps.

The point I was making when I started the series was they’re going to have to perform this Ship of Theseus transformation of Google Search into a conversational chatbot-like experience over time, because that’s what consumers are getting accustomed to with chatbots. They can’t do it all at once, and when they do that, though, they’re going to cut off the open web, they’re going to capture way more of the value, and they’re going to turn Search from a distribution mechanic where they just distributed clicks and distributed traffic, into an engagement sync where people spend time in search.

That’s a foreign concept 18 months ago, people don’t spend time in Search, they go there for a specific purpose, they go there to go away, they go there to click away, and if they don’t click away in the first link, that’s a failure, that means Search did a poor job, so they go there to get the result that they want to click away to very quickly, and they needed to transform Search into something where I go there and I have a conversation. Meta’s Models

*Where’s Meta in this? Are you encouraged by Spark? Are they going to be competitive here? Or is the actual Facebook opportunity, to tie back to what we talked about at the beginning, actually the product and the ads are all the same thing, every pixel is a monetization opportunity, stick with that.*

*ES:* Products and ads are exactly the same thing, right? These systems are unified — they’re not literally unified, but they are informed by the same research. And my sense is, I was just writing this today , but it’s something I’ve been thinking about a lot lately, there’s this quiet revolution going on right now within RecSys.

It’s transitioning from this traditional DLRM [Deep Learning Recommendation Model] model, which was introduced by YouTube in 2016, so this predates the Attention Is All You Need . This idea of what’s called the two towers, you’ve got a user tower and you’ve got a content tower, and then what you’re doing is you’re building these large embedding tables and you’ve got the user history and you’ve got all the possible content they could consume and you’re doing just dot product similarity and you’re trying to figure out what to show the user next.

That was tremendously powerful idea when it was introduced by YouTube in 2016, but this is giving way now to generative recommendation, and so this is also essentially invented by Google, I would say. They introduced this idea of Semantic IDs in 2023, this paper, this very famous TIGER [Transformer Index for Generative Recommenders] paper , and the idea here is that, I won’t go too deep into it because it’d be a distraction, but instead of saying, “Here’s all the possible content, and here’s all the sequence of activities we have about this user, and let’s condition the combination of both for every single possible piece of content that this user could consume”, what if we just predicted the next thing that the user would be likely to engage with? And what they do is they flip it around.

*Totally flipping it around, yeah.*

*ES:* So what they do is you can use an LLM for that, what the TIGER paper did was they trained a sequence-to-sequence model, but they trained an encoder and a decoder, and they did this codebook model with a methodology called RQ-VAE, [Residual Quantized Variational Autoencoder]. But what they did is they say, let’s say you have a billion items in your content catalog, well, if you wanted to use like sequence modeling for that, or if you wanted to use an LLM for that, you need to create a billion, essentially, a billion representations of tokens. But you can’t put that into a tokenizer because that would overload the vocabulary, you can’t do a softmax on that.

And so what they do though, is they use this, the Google paper uses RQ-VAE, and what they do is they train code books, and so what they do is they use quantization to basically — what happens is you create these hierarchical code books where you, let’s say it’s a code book of size 256, so you’ve got four, so you’ve got 1,028 possible options, but it’s the combinations that create the variation volume, and so you train these codebooks. Codebook one, I’m just basically grouping things, I’m classifying things into 256 classes. The second one, I take the residuals on the first one and I classify the residuals and I take the residuals of those, I do the third one and the fourth one. Right now, with a combination of four codebooks of 256 size each, I can capture the entire size of my catalog. Now, each of those turns into a token, so instead of 10 million or whatever tokens that I have to push into the tokenizer, I’ve got 1,028, and I push those into the tokenizer, and then I mid-train an LLM to accept those as potential output as next token prediction. So I say, “Here’s a sequence of the things that the user engaged with, predict the next one as a token”.

That has been revolutionary, I think. And now you’re seeing a lot of these big advertising platforms publish papers are saying like, “We’re going to rebuild our entire architecture around this”, and it’s not just Google, it’s Meta. They’ve talked about LLM for ad ranking, they talk about it in their earnings, that’s the altitude that this has reached. They talk about the power of LLM for ad ranking, but also it’s Kuaishou in China. And so the thing is, if you think about all of the semantic and the world knowledge, what Meta says when they talk about this in earnings, all the world knowledge you bring to bear on predicting the next thing the person will be interacting with if you use this methodology, so I think there’s like a big leg of growth that is yet to even really be tapped into with the application of LLMs here.

But also think about the value that owning the LLM model has in that world, because I think we’re probably entering a world where, hey, maybe the most state-of-the-art LLMs, and we’ve already seen this with Mythos, “The most state-of-the-art LLMs, we’re going to keep those for ourselves, we’re not going to make that available”.

*Mythos and Meta Spark came out the same week , which on one hand would seem negative for Meta, their model is relatively far behind — in my head, I’m like, this is the greatest endorsement of Meta building their own models that you could ever get, it’s existential. They absolutely have to be doing it, and the fact that Spark is not terrible means they’re on the right path, so everyone should be happy about this.*

*ES:* Yeah, it was competitive. It’s not the tip of the frontier but it was competitive.

*That’s fine, it’s on the right path, and it’s a path they have to be on.*

*ES:* They own it, you can’t block them from using it, they own it. And what happens if owning that means that you are the best ad platform because you have the access to that LLM to do this kind of mid-training? I think that people discount that, but again, it’s because Zuck doesn’t talk about this, he doesn’t talk about why this is important, all these investments that they’re making in GEM [Generative Ads Model] . *Has phenomenal results, that in and of itself justifies all the infrastructure investments they’re making.*

*ES:* But if you think about, “What does a research team do?” — they make foundation models! Well, they made one, they made GEM. And the thing is, if you look at the application of GEM, you can’t use GEM for inferences, it’s too big. Meta published a paper called SUM [Scaling User Modeling] in 2024. *This is what ultimately, to your point, ads and recommendations have always been the same problem, but this is like the pivot point to actually make them into the same solution where you flip it around and you’re understanding the user and what they actually want to see next. *ES:* Another piece here, I was reading some analysis yesterday or the day before, and someone was making the point that, I genuinely don’t remember who was writing this, but someone was making the point that it’s all the adoption, all the economics of these models are being absorbed at the frontier, so it’s the latest versions of the models that are capturing all the value and doesn’t that show support for the idea that this will continue to move in that direction.

My sense is that’s probably true because a lot of people are adopting these models and they’re integrating them into their own commercial workflows for the first time, but what happens when they’re not? If it’s already done and there’s a new frontier model, would you upgrade? And I think you made the point on Flash 3.5, it uses more tokens and it’s a higher cost per token why would you upgrade? If I built a tool that uses Flash 3 and it works perfectly, I tested it, it gives me the output I want, what incentive do I have to upgrade in the first place, especially if it costs more money? And then the other thing I think people don’t recognize here, it’s like every time I query from a model, it’s essentially like sampling from a distribution. Well, if I’m querying from a new model, it’s querying, it’s sampling from a different distribution, I’m going to get different results and so I might have to do a lot more than just change out the variable name. I have tools that I’ve built, the model that’s used is a variable name, I could just change that and I’d be querying from 3.5, but that’s going to change the entire output, I’m going to have to then change the system prompt that I use, I’m going to have to test it a bunch to make sure I’m getting what I want.

If I’ve already done that and I’m getting stable results from 3, then I don’t know why I need to upgrade. Now, think about like, what happens if these models are actually so powerful for my use case, which is RecSys, which is ad ranking, it’s re-ranking, that I don’t want to make them available to anybody else, this is proprietary to me, I spent a lot of money, but I’m getting a lot more in value out of it in my 5%, 6% every quarter improvements in time spent — that’s RecSys, in conversion rate, that’s ad ranking. In addition to all, we got very tactical with a lot of these questions, you put together a four-part podcast series expressing AI optimism called The Prosperous Society . I’d love for you to walk me through the arguments here. Part one is The Primacy of Distribution , this certainly sounds right in my wheelhouse, so give me the overall view but then I’ll ask you about each of the four parts.*

*ES:* Let me give the big picture thesis, which I kind of encapsulate in the fourth episode . Let me give a little bit of the background.

I was writing this as a book, and then the Citrini short report dropped and I just couldn’t bite my tongue. So I scrapped the book and I tried to break it up into four podcast parts, the whole running time is like three-and-a-half hours, I’m going to release one combined episode soon of no ads. I wanted to make it episodic, but I just felt like I just viscerally needed to respond to the Citrini report and so I came out with episode one just as a kind of a response to that and I cobbled it together from what was the manuscript.

My point is when you get the explosion of output that AI is allowing for, you shift the binding constraint to distribution, because you’ve got this massive pool of stuff to pull from.

*You’re talking to the right guy , you have an explosion of supply, the problem becomes how do you sort through this? How do you actually find what you want?*

*ES:* Exactly, and so the distribution becomes the principal allocation mechanism, but these allocation mechanisms with digital ads are very, very good, they’re very, very efficient. So that’s great, you’re shifting a lot, a big chunk of the economy to these systems that are very, very efficient and they’re very, very workable, and that’s good, that automatically creates growth, that automatically creates value.

But the other thing is in that explosion of things that are being created — and it’s not just slop output, but it’s all types of content. People are getting more efficient at creating great podcasts, great books, great blog posts, and it’s not that the AI is writing it, it’s just they’re getting more efficient at pulling ideas together, doing research, packaging it. You get this larger exploration of the product space, you’re creating more and more granular products that could satisfy very specific and particular needs. And then you’re getting more products that meet more very specific particular needs, you’re getting more efficient matching and you’re getting people that are on-boarded to the advertising economy that never could have done so in the first place because of this primacy of distribution that all the ad platforms are investing into making these systems end-to-end automated that brings in ever smaller SMBs [Small and Medium-Sized Businesses] — so across these three axes you’re creating more economic value and I think that’s what leads to the prosperous society.

Actually the foil for this was this book, I’ve got it right in front of me, John Galbraith’s Affluent Society — he wrote this in the 50s, but his point was advertising was just introduced as a means of maximizing consumption because the conventional wisdom at the time, what he called the conventional wisdom, is that we need to be at full economic output all the time, that means producing as much as possible. We’re producing more stuff than people demand, and so we need to manufacture demand, and that’s what advertising is.

And my point with the prosperous society is actually, the demand-matching system is totally indifferent to what you want, whatever you want, it’ll find you the thing that you want most and that you’re going to enjoy the most and so people are getting more value and more personal satisfaction out of the things they discover. There’s more things to discover, so they’re discovering more granular things, and the matching is happening at the maximum possible efficiency. So the advertisers are getting the most value and the customers are getting the most value and the platforms are getting the most value. And in this way, what we can do is we can take that 83% of all commerce, of all retail that’s not happening online, and let’s say we double that and when we double it, it’s much more efficient. All of this distribution is much more efficient, all the consumption is much more efficient and satisfying, that is a prosperous society, that’s everyone wins, that’s growth across all those axes, and this is not the doomsday scenario that Citrini pointed out, this is actually a much happier, much more economically satisfied society.

*It’s such a good point. And the last question I had here, I’m going to jump to it right here, there’s an aspect where to what extent can you separate your and my relative optimism from your and my relative understanding of and appreciation for the power of individualized advertising? Because there’s a bit about this that I think the comparison to Galbraith is exactly right. There is an assumption in there of the power and primacy of the supply side and the stupidity and naivety of the demand side, that it can somehow be induced and can be controlled, and the thesis that I think we have, I’ll speak for myself, but about the reason why I’m such a advocate for Meta-style advertising is the belief that human desires and needs and wants are effectively infinite and it’s infinite in a combinatorial way .*

*It’s not just that humanity broadly wants things, it’s that every individual wants different things and the fact that on the production side, we’re getting the capability to meet those needs, but we just need to match them, how do we match the need provider to the need haver? And because we believe in advertising, we know it’s possible and I think it’s not an accident that you have — go back to OpenAI, why are they so resistant to advertising for so long? Because they don’t believe it works , they don’t understand it and it gets to the whole Silicon Valley blind spot about ads that, by the way, seems to apply to Mark Zuckerberg as well and it falls on us to sit over here and say, “Actually, ads are amazing”. They’re not just amazing because they pay for cool toys, they’re amazing because they actually understand price and by extension meet consumer needs, and if you understand the massive value explosion that is downstream from ads, it’s like, oh my God, AI makes this all a million times better, not worse! It’s such a poverty of mindset to think that because AI can just generate a gazillion Soviet-style gray apartment blocks that we’ve solved the problem, that’s not what humans are interested in.*

*ES:* First of all, amen brother. Second, we are, I think, we are like facing this, call it a failure of imagination or call it a moral malaise, but if you look at a lot of the discourse, let’s call it and who it’s dominated by, it’s people that have firmly internalized a degrowth mindset and the affluent society in Galbraith’s book is the degrowther manifesto. It’s quoted to this day by a lot of these degrowthers and that’s really scary to me, and I think it’s really important for people to advocate for the opposite.

Capitalism is good, capitalism enriches people, capitalism creates fair societies, capitalism creates happier people, capitalism creates more human satisfaction. And yeah, you could obviously fix things and optimize things at the margin, but largely it’s better, it’s objectively better than the alternatives. And my worry here, and if you don’t, if someone doesn’t actually make the case and actually go through and analytically make the case and make the case with support and make the case by tying it to books that we all agree are Western canon, then if you don’t do that, then the degrowther mindset just by default dominates and that’s a really scary proposition.

*Well, and it’s combined with this. People in Silicon Valley are smart, the Communist theorists were always smart, and implicit in that is this sort of looking down on the general consumer and how dumb they are and this lack of imagination for the tremendous capacity of human wants and desires and the willingness and innovative capability of humans to meet those desires. You talked about in part two, The Human Nexus of Commerce and The Collapse of the Pareto Principle , I think both of them touch on this infinite customization aspect and that to the extent we accelerate both sides, that’s a huge positive.*

*ES:* And to be fair, in part four , I call out some potential issues with endless atomization and you could think about people becoming alienated and social cohesion breaking down, those are risks, but my bigger worry is not that those take root, because they won’t, because consumers will reject that, my bigger worry is that this is what the companies invest all of this CapEx expenditure into, and then it doesn’t work.

Then we’re in a bubble because we’re not in a bubble — if it works, we’re not in a bubble, we’re on a growth trajectory. If it doesn’t work, we’re in a bubble and then the bubble bursts. And then we have a recession, and that’s a bad outcome. But the thing is, my sense is you’ve got the lump of labor fallacy , which I think most people recognize that as just broken on its face.

*But the lump of labor fallacy is the exact same mindset that leads to this total, “Human labor is going to be worthless”, it’s like two sides of the same coin.*

*ES:* And then that’s coupled with this deep cynicism and nihilism that is really destructive and corrosive and I think you’ve got to match that with optimism and you have to shout it from the rooftops and I’m doing my part, I know you’re doing your part, but the thing is like, if a Citrini publishes this thing and it tanked the S&P the next day, you need to come back with something else, there needs to be a rebuttal, there needs to be a very pointed rebuttal there.

That’s essentially what I was trying to do, I hope some people enjoyed it, I just think it’s incumbent on the people that have any sort of voice to make this case, because if you don’t make the case, the other side’s going to dominate.

*I like this thesis. People who like ads are optimistic about AI.*

*ES:* There you go.

*I think there’s honestly something to that. There’s this suspicion of commerce, this sort of assumption that people are dumb, that is very much tied in this lack of imagination for the expanse of potential products and services to be sold and acquired that are absolutely absurd. I was on another podcast last week and someone was like, “They made this leap from planting seeds in the ground and eating your own food to losing value in your office job from AI” — I’m like, “Wait, there’s a lot of steps here from the intrinsic value of feeding yourself to email jobs”, we’re far departed from that, and our ability to invent completely new needs and functions and to create solutions to that and then to match them together — it already works pretty well, that’s why so many people have missed out on all this Meta upside all these years.*

*ES:* That’s right, and Google.

*Eric, good talking to you, congratulations on your thesis and very excited to see what happens next.*

*ES:* Always a pleasure Ben, thank you for having me.

text:
YouTubers are ruling the box office, and it shouldn't be a surprise: succeeding on YouTube is a much higher bar than the gates that currently govern Hollywood.

YouTubers Win the Box Office, Goodbye Gatekeepers, The YouTube Bar

Monday, June 1, 2026

On Thursday’s episode of Sharp Tech , Andrew and I discussed SpaceX and Elon, Nvidia and the Neoclouds, and the Ferrari Luce backlash.

On to the Update:

YouTubers Win the Box Office

From Bloomberg :

The two most popular movies in the world were directed by YouTube creators under the age of 30. Backrooms grossed $81.7 million in North America this weekend, the biggest opening in the history of A24. It was directed by Kane Parsons, who rocketed to fame as a teenager with a YouTube series. Obsession, directed by Curry Barker, has increased its grosses two weekends in a row and eclipsed $100 million worldwide.

Their success signals a potential shift in audience taste and a hunger for new voices. These two movies, which cost less than $15 million to produce combined, are proving more popular with young viewers than a new Star Wars film.

There is one caveat for these results, courtesy of the New York Times :

These box office victories come with caveats. “Backrooms,” “Obsession” and “Iron Lung” are all horror films, the genre that has long been the most forgiving for first-time filmmakers, in part because horror is relatively cheap to produce. For some studio executives, that context is a reason for caution: The real shift, they say, will come when horror isn’t the only proof of concept. (To be fair, there have been a few comedy examples over the years, including A24’s “Eighth Grade,” which was Bo Burnham’s directing debut. Mr. Burnham was one of YouTube’s earliest stars.)

“Backrooms” and “Obsession” were also produced by powerful people. The mogul Peter Chernin, the horror maestro James Wan and the A-list filmmaker Shawn Levy have producing credits on Mr. Parsons’s film. Jason Blum, perhaps the most successful horror producer in Hollywood history, was involved with “Obsession.” Even Mr. Kujawski of Focus Features urged caution. “There’s a moment happening with YouTube talent, for sure, and it’s really exciting,” he said. “But not everyone who finds success on the Internet is going to translate. Curry Barker, for one, is a very, very special storyteller.”

With that out of the way, let’s do a bit of a victory lap.

Goodbye Gatekeepers

In 2017, when the first public allegations were made against Hollywood producer Harvey Weinstein, I wrote in Goodbye Gatekeepers how the traditional structure of Hollywood — where the supply of people who wanted to make and be in movies far exceeded the demand for movies to be made by Hollywood — created the conditions for his predations.

What made Hollywood’s structure particularly nefarious was the fact that selecting actors is such a subjective process. Movies are art — what appeals to one person may not appeal to another — making people like Weinstein cultural curators. If he were to not select an actor, or purposely damaged their reputation through his extensive contacts with the press, they wouldn’t have a chance in Hollywood. After all, there were many others to choose from, and no other routes to making movies.

As I noted in that Article, a similar structure used to be the case in newspapers, which not only gated what news was reported, but also leveraged that gate to monetize via advertising; however, the Internet had long since broken down the gate in both regards. Meanwhile, I raised the spectre of something similar happening to movies:

Don’t forget YouTube: video is a zero sum activity — time spent watching one source of video is time not spent watching another — and YouTube showed over a billion hours of video worldwide every day in 2016.

YouTube represents something else that is just as important: the complete lack of gatekeepers. Google CEO Sundar Pichai said on an earnings’ call earlier this year that “Every single day, over 1,000 creators reached the milestone of having 1,000 channel subscribers.” That is an astounding number in its own right; what is even more remarkable is that while Hollywood has only ~3,500 acting slots a year (including all movies, not just major studios), YouTube creates 100 times as many “stars” over the same time period.

It’s not a surprise that the breakthrough moment for YouTube stars in film took nearly a decade to materialize after that Article; I’ve long noted the sequence through which the Internet and digital has affected media: text first, then music, then short-form video, etc. Movies, the pinnacle of traditional media, are the hardest to both make and distribute, particularly if the goal is to make it into theaters. And, of course, movies ask the most of customers in return: they have to actually leave the house!

That leads to two true but ultimately unsatisfying answers as to why YouTube stars might succeed in movies. The first is that this is simply a new place to discover talent, and that’s certainly true. The analogy I would draw is to the impact AWS had on venture capital : cloud computing reduced the cost of starting a company to nothing more than opportunity cost for the founder’s time, and perhaps a bit of seed funding for a few engineers; that created an entirely new asset class of angel investors. Venture firms, meanwhile, didn’t evaluate companies based on a powerpoint to fund Sun servers, but rather on actual products and market signals. So it is with this new wave of talent: the cost of production has plummeted such that creators can be evaluated on their creations, not just their ideas.

The second true but unsatisfying answer is that YouTube creators bring their own audience. That’s almost certainly true: Kane Parsons, who made Backrooms , has 3.2 million subscribers , and Curry Barker, who made Obsession , has 1.2 million subscribers . Mark Fischbach, who made Iron Lung , has 38.7 million subscribers , which he purposely leveraged to get distribution. From Bloomberg :

In January, Mark Fischbach, known to his YouTube fans as Markiplier, was set to release his $3 million film Iron Lung in 60 independent cinemas. Fischbach led a grassroots campaign encouraging his followers to phone up their local theaters and request Iron Lung screenings. The film was ultimately picked up by major chains including AMC Entertainment Holdings Inc., Regal Entertainment Group and Cinemark Holdings Inc. and grossed $41.4 million in the US and Canada.

At the same time, Obsession ‘s results actually increased for the second week in a row, with the box office up 10% from last week, which was itself up 39% from the film’s opening; this isn’t just fans, and gets to the unacknowledged third factor.

The YouTube Bar

The “unsatisfying” aspect I’m referring to is best understood through the lens of the movie Backrooms and Obsession finished ahead of; from Variety :

The original fare ruling is especially striking at the start of summer movie season, a period that’s usually dominated by major franchises. Yet Disney’s “Star Wars” spinoff, “The Mandalorian and Grogu,” suffered a catastrophic 70% drop in its second weekend, signaling the property isn’t catering beyond an aging group of core fans. Despite playing on far more screens, “The Mandalorian and Grogu” landed in third place on weekend charts behind “Backrooms” and “Obsession.”

Star Wars was created by George Lucas, whose initial claim to fame, American Graffiti , is one of the closest analogies to Obsession ‘s crazy profitability ( American Graffiti made over $200 million on a $777,000 budget; Obsession is at $148 million after three weeks on a budget of $1 million). That success gave him the support to make Star Wars , the entire empire of which he would sell to Disney for $4.05 billion in 2012.

Star Wars seemed tailor-made for Disney’s business model, which is about IP, i.e. a capital investment, not an operational one in talent. Disney wants properties that sell themselves, in which talent is incidental, and which it can leverage first in movies, then TV, then merchandise, and ultimately in parks.

It turns out, however, that actually making good movies still matters: a late Gen X’er like me, who as a teenager saw The Phantom Menace twice in its opening weekend, so excited was I by the return of Star Wars (and did the same for The Force Awakens ), has basically no interest in The Mandalorian and Grogu , and I’m clearly not alone. It’s been clear for a while now that of all the things that Disney worries about when making a Star Wars film or TV series, actually making it good has not been one of them (the first season of Andor was a notable exception in this regard).

That’s the thing with an IP-based business model, however: Disney seems to have assumed that, because they controlled distribution, thanks to the massive consolidation in movie studios over the years, that they could shove whatever supply they wanted through the tubes and audiences would slurp it up because they had no other choice.

This is the exact opposite of YouTube specifically, and the Internet generally: on the Internet distribution is free. Anyone can set up a website, or start a YouTube account, and they can post whatever they want. The content that breaks through has to do so on its own merits: is it good and compelling or is it not? If it is, it gets more and more views — that’s what the algorithm does, is respond to and amplify interest — and if it’s not, it, like 99.99% of YouTube content, is barely seen by anyone.

In short, the reason these movies are successful is not just because their makers were spotted by powerful producers, or because they brought their own fans. It’s because the necessary precondition for those two things happening is actually becoming popular on pure merit. These movies are successful because their makers are good, and we know they’re good because they’re successful on YouTube. No, that doesn’t mean everyone on YouTube is good — indeed, that’s the entire point. There is no quality bar to get onto YouTube, which means the quality bar to get noticed on YouTube is much higher than any gate. Indeed, as much as Hollywood types might look down on YouTubers, it’s the latter who are far more impressive, at least if the goal is actually making something that resonates.

title: The Google Capital Company
subject: The Google Capital Company (Stratechery Article 6-2-2026)
dek: Google has issued equity to Berkshire Hathaway in a deal that signals far more demand and a future where capital is the ultimate commodity. View in browser | Listen in your podcast player STRATECHERY
text:
Google has issued equity to Berkshire Hathaway in a deal that signals far more demand and a future where capital is the ultimate commodity.

The Google Capital Company

Tuesday, June 2, 2026

What does the most beautiful business model of all time look like?

First, imagine that your supply is free. Second, imagine that your customers willfully compete against each other to raise your prices. Third, imagine that your users decide which of your customers gets the privilege of paying you. All you have to do is build a bit of infrastructure to make it all happen, pay a nominal bit of depreciation on that infrastructure, and make billions of dollars on some of the greatest margins in the history of business.

I am, of course, describing Google, a company so good that Warren Buffett, the legendary investor, could never quite bring himself to invest in it. Buffett explained in the 2017 Berkshire Hathaway annual meeting :

We were their customer very early on with GEICO, for example, and we saw — these figures are way out of date — but as I remember, we were paying them $10 or $11 a click, or something like that. And any time you’re paying somebody $10 or $11 bucks every time somebody just punches a little thing where you got no cost at all, you know, that’s a good business unless somebody’s going to take it away from you. And so we were close up seeing the impact of that…But, you know, you’ve almost never seen a business like it.

One of the characteristics of an Aggregator like Google is the way in which they maximize absolute value at the expense of relative value. For supply — i.e. content on the web — Google dramatically increases the number of visitors, even as the value of any one visitor who comes from Google is worth much less than a visitor who visits directly; for an advertiser, the value of one click makes up for thousands of impressions of an ad that make no difference; for a user, Google helps them discover what they are looking for amidst the overwhelming abundance that is downstream from distribution being free. In every case the Aggregator increases quantity at the expense of relative quality, confident that the absolute amount of quality will be more in the long run.

What is interesting is that this is the exact inverse in terms of why these companies have been valued by investors. The best tech companies are “asset-light”, predicated on maximizing zero marginal costs. Yes, they spend a lot of money on R&D and on the infrastructure to make markets happen, but they don’t actually participate in those markets; simply taking a skim and keeping the vast majority of that skim is what gets Wall Street excited. In other words, it was the relative amount of money made that was generally more important to the market than the absolute amount of money.

Berkshire Hathaway and Productive Capital

Berkshire Hathaway was, before Buffett acquired it, a failing textile business; Buffett originally invested because the stock was worth less than the liquidation value, and ended up owning it outright after a dispute with management. It was a decision he regretted; from the company’s 1989 letter to shareholders :

If you buy a stock at a sufficiently low price, there will usually be some hiccup in the fortunes of the business that gives you a chance to unload at a decent profit, even though the long-term performance of the business may be terrible…Time is the friend of the wonderful business, the enemy of the mediocre…

I could give you other personal examples of “bargain-purchase” folly but I’m sure you get the picture: It’s far better to buy a wonderful company at a fair price than a fair company at a wonderful price. Charlie understood this early; I was a slow learner. But now, when buying companies or common stocks, we look for first-class businesses accompanied by first-class managements.

One of the first-class businesses Berkshire Hathaway acquired was See’s Candies in 1972. Buffett explained in the 2007 shareholder letter :

We bought See’s for $25 million when its sales were $30 million and pre-tax earnings were less than $5 million. The capital then required to conduct the business was $8 million. (Modest seasonal debt was also needed for a few months each year.) Consequently, the company was earning 60% pre-tax on invested capital…

Last year See’s sales were $383 million, and pre-tax profits were $82 million. The capital now required to run the business is $40 million. This means we have had to reinvest only $32 million since 1972 to handle the modest physical growth – and somewhat immodest financial growth – of the business. In the meantime pre-tax earnings have totaled $1.35 billion. All of that, except for the $32 million, has been sent to Berkshire (or, in the early years, to Blue Chip).

The “problem” with a See’s Candies is that there is nothing to be done with all of that profit; if it’s privately held then its owners end up with more cash than they know what to do with, and if it’s public, then the job is to figure out how to return that cash to shareholders through some combination of dividends and stock buybacks. What Berkshire Hathaway did, however, was use that cash to grow:

After paying corporate taxes on the profits, we have used the rest to buy other attractive businesses. Just as Adam and Eve kick-started an activity that led to six billion humans, See’s has given birth to multiple new streams of cash for us. (The biblical command to “be fruitful and multiply” is one we take seriously at Berkshire.)

One of the businesses Berkshire Hathaway used the See’s profits for was on the opposite end of the spectrum in terms of capital utilization: BNSF Railway. Railways require a lot of capital to operate; BNSF consumed $3.8 billion last year; they also make a lot of money: BNSF’s net income was $5.5 billion on revenue of $23.4 billion. To put that in perspective, the total amount that Berkshire Hathaway has made from See’s Candies is probably less than $3 billion (the last disclosure was “over $2 billion” in 2019), i.e. less than BNSF made last year.

So which is the better business?

Google Cloud’s Runway

In Q4 2019, the first year that Alphabet disclosed Google Cloud revenue, Google Services — the high margin beautiful business I described at the beginning — made $43.2 billion in revenue and $13.5 billion in operating profit; Google Cloud made $2.6 billion in revenue and lost $1.2 billion. Google Cloud revenue was 6% the size of Google Services.

In Q1 2023, Google Cloud made a profit for the first time. In that quarter Google Services made $62.0 billion in revenue and $21.7 billion in profit; Google Cloud made $7.5 billion in revenue and $0.2 billion in profit. Google Cloud revenue was 12% the size of Google Services, and its profit was 1% the size of Google Services.

In Q1 2026, Google Services made $89.6 billion in revenue and $40.6 billion in profit; Google Cloud made $20.0 billion in revenue and $6.6 billion in profit. Google Cloud revenue was 22% the size of Google Services, and its profit was 16% the size of Google Services.

Google Services is, needless to say, a much more scalable business than See’s Candies. The growth just over the last seven years — more than doubling revenue and tripling profits — is astounding. And yet, at the same time, Google Cloud is growing faster, and while its margins are worse — 33% last quarter as compared to 45% for Google Services — they are expanding more rapidly.

The bigger question is how big can those numbers go? Google Services’ advertising business is inherently high margin, but advertising is definitionally but a fraction of the overall economy; Google Cloud’s growth, meanwhile, is AI, which many people think/worry/hope might take over the entire economy. In other words, might we one day look back and realize that Google Services provided the cash flow to build a business with relatively worse margins but absolutely higher dollars, much like See’s helped fund BNSF?

Berkshire Hathaway and Google Equity

The context for this discussion is this news from Bloomberg :

Google parent Alphabet Inc. is raising $80 billion through a package of equity offerings, including an investment deal with Berkshire Hathaway Inc., as the company races to fund its ambitious artificial intelligence spending plans. The undertaking includes a $40 billion so-called at-the-market program to sell shares from time to time beginning in the third quarter, according to a statement Monday. The company will also offer $30 billion in underwritten offerings of shares and mandatory convertible preferred stock, as well as the $10 billion deal with Berkshire. Together, the transactions represent one of the largest equity deals of all time — and they bring an unexpected twist to a blockbuster year for initial public offerings.

First off, a decent portion of the ATM program, launching in the fall, is going towards paying tax obligations on Google equity awards (which are quite large thanks to the stock’s run-up in value).

That leaves equity being issued now, particularly the $10 billion to Berkshire Hathaway, which is fascinating for a number of reasons. The first question is why did Google issue equity instead of debt? Debt is, all things being equal, the preferred instrument for investment: the proceeds of the latter pay off the former, and existing equity holders reap all of the benefits. Equity, on the other hand, removes the risk of debt, but at the cost of giving up a share of future profits.

Google has to date funded its massive AI-related capital expenditures with free cash flow, and while the company does have around $81 billion in debt, that is more than balanced by $126 billion of cash. In other words, Google’s capacity to issue more debt — and to reap the financial benefits of doing so (because interest is tax-deductible) — is substantial.

That leads to what may be the Occam’s Razor explanation: Google is also going to start issuing a lot more debt as well, which is to say that everyone continues to underestimate the amount of demand there is for compute. Of course that’s not far off from a more bearish interpretation: Google is uncertain about the return on investment of all that capex, and would prefer to share the risk (along with the upside). If there isn’t a substantial debt issuance down the road then this might be the right answer.

The second question is why is Berkshire Hathaway suddenly, after all these years, interested in Google, and at only a slight discount to its all-time high price? Does it really just come down to the fact that Buffett is no longer making investment decisions, and Greg Abel, his successor as CEO, is?

In fact, you can make the case that Abel is actually just replaying Buffett’s strategy, only this time Berkshire Hathaway is See’s Candies, and Google is BNSF. At the end of last quarter Berkshire Hathaway had $373 billion in cash, and $25 billion in free cash flow in 2025. How many companies could actually employ that cash in a way that generated a high rate of return?

It’s hard to imagine a better option than Google. The company is not only investing in AI, but has optionality in terms of outcomes: its Services business benefits from the investment, it is in contention at the model layer with Gemini, and it can sell capacity to the frontier labs. Moreover, that capacity has a sustainable cost advantage because of TPUs, which means that in a world where compute becomes a commodity — as hard as that is to imagine right now — Google is the hyperscaler that is poised to make the most profit.

It is worth noting that $10 billion is a relatively small amount of money to both companies. To that end, perhaps the primary utility is as a signaling mechanism. On Google’s side, the signal is that the expected demand is actually far greater than anyone thinks, and that the company is ready and willing to fund supply using all means at its disposal, including equity; for them Berkshire Hathaway’s investment is an endorsement of this view and a validation of the wisdom of the investment. And, on the flip side, if the signal is correct, then Berkshire Hathaway is getting a deal and putting its cash flow machines to work building the future.

Cash the Ultimate Commodity

A couple of months ago, when Anthropic was clearly ascendant, OpenAI backers tried to make the case that actually OpenAI was in the driver’s seat because the frontier lab had secured more compute; I made the case in Mythos, Muse, and the Opportunity Cost of Compute that this was not at all dispositive:

OpenAI is betting that this compute constraint — and the deals they have made to overcome it — will matter more than Anthropic’s current momentum with end users…I’m less certain that this will be dispositive. When it comes to AI, distribution and transaction costs are still free — the two preconditions for Aggregators — which means that the winners should be those with the most compelling products. Those products will win the most users, providing the money necessary to source the compute to serve them; consider Anthropic’s deal to secure a meaningful portion of TPU supply, which, given the capacity constraints at TSMC, is ultimately an example of taking supply from Google. I suspect that Anthropic can take more, including already built hyperscaler and neocloud capacity. Yes, that compute will be more expensive, but if demand is high enough the necessary cash flow will be there.

That thesis was proven correct just weeks later when SpaceX ponied up the supply Anthropic needed (and yes, it was expensive):

This deal is a perfect example of what really is basic economics. First, if demand exceeds supply, then prices should increase. At the same time, prices are elastic: if they are lower there is more demand, and if they are higher there is less demand. In this case, while there is broad demand for computing, Anthropic has arguably the most demand; furthermore, Anthropic has the most willingness to pay, not just because they are making meaningful revenue, but also because they have the capacity to raise money in the pursuit of winning in AI.

Implicit in this analysis was that there was enough compute capacity in the world to be bought; what happens, however, when and if there isn’t? What if the ultimate battle — the one that determines who gets compute — becomes a matter of who can bring the most cash to bear? And what if that advantage compounds, such that the company with the most cash capacity ends up with the most compute capacity (which we already know they will sell, in addition to using themselves) driving the ability to generate more cash? In that world, what company would be your best bet?

We now know which one Berkshire Hathaway is betting on. 1 ( #a8f2c738-d146-41d0-8c2f-0ca7cc2a3f23 )

* As an aside, it’s notable that Alphabet has another business — Waymo — where the company has so far rejected an asset-light model of licensing their software to OEMs, and has instead to date pursued a much more capital intensive approach of owning and operating their own cars; that’s a choice that has always felt at odds with Google Services, but is perhaps more compelling and aligned with Google Cloud and the Google Capital Company. ↩︎ ( #a8f2c738-d146-41d0-8c2f-0ca7cc2a3f23-link )
