An interview with Ben Bajarin about WWDC and the status of the AI compute industry.

An Interview with Ben Bajarin About Apple, AI, and Compute

Thursday, June 11, 2026

This week’s Stratechery Interview is with Ben Bajarin . Bajarin is the CEO and Principal Analyst for Creative Strategies , one of the oldest technology-focused market research firms. Bajarin and Creative Strategies have a particular focus on semiconductors, and Bajarin also hosts The Circuit Podcast about the semiconductor industry with previous Stratechery Interview subject Jay Goldberg. Recently Creative Strategies launched a new Substack called The Diligence Stack , featuring original market research and industry analysis. I previously spoke with Bajarin in September 2024 and October 2025 .

In this interview we discuss WWDC and Apple’s AI announcements. We talk about what they launched, not just in terms of AI, but also why the company was focused on improving the underlying platform. We also discuss their architectural choices, including on-device inference and using Nvidia chips on Google’s Cloud. After that we discuss AI compute broadly, including Nvidia’s new PC chip, Vera, CPUs and agents, and Intel’s change in fortunes. And, at the end, we talk about Creative Strategies’ new offering.

As a reminder, all Stratechery content, including interviews, is available as a podcast; click the link at the top of this email to add Stratechery to your podcast player.

On to the Interview:

An Interview with Ben Bajarin About Apple, AI, and Compute

This interview is lightly edited for clarity.

*Topics:*

WWDC Foundations ( #wwdc-foundations ) | Consumer vs. Enterprise AI ( #consumer-enterprise-ai ) | Apple’s AI Architecture ( #apple-ai-architecture ) | Project Solara ( #project-solara ) | The Nvidia PC ( #nvidia-pc ) | CPUs in the Data Center ( #cpus-data-center ) | Compute Capacity ( #compute-capacity ) | CPUs in the Data Center ( #cpus-data-center ) | The Diligence Stack ( #diligence-stack )

WWDC Foundations

*Ben Bajarin, welcome back to Stratechery.*

*BB:* Hello, Ben Thompson. Thanks for having me again.

*I’ve been wanting to have you back on for a while, and we finally got a good occasion this week, which is WWDC , so let’s start there. What was your overall take on the keynote, beyond it being shockingly short?*

*BB:* Shockingly short, which I thought was interesting, because any of us who’ve watched this for a while know WWDC used to be a product or vertical operating system set of narratives — here’s macOS, here’s iPadOS, here’s whatever. This was a platform conversation, and so I thought that was different.

My read on that — and I don’t think this was my overall take coming into this, but the realization afterwards — is that to do all the things we want them to succeed in or do with generative AI, and AI in a smart Siri, a lot needed to be re-architected at the platform level.

*And by platform, do you mean not just at the operating system level, but Apple as a platform broadly?*

*BB:* Correct. Every platform essentially needed to be re-architected, you probably felt this too — we have a lot of conversations, and they’re always like, “You know what, operating systems and platforms just get crusty, they’re old, they’ve been built on something that was great 10 years ago and not now”. This is the same problem that Microsoft’s been trying to go through with Windows to modernize it, a lot just needs to be modernized, and that’s hard to do when you’ve got billions of customers.

So that I thought was the take of, “We need to do these things” — when’s the last time Apple’s mentioned a CPU scheduler? They update CPU schedulers all the time — they just felt the need to call out that they’ve actually done it even more, and the index, when’s the last time they talked about, “Hey, we rebuilt the index”? That’s boring on the surface, but necessary to do all this stuff with Siri and Apple Intelligence.

*I thought the index was a really notable point, because if you understood broadly what the point of Siri was, it was notable that they spent so much time on the index. This was my overall take on the AI story, they’re perfecting a 2024 AI story, which is when they announced Apple Intelligence . This was basically, “Let’s do what we said in 2024, but for real this time”. To what extent was there the realization that the reason why Siri failed wasn’t just because the models were bad or whatever it might be, but because if we’re going to do RAG , we actually have to have a functional search index, and they didn’t have that”?*

*BB:* I think it’s related — that’s exactly right. Obviously, we wanted them to get here sooner — I don’t think any of us perhaps appreciated the magnitude of the platform re-architecture that was needed to do this.

*What about us? What about Apple?*

*BB:* Well, that’s the thing. The broader question would be, “Could you have done some of this sooner? Is it all necessary?” — maybe that’s the case, but the reality is, and you’re exactly right, I would imagine that search, and semantic search, and better contextual search, is actually going to be one of the things that people do a lot of, and so having the index get redone was a key part of being able to do that. Maybe it wouldn’t have worked before.

*Well, all the Siri demos that are super obviously useful, and that, from what I’ve seen, seem to clearly work, are basically just fancy search at the end of the day. Is that a fair characterization?*

*BB:* Correct, yes, absolutely. And again, that’s one of the things where that’s been like a black hole for a lot of people — you lose a lot of stuff, you’re not organized.

*And also, if you ever tried to search in Messages, you realize that — I mean, that was almost like a tell, right?*

*BB:* It doesn’t work at all.

*If you go back to the “When does my mom land in San Francisco?” demo, which was never actually demoed, but just talked about in 2024, you realize I can’t actually find a message from my mom in iMessage today.*

*BB:* Ever!

*So on what aspect is Siri going to be able to find it?*

*BB:* Yeah, 100%. Or I could say, “Search for something from Ben Thompson”, and you don’t show up at all. And I was like, “He’s in my contacts, how can you not find this message?”, it’s just stuff that now, in a gen AI world, you’d walk back and say, “If it didn’t do those things, I would view it as a failure”, and so it needs to do those things, and that’s why the platform needs to be updated.

So broad picture, taking a platform approach was kind of what they did, because all those pillars led up to now trying to mainstream generative AI and bring it to the masses — they had to do those first two things first.

*Do you think that is enough? Is actually just being, “State of the art in 2024 but it actually works, and you happen to own the operating system and have all that data” — do customers actually want anything more than that ?*

*BB:* I think there’s a base level of expectation that my device does these things, and I think that’s where they landed. If you just look at even Gemini — Gemini is fine, it’s definitely not OpenAI or Claude in terms of its capabilities yet, it does what you need it to do when you’re searching and might want to interact with your calendar. These are basic things, and I also step back and say most consumers on the long tail of adoption are not using this for anything more than search. When they use GPT or Claude, it’s just search.

*The two big use cases that I seem to see for normal people are recipes and do-it-yourself projects, which are fancy search at the end of the day.*

*BB:* Yes, fancy search. So that’s why I think the interesting part here is, if we know that a lot of people kind of don’t do these things other than search — most people are not doing full workflow automation for their lives — they might do this for some work stuff, but they’re not doing it for their lives. That connecting to a consumer job, or the agent that I hire to go make a change in my calendar or find this image or have deeper semantic search — these are still new behaviors, and having a way that Apple mainstreams that in a way everybody can use it, for me, was always the key. Could they do it in a way that even grandma can use and find useful? That I just don’t think was an easy mountain to climb, and it looks like what they’ve got has gotten to a point where, honestly, it doesn’t always even mean you need to use Siri — it will be invisible in the background, but still be useful.

So this useful AI in an application, or applied AI, which is kind of the term I was using — if you just use robotics and applied robotics as a term, it moves from the lab to the mainstream — this is applied AI at a consumer level, and I think they got to that point and honestly, that’s all people will need. If they want to go off and do advanced other workflow stuff, there’s other models, and that’s totally fine.

*When do you think Apple realized they needed to have their own — because they tried to draw this clear line between world knowledge and personal knowledge in 2024 — when did they realize that actually this is a line that does not make sense at all?*

*BB:* I think for them — and we’ve talked about this too — there needs to be value in general search. The assumption when I heard, “Hey, we might be working with Gemini”, or when the rumor was out, was, “Oh cool, search is going to get good, because I use this on my device a lot”. So the idea is that they are bringing what they’re calling Apple world knowledge to this, and to some degree it sounds like it’s their index — they’re trying to separate themselves from Google. But that’s a core function that’s necessary, and to be honest with you, that’s a core function that’s necessary if we assume that they want to do glasses someday, and you might ask it about not just your food, but a flower or a bird or whatnot. So it needs to have that broad world knowledge, as they call it, and be something that they own and maintain.

Consumer vs. Enterprise AI

*Do you think consumers will ever care about agents and things like that?*

*BB:* No, I don’t. This is actually something I want to talk to you about.

*Oh, I’m getting interviewed now.*

*BB:* Yes! You and I were both born in the era of disruption theory and Jobs to Be Done . Is this not one of the most cleanly interesting examples? I’m hiring something, I don’t need to think it’s an agent, but I’m hiring something, in this case it’s Siri, or is it GPT, or is it Anthropic, to go do something for me to get jobs done, and how I disintermediate what those jobs are. Is it summarize an email? Is it do this for my calendar? This to me is a super interesting jobs to be done, in its purest definition, of, “Why would I choose this control plane layer?”. Don’t even think agent — just think something I interact with, and it goes and does this stuff for me. Consumer jobs, enterprise jobs, whatever it is, this is purely jobs to be done competition in the mental model. It doesn’t have to be an agent, it’s just I use this one thing and it can go do these things for me, because it has system-level access, app-level access, Internet-level access, all of those things.

*My view on this has gotten quite coarse, which is, enterprises want to do work , they want their employees to be productive, because they’re paying the employees, they want to get more bang for their dollar, or perhaps replace those employees with something that is at least theoretically cheaper. Consumers don’t want to do work! The whole point of being a consumer is you don’t want to be at work, you want to be entertained, and in that context, I’m just broadly skeptical.*

*Again, as I put in my Article this week , I think this is a lesson that tech has had to relearn every decade or so. OpenAI is like the modern Dropbox — sort of timely with Drew Houston stepping down these days. Remember Dropbox, they wanted to be a consumer company so bad, even after it was clear their only market was enterprise, they launched that Carousel product, this beautiful photos thing, and I remember I wrote at the time that Houston was so clearly so much more enthusiastic and passionate about this product — which they then killed a year later — because finally it penetrated the consciousness that consumers don’t pay, because they don’t care about being productive. What are the things they do pay for? Netflix.*

*BB:* Entertainment. Yep.

*What they don’t pay for is productivity applications. That’s always been the case, and OpenAI had to learn that lesson. I had Sam Altman telling me, in the chair you’re in right now, multiple times , “I don’t like ads, we think that consumers will pay”. Nope, they won’t! And given that — and this isn’t short-changing AI, I’m obviously incredibly optimistic about a lot of these workflows and more and more autonomy and agentic stuff, and I think that enterprises will pay for that — I don’t think consumers are going to care.*

*BB:* I don’t disagree with that but my mental model is using this to plan a party, and having a seamless culmination of emails from three sources to plan it — that’s still a job.

*Right, fancy search is a great outcome.*

*BB:* But it’s still a job, right? It’s just not an enterprise workflow. It’s still, in your mental model, an outcome — you are searching for an outcome.

*But it’s a human-in-the-loop job. It’s not like the agent is going to go out and plan a party and buy supplies and they’re just going to show up at your door.*

*BB:* Do everything — agreed.

*And there’s another thing here, this gets at the whole agent — sorry, I’m sort of ranting on my own interview.*

*BB:* Please go.

*The whole agentic shopping sort of thing — there’s a fundamental variable that is missing in it. Silicon Valley just has such a bad mental model for the rest of humanity — people like shopping, they do it for fun! It just doesn’t even occur to folks, it’s like, “Oh, let’s make it so you never have to shop again” — okay, then what are they going to do, watch more Netflix?*

*BB:* But you hit it again — even in all of these, the best application is still some form of human-in-the-loop, even if that’s reviewing or guiding or it collaborating with you, which to me is the most interesting thing. Something that works with you, that essentially has some level of autonomy, but you are still collaborating with it, is ultimately the thing that I think gets to the most interesting endgame here for everybody.

But again, when I use this jobs to be done framework, I’m saying if we just separate these two things, we understand what the enterprise jobs look like. There are still consumer jobs, endpoints of outcomes, and there needs to be a middle layer there that they interact with, that control plane, to go do those jobs. I think that’s the more interesting role for Apple and Siri — to be that control plane for a whole host of outcomes, in this case in a pure consumer sense.

*Basically, zooming out, there was this whole consumerization of IT theme, or whatever, and people wanted to tell themselves that consumer and enterprise were conflating. In some respects they were, and I think the broader takeaway I have from AI is actually we’re way back — it’s another back-to-the-future angle, they’re just completely and utterly different markets when it comes to AI in particular.*

*BB:* Absolutely, and most people don’t love working, but you probably like being a consumer of things — that’s an enjoyable life.

*I’m not going to pay Anthropic $50 per million tokens or whatever so I can have an agent managing my kitchen.*

*BB:* Go outside, touch grass.

Apple’s AI Architecture

*All right, let’s get into some of the architectural changes Apple made. So first, where exactly is Gemini showing up? Is it fair to characterize it as Apple using it as the teacher model for their on-device models, which are basically distilled from Gemini, but then it is the core of the foundation model — with a lot of post-training and stuff from Apple — for Apple’s models in the cloud. Is that a good characterization?*

*BB:* Yeah, but only for the models in the cloud. They went out of their way to explain that the AFM [Apple Foundational Models] models that run on device are theirs — their training, their evolution.

*Theirs, but using Gemini to train?*

*BB:* They didn’t even say that for four of the five models. The only place they said they used a Gemini-based model is for Apple cloud, the Pro model.

*What I’m saying though is, are the on-device models, which are not Gemini, basically distilled from Gemini?*

*BB:* We did not get that impression. They wanted to go out of their way to say that they’ve been doing AFM for a handful of years, and those are all their models. Whereas in the cloud model, that is base Gemini, and then they trained a whole slew of things on top of that. They want to make sure it’s clear: we’re not using Gemini, we’re using ours — but the base model for hybrid cloud compute is whatever they licensed from Gemini.

*Got it. So they have a new on-device model, a 20-billion parameter mixture-of-experts model. Usually for mixture-of-experts — broadly speaking, I’m going to bastardize this explanation — a model is divided into multiple experts, of which only some are lit up at a time, and usually almost all leading-edge models at this point are mixture-of-experts, they’re more efficient, there’s lots of things that go into it. But usually you light up a different expert per token, so there’s a decision at every token that’s produced, “Which expert should I be looking at?”. But that requires all the experts — the entire model — to be in memory, and that’s not viable for a 20-billion parameter model on a phone. So what Apple is doing is actually lighting up an expert per query so it’s like, “This is mostly an audio-oriented question, there’s a specific aspect of the model that’s good at that, we’re going to light that up”, this only works on the latest A19 Pro, and basically you need at least 12 gigabytes of RAM for this to work. Did Apple screw up by not putting 12 gigabytes of RAM on the regular A19, such that phones from last year can’t run this model?*

*BB:* Well, remember too, that’s for the audio model — it’s for the voices, it’s not for the entirety of what you’ll get in Apple Intelligence. They were very clear that there are certain things they did, exactly like you said, where they can just run — call it maybe a three-to-four billion parameter model — to do these new voices, and that level of memory management needs the latest devices. The other stuff we’re talking about — contextual Siri, contextual search, the app — that comes back to all the devices, they said, but it was specific to a few things, voices namely, that are reserved for only the A19 Pro and above.

*Let’s get to the cloud aspect of these models. Is Apple Silicon in the cloud dead?*

*BB:* You know, it’s a great question, I struggle with this to be honest with you, because we understand all of the reasons why they are pushing and highlighting confidential compute . I mean, when’s the last time Apple has even mentioned Nvidia? It’s been at least a decade and a half, if not longer. Everybody that follows this knows these two companies did not love each other — there was a huge feud.

*Did not love, they hated each other, let’s be clear here.*

*BB:* I was being generous, Ben, I was being generous!

*They’re too alike.*

*BB:* Yes, exactly. But they called them out, I did not expect this — I did not expect them to specifically say we’re running on Google Cloud and Nvidia for confidential compute, and Intel for that matter — you actually have two steps of confidential compute. So they made a big deal of confidential compute.

Okay, so then the question is, “Why would you make a big deal of this?”, to me, this is a very geopolitical thing. Think of Apple as a sovereign at this point, you need to be global and bring this to all your customers, and you’ve got to pass scrutiny tests, because people freak out about AI and whatnot, obviously with Europe and China — so confidential compute becomes table stakes to do some of these things, so they call that out.

So now the question is, do they just keep relying on others? Is it so important that they can’t do it or don’t want to do it, or will they eventually do it because it’s so critical to their ability to bring this at a global level? That’s what I don’t know. I think you would argue they want to be as vertical as possible, they would rather do these chips, and there’s rumors they’re doing something with Broadcom on cloud ASICs . But to go so far out of their way — and is this temporal? — to call out what they’re doing with these other vendors in confidential compute is pretty significant, that has to have a lot of weight.

And so again, the debate is, do you verticalize there, or do you allow others to do it, because your belief is they will help you pass regulatory scrutiny by nations, because they have established confidential compute in their environments?

*I agree with you in part, disagree with you in part. So number one, I don’t think the regulatory angle has anything to do with it, personally. I think the fact of the matter is that it wasn’t good enough and sufficient for what they needed to accomplish, especially this image generation stuff. It’s sort of interesting, because they’re not running long-context sessions — part of the whole point of Private Cloud Compute is that it’s not retaining the data. This gets to our earlier point, where they are building state-of-the-art 2024 answer models — they’re not building anything remotely useful for agentic inference. But at the end of the day, what differentiation are they actually providing, especially once they’ve already opened the door here? And I think the callout for Nvidia and Intel is because they do have initiatives for exactly this sort of confidential computing. At this point, once they’ve broken the seal, what’s the point of wasting resources on building their own thing, unless they want to claw back margin? I don’t know.*

*BB:* So I’ll give you two other points. The reason I land on the sovereign point is just because you do confidential compute, you pass this regulatory scrutiny when you—

*Sorry, what’s the regulatory scrutiny around confidential compute?*

*BB:* Again, think of them as a sovereign. It may not even all just be Europe, but where might people continue to be concerned about that data, where that data lives, and where that data is processed? Confidential compute adds, I think, another layer of security, privacy, trust.

*So are you talking about data transfer rules from the EU to the US?*

*BB:* Yes, correct.

*Got it, okay.*

*BB:* And again, think about this for China. How do they do this in China? I don’t know — they’re certainly not going to do it on Nvidia GPUs, so they will need a very similar set of standards that they pass in order to deploy these in nations.

*Why not do it on Nvidia chips in China? I could see China letting Apple put Nvidia chips in their data centers.*

*BB:* Okay, well, that would be an ideal scenario, but contentious to begin with. They’re the only one that gets to bring a cloud and stick it in Baidu, or Alibaba?

*Apple gets lots of special exceptions in China.*

*BB:* You’re right. But I think the broader point here is, it is more expensive to do confidential compute — there is a cost to the CSP to do it, so you’re right, it could be margins. There’s also a compute tax, there’s latency involved. So is it the kind of thing they could speed up? It’s not just margins — could they do it better, take some of that compute tax, verticalize it, make it faster so there’s less latency, etc.? That would be my argument for where they could maybe add value.

But again, it comes down to how critical they think that one thing is to the core experience, because as you know, Apple verticalizes when they think they can add value in a core experience that differentiates them. If they have all those dots aligned and say yes, then they still do the cloud ASIC. If no — if you’re fine with the price, and you’re fine believing that it will be sped up by these vendors over time — then maybe it’s not that big of a deal.

*You mentioned Apple and Nvidia together at last — is this the greatest Nvidia endorsement ever?*

*BB:* For confidential compute, yes. You’d imagine [Nvidia CEO] Jensen [Huang] and others would be like, “Yes, we got Apple”, but I think he’s equally proud of, let’s just say, others who named them.

*Why isn’t this run on TPUs?*

*BB:* We have good evidence it was trained on TPUs, they obviously want to serve the inference side of this, which is a little bit broader of an equation. And again, they very specifically called out Intel as a head node for some of the additional confidential compute, and as we’ve talked about before, agentic CPUs are now a full-blown thing, and so you need that dedicated install base as well. TPUs are fine, but to what CPU head node? Google is just now bringing Axion to those.

*Do TPUs have this sort of — what’s the framework for Nvidia GPUs, the secure compute?*

*BB:* I forget the name of their secure enclave.

*Yeah, do TPUs have that?*

*BB:* They have a version, but definitely not as complex.

*Not as robust. So my view on this is, I think your point about data moving around is a very good one, that’s why Apple needs to rely on an external cloud provider first and foremost, because they’re not going to build data centers in every country, so they need someone that has broad geographic dispersal. But number two, it’s fine to be dependent on Google for training, because that’s a one-time thing. Inference is ongoing, and if you’re on Nvidia, then you, in theory, can always go to Amazon or you can go to Microsoft. If you’re on TPUs, you’re stuck with Google, and I think that’s something that Apple would want to avoid.*

*BB:* Portability and also there’s a lot of programmability that goes into GPUs — they’re still general purpose, so there’s a lot of software.

*They’re not doing anything that fancy though, let’s be honest. They’re generating some images.*

*BB:* Okay, but again, in that vein, why not someday move toward your own cloud ASICs? If you want to just specially optimize, then verticalize there as well, if this will always be a core part of your offering, and you’re going to consistently need to do hybrid, you could make an argument that they should verticalize and do their own ASICs there.

*Is this Apple deal the driving factor behind Google’s SpaceX deal to get a bunch more Nvidia GPUs?*

*BB:* Oh man, this was so much talked about in numerous investor events, it’s a very good theory. Obviously, we don’t know — when they say we’re running this with Google, we don’t know where that is.

You can look at this two ways — either Google needs more capacity and they’re willing to use SpaceX GPUs and then give Apple something else internal, or they’re like, “Hey, we need this deal for Apple” — and this is the most speculation. But my concern with the SpaceX deal is that [SpaceX CEO] Elon [Musk] can take these back. It’s not guaranteed infrastructure — I don’t think he would, and he has to give what I think is 90 days notice, but regardless, if you’re Apple, why would you even do a deal where somebody could pull the rug on me and then I’ve got to change?

But Google might be able to use those and guarantee Apple internally so it might be more that Google cares — they freed up capacity, and now they’ve got more GCP because of this deal.

*So when we zoom out, it was kind of weird — why is Google giving Apple Gemini for a billion dollars a year ? That doesn’t seem like very much money. Is this actually the answer, they now have a massive new Google Cloud customer?*

*BB:* Yeah, for sure, I think that’s definitely part of it. And again, it’s ongoing — Apple will still want to update that model with Gemini as a base in the future, it would obviously be bad if they didn’t, because then it would get stale. And exactly to your point, I think this is an interesting part of this discussion too, I think Google had just sort of assumed Apple would do something and they wouldn’t have much opportunity in Apple’s ecosystem with Gemini so they don’t want to lose that entirely — get something from it, that’s part of this deal.

*I just think the whole thing makes so much more sense once they talked about this actually running on Google’s cloud — I think they’re giving up, or they should give up, on Apple Silicon in the cloud. Just view it like the world is Lego — you can assemble it and connect it, and you’ve got to put it on a baseboard, your base Lego tile, and those need to connect together. So that’s their packaging chops in terms of EMIB.

In a world where you are capacity-constrained — meaning that you can only get so much capacity for CoWoS and future versions of CoWoS from TSMC — and you have so much demand, the idea of dual-sourcing makes sense. *So there’s sufficient GPUs available to do this?*

*BB:* They’re moving internal teams off to those.

*That’s what I’m saying — but it’s a pretty remarkable claim, Google is putting internal workloads on GPUs because when they go to their customers, they don’t want to say they have GPUs available, they want to say, “Oh, come over, we have TPUs” — but they do have GPUs available, they’re just not telling their customers, that’s basically the story here?*

*BB:* This is why they’re doing deals with, like we talked about, SpaceX and other neoclouds who have GPUs — it’s for that workload diversity. But you can see that they knew they needed to get customers on this, if they can’t get customers on their custom ASICs — it’s very hard if it’s just internal. So they’re willing to give those internal teams the GPU side and then bring customers TPUs to make this money, make their CapEx, return their ROIC, etc.

*This is very interesting. Okay, so Google — setting aside Apple — Google getting SpaceX is not because customers want GPUs, it’s because Google wants to offer customers TPUs so they’re locked in, and Google, in the meantime, will use the GPUs. Just to make sure I got the take — it’s a very compelling take, it’s kind of blowing my mind here.*

*BB:* Yeah, and we think Amazon’s doing the same thing. Again, you’ve known the contention of internal teams sitting there going, “We’re tired of being in line, we’ve got to get stuff done” — but they want to monetize that infrastructure.

*Well, they want to lock people in. Once you get your stuff working on Trainium or TPUs, then the work’s done.*

*BB:* You’re stuck. Exactly, yeah.

*Interesting. So in the long run, who holds the ultimate value? What’s going to be the most valuable part of the stack — is it the model companies, is it the hyperscalers, is it Nvidia, is it TSMC? Give me a stack ranking of 2035 market caps.*

*BB:* 2035! I would lean towards still the hyperscalers at this point, but then I’m going to make a somewhat different point on the token spend, because a lot of this comes down to just what token costs are. They are still the meters in this, and as long as you are the meter — from infrastructure to power, all the things that are scarce and hard to control — especially at an enterprise software layer, where you’re going to see the vast majority of enterprises move to some degree of cloud for AI, your hyperscalers sit right there as the control point of those platforms, so they’re well-positioned.

But the token side of this — and this would be where you could claim infrastructure takes a different shape — is if we start to see more on-prem infrastructure, meaning on-prem servers too. What if enterprises start buying Nvidia to put in their internal data centers, in order to do more token generation at the edge? Then there’s a long tail there of infrastructure, of compute. Think of it like PCs in that cycle, but in this case, it’s on-prem servers.

So there’s the two sides of those, where I don’t know which way that goes. You could argue — again, I would rather just do all my token generation at the edge if I can, it’s going to save me money, because this is OpEx, not CapEx, for these companies. But the model labs and the hyperscalers are going to keep trying to pack as much as possible, so that the best model compute is there, so they can meter it, and in a metering world, they will be the best-positioned — the hyperscalers as the allocators of that power, that compute, that meter. But my concern is the fight for token generation moves some of it back to the edge, at which point that’s infrastructure — compute as a chain.

*When do the supply-demand balances in terms of compute even out?*

*BB:* Not before 2030. Honestly, it could extend to your timeline of 2035. And I think, again — I think we talked about this — it really depends on your view of AI software. I tweeted this the other day, you’re bearish on the long haul — and I mean, this could last for some time — if AI is Internet software or client software, because that all got good enough at some point, there was no reason for me to keep updating my infrastructure on three-to-four-year timelines when the gains in software were marginal.

But if this is like graphics, for example — that industry has never had enough compute. They’re chasing fidelity, they’re chasing real life — that’s a 30-year set of advancements. If you believe that AI is more like fidelity — that tokens and pixels are the same thing — you’re a lot more bullish, because this could be a much longer cycle. So you just really need to pick your software philosophy — is this 10 years, or is it maybe 20 or 30 years?

*I love this tweet — that was going to be my closing question, this tweet, so you just did it, I’ll link it in the show notes. Do you think AI is software or graphics? It’s a great question, a great way to frame it, and it really speaks to why Nvidia is doing as well as they are.*

*BB:* It is. And again, to the degree that Jensen knew this — I sort of landed on this because he’s said this framing so many times — generative AI is generative in the same way that graphics is generated. It’s generating a scene, and then you move to the left, and it generates that scene in real time. If this is true — and this is why the graphics one holds for me — Jensen’s insight was that the same computational problem for pixels is for tokens, and that architecture is the same problem.

The Diligence Stack

*One last question related to this, but not related to this. Of course, I love chips, I love talking about products. I really love publishing and publishing business models, and you have a new one! You’ve traditionally been a boutique research firm serving clients, you now have a Substack , tell me about it.*

*BB:* We started this new Substack called The Diligence Stack. And exactly like you said, we do a lot of research for the industry that’s largely private and so now we wanted to make that more accessible to a wider audience, so we’re publishing a lot of our research, our thesis, our market forecasts, our TAM sizing, things that we love doing, we’ve done for clients and publishing that.

*And this is instead of like, “Go out and do this market forecast”, you’re doing market forecast and putting it up for sale, basically.*

*BB:* Correct. Yeah, full data models. Another good example, we do a lot of CIO interviews so we published our whole CIO interview there. You could get something like that at Gartner, IDC, we’re sharing that now much more publicly than just internally. So it’s really just our firm kind of taking an approach now and doing more in a one-to-many model, making that more accessible than just what we did.

*Right.*

*BB:* But we’ve got decades of research, we’ve been doing this for 30, 40 years, our firm and so making that more as a publishing model, it’s a first for us, and it’s been great, and the feedback’s been amazing.

*Well usually it’s a lot harder to go from like small set of customers at very high prices to making it up in volume, so I’m curious — you don’t have to give any numbers — but it’s been a few months, how’s it going?*

*BB:* It’s going extremely well, it’s far exceeding my my expectations.

*Amazing.*

*BB:* We are getting a lot of the buy side in the institution who I’ve worked with for you know dozens of years and they were like, “You should put something out because it’s great that we talk to you, but it’s better for us to circulate research that you’ve done, it’s just more useful”. So we packaged this up, which is why it’s a whole publishing product.

*It’s an interesting price point because it’s $300 a month, $3,000 a year, it has real data, it’s not just an institutional investor, but it’s not just a “read my newsletter” sort of thing. It’s sort of in the middle.*

*BB:* Really just leveraging the decades of research and presence that our that our firm has had and my time in this industry and just bringing all of that experience, all of that data, our thesis, things we’ve seen, our ability to size markets, do TAM forecasts, estimate things I don’t see others do and I’m just intellectually curious of and publish that.

*Right, that’s the key thing is you get to go out and do it and then sell it as opposed to waiting for someone to hire you to do it.*

*BB:* Yeah, exactly, which makes it more worth it. And I think we do a good job of surveying the big hairy questions of the industry that aren’t answered, and I want to go try and solve some answers or form a thesis around that.

And again, just our decades of doing this is having good experience to build these models because this is not our first rodeo, it’s our third or fourth rodeo. That’s where I think the broad demand has been really interesting and a wider audience finding that compelling, which is validating for me to keep doing this, which has been a huge positive because it’s a lot of work.

*Yeah, it’s very exciting, I’m very excited for you. We’ll have to check back in on both the business model and the industry later this year. Good talking to you.*

*BB:* Yeah, I look forward to it. Thanks for having me on.

title: Anthropic's Safety Superpower

text:
Anthropic's belief in its own commitment to safety gives the company license to aggressively favor its business and even challenge the U.S. government.

Anthropic’s Safety Superpower

Monday, June 15, 2026

I’m sympathetic to the cynics who consistently characterize Anthropic’s public statements, particularly those surrounding their model releases, as scare-mongering for the sake of marketing. It was only two months ago that Anthropic announced Mythos Preview, a model that they said was too dangerous to make publicly available, thanks in particular to its advanced cybersecurity capabilities. Then, two months later, the company publicly released Fable, a version of Mythos with various safety guardrails.

Fable is, in my limited experience, a very impressive model. It’s increasingly difficult to objectively evaluate models for anything other than coding performance, but there is subjective feel, and I found my interactions with Fable to be extremely impressive; it made other models, including GPT 5.5 and Opus 4.8, feel small and dumb. The two times I felt that way previously were with GPT-4 and Grok 4, both of which represented new generations in terms of base model size and complexity; my sense is that Fable is downstream of a new pre-train and the first of a new generation.

To that end, I can certainly buy the case that Fable/Mythos is in fact more capable when it comes to identifying and exploiting security issues, and that Anthropic’s cautious roll-out was justified. The problem with publicly releasing models, however, is that guardrails can be jailbroken, and apparently that is exactly what happened shortly after the release.

Anthropic vs. the U.S. Government, Again

What happened next is somewhat unclear. Anthropic wrote in a blog post :

The US government, citing national security authorities, has issued an export control directive to suspend all access to Fable 5 and Mythos 5 by any foreign national, whether inside or outside the United States, including foreign national Anthropic employees. The net effect of this order is that we must abruptly disable Fable 5 and Mythos 5 for all our customers to ensure compliance. Access to all other Anthropic models will not be affected.

We received the directive from the government today at 5:21pm (ET). The letter did not provide specific details of its national security concern. Our understanding is that the government believes it has become aware of a method of bypassing, or “jailbreaking” Fable 5. We reviewed a demonstration of this specific technique being used to identify a small number of previously known, minor vulnerabilities. These vulnerabilities all appear relatively simple, and we have found that other publicly-available models are able to discover them as well without requiring a bypass.

Anthropic went on to make the case that non-universal jailbreaks were inevitable and also narrow, and that there was no evidence of a universal jailbreak; the jailbreak that was found, meanwhile, appears to have been reported by Amazon , which is notable given Amazon is both an investor in Anthropic and a major provider of inference to the company. As I write this, senior Anthropic staff are in Washington D.C. seeking to resolve what they insist is a misunderstanding, and which White House officials are suggesting is insouciance by the company’s leadership to legitimate national security concerns.

I don’t actually have much to add to the current conflict given how many facts are in dispute; what I am not surprised about is the fact that the conflict is happening: I already explained in Anthropic and Alignment why conflict between the U.S. government and Anthropic was inevitable. To that end, people who are arguing that Mythos isn’t powerful enough to warrant the government’s drastic action are missing the point: if it’s not powerful enough now, the next one will be, or the one after that, particularly now that models are increasingly useful in creating their successors.

That, however, raises another question — one that seems to validate the cynics’ viewpoint: if Mythos is so dangerous, why even release Fable in the first place, and why fight with the government doing exactly what you claim to want? In fact, I think that Anthropic’s actions are quite understandable; what makes the company unique is how it justifies them, and it is those justifications that both give the cynics their fuel and Anthropic its magic.

The Economic Imperative

For the first few years of AI the most economic value has flown to compute, for obvious reasons: we don’t have enough supply to meet demand, which has meant skyrocketing prices; the biggest beneficiaries have been Nvidia, TSMC, and the memory makers (SK hynix, Samsung, and Micron). Anthropic and OpenAI, meanwhile, have collectively lost tens of billions of dollars building leading-edge models that, once released, are distilled and commoditized by open source models, primarily from China.

This represents the bear case for the labs — they never cover their costs because their differentiation is fleeting, while free alternatives become “good enough” — and I think it’s a legitimate one. A world where models are interchangeable is one where models are commodities, while most of the value flows elsewhere. Right now that’s compute, but in the fullness of time, whenever we have enough compute, the most valuable place to be in the value chain will be the place that has always been the most valuable: owning the user touchpoint.

To that end, it has long been clear to me that the frontier labs have the economic imperative to move closer to the user. If you own the user touchpoint, then you have meaningful lock-in, and the best way to own the user touchpoint is to be the canvas for everything they need to do. This, by extension, means that the frontier labs are on a collision course with software companies: it’s software that owns the user touchpoint, and it’s in the frontier labs’ long-term interest to not simply be a commodity input into software but to simply replace software outright.

Software companies, meanwhile, are working to do the opposite. Satya Nadella laid out his vision for how companies should build on models in an essay on X :

Every company is going to have to build what I think of as human capital and token capital. Human capital comprises the knowledge, judgment, relationships, ingenuity, and pattern recognition of its people, while token capital is the firm’s AI capability it builds and owns. Importantly, human capital does not become less valuable as token capital grows. It only becomes more valuable! I believe human agency will be the driver of token capital growth. Humans will set ambitious goals, connect dots across domains, build relationships, and recognize patterns that matter most. Without human direction, you have compute running in circles.

This means the real opportunity is not in picking the best model but instead in building a learning loop on top of models where human capital and token capital compound. You can offload a task, or even a job, but you can never offload your learning. The future of the firm is the ability to compound that learning across people and AI. This requires a new architectural approach where every business is able to build agentic systems that improve over time, while still retaining control over their IP. A company should be able to switch out a “generalist” model without losing the “company veteran” expertise built into their learning system. This is the key “test” of your control and sovereignty in the era ahead.

Nadella set this vision off with a warning:

The last thing any of us want is a world where every company across every sector is ceding value to a few models that eat everything they see. If all the value is accrued by only a few models, the political economy will simply not tolerate it. There is no societal permission for an AI future that hollows out entire industries.

Think about what happened in the first phase of globalization where entire industrial economies were hollowed out by outsourcing. The GDP numbers looked fine on the surface, but the displacement was real and the consequences are still being felt. Let us not bring that dynamic into the AI era, with a small number of AI systems capturing all the economic returns, while entire industries find their knowledge commoditized right out from underneath them.

Here’s the problem with that analogy: the globalization happened, and the industrial economies were hollowed out. There’s a possibility that this isn’t a warning but a prophecy; small wonder Nadella is raising the alarm given that Microsoft could be one of the casualties. And, by the same token, the economic imperative for the model makers is to accomplish exactly this.

The Data Imperative

The models — not even Mythos — are not yet at this point. What they need, beyond more compute, is more and better data. Model improvements increasingly come from reinforcement learning; some of this can be generated synthetically, but the most powerful lever for a frontier lab is real world use.

This, I think, is a major reason why both OpenAI and Anthropic offer their heavily subsidized subscription plans. SemiAnalysis recently estimated that a $200 plan gets you $8,000 worth of Claude tokens and $14,000 worth of Codex tokens. Of course both are fighting for user and developer mindshare, but they’re also fighting to have access to actual usage data to make their models better.

Anthropic upped the ante in a major way with Fable, announcing that they would retain the data for all usage for 30 days, even for their enterprise plans that previously promised zero data retention. The company said they would not train on this data, but they didn’t put in any sort of safeguards to guarantee they wouldn’t do so in the future (like storing the data with a third party). If this policy change (whenever Fable is restored) doesn’t lead to a significant loss of customers, I suspect it’s only a matter of time until they start using the data: it’s simply too valuable to their end goals.

Note also the virtuous cycle with moving up into user touchpoints: the more workflows that are done directly with Claude or Codex, the more data each company gets to feed back into their training, which makes their products that much more capable and useful, expanding the number of workflows they can serve, expanding their access to data.

Nadella, in his essay, highlights the importance of this data, but naturally thinks it should be independent from the model:

Companies need to turn their workflows, domain knowledge, and accumulated judgment into AI systems that improve with each use. Private evals should capture whether a model is actually improving against outcomes that matter to the business (not just external benchmarks!). Private reinforcement learning environments should let models grow stronger on real traces from inside the organization. Its knowledge base makes institutional memory queryable and use of tokens more efficient.

This loop becomes the new IP of the firm. I think of it as a hill climbing machine. And unlike most assets, it compounds. Every improved workflow generates better training signal, which accelerates the accumulation of tacit knowledge unique to the firm. The companies that build this early will have an advantage that is hard to replicate, regardless of any new individual model capability.

What if, however, the companies that give in to Anthropic’s data policies get better results right now? Or what if existing companies resist, leaving the door open for new companies — or the model makers themselves — to outcompete them in the market? Anthropic is certainly putting the resolve Nadella is calling for to the test.

The Power Imperative

The data retention policies around Fable/Mythos were, amazingly enough, not even the most controversial part of the launch. Rather, Anthropic said at launch that it would silently degrade Fable performance if it were used for LLM development; from the System Card :

We have also added safeguards related to frontier LLM development. As discussed in Section 6.1 of our February 2026 Risk Report , we are concerned about the risks of accelerating the overall pace of AI development, though we remain uncertain about the severity of these risks. In particular, our concern is with — as we wrote then — “accelerating other AI developers in building powerful AI systems that pose similar risks to the ones ours pose – without necessarily having commensurate safeguards.”

In light of the ability of recent models to accelerate their own development , we’ve implemented new interventions that limit Claude’s effectiveness for requests targeting frontier LLM development (for example, on building pretraining pipelines, distributed training infrastructure, or ML accelerator design). Using Claude to develop competing models already violates our Terms of Service , but enforcing this restriction through our safeguards avoids accelerating the actors most willing to violate these terms.

Unlike our interventions for cybersecurity, biology and chemistry, and distillation attempts, these safeguards will not be visible to the user. Fable 5 will not fall back to a different model. Instead, the safeguards will limit effectiveness through methods such as prompt modification, steering vectors, or parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). These interventions will not affect the vast majority of coding work. We estimate they will impact ~0.03% of traffic, concentrated in fewer than 0.1% of organizations. When these interventions are active, we expect them to have minimal behavioral impact on the model except to limit its effectiveness in developing frontier LLMs. Claude will still respond helpfully to user requests. We’ll continue to improve the precision of our detection methods following the launch of this model.

Anthropic walked back this change — Fable will simply hand off LLM-related requests to Opus 4.8, and disclose this hand off to the user — but I think the initial policy was very illuminating. On one hand, I actually don’t begrudge Anthropic not wanting to help its competitors; on the other hand, what should be blisteringly clear is that Anthropic does not think that anyone else other than them should even be making frontier LLMs.

What makes this policy all the more remarkable is the fact that it was enacted only two months after Anthropic had that dispute with the Department of War: the latter wanted to use Claude for any legal use, while the former wanted more stringent controls around surveillance and autonomous weapons. What this degradation represented was both the capability and willingness of Anthropic to silently alter its models to achieve its policy preferences. In other words, Anthropic willfully validated some of its critics’ worst fears in terms of being a supply chain risk.

The broader takeaway from that previous episode, however, is that Anthropic believes that they are the ones who should have final say over how Anthropic is used; given that they think only they should be developing leading edge AI, they by extension think that only they should have final say over AI generally. When you further combine this realization with the company’s pronouncements about AI’s ability to conduct all economic activity, you realize that Anthropic’s leadership effectively wants to have power over everything and everyone.

The Safety Story

Of course Anthropic would never put things so baldly; the story, rather, is safety:

* I expect Anthropic to increasingly expose their model’s capabilities to end users through endpoints increasingly tailored to different workflows, even as they start to restrict the API. This replacement of software and restriction of access will be done in the name of safety, even as Anthropic fulfills its economic imperative of getting closer to end users.
* Anthropic’s explanation for their dramatic change in their data retention policy was safety. Specifically, the company claims that retaining all user data for 30 days is necessary to prevent the jailbreaks the U.S. government is worried about. I can certainly imagine a future where safety compels them to train on this data as well, to better protect against malicious usage.
* The entire Anthropic origin story is rooted in the founders’ belief that OpenAI wasn’t taking safety seriously enough; the company believes that only they can control AI, and that because they uniquely care about safety, they are justified in trying to control everyone else, up to and including the U.S. government.

Here’s the thing about these safety justifications: I think they work because, to Anthropic, they aren’t justifications. The company really believes that they are the only ones who believe in super intelligence, and thus are the only ones who are sufficiently concerned about the dangers. That excuses decision after decision, policy after policy, and confrontation after confrontation that, to people on the outside, look like a bizarre combination of cynicism and naiveté.

The contrast to OpenAI is massive: I think that one way to understand how and why OpenAI lost its lead is that, in the years following the release of ChatGPT, the company has been at war with itself internally as what used to be a research lab was suddenly seized with the burden of being the accidental consumer tech company ; to the extent OpenAI solved that conflict, it was by bleeding huge amounts of talent to Anthropic in particular.

Anthropic, on the other hand, has perfect alignment between talent and mission and business. The company gets to sell to researchers the creation of a machine god, with the mantle of being the sort of person who cares about the dangers and is smart enough to navigate them on behalf of humanity; that every policy change that falls out of that happens to be great for business is the most beautiful coincidence in the world.

I respect this alignment, and I fear it. I respect it because it is so clearly effective; the closest analogy is probably Apple, which has always framed every self-serving action in the guise of doing right by users — and often they were. So it is with Anthropic. What I fear, however, is that it is one thing to have people convinced they know best building a smartphone that I can take or leave; it’s considerably more concerning to have them building superintelligence that has the potential to rival or exceed the power of nation states, or merely massive corporations. The history of brilliant people convinced they know what humanity needs is a sordid one, precisely because they have convinced themselves that their intentions are good, justifying actions that very much are not.

text:
The market hates Fox's acquisition of Roku, but the company is trading extraction from rights holders for leverage as a renter.

Fox Buys Roku, The Problem With Fox’s Smart Strategy, Streaming That Works

Tuesday, June 16, 2026

On last Thursday’s episode of Sharp Tech , Andrew and I discussed WWDC and Fable 5.

On to the Update:

Fox Buys Roku

From the Wall Street Journal :

Fox Corp. said it is acquiring Roku in a deal valued at around $25 billion, making a major bet on the future of ad-supported streaming. The deal — Fox’s largest to date—brings together a media company known for its live news and sports programming with the biggest provider of streaming platforms for connected TVs. It will add scale to Fox’s streaming business, currently home to free, ad-supported streaming service Tubi, which the company bought for $400 million in 2020, and subscription-based Fox One and Fox Nation. In addition to distributing other streaming services through connected TVs and devices, Roku has its own ad-supported Roku Channel. The combined company will better compete with the likes of Amazon.com and Netflix for ad dollars…

Fox will pay around $160 per Roku share, with $96 in cash and 0.9693 Fox Class A shares. The deal is valued at around $22 billion on an enterprise basis. Fox expects to fund the cash portion of the transaction with $12 billion in new debt, as well as cash on hand. The combined company expects to cut about $400 million in annual costs. Fox plans to keep Tubi and the Roku Channel as separate offerings, Murdoch said on the call, noting the two services complement each other.

The market was not very happy about this deal; from Bloomberg :

Roku shares jumped 20% on Friday after Bloomberg reported the company was in talks about a sale. On Monday, Roku shares slipped 1.9% to close in New York at $140.90. Fox shares fell 17%, a record, to $54.76. The sharp decline in Fox shares means the stock component of the agreement would be worth less if it holds through the closing of the deal. Based on where Fox traded Monday, the ratio of stock and cash the company would pay Roku shareholders was roughly $149 per share, about 5.8% above where Roku stock ended trading.

I have to admit I was pretty surprised by the market’s reaction; my immediate reaction to the deal was very positive. However, after looking more into the deal…I’m still very positive, but I get the skepticism.

The Problem With Fox’s Smart Strategy

The first reason I was optimistic about this deal was because of recent history. Specifically, I hold Fox’s business acumen in high regard, as I feel the company — along with Sony — has handled the shift to streaming better than anyone. The company set its course back in 2017 when it sold 21st Century Fox, its studio business, to Disney; I wrote in an Update at the time :

In that last sentence I actually put forth two distinct strategies: selling direct to consumers, and charging distributors significantly more. Both do depend on having differentiated content, which was the point of that Daily Update, but the similarities end there. To explain what I mean, this deal actually offers two great examples: if it goes through, that means Fox is pursuing the second strategy, and Disney the first.

Start with Fox: its news and sports divisions — particularly the former — are highly differentiated. That gives Fox significant pricing power with shrinking-but-still-very-large TV distributors. Moreover, given that both news and sports are heavily biased towards live viewing, they are also a good fit for advertising, which again, matches up with traditional TV distribution. What Fox would accomplish with this deal, then, is shedding a huge amount of that detritus I mentioned earlier: sure, more was better when there was only one distributor, but now that there is competition for viewer’s attention, filler is a drag on the content that actually gives negotiating leverage. Fox could come out of this deal with the same pricing power it has today but a vastly streamlined corporate structure and cost basis.

Disney, in contrast, decided to double down on content in order to build its own streaming service; and it hasn’t gone so well. On March 20, 2019, when the deal closed, Disney’s stock opened at $106.47; Fox’s newly listed stock opened at $35.89. Last Friday, meanwhile, Disney’s stock closed at $100.04; Fox’s closed at $58.92.

Even with Monday’s market reaction, Fox’s Class B stock is still at $49.95, a 32.86% increase. No, that’s not the most impressive growth in the world, but it is growth, and it’s a lot better than Disney.

News remains a great business for Fox, but where the company has really doubled down has been on sports rights. Back in 2022 , when the Big Ten expanded to the West Coast, I praised Fox’s decision to not only not launch a streaming business, but also exit original content completely; I also noted that its focus on the bundle left it at the mercy of rights owners determined to extract ever more value from their fans:

The logic of the Big Ten’s expansion into California is obvious: the more of an audience that the Big Ten can command, the more of the money flowing through that value chain it can extract. Sure, it’s not quite to the level of the NFL, but it’s the next closest thing. This is also the downside to Fox’s bet on live: while the company owns the content it produces on channels like Fox News, it has to buy sports rights, and it is the Big Ten that is determined to take its share, even if that means an expansion that otherwise makes no sense at all.

In other words, I think the tweet above has it backwards: Fox and ESPN are not “grandmasters calling the shots behind the scenes”; they are essential but ultimately replaceable parts in the movement of money from consumers to the entities that provide the content those consumers want.

Still, the tweet is instructive: perhaps the most essential role Fox and ESPN play for universities is taking the blame as the latter make more money than ever.

This is the biggest problem with the demise of the bundle. Once Fox was reduced to news and live sports, it was increasingly just a conduit for transferring money from fans to sports leagues, because the latter had wholesale transfer pricing power , given Fox wasn’t really selling distributors anything else other than Fox News (which, to be fair, achieves very high affiliate fees in its own right). This did not, to be clear, mean that spinning off 21st Century Fox was wrong; it did, however, mean that Fox was both dependent on an ecosystem in secular decline and had decreased bargaining power within that ecosystem (especially as cable news viewers, one of the oldest demographics there is, started to die off).

Streaming That Works

There is one other important part of recent Fox history that made me enthusiastic about this deal. Fox may have decided to not even try and compete in the paid streaming game, but that doesn’t mean it wasn’t a streamer. In March 2020, Fox acquired Tubi , a Free Ad-Supported Streaming Television (FAST) service.

FAST services are free and full of ads, and they look a lot like the cable television channels of my youth: lots of syndicated TV shows (including ones that first appeared on streamers), movies, and the occasional low-budget original series. They are also one of the fastest-growing TV categories, collecting a combined $3.5 billion in revenue in 2025; Tubi grew viewership by 16% and revenue by 27% in 2025, to $1.1 billion.

Roku, meanwhile, has a FAST service of its own called the Roku Channel, as well as advertising throughout its TV OS. In April, Roku finally broke out its advertising revenue for the first time — almost certainly because they were looking for a buyer! — and it’s a healthy business: $2.3 billion in 2025, a 13% increase.

Now, not everything is perfect in the FAST world: Paramount’s Pluto TV declined 14% in revenue, and the segment as a whole saw its growth slow from 17% in 2024 to 10% in 2025 as Amazon and Netflix in particular grew their advertising businesses. That, though, makes this acquisition all the more compelling. First, Fox is taking a dominant position in a space that is still growing, and second, Fox is increasing its bargaining power for those old shows and movies that struggling studios do still want to make money from, right as Paramount is taking on a massive amount of debt to acquire Warner Bros., and will likely be incentivized to use Pluto as an outlet for its own content. Fox is well-positioned to earn more money from advertising thanks to its increased scale, even as it reduces its costs to operate the business, and acquires content for better prices than it might have otherwise.

This also has the potential to benefit Fox’s core business as well. First, increasing profits from FAST will give Fox more capacity to absorb sports rights increases. Second, Fox can explore putting games on its FAST channels, increasing customer awareness and downloads. Third, Fox can go to advertisers with a scaled offering that extends across all of its properties, including Fox One, the streaming service for its linear TV offerings.

Roku also makes money in other ways, most notably through being a storefront that sells subscriptions to other streaming services. This also means that Roku has a better handle on who its viewers are, which could help with targeting. At the same time, Fox will need to take care to not alienate those partners, or get distracted by driving people to Roku; the value here is in the scale that comes from combining multiple advertising-supported streaming services, not in owning a vertical device business (and, it’s worth noting, the device business isn’t exactly high margin).

So why did the market hate this deal? There is the debt, which is always risky for a company predicated on a sector in secular decline; we already saw how that drowned Warner Bros. Discovery. There’s also the general mistrust of media companies, particularly when it comes to acquisitions. And most pertinently, while the premium Fox paid for Roku was relatively small compared to Roku’s current stock price, it’s much larger compared to Roku’s price a year ago, and it’s massive compared to Roku’s actual profits — about 52x Roku EBITDA. Fox’s investors thought they owned a focused and eminently understandable company with knowable risk and strong cash flows; now, thanks to dilution from new stock issuance, they own much less of a much more complicated business with real execution risk and a big debt load.

Ultimately, however, I like the deal. Not only is Fox a company that deserves the benefit of the doubt, but also advertising is a business that needs scale: Fox is getting exactly that, pointing towards a future where the current rights-renting business that bleeds leverage to rights holders funds the build-out of a new rights-renting business — FAST — that builds leverage for the renter in a way that only advertising can. Advertisers should be buyers; it’s the subscription models that struggle with scale.
