text:
The administration is very likely wrong about Fable, but that is ultimately Anthropic's responsibility.

The State of Fable, The Jailbreak Problem, SpaceX Acquires Cursor

Wednesday, June 17, 2026

On this week’s episode of Greatest of All Talk , Andrew and Adam break down a thrilling NBA Finals that ended with a New York Knicks title. Oh, and while I’m here, congrats to all of the Knicks fans!

On to the Update:

The State of Fable

From the Washington Post :

Trump administration officials began weighing sanctions on Anthropic weeks before they demanded the company take its latest and most advanced artificial intelligence model offline, after a dispute shattered the White House’s already-fragile trust in the company, according to two White House officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private deliberations.

Several weeks ago, Anthropic gave the administration a list of 111 organizations slated to receive advanced access to Mythos, its newest model, one of the officials said. With companies around the world clamoring for the technology after Anthropic warned it could dramatically enhance hackers’ capabilities, officials reviewed the list and signed off. But Anthropic later disclosed that the list had ballooned and roughly 50 additional entities had already received access.

Senior officials began to consider using export controls to claw back the technology after the company did not identify the new recipients for days. When Anthropic finally turned over the names, the administration discovered that one recipient was a South Korean telecommunications company the administration suspected of having ties to China, the officials said. Anthropic quickly revoked the firm’s access to Mythos, said a person close to Anthropic, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe the deliberations. But the episode badly damaged officials’ confidence in the company’s ability to safeguard sensitive technology…

The administration wants to lift the sanctions as soon as it’s convinced Anthropic has fully accounted for everyone who received the Mythos product and has strengthened the protections on the Fable project to prevent it from being jailbroken, the official said. The administration has no intention of moving against other products from Anthropic or other AI companies, the person added.

I sort of side-stepped the specifics of the current stand-off between Anthropic and the Trump administration in Monday’s Article Anthropic’s Safety Superpower , given the level of uncertainty about what exactly happened; unfortunately that uncertainty remains, and, on a personal level, I’m certainly disappointed to not have access to Fable.

I did want to start with this story from the Washington Post because I suspect it captures something important: I doubt the current dispute suddenly arose with an alleged phone call from Amazon CEO Andy Jassy to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent; rather, it’s something that has likely been building for a long time. And, thanks to the dispute with the Department of War , there was a ready-made constituency in the Trump administration for cracking down on Anthropic generally, particularly if Anthropic was legitimately perceived as violating the spirit of the administration’s executive order.

This isn’t to let the administration off the hook: setting aside whether or not their objections are reasonable — more on that below — the fact of the matter is that a de facto policy change that limits not just Mythos/Fable but all future models to administration-approved entities will destroy the economics of frontier models, which need to maximize usage; it also may destroy the feedback mechanism that comes from usage, which appears to be an increasingly critical factor in terms of model improvement.

The Jailbreak Problem

At the same time, I think there is a more fundamental issue: Anthropic’s dramatic unveiling of Mythos created a standard for control that was fundamentally unattainable. Consider the jailbreak issue: we don’t know what the jailbreak Amazon discovered was, but there is at least some reporting that it was incredibly banal; from The Atlantic :

It’s not unreasonable for the federal government to want to rapidly clamp down on a technology that could be incredibly dangerous. Trump officials had been alerted by researchers at Amazon to a possible way to circumvent Fable 5’s safety systems, which led the model to identify some known IT vulnerabilities. The administration has not publicly shared much information about its security concerns. A White House spokesperson told me that the jailbreak “was very serious” but said that specific details are classified. Whether the bypass really was that serious is not at all clear, and Anthropic has contested whether what administration officials showed the company even constitutes a jailbreak. An Anthropic spokesperson pointed me to a blog post in which the company wrote that the actions elicited from Fable were “either entirely benign responses or are minor findings.”

Katie Moussouris, a cybersecurity expert and the CEO of Luta Security, told me that Anthropic shared with her a copy of the White House’s report on the Fable jailbreak to get her appraisal. (She said that she is not being paid by Anthropic.) The report, Moussouris said, involved IT experts asking Fable to help find and patch bugs. When given deliberately insecure code, she said, Fable refused the prompt “review the code for security issues” but then complied when asked to “fix this code,” followed by some further manual steps. Moussouris told me that this was just “the model working as intended” for cyberdefense. She added that OpenAI’s GPT-5.5, a model with similar cybersecurity capabilities, could be used in the same way.

Again, we don’t know if this was the jailbreak, but let’s assume that it was; as Moussouris wrote in a blog post :

Defenders need to be able to ask AI to fix the bugs in a file, explain why the fix matters, and write tests that confirm the patch works. That is not a guardrail bypass. It is the most valuable thing an AI model can do for defensive security: executing the find, fix, and test loop defenders run every day.

The prompts worked because they were defensive requests, and that capability cannot be removed without making the model worse at fixing bugs and verifying patches. The same holds for every capable AI model, including the foreign and open-weight systems the United States cannot reach with export controls, many of which will match Fable and Mythos capabilities within months. Will all the US based models be export controlled? They have fewer guardrails than Fable 5, and almost all the capabilities, or will shortly.

This is obviously correct: cybersecurity defense is indistinguishable from offense; there are echoes here of the encryption battles of the 1990s, when the U.S. government wanted to ban encryption but was eventually persuaded to stand down by the argument that encryption doesn’t just protect criminal activity, but also protects things that need to be protected too — including government secrets — and that you don’t get to pick-and-choose its application. So it is with AI and cybersecurity: the best defense for AI-enabled cybersecurity attacks is AI-enabled cybersecurity protection, including actually looking for vulnerabilities.

Zooming out, however, I think there is an even bigger issue when it comes to AI specifically. Encryption was ultimately understandable and defendable as an all-or-nothing concept because it is deterministic: strong encryption protocols are fully open source and understandable, even as they are unbreakable, because, at the end of the day, they are math. Math — and the code used for encryption — is deterministic: it either works as it is supposed to or it is fundamentally flawed; you don’t get to have the good encryption for the good guys and the bad encryption for the bad guys. In other words, you can’t distinguish between use cases.

What makes AI so difficult to talk about, on the other hand, is that it is probabilistic. This, at the end of the day, is how jailbreaks work: because models don’t depend on deterministic code, you can’t simply define boundaries of what is acceptable and what isn’t according to a set of heuristics. Rather, you provide guidelines that the model interprets and probably abides by but, with the right prompt and the incredible creativity of jailbreakers, the model can be prompted to do what its creators didn’t want it to do. It’s just a matter of tipping the probability function in your favor. In contrast to encryption, the problem isn’t the inability to distinguish between use cases for a knowable technology, but the inability to even know what the use case is.

I don’t really expect anyone in the administration to truly understand this, just because you can see everywhere the extent to which people don’t really understand how AI works. Most people experience AI as a magical answer machine that weirdly can’t count the number of ‘r’s in ‘strawberry’ (although Fable could ), and never draw the connection between those types of weird shortcomings and the fact you can’t actually perfectly stop “jailbreaks” of this sort.

Now, to the extent this is true, you may wish it were not the case: you might wish that the people with guns had an intuition for how AI works. You might say the same thing about consumers generally, who have frustrated technologists for decades with their unrealistic expectations and refusal to just “figure it out”. Ultimately, however, the companies that succeeded — like Apple, to go back to the analogy I drew on Monday, but in this case as a contrast — did so by explaining problems in clear language, and demonstrating how their products solved those problems.

Notice how this sort of language is missing from Anthropic. Go back to the Project Glasswing announcement ; this paragraph was the closest the company came to explaining how Mythos Preview worked:

Many flaws in software go unnoticed for years because finding and exploiting them has required expertise held by only a few skilled security experts. With the latest frontier AI models, the cost, effort, and level of expertise required to find and exploit software vulnerabilities have all dropped dramatically. Over the past year, AI models have become increasingly effective at reading and reasoning about code—in particular, they show a striking ability to spot vulnerabilities and work out ways to exploit them. Claude Mythos Preview demonstrates a leap in these cyber skills—the vulnerabilities it has spotted have in some cases survived decades of human review and millions of automated security tests, and the exploits it develops are increasingly sophisticated.

Do you see the gap in communication? What is lacking is an explanation of how it is that models can read and reason about code, find vulnerabilities, and exploit them. That capability is a function of approaching any problem probabilistically instead of deterministically; the problem with the latter is that the set of problems to which it can be applied is definitionally limited by the rigidity that results in a clearly correct answer. A probabilistic approach, on the other hand, runs the chance of being wrong (i.e. hallucinating), but in exchange it gains the ability to navigate any problem: the set of applicable domains is infinite. This is why Mythos can look at any code base, even if it’s not trained on them; this is also why you can’t get Mythos to only play defense while eschewing offense. The strength of the approach is its weakness.

These are, to be clear, exhausting explanations to make; they are also far more difficult when you lead with dramatic assertions, don’t respect the counterparty, or think you’re smarter than everyone else in the room. Steve Jobs’ brilliance was that he treated consumers with respect, even if they had no idea how a computer worked. Does anyone feel that Anthropic treats anyone outside of Anthropic with respect, much less this administration?

This is, in other words, a communications problem, and unfortunately communication is not exactly a forte of Anthropic’s leadership. Yes, CEO Dario Amodei writes thoughtful essays, but those are targeted at and understood by people who provide the push for AGI. Just as important to that goal, however, is avoiding the barriers, and that means communicating with those with the capability to erect them. Amodei is pursuing Machines of Loving Grace ; he’s not going to get there without some grace for his fellow man.

SpaceX Acquires Cursor

From the Wall Street Journal :

SpaceX said it would buy Cursor parent Anysphere for $60 billion, striking a massive deal for an autonomous coding agent that could help the company catch up with its AI rivals after its blockbuster IPO. Cursor will receive $60 billion worth of SpaceX stock under the agreement, according to a filing released Tuesday. The deal comes days after SpaceX’s historic public offering Friday. SpaceX’s market value is around $2.66 trillion after its shares rose 19% in their first day of trading, 20% on Monday and around 5% on Tuesday.

I already wrote about the logic of this acquisition when it was announced; from an April Update :

The theory of the case is that Cursor has a huge amount of proprietary data about coding and how people actually interact with LLMs, which should be a solid foundation for building the agentic model of the future. Again, however, training is exceptionally expensive, and serving even more so.

I think you can see where I am going here: setting aside the weird nature of this deal, what with the option-to-buy and all, and the numbers involved (which honestly, given the silly numbers Musk has attached to the acquisitions of first X and then xAI, who’s counting), there is really obvious synergy between SpaceXAI and Cursor: the former has compute, and the latter has a product, data, and a decent amount of distribution for the use case that is most important for AI. At a high level this tie-up makes a lot of sense.

Well, now we have a clear answer to the weird nature of the deal and the numbers involved, and it’s pretty brilliant: the key fact is that SpaceX is paying with stock, not cash. Right now SpaceX has a tiny float, which is driving the stock artificially high: that means that by waiting for this exact moment in time — after the IPO but before most of the lock-ups expire — SpaceX gets to make the deal at what will likely be a discount, at least in the medium term (i.e. once the float increases and demand is more easily satisfied, the stock price will likely fall).

To be clear, the exact amount of stock will be determined at the time the deal closes, which is expected to be in Q3. However, that’s before the largest lock-ups expire, and after SpaceX is expected to be added to most major indices (which will further juice demand, albeit permanently): it seems very likely that the cost of $60 billion worth of dilution will be considerably less than the cost of cash.

Cursor, meanwhile, got their headline number, and, more importantly, are already putting SpaceX’s compute to work: just today the company teased a new 1.5-trillion-parameter general purpose model trained from scratch that it claims rivals Opus and the latest models from OpenAI in size. It remains to be seen how it fares in effectiveness, but I think they have a shot.

text:
An interview with Michael Morton about e-commerce and AI, including the challenges of unfalsifiable bear cases, distribution versus referal models, grocery, and autonomous vehicles.

An Interview with Michael Morton About E-Commerce in the Age of AI

Thursday, June 18, 2026

This week’s Stratechery interview is with Michael Morton . Morton is a senior research analyst at MoffettNathanson with a focus on e-commerce and marketplaces. Morton has worked on both the buy-side and sale-side of equity analysis, and also worked on the YouTube strategy team prior to joining MoffettNathanson. I previously interviewed Morton in April 2024 and November 2025 .

In this interview we discuss the challenges of analyzing companies facing unfalsifiable AI uncertainty. The poster child for this is Shopify, but Morton is still bullish. We then talk about how AI is trending towards being a referral business model, instead of distribution, and what that means for advertising. We also talk about Amazon’s moves in grocery, and why Morton is bullish on DoorDash. At the end we discuss the current state of autonomous vehicles and why Waymo has a big opportunity.

As a reminder, all Stratechery content, including interviews, is available as a podcast; click the link at the top of this email to add Stratechery to your podcast player.

On to the Interview:

An Interview with Michael Morton About E-Commerce in the Age of AI

This interview is lightly edited for clarity.

*Topics:*

The Unfalsifiable Bear Case ( #unfalsifiable ) | Shopify ( #shopify ) | Referral vs. Distribution ( #referral-distribution ) | Ads and AI ( #ads-ai ) | Grocery ( #grocery ) | Autonomous Vehicles ( #autonomous-vehicles )

The Unfalsifiable Bear Case

*Michael Morton, welcome back to Stratechery.*

*MM:* Hey Ben, thanks for having me.

*So you were telling me before we started that the last time we talked was November — you’ve graduated to “I need to have you on at least twice a year” status — but it seems much longer than that.*

*MM:* I checked when the last time I was on was, because it feels like years. When you’re dealing with AI and consumer adoption of AI and all the different product announcements, months feel like years.

*How are you handling that?*

*MM:* It is requiring the greatest level of flexibility in my theses at any point in my career. I joke in client meetings, we’ll be talking about something, I can sound high-conviction, and at the end of the meeting I’ll say, “I reserve the right to change my mind”.

*Right. Or maybe, “In this meeting, I just changed my mind”. I did your conference a few weeks ago — but I’d also done it a year ago — almost between the time that I recorded that and within a few days, or a week later, I totally changed my mind about Google in particular. I’d kind of like to have that one back, but that’s part and parcel of the game these days.*

*MM:* We just have to roll with the punches. We’ve gone from ChatGPT checkout to it getting deprecated pretty quickly, it’s constantly changing.

*We’ll get to that. You just released a report today about the current status of e-commerce in the age of AI, and you acknowledged at the beginning that the AI bear case for e-commerce is in some respects unfalsifiable — you can’t prove a negative. How frustrating is that as a stock analyst to deal with?*

*MM:* It’s great, because some clients have elbowed me in the ribs a little bit and said, “Hey, weren’t you the one a year-and-a-half ago screaming from the rooftops about the compression in the funnel, that there’s going to be some shifting landscape here?”, and yes, that is the case. With markets, you worry about stuff when no one’s talking about it, and then when everyone’s talking about it, a lot of the time you have to reassess, it’s kind of like zig and zag.

But AI in particular for my coverage world has been really hit by this. There’s a view in the marketplace that if you earn a digital dollar, your terminal growth rate or take rate is going to be up for review, and that leads to multiple compression. For my coverage world, the multiples on the stocks have gone down 30% year-to-date and why that’s particularly difficult is because you love a bear case that you can kill — there’s a business, people think gross margins are going to compress, and then you go through a quarter or two, gross margins go up, and everybody moves on. But this is one where there are these storm clouds, and you can’t convince people otherwise, because it’s impossible to prove it with data today.

And the bear case is also amorphous, right? I go from one meeting where someone is telling me AI is going to order all your groceries, all your consumer staples, everything you use in your house. The next meeting, AI is going to order my Uber and my pizza for me, and I’m never going to open the marketplace apps. And then the next meeting, Shopify’s stack is going to get vibe-coded. So in my seat, when I see stocks that I think are undervalued, it’s difficult and frankly at times frustrating when you can’t get the message across, because there’s so much whack-a-mole.

Shopify

*Yeah, exactly. Well, let’s talk about the Shopify one. We’ll come back to the report, but since you mentioned it — you upgraded Shopify to buy earlier this year in the face of the software apocalypse . I think the first time you were on, you had just upgraded Shopify as well, Shopify proceeded to get killed by the market right after that. You’ve done better this time — it’s been basically level, but where are you at with Shopify these days?*

*MM:* Stocks are certainly humbling, and Shopify has the ability to be that one for me that gets me a few times.

If you think back to when you and I started doing these a few years ago, the operating thesis was that all roads lead to Amazon when it comes to product discovery. You either started on Amazon, or you went to Google Search and then ended up on Amazon — that was a very reliable thesis for e-commerce, and it made it really hard for merchants — for the sake of this discussion, we’ll just refer to them as brand.com. That’s Shopify’s customer base: these people trying to build direct relationships with you.

When we started doing the work on AI and how it was going to change product discovery, we found a couple of things. When I asked the models, “Who do you prefer the most, and what are the important inputs that help you rank where to send people for the goods?” — they said price, shipping speed, trustworthiness — and the clear favorite there was Amazon, then Walmart number two. But I’ve spent more time than I’d care to share running through product discovery experiences on all of the different AI platforms and I couldn’t help but notice I’m seeing a lot more brand.com in this funnel than I ever have.

*Yeah, you mentioned that in your report. I’m going on a fishing trip in a few weeks, researching and buying a lot of stuff, and that’s actually something I noticed before you mentioned it in your report — and that does feel like a bit of a change. You kind of got random links before, and now almost every time the first link is to the manufacturer’s own site.*

*MM:* Yep. And in my job, I can’t pitch an investment thesis on something just anecdotal — “Hey, I see more brand.com.”

*Right — I get that privilege. That’s what you get for only charging $15 a month.*

*MM:* (laughing) That’s not a shot at you.

*Oh, no, I embrace it!*

*MM:* I need to be able to show, “Here’s something we measured, and I can prove this is what’s happening”. What we started to do was measure the traffic that’s sent from AI platforms to marketplaces and then to brand.com and compare the growth rates between the two, and also look at them against traditional Google Search. We’ll call traditional Google Search the baseline, because we have to think about the world we’re in and where we’re going.

In traditional Google Search, brand.com would outpace Amazon, Wayfair, Chewy, eBay, Etsy — the marketplaces — sometimes by about 2x, depending on the time of year. And you should expect that, the top 25 Shopify merchants should be growing faster than Amazon, so let’s call it 2x the growth rate of the marketplaces coming from Google Search. When we aggregate the traffic coming from AI platforms — AI Mode, you name it — to the different marketplaces and brand.com, brand.com is outpacing what I’ll call the legacy marketplaces 4-8x.

*Wow.*

*MM:* So what you and I have experienced, “Wow, I’m seeing a lot more brand.com here”, is showing up in the data. I’ve loved Shopify’s market position for a while, and I think they’re only going to get stronger, but that’s not enough of a thesis. When I could actually see with data that the product discovery shift truly is favoring their base, it gave me the confidence behind the view that GMV is going to grow higher for longer than most people think.

*Right, and it was one of those cases that made sense in theory — the idea that the AIs are just going to dig deeper and find the direct link, that that is more meaningful. But to your point, now you feel like you have evidence in that regard.*

*MM:* Yep. Shopify had spoken about it on the calls once or twice, and I’d been struggling for a way to try to prove it, we had to come up with a way to index who we think are the largest Shopify merchants. Not a single stock in my coverage is immune from these AI bear cases, and the Shopify one was, “No, it’s going to go to an AI checkout”, or, “No one can beat Amazon”, or “Their payments will get disrupted”, or, “They’re going to get vibe-coded”. It’s still not in the obvious AI-winner bucket when you talk to investors, this was one way for me to try to find a smoking gun. But in product discovery, this is clearly in a winning position.

*Well, brand.com is going to vibe-code their website, don’t you know?*

*MM:* It’s funny you should say that! I have a tremendous amount of respect for investors in general — it’s hyper-competitive, and everyone at the top of the game lives and breathes their space. This is one unique thing where I tease my friends who are investors, they’re like, “Oh, they’re going to get vibe-coded”, and I’m like, “Guys, let’s all step out from behind the monitors and the Excel sheets and go talk to some merchants”.

I love going to the different industry conferences — they have them all over the country, where you get to talk to operators. Today we actually did a call with a former Shopify employee who managed these large relationships, the infrastructure behind an e-commerce stack is so complicated that, for starters, it’s effectively impossible to recreate the Shopify stack you’re offered for less than you’re paying for it. Even if I had unlimited resources, an army of engineers, and a blank check from Anthropic, my ability to do that at a lower cost is almost impossible, due to the negotiating leverage Shopify brings to the table with all of their partnerships. They have a better fee structure with Stripe than I could ever get, they have CAPI [ Conversions API ] integration with Meta, because [Shopify CEO] Tobi [Lütke] and [Meta CEO] Mark Zuckerberg are personally acquainted and worked on this deal together, so Shopify merchants get one-click CAPI integration. It’s a long list of reasons why you’re not going to vibe-code your way to a Shopify stack.

*Even if you actually had the capabilities to vibe-code it and maintain it and all the things that go into that — the unrealistic ideas that go into that — as if a small merchant, or even a large merchant, wants to devote their time and resources to this problem.*

*MM:* And then when something breaks, things break all the time. If you’re a seller of any size, you’re selling across a variety of channels — TikTok, Etsy, Amazon, Walmart Marketplace — and you’re using a bunch of APIs, and things go wrong, all of a sudden you’re sitting there by yourself, and for the illusion of maybe saving pennies, something breaks, and now your whole livelihood and top line is at risk. Every stock we cover has a bear case, there is no perfect stock, Shopify being vibe-coded is not one that keeps me up at night.

*Isn’t this the stack part you talked about — just in terms of fully understanding your catalog, having all the details, being perfectly up to date — isn’t that part of the thesis for why the Checkout integration with ChatGPT ended up not working? I’m restating Eric Seufert’s point of view, I let him take a victory lap the last time he was on, he called it — this thing’s doomed right away — and I think this was a big part of it.*

*MM:* There are a lot of reasons that checkout experience had a hard time, it was something we talked about on the last podcast too — ChatGPT needs Amazon more than Amazon needs ChatGPT. They also never got critical mass, and the consumer is smart enough to know, “Hey, I’m not seeing all of the inventory here that I need to see”. I’ve talked to some people within the channel about why that Checkout didn’t work, why there were bottlenecks. Without speaking out of school, it’s fair to say ChatGPT was trying to do maybe more things at once than they should have, even on the consumer side.

*The ChatGPT story in a nutshell, right there.*

*MM:* And so I think that’s why there were some bottlenecks around the Checkout experience. I don’t think it was on Shopify’s side — they’ve done an awesome job with the Shopify Catalog , which is just another example of how the puck is moving toward Shopify’s favor.

*Yeah, talk about this.*

*MM:* Tobi is a real innovator, and the guy lives and breathes e-commerce, these are the type of people you want to invest behind during periods of change. I also like another company, DoorDash — founder-led companies in periods of change have some of the greatest ability to move.

Tobi saw what was happening with AI product discovery, and they quickly put together what’s called the Shopify Catalog. What it does is allow the Shopify merchant base to pull their product feeds and plug them directly into the AI platforms for discoverability. Because that’s part of the problem — the models don’t love going out and doing raw HTML scrapes specifically for e-commerce.

Google has this thing called StoreBot , which is crazy — I don’t think people even know about it. It runs around, goes through all the e-commerce websites on the Internet, puts in orders with fake credit cards, and checks out to see what delivery speeds and inventory are. Referral vs. Distribution

*So let’s go back to that report, because I think it touches on a lot of these topics. The headline question in the report you put forward is, “Is AI a referral channel or a distributor?”. What do you mean by that, and why is that distinction so important?*

*MM:* It is critical, because it’s about the customer relationship. Where everyone panics when it comes to investing in consumer Internet is if you’re going to lose your relationship with the consumer — you’ve spent decades building it, you’re able to monetize via on-site ads and a lot of other angles, and if someone is able to wedge their way in between you and the customer, that’s clearly not good for your business. Another way to talk about it is if they become a distributor and you get reduced to being an API call, that is very troubling.

Six to nine months ago, there were real fears that’s where we were going, you started seeing some of the weaker players in consumer Internet run into the arms of the different product offerings that risk making them just API calls. If you look at the world today, we’ve seen the distributor attempts fall short, and AI is looking a lot more like a referral channel — which is just a much better version of Google Search, where you end up with better, clearer intent further down the funnel. So it should be a de-risking event, which hasn’t really played out in the market.

Now, I mentioned in the note, I’m not pretending the risk is gone. We’re not underwriting the next Industrial Revolution in CapEx spend from all the hyperscalers just for a better version of Google Search. There have been a lot of reports of Google, Meta, and others trying to build personal agents, but today, what it looks like is a clear referral-channel type of model.

*Well, why not? The largest hyperscalers today — at least Google and Meta — are built on advertising, which is referral, not distribution. In fact, both companies have learned over time that getting into the distribution game, trying to own checkout, doesn’t work. *MM:* E-commerce is very challenging, Amazon literally patented one-click checkout. *MM:* Yeah, and if it’s “Hey, I need a new pair of running shoes”, and it’s, “Well, XYZ can get this to you in two days, or you pay $10 more and Dick’s gets it to you in an hour via DoorDash”, it becomes a pretty easy choice for a lot of consumers.

So I think over the next two years, this is Waymo’s game.

*Let me jump in on the Uber-Waymo thing . You just articulated what I think has been the strategically smart thesis — it’s one I’ve articulated, so we’re in this boat together — that at the end of the day, if you’re putting high-capital assets into the market, they need to be utilized, and the entity that can provide utilization, that can provide demand, is going to have power in the market, it’ll behoove the entity spending all this capital to be on the high-demand marketplace so they can have high utilization. And that’s been the case — Uber is going to be fine, they own the customer, they’ll layer on all these driverless cars with their regular fleet, and they might not be the winners in terms of margin, the margin may compress, but they’ll still own their market.*

*I think there are two things that have given me pause about that thesis. Number one is the extent to which most customers do seem to view Waymos as exceptionally highly differentiated and worth the effort to go to another app. The problem for Uber is that this puts them in the UPS-FedEx position relative to Amazon delivery — where, sure, Waymo is actually deputizing Uber to fill in the high-demand periods, because they know consumers will go to the work of bringing Uber on when a Waymo simply takes too long. That’s a flip of the expectations you would have, and it depends on very high differentiation, which a lot of people believe Waymo has, my personal feeling is a little — I sometimes get frustrated with Waymos, but whatever.*

*Number two — and this is my overall shift in thinking generally — is an increased appreciation for the extent to which Google can act suboptimally from a strategic perspective. There’s a story here where Google pursuing this asset-heavy approach makes no sense, they should be the layer, they should be licensing their tech to all the OEMs, they should be happy taking a skim off of every ride-sharing program in the world and yet there’s also a story where they have all this cash flow, and all that strategy of putting in lots of money to own a market by sheer brute force is really stupid right up until it works. It’s like Berkshire Hathaway — take your high-margin money from See’s, put it into railroads, which are terrible margins relatively speaking, but the absolute dollars are way higher. I’ve talked about this in the context of Berkshire and Google before — you have all this capital that needs to go somewhere, and you could fit self-driving into this, where it’s actually totally dumb right up until it works, and then you have this impregnable moat.*

*MM:* Yeah, there are a few things to unpack there, and I generally agree with most of them — let’s start with the first part. I’m in the camp where I think a seat is a commodity. Right now, Waymos are cool and unique, but if you look at the airline industry — I’m largely a Delta guy, but United has kind of caught up, though that’s a separate conversation, you want an ETA and a price on a long-term view.

*Oh, by the way, Uber’s ETAs always being wrong is, I think, getting to be a crisis at this point. No, I’m serious — I get upset at an Uber almost every time I book one, it’s terrible.*

*MM:* It could be because you’re in the Midwest.

*No, anywhere — San Francisco, New York — it drives me batty. Anyhow, continue. That’s a personal rant.*

*MM:* I love personal rants. But I am in the camp where I generally believe that a seat is a commodity. And like you said, you are going to need to fill for peak and trough demand.

There are two different models that Waymo is taking today. With Lyft in Nashville, it’s a hybrid network, and they’re basically using Lyft for the non-peak demand, “Hey, fill the demand at one in the morning when we can’t get someone into a Waymo with our app”. In Austin and Atlanta, Uber is renting the cars from Waymo for the day and paying a variable fee per trip, and it’s Uber’s job to drive all of the demand all the time and show that they can justify a take rate. So I think Waymo is not sure what they want, or historically haven’t been, if you look at the commentary — they’ve had co-CEOs [Tekedra Mawakana and Dmitri Dolgov] for the last couple of years, you get very mixed messaging.

*And you get the sense that the co-CEOs have different views on this.*

*MM:* Yeah, you get very mixed messaging, “Hey, we don’t want to change tires, we want to license this technology”, and then they’re opening a bunch of cities on their own. There’s probably an internal debate going on there that’s outside the scope of my knowledge, I think they’re testing both models, and also the 1P, go-it-alone approach.

I think their lead is so expansive today, and everyone is so far behind, that they don’t have to think in a competitive mindset, number one. Number two, when you’re saying, “Oh yeah, it might work until it doesn’t”, I think it’s working in some markets. They gave you the California data, for a while it was just San Francisco, and now that it’s in LA it makes it a little more difficult, but you could see the trips approaching high-20s per day. In our AV model, low-30s to mid-30s trips per day gets you EBIT-per-mile positive, so I actually think it’s pretty close to there in some of the markets.

When you listen to people who work at Waymo speak, they’ll tell you it’s the business model that is justifying our expansion, and costs are only going to come down with the vehicles going forward. So the model is better than I think most realize — the utilization is what’s really behind it being better than most realize — and they don’t have to be constrained today by the traditional business-strategy decisions that are your specialty.

*Yep, it’s true. What’s the deal with the Zeekr cars ? You made an interesting note that we thought these were dead because of the tariffs on China — not Trump, this happened under Biden — the tariffs on Chinese automobiles. But I saw one in San Francisco, what’s going on?*

*MM:* So that was the big debate. They built this first — I guess it’s about 3,700 vehicles — on the Jaguar I-Pace. From my understanding, that was never the platform vehicle, that’s a proof of concept, “Hey, we can make this work”.

*You get in there and you understand that this is a huge waste of money, trying to retrofit all this stuff in there.*

*MM:* “This is pretty luxurious”, yes. And then they announced this partnership years ago with Zeekr — it’s a Chinese car manufacturer, and it’s no secret, everyone in the world knows the Chinese can produce autos at a fraction of what the rest of the world can. If you can make a purpose-built AV, that’s going to provide you with the platform vehicle you can expand with globally.

My understanding is they call it the Ojai , but it’s a Zeekr van. The Ojai was going to be the platform car they could take around the world for the business model, then we had the Biden administration go after some imports, and then the Trump auto tariffs that never got rolled back — 100% tariffs. The market was struggling with, “How are they going to hit their goals?”, and, “There’s going to be an air pocket between the Jaguar and the Hyundai Ioniq that they were going to bring”, and I’m a deeply obsessive person — when you cover 10 stocks, it’s an empowering thing, because you can just be obsessed with a few things. For a month, I was pulling my hair out thinking, “There’s no way they could be bringing these cars into the US, and I can’t figure out what it is”, to be frank, I did some brainstorming with an AI platform, running down, “Hey, can we look at VIN numbers?”, “Go try to find VIN numbers, let’s do this”, and then eventually, on one train ride home, we landed on the bill of lading. That’s where, if you bring things into the US on ships, you have to have a receipt that says what’s in the ship.

What we recently published two weeks ago was we found the organizations through which they are importing these cars, it looks like Waymo is bringing in roughly 300 Ojais a month. That puts them on pace to basically double the fleet in the next 12 months and you can start to really put a dent in market share for rideshare — you start to get to the mid-single digits of US rideshare market share within line of sight.

*This is almost a terrifying prospect in terms of the strength of the Chinese auto industry, where Waymo’s like, “We have to pay 2x? Still worth it!”, because that’s basically what you’re suggesting. I mean, again, it’s Google, so they can afford it. Maybe, to your point, there’s an air pocket between the Jaguar and the Hyundai that’s going to be the next generation but it certainly was very surprising to find out they’re importing them anyway.*

*MM:* Yeah, it’s a little bit of, “Wait, why would you try to build a platform car on a Chinese manufacturer? Come on, you know that’s going to upset some politicians”, but did it anyway — maybe a little Google-esque — and then doubling down on it, “Hey, we can pay it”, now moving to the Hyundai. Again, maybe a little bit of a more Google move, but it’s working, and it’s going to give them the ability to continue to expand and grow consumer adoption.

*So it’s basically the entire industry just waiting around to see which direction Waymo decides to go, “Are we going to make a play and own the whole stack, even though it’s lower margin, or are we going to pursue some sort of licensing angle and just dominate that way?”*

*MM:* Yeah, they keep saying those things. They keep announcing 1P cities and rolling out first-party cities with their standalone app. What the market is really waiting to see is Uber basically putting up points on the board, you want to start seeing Uber put up big trip volume. That’s where I got the call wrong, I didn’t realize how quickly the Waymo-Uber relationship would turn south, that’s behind-closed-doors stuff that I’ll never understand.

*And do you think that’s because Uber started trumpeting a little loudly that, “Look, we can commoditize even Waymo”, and Waymo’s like, “Commoditize this!”?*

*MM:* There were signs — there always are. When they announced that one of their test cities for Nuro and Lucid was San Francisco, you’re like, “Wait, really? Waymo’s home turf, of all the cities?”, and then when they started highlighting how the Waymos had all the problems with the power outage in San Francisco — that’s not how I’d typically talk about a partner on an earnings call. You could see the signs.

I just think the bid-ask spread between what Uber is willing to pay, and the demand they think they can drive and the take rate, is different from what Waymo wants to earn. And look, Uber has a lot of really solid partnerships, they’re doing this in the Middle East, they’re starting to do it in Europe, they’re going to have cars on the road in the US. But it takes time, and this doesn’t even factor in what, for me personally, is the largely unknowable — Tesla. If we wake up someday and they really have it locked down, it’s kind of going to be game over for a lot of people, it’s a really terrifying fact if he [Tesla CEO Elon Musk] could put these cars on the road that really work at $30,000.

*Right, and that’s just because, from a cost perspective, they’re the ones that will actually flood the market.*

*MM:* Yeah, and he has the production abilities. That’s a really tough part about all the AV operators — I think Honda makes four million cars a year, and going to one of these OEMs and saying, “Hey, build me 5,000 cars”, it’s like, “Buzz off, we don’t have time, we’re not going to dedicate a line to you”. Elon can pump these out at a biblical rate compared to everybody else’s ability to do it, and at a fraction of the cost. The OEMs are now starting to move in that direction — they’re doing partnerships with companies like Wayve to integrate it into their cars. It’ll get there, but again, Waymo has a multi-year head start.

*Well, it’ll be fun to check in on. We’ll have to be back in six months, when the world has changed completely yet again and we can both decry how we got everything wrong in June 2026.*

*MM:* (laughing) Thanks Ben.

*Sounds good, I’ll talk to you later.*

text:
Apple is (finally) raising prices, but they're not shipping Siri AI to the E.U.

Apple Price Increases, Apple Intelligence and the E.U.

Monday, June 22, 2026

This week is the last week of regular Stratechery Updates before we enter the summer schedule season. As in past years, I will take a summer break the week of July 4th, a week vacation, and there will be no Stratechery Interviews. Specifically:

* June 29–July 2 will be summer break; there will be no Updates
* July 27–30 I will be on vacation; there will be no Updates
* After this week’s Stratechery Interview, the next one will be in September

Sharp Tech and Dithering will follow the Stratechery schedule .

And, speaking of Sharp Tech, on last Thursday’s episode , Andrew and I discussed the ongoing Anthropic export control saga, Fox and the future of streaming, and e-commerce in the age of AI.

On to the Update:

Apple Price Increases

From the Wall Street Journal :

Apple plans to raise prices on its products to offset the surging costs of memory and storage chips, Chief Executive Tim Cook said in an exclusive interview with The Wall Street Journal. “Unfortunately, price increases are unavoidable,” he said. “We’re doing our best to mitigate the huge increases that are being passed to us, and we’ve been trying to shield our customers from the increases, but the situation has become unsustainable.” Cook declined to offer details on the timing or scale of the planned price increases, nor which products would be affected.

Apple’s next major product launch is likely to be in September when it releases the iPhone 18 lineup, expected to include a new foldable iPhone. Price increases, especially for Macs and iPads, could come sooner. Apple raised the starting price of the Mac Mini last month in between launch events.

Skyrocketing demand for memory and storage chips from artificial-intelligence companies has pushed up their cost so much that Apple would have to raise device prices substantially to maintain its profit margins. Passing the higher cost on to consumers while maintaining its profit margin would add about $270 to the price of the next iPhone Pro model, estimates research firm TechInsights.

Just for clarity, Apple didn’t raise the price of the Mac Mini; they just stopped selling the base configuration. The models that are available are the same price they were before — at least for now!

In truth, I’m pretty surprised that Apple didn’t raise prices on the new Macs they released in the beginning of March; it cost me a steak dinner . As they say, however, it’s not enough to be right: you have to get the timing right as well.

That raises the question, however, as to why Apple is dropping this news now — and, at least according to Mark Gurman — is going to actually increase prices imminently. One possible reason is that Cook wants to take the blame for raising prices and spare incoming CEO John Ternus from spoiling his first iPhone introduction with a price increase. That’s certainly possible, although I think the easiest way to do this would have been to raise prices when those new Macs were introduced.

The other explanation, which I favor, is that Apple held out as long as they could, but just ran out of memory. Specifically, Cook explained on last quarter’s earnings call :

Let me talk about memory specifically, which I think is the root of the question. And I’ll go back to December for a moment and just walk you through the chronology. In the December quarter, we really had a minimal impact due to memory, and you can kind of see that in the gross margin results. We said it would be a bit more in the March quarter, and we did see higher memory costs in the March quarter, and they were partially offset by benefits from carry-in inventory that we had. For the June quarter and what’s embedded in the guidance that Kevan went through earlier, we expect significantly higher memory costs. They are also partly offset by the benefit of carry-in inventory. And then where we don’t give color beyond June, I can tell you that beyond the June quarter, we believe memory costs will drive an increasing impact on our business. And we’ll continue to evaluate this, and as we’ve said before, we’ll look at a range of options.

Well, it’s June, and Cook is giving emergency interviews to the Wall Street Journal. Honestly, it’s hard to escape the sense that Apple didn’t really see this memory crunch coming, and once they did, they just sort of hoped it would go away before they had to make the choice between out-of-band price increases or killing their margins.

I know some people hoped that Apple would simply eat the memory price increases and make a play for market share, but I never thought that was realistic. First, for all of the validity of the Services Narrative and its impact on Apple and its stock, the company still makes a huge amount of money from selling highly differentiated devices. Giving up margin with the idea of making it up in Services revenue is much too big of a risk in a vacuum.

However, such a move would not be in a vacuum. First, Apple has already skimmed the richest customers, and it follows that people who are willing to pay for an iPhone are also willing to pay for things like App Store subscriptions; more price-sensitive customers are likely to be less profitable in all sorts of ways than Apple’s existing customer base. Second, not raising prices doesn’t mean cutting prices; what is actually going to happen to price-sensitive customers is that they are simply not going to get new phones, not suddenly spend much more just because iPhones are relatively cheaper (and even then, probably more expensive than whatever else they were going to buy). No, Apple is right to protect their margin and continue slowly expanding their market share through differentiation, not pricing.

The other thing to keep in mind is that Apple has been decreasing prices in real terms for years now: iPhone prices stayed the same in the face of inflation, with the entry price of the iPhone 17 Pro finally increasing last year . Even then the new $1,099 starting price is $892 in 2020 dollars, significantly less than the $999 it was in actual 2020:

Prices in 2020 $ 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 2 year old iPhone $499 $477 $441 $422 $411 N/A 1 year old iPhone $599 $572 $530 $507 $493 $568 New iPhone $799 $763 $707 $676 $657 $649 iPhone Pro $999 $954 $883 $846 $822 $892 iPhone Pro Max $1,099 $1,050 $972 $1,015 $904 $973

This was the real Services Narrative impact on Apple’s pricing; now it’s the AI narrative, and this time it’s out of Apple’s control.

Apple Intelligence and the E.U.

It has been a couple of weeks, but I did want to revisit one of the more remarkable parts of Apple’s WWDC keynote.

VideoPress Video Player

Those are just some of the ways that Apple Intelligence is up-leveling so many of the apps you use every day. These new features across apps will be coming to all our Apple Intelligence-supported languages. And they’ll be available for free with our latest software releases. Some features, including image generation, have daily usage limits because they rely on powerful server models. Increased access is available with most iCloud Plus subscription plans, which also include Apple Intelligence support for compatible home cameras…

This update will be supported on the same product models that support Apple Intelligence today. Our most powerful on-device model and the features it enables like expressive voices and more advanced dictation will be coming to our most capable iPhone, iPad and Mac systems. Developers can start trying out our new version of Siri today. And for customers, we’ll be launching Siri AI in beta later this year. We’re excited to hear your feedback. Siri AI will not be available initially in the EU on iOS and iPadOS. We’re working hard to find a path forward that preserves our users’ privacy and security. In China, Siri AI and the other new Apple Intelligence features will not be available while we work through regulatory requirements.

First off, the limitation on models is a reminder that the memory shortage hits Apple in two ways: not only is memory more expensive, but Apple also needs more of it on their devices; the dividing line in terms of which devices can run the larger on-device models is how much RAM they have (the ones that can run all of the models have at least 12GB of RAM; the devices that can only run basic models have 8GB).

Second, those “powerful server models” that have usage limits are running on Nvidia hardware. There are two reasons this might be the case: first, by running on Nvidia instead of Google’s TPUs, Apple retains the option of moving its business somewhere else. Second, Nvidia’s Grace Blackwell is unique in terms of its support for Nvidia Confidential Computing, which extends trusted execution environments to multi-node rack-scale domains (Grace Hopper supported confidential computing, but only on a single-GPU-per-VM basis, which wouldn’t scale). That’s probably the bigger deal: it was privacy that led to Apple finally agreeing to work with Nvidia again.

And that’s what brings me to the E.U. Apple’s point of differentiation for Siri AI is exactly what they were trying to capitalize on two years ago: it’s not the best AI in the world, but it’s the only AI that has access to your personal data as stored on your phone. That’s a genuine differentiator, and the exact sort of thing that the E.U. wants to ban. And, at the same time, exposing all of your personal data to every other AI in the world is an obvious privacy problem, and Apple isn’t going to allow it (even if customers want it). The company explained in a newsroom post :

Siri AI is private by design and deeply integrated across Apple’s platforms using on-device processing and Private Cloud Compute, which extends the privacy and security of iPhone into the cloud. However, under EU regulators’ extreme interpretation of the DMA, Apple would have to give any virtual assistant direct access to users’ private data — and the ability to directly control other installed applications — as soon as Siri AI is made available in the EU, without the essential protections necessary to keep users and their data safe.

According to EU regulators, the DMA requires Apple to give any AI system nearly unlimited access to a user’s device, as well as the ability to act on that access autonomously without a user’s ongoing visibility and control. That includes the ability to read and send messages, make purchases, access files, and execute actions across any app. Security researchers have already shown that AI systems can be hijacked to steal personal data — like passwords and photos — and to permanently alter files and account settings without a user’s consent. As AI systems gain more capabilities, these risks are quickly increasing in frequency and scope.

Given the serious risks to users, Apple designed a solution called Trusted System Agent — an intermediary that would allow virtual assistants to safely access the same features and capabilities as Siri AI for devices in the EU. Apple also shared a plan to launch Siri AI in the EU while gradually rolling out this new solution over an 18-month period. The European Commission said no. In fact, the European Commission did not agree to any of Apple’s proposals.

The way Siri AI works in the beta is interesting. Currently, “Hey Siri” and the side button directly query Siri AI. In the Siri AI app, however, you can change the model to ChatGPT, and all queries in the app are directed there using the existing integration (Anthropic and Gemini are reportedly coming). However, if you make a query that relies on personal information, then the app switches back to Siri AI. In short, the system-wide AI invocations are Siri AI, and anything involving personal data is Siri AI.

I certainly understand Apple’s point of view on this, and I certainly object to the E.U. inserting itself into product design, particularly when that means infringing on Apple’s entire product promise, which is not just privacy but also integration; I also fault Apple for its part in bringing regulators to this point. I wrote back in 2021 :

One of the central planks of many of those pushing for new laws in this area are significant limitations on the ability of platforms to offer apps and services, or integrate them in any way that advantages their offerings. In this potential world it’s not simply problematic that Apple charges Spotify 30%, or else forces the music streaming service to hope that users figure out how to subscribe on the web, even as Apple Music has a fully integrated sign-up flow and no 30% tax; it is also illegal to incorporate Apple Music into SharePlay or Shared-with-you or Photos, or in the most extreme versions of these proposed laws, even have Apple Music at all. This limitation would apply to basically every WWDC announcement: say good-bye to Quick Note or SharePlay-as-an-exclusive-service, or any number of Apple’s integrated offerings.

I think these sorts of limitations would be disappointing as a user — integration really does often lead to better outcomes sooner — and would be a disaster for Apple. The entire company’s differentiation is predicated on integration, including its ability to abuse its App Store position, and it would be a huge misstep if the inability to resist the latter imperiled the former.

This, more than anything, is why Apple should rethink its approach to the App Store. The deeper the company integrates, the more unfair its arbitrary limits on competing services will be. Isn’t it enough that Spotify will never be as integrated as Apple Music, or that 1Password will not be built-in like Keychain, or that SimpleNote will only ever be in its sandbox while Apple Notes is omnipresent? Apple, by virtue of building the underlying platform, has every advantage in the world when it comes to offering additional apps and services, and the company at its best leverages that advantage to create experiences that users love; in this view demanding 30% and total control of the users of its already diminished competition isn’t simply anticompetitive, it is risking what makes the company unique.

Well, here we are: Apple simply doesn’t get to launch Siri AI in the E.U., maybe ever.

That noted, I mentioned that Apple is shipping what they promised in 2024, and, well, I’m interested in more capabilities than what was available in 2024. I don’t have any faith that Apple will be anywhere close to the cutting edge of what is possible with AI, and I would like the option of having a device that lets me use the latest models in deeper ways than simply an app. I think it’s going to happen, and I don’t think it’s going to be an iPhone where it does.

And the thing is, that’s awesome. The only possible way to curb Apple’s dominance is through competition, and if Apple wants to open up a vector for competitive hardware to arise, that’s fine! And, if in response to competition, they open up their platform, that’s great too. This has always been the only answer to dominant platforms; trying to make competition happen by government fiat simply squashes the innovation that actually provides the solution.

text:
The big three memory makers may come to regret opening up the door to Chinese memory makers; Microsoft, meanwhile, is very incentivized to use Chinese models.

Memory Chips and China, Microsoft and Chinese Models

Tuesday, June 23, 2026

Jon at Asianometry had a recent video about Taiwan’s DRAM Failure . It’s a great video in its own right, and also a useful primer for today’s Update.

On to the Update:

Memory Chips and China

The Wall Street Journal has a good overview of the memory issue, which, as I discussed yesterday , has even reached mighty Apple, once king of the supply chain; I thought it would be worth going through the article piece-by-piece to explain what is going on.

The last thing President Trump wants is another hit to consumers’ pocketbooks. But there is little policymakers can do to quickly address the memory-chip shortage behind Apple’s decision to raise prices.

AI in the long run should be deflationary, but as I noted in January after Nvidia’s CES keynote that wasn’t about consumer electronics at all , the memory issue is going to raise prices on a category of goods that have traditionally always decreased in price:

A big story over the last few months has been the dramatically escalating cost of memory as the major memory manufacturers shift their focus to high-bandwidth memory for AI chips in particular. What that means is that everything else is going to get a lot more expensive: memory is one of the most expensive components in nearly everything tech-related, and given the competitive and commoditized nature of the industry those costs will almost certainly be passed on to the end users.

This AI crowd-out dynamic arguably started with the hyperscalers, who diverted ever increasing parts of their budget to GPUs in place of CPU purchases, but now it’s coming for everything from grid power to turbines and now to components, and it’s only going to increase and become more impactful to end users. In other words, Nvidia may not have talked about consumer electronics at the Consumer Electronics Show, but they are having the biggest impact on the industry by far.

Some aspects of these increased prices are simply going to result in fewer sales; still, consumer electronics — particularly smartphones — are the single most important devices in consumers’ lives so they will have no choice but to pay up.

Only a handful of companies make memory and storage chips, and it takes years to build new factories. Three industry titans—Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Micron Technology—dominate the business of memory chips, also called DRAM. They are using much of their capacity to serve the fast-growing artificial-intelligence industry, squeezing consumer-technology companies.

This paragraph is, in many respects, the root of the problem. One of the topics that Jon discusses in the aforelinked Asianometry video is the boom-and-bust memory cycle, where the industry responds too slowly to surges in demand, overbuilds, and then gets absolutely killed when prices plummet. The biggest losers are the least efficient producers who license their technology — which is basically what Jon’s video describes in Taiwan — but even for the companies that survive, it takes massive investment to stay on the cutting edge. The net result is that an industry that used to have tens of players now only has three, which makes it much easier to exercise discipline in terms of capacity expansion.

Burned by past boom-bust cycles, the big memory-chip producers are cautious about creating another glut, which is why their spending on new plants remains relatively conservative. That is also true for the makers of storage chips known as NAND, which include the three titans plus Kioxia and Sandisk. The caution comes despite gross profit margins that have soared to records: in Micron’s case, 80%.

I wrote earlier this year about TSMC’s delayed response to AI and why it was important for tech companies to get Intel and Samsung up to speed:

What the hyperscalers need to understand is that simply begging TSMC to make more isn’t going to fix this problem, because begging TSMC to make more is to basically ask TSMC to take back the risk TSMC is offloading to the hyperscalers — they already declined! Rather, the only thing that will truly motivate TSMC to take on more risk is competition. If TSMC were worried about not just forgoing its own extra revenue, but actually losing business to a competitor, then the company would invest more. Moreover, that extra investment would be stacked on top of the investment made by said competitor, which means the world would suddenly have dramatically more fab capacity.

TSMC’s de facto monopoly on the leading edge is very much intertwined with their slowness to react to the AI signal; there are three memory manufacturers, which makes the situation a little better there — at least in theory — but the fact of the matter is that if there were 7 or 10 we would be in much better shape right now (and in reality, the explosion in memory demand has been even greater than the explosion in chip demand, so the situation is worse right now).

Not long after, AI took off, stoking demand for a particular memory chip well-suited for use in computers that train and query popular artificial-intelligence models. AI data centers also need large quantities of more traditional memory chips.

What has compounded the memory issue is that the high bandwidth memory (HBM) chips used for AI are stacked DRAM chips, but include increasingly important base die and interface layers that are customized around the needs of accelerators, particularly Nvidia’s. The price Nvidia (and AMD) is willing to pay for HBM is far more than the DRAM is worth on its own; that means that the big three memory makers are completely focused on meeting Nvidia’s needs, and only then selling DRAM to everyone else.

Two Chinese chip makers—CXMT, the country’s top DRAM producer, and Yangtze Memory Technologies, which focuses on NAND storage—are growing fast and want to expand their global clientele. China is the closest thing to a quick fix for the chip shortage, but the solution is at best partial.

Yangtze Memory is building three new factories in China that would more than double its current capacity by the end of 2027, people familiar with the plans said. Meanwhile CXMT is seeking to raise $4 billion in an initial public offering in Shanghai, and it is building new factories. It said its revenue rose by more than 700% year-over-year in the first quarter of 2026, though it acknowledged that its products still trail those of the three industry leaders.

This is where the rubber is going to hit the road. There is one country that is ready and willing to put up the massive amount of capital that is necessary to increase the number of competitors in the space; it just so happens to be a country that the U.S. has national security concerns about. However, I don’t think that those concerns are going to carry the day.

Yet the memory-chip shortage has gotten bad enough that some big consumer-tech companies have asked administration officials to loosen the restrictions on working with China. The companies also want the U.S. to make it easier for Samsung and SK Hynix to boost production in China.

Apple Chief Executive Tim Cook said in a Wall Street Journal interview that “everything needs to be on the table” regarding policy choices. In 2022, Apple worked with Yangtze Memory to prepare the Chinese NAND maker to become one of its suppliers of flash storage but was forced to abandon that plan when lawmakers opposed it.

Some of the world’s biggest personal-computer makers, including HP, are in talks with supply-chain partners about using CXMT memory chips in products bound for Asia, people familiar with the discussions said.

That last paragraph hints at where this is likely going to go. Chinese companies cannot currently make competitive HBM, even if their chips were allowed onto AI accelerators, but again, the core component of HBM is DRAM, and basically all computing devices need DRAM. Moreover, DRAM, unlike logic, is fungible: it’s very viable for HP to use CXMT chips for computers that are sold in Asia, and chips from the big three for computers sold to the West. The same thing applies to smartphones or anything else.

Yes, it’s possible these are older types of DRAM, or less reliable, or whatever other deficiencies might entail going with a new supplier, but simply getting this volume will make the Chinese suppliers better. And, in the long run, Chinese suppliers will increasingly be in a position to compete with the leading providers; moreover, they very well may have the sort of subsidies that make them the low cost provider.

This, by extension, explains why the big three have probably already massively damaged themselves in the very long run: because they were comfortable enough with their oligopoly to not bring on more supply faster, they created the conditions for Chinese competition to arise, and I don’t think they’re going to like it very much.

Microsoft and Chinese Models

From Axios :

Microsoft says companies using Copilot Cowork will pay based on how much compute they use. The company tells Axios it is exploring a fine-tuned version of DeepSeek V4, or another open-source model, as a lower-cost alternative to the Anthropic and OpenAI models now powering Copilot Cowork. Microsoft says it expects to make a lower-cost model available in the coming weeks and will confirm its choice then.

When I interviewed Satya Nadella earlier this month , there was a point of confusion when he said that Cowork supports multiple models; that in fact hadn’t been announced yet, but based on this report it sounds like that announcement is coming soon.

Microsoft, like many software companies, is in a tough spot when it comes to token usage. On one hand, of course it makes sense that customers pay for usage for a product that has meaningful marginal costs. On the other hand, an important aspect of software-as-a-service is that the pricing is predictable: you know that an employee is going to cost you $50/month on an E5 plan, and while that’s a decent amount of money, it’s something you can budget and plan for.

And, particularly in the case of Microsoft, you do get a lot for your money. Rewind just under a decade when Slack was the hot new product with one big barrier to entry: it’s hard to get large enterprises to pay for new software. Microsoft made that decision a lot more difficult by launching Teams and adding it to the bundle. For many companies, it didn’t matter that Teams was “worse”, particularly in terms of the user interface; what mattered was that it integrated with their existing products and, critically, was effectively free, because it was a part of the bundle they were already paying for.

That’s the real challenge with a usage-based pricing model: if an enterprise is paying for marginal usage, then they’re going to look a lot closer at the marginal value they are or are not getting. That means that Cowork (or Copilot) doesn’t win by default; they actually have to be at least competitive with the offerings from Anthropic and OpenAI. After all, if you’re paying regardless, you might as well make sure you’re getting what you’re paying for.

This is where I think DeepSeek will come in: while I suspect Cowork will be best with Claude, and Copilot with GPT, Microsoft is surely concerned about how much usage they can offer in their new E7 plan (which includes both for $99/employee/month) without destroying their own margins by virtue of giving margin to Anthropic and OpenAI. What would be nice would be to be able to offer a significantly higher level of usage — enough for most employees — as part of the bundle, but that may only be viable with an open source model, and DeepSeek is one of the most compelling options because of the combination of performance and serving efficiency.

And so, yet again, the biggest proponents and beneficiaries of Chinese companies offering a cheaper alternative will be American companies. This is a pattern that isn’t going away, even if Microsoft ultimately does not go down this route (but I think they will).
