text:
Microsoft's Xbox division is conducting big layoffs, as the company deals with abject failure of its Game Pass strategy.

XBOX Cuts; Bundling and the Internet Solvent; Transaction, Coordination, and Sunk Costs

Wednesday, July 8, 2026

It’s good to be back from what was a relaxing summer break, although, due to some logistical challenges and a lack of foresight on my part, said return was a day late. I will make it up to you with an Update on Thursday — and will probably stick with a Tuesday–Thursday schedule for most of the summer.

On to the Update:

XBOX Cuts

From Bloomberg :

Microsoft Corp.’s XBOX plans to eliminate 3,200 jobs, or around 20% of its staff over the next year, as part of a massive reorganization to spur growth in the struggling gaming division. XBOX will also divest four of its video-game development studios and is beginning the process to part ways with a fifth. “Our business today is not healthy,” Chief Executive Officer Asha Sharma wrote in a note to staff Monday morning, adding that XBOX is operating at margins three to 10 times lower than comparable businesses. “We must reset XBOX.”

Sharma’s note was bracing in terms of the picture it painted of XBOX’s ( now ALL CAPS ) precarious position. The full paragraph containing the above quotes was right at the top of her email:

Our business today is not healthy. We are operating at margins that are 3–10x lower than comparable platform and publishing businesses. We entered Gen 9 with a smaller install base and a higher cost structure. To grow, we bet on Game Pass, multi-platform, and a broader portfolio of content. While those businesses have created meaningful value, they did not grow at the pace we expected. As that happened, our core business weakened, and we added more teams, more investment, and more time, hoping for a better outcome. And now the industry is facing the most severe hardware crisis in its history. We must reset XBOX.

I explained what happened to XBOX in the context of the overall evolution of console gaming in 2022’s Consoles and Competition . In brief:

* Consoles used to be differentiated by hardware, and developers generally committed to one platform.
* The shift to 3D and high definition graphics drove the emergence of game engines on one hand, and increased the cost of asset creation on the other; developers responded by making games cross-platform, which particularly burned Sony’s PlayStation 3, which was predicated on hardware differentiation.
* Sony responded by buying multiple studios and making their games exclusive, which made PlayStation 4 and then 5 clear winners over XBOX (Nintendo, as always, was doing their own thing with the Switch).

That Article was written in the context of Microsoft’s acquisition of Activision, one of the first 3rd-party developers, an important part of the company’s effort to compete with Sony by brute-forcing a new business model; from the Article:

Microsoft is willing to cannibalize itself to build a new business model for video games, and it’s a business model that is pretty darn attractive for consumers. It’s also a business model that Activision wouldn’t pursue on its own, because it has its own profits to protect. Most importantly, though, it’s a business model that is anathema to Sony: making titles broadly available to consumers on a subscription basis is the exact opposite of the company’s exclusive strategy, which is all about locking consumers into Sony’s platform.

Unfortunately, what is clear is that the attempt to shift gaming from an up-front purchase model — which increased the barrier to entry for games, but maximized revenue per game — to a subscription-based services model — which gave you all of the games, at the cost of the most popular games’ profitability — was anathema to actually making money. Or, to put it another way, this was a bundling disaster.

Bundling and the Internet Solvent

Everyone is familiar with that famous Jim Barksdale quote, “There are only two ways I know to make money in business: bundling and unbundling.” Barksdale was most well-known as the CEO of Netscape in the late 1990s, and reportedly coined the aphorism during Netscape’s 1995 IPO road show. And, in the three decades since then, it’s just sort of been taken as a given that you can make money in either direction. However, I’m not sure that that is actually the case.

Consider television, the most famous bundle of all. The unbundling of the pay-TV ecosystem is well-documented by this point — and Netflix made a lot of money in the unbundling — but it’s not at all clear that things will re-bundle, at least in the way that people understand bundling. Yes, there are various special offers to subscribe to this or that collection of streaming services, but as long as everything is available a la carte it seems unlikely that there will ever be a collective offering like before; bundles work best when you don’t have a choice.

One counter to this is that Netflix didn’t just unbundle, they also bundled: ideally you can subscribe to Netflix and get something for everyone, including an ever increasing amount of low-budget filler content . This bundle, however, isn’t at all comparable to the cable bundle: no matter how much stuff Netflix gets, content you want will be streaming elsewhere; bundles work best when they have everything.

This is the key to what I think is the only real bundle that has been created by the Internet: Spotify specifically, and music streaming services generally. Technically, you still have a choice to buy music a la carte; in reality, the value proposition of Spotify is so compelling that for most people it really isn’t a choice at all. For a relatively low monthly price you get basically everything , thanks to the technological breakthrough that is streaming and cellular connectivity. This is in fact critical: economics don’t make bundles work; technological changes do, particularly when the technological change doesn’t just provide carrots but also sticks in the form of piracy (and before you bring up Amazon Prime, that is first and foremost a logistics-based bundle, i.e. it’s rooted in the physical world).

Go back to TV: the technological change that mattered there was the initial creation of cable networks to connect rural communities to large antennas capturing signals from far-off cities, followed by satellites that beamed the signals anywhere in the world. The bundling was enabled by technology — that’s the only bundling that works. The same story applies to print: newspapers were bundles that were enabled by the centralizing nature of printing presses; on the Internet, where anyone can publish, bundles are impossible.

With this framing it’s much more obvious why Game Pass failed. Microsoft’s case for Game Pass was purely an economic one: get more games for less money, and make it up in volume. What limited that volume, however, was not the fact that games were too expensive, but that the people who cared to game already did; now they simply paid less, and Microsoft lost the difference. From the Wall Street Journal :

Microsoft bought game production companies including Activision Blizzard to beef up the offerings on Game Pass, its Netflix-style subscription service. The company had projected Game Pass subscriptions would reach around 77 million this year, according to a document revealed during legal proceedings related to the Activision acquisition. It currently has about 30 million, a person familiar with the matter said.

Game Pass existed in a world of choice, it didn’t have everything, and it was fighting technological paradigms; is it any wonder it failed?

More generally, the Internet, by virtue of eliminating distribution costs, is a bundle solvent; you make money by unbundling, and lose money by trying to fight gravity. What actually works is an approach that starts with the assumption of abundance, which is to say markets. The companies that make the most money in gaming are the market makers, i.e. the storefronts, like Apple’s App Store or Valve’s Steam. Markets benefit from abundance and liquidity and maximizing consumer choice and are the most natural way to make money on the Internet.

Transaction, Coordination, and Sunk Costs

Two more paragraphs from Sharma’s email:

Since 2018, we have aggressively expanded our studio portfolio while the number of games created each month across the industry now outpaces the last ten years combined. We now find ourselves competing not only with the largest publishers, but also with smaller independent studios. It is neither possible nor desirable to own every great independent studio. We have also learned that we are not the best home for every type of studio; in a typical year, we lost 64 cents for every dollar we invested. As we reset XBOX, we will help independent creators succeed by providing open development tools and audiences to realize their vision…

We know that great technology gets better when it gets simpler, not bigger. Today, in some parts of the company, work passes through as many as 14 layers of management. Our platform teams are 40% larger than they were at the start of this generation, even as our player base and playtime have declined. That complexity has slowed decisions, blurred accountability, and made it harder to deliver for players. As we reset XBOX, we will simplify.

That first paragraph recognizes the reality I just described: trying to own everything on the Internet is impossible; it is better to own demand and facilitate users buying what they want.

The cost of fighting gravity, however, is more than the money lost: it’s the internal complexity that comes from trying to own everything. Ronald Coase wrote a famous treatise about The Nature of the Firm , which posited that companies exist because markets have costs: searching, negotiating, contracting, monitoring, enforcing, coordinating etc. are all costly transactions that can be more easily accomplished by internalizing them in a command-and-control structure. At the same time, that command-and-control structure had costs of its own — coordination costs, Coase called them — and the natural size of a firm was the point at which coordination costs roughly equaled market transaction costs.

Technology’s impact on this equilibrium has cut in both directions. On one hand, it is easier to scale because of technology; on the other, it is easier to create efficient markets because of technology. The way this has played out is that there are massive market makers on one end of the spectrum — the Aggregators — and a plethora of small actors on the other; it’s companies in the middle that have gotten squeezed.

XBOX’s Game Pass strategy, unfortunately, pushed the company right into this middle zone. Trying to own too much meant Microsoft was simultaneously not big enough to serve the smallest players (contra Steam) and also too large to efficiently serve the customers that they had. What made all of this worse is that the way that Microsoft got itself into the position of paying massive coordination costs was by also paying a massive premium to override market signals that, in the end, were perfectly rational (i.e. no independent studio wanted to join Game Pass). It really was the worst of both worlds!

This analysis is, to be clear, being done with the benefit of hindsight; I was amenable to the company’s Game Pass plan, and obviously should have considered many of these points previously. The best I can do now, then, is point out what went wrong. The considerably more difficult challenge for Microsoft is to figure out what to do with the mess they have on their hands.

There are two options that make sense. The first is to accept that the studios they bought are sunk costs, and go all-in on an exclusive strategy, even as they end Game Pass and charge full price for their titles. The other is to give up on Xbox (I haven’t even touched on the memory crisis) and simply become a game publisher. I have, for years , favored the latter, and I don’t see any reason to change. The allure of Game Pass is that it at least had some theoretical alignment with Microsoft’s services strategy; it’s hard to see any sort of synergy otherwise. Indeed, maybe that points to where we are actually headed: unwinding and/or spinning out the division completely. Sometimes it’s Game Over.

text:
The batter for verifiable data is increasingly defining the AI race, from Meta to Grok to the frontier labs.

Muse Image, Grok 4.5, Alex Karp on CNBC

Thursday, July 9, 2026

On this week’s episode of Sharp China , Andrew and Bill discuss Chinese missile tests, the CITIC plane crash, and America’s interest in preserving the Taiwan status quo.

Meanwhile, Jon at Asianometry produced a video about one of my favorite companies : Toto. You know them and I love them for their toilets; they also happen to be indispensable to the AI supply chain.

On to the Update:

Muse Image

From Bloomberg :

Meta Platforms Inc. debuted a new image-generation artificial intelligence model, its first such release since the company spent billions to rebuild its AI lab under Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang a year ago. The model, called Muse Image, is rolling out Tuesday inside the Meta AI chatbot, the company said in a blog post. It will also be embedded in Meta’s various social apps, including Instagram and WhatsApp. People can use it to generate images based on text prompts or by asking it to alter existing pictures. Advertisers, too, will soon have access to the model to create marketing materials. Users can also make images featuring friends or creators based on their publicly available Instagram posts, part of an effort by Meta to make the platform feel more personal. Those who don’t want others to “reuse or remix” their content using AI can opt out in the settings menu, according to the blog post.

The headline for Muse Image is exactly what Bloomberg leads with: end users have a new image model on Meta’s properties, and by all accounts it’s very good, thanks in part to incorporating many of the advancements that have transformed large language models. Meta’s blog post about Muse Image detailed these features, including:

* Tool use, including coding (for things like plots, QR codes, interactive games, etc.) and search (for grounding images).
* Self-Refinement, which is Meta’s term for reasoning: the model iterates on images to correct mistakes and make them better.
* Test-Time Compute Scaling, which incorporates both of the first two items: the more compute you spend on an image the better it is.

What is most compelling, however, is the advertising angle; these were the headline takeaways from Meta’s business blog (which, interestingly enough, still lives at a facebook.com URL):

* In the coming weeks, Muse Image, the first image generation model from Meta Superintelligence Labs, will help power image generation in Meta Advantage+ creative — bringing smarter reasoning and iterative refinement to our popular gen AI ad creative tool.
* Early results with Muse Image-powered generation variants show strong promise — advertisers who tested the experience cited higher-quality creative, with photorealism and product integrity standing out.
* Muse Image now enables room restyling in Meta AI Shopping, letting people visualize products from your business’ catalog in their own spaces—creating a richer, more immersive path from discovery to purchase.

I’ve been talking for years about the obvious application of image generation to advertising: instead of creating 10 or 15 pieces of creative and A/B testing which ones work best, you will be able to have exponentially more possibilities that you can rank with a built-in scoring system — i.e. did the ad convert or not?

However, there is a deeper implication to this capability that was highlighted by Eric Seufert at MobileDevMemo :

More conceptually, Meta’s integration of its own ad platform tools with a foundation image generation model that it owns is an incredibly profound commercial advantage. There are immense benefits to proprietary model ownership for the purposes of establishing closed-loop creative optimization. The most obvious is that Meta is not dependent on an outside model provider whose access, pricing, roadmap, or availability could be limited or adversely changed by export controls, competitive pressure, or government intervention; see the case of Fable 5 and Mythos 5 for a recent relevant example of this.

But the more fundamental benefit of direct integration of Muse Image into Advantage+ is that Meta can train, tune, align, and evaluate its own model against domain-specific advertiser performance data that only it possesses, producing results that are more differentiated and more use-case-native than what could be achieved through fine-tuning a generic model. A foundation model can be trained in alignment with Meta’s own retrieval and ranking infrastructure, with output controls that differentiate its ad creative from that of standalone or other platforms’ tools, in ways that enforce brand safety and preserve product integrity, with latency and cost controls. These are enormously powerful advantages for an ad platform, and they sit at the heart of my argument over why Meta is reaping real rewards, now, through its AI investments.

Integrating Muse into Advantage+ is exactly the kind of narrative-supporting development that Meta should be pursuing to assuage investor anxiety over its AI investments; it is more visible, given the creative applicability, but it also showcases the power of foundation model ownership because an open weight model might have been fine-tuned for this use case instead (compare that to GEM, which is also a foundation model but for which no open weight alternative exists).

One of the single most important contributors to model improvement is verifiability. A major reason why coding has been such a fruitful area of AI development is because code is verifiable: does it work or not? That, by extension, means that the more that a particular task is verifiable, the faster it will be done by AI. Or, to put it another way, owning verification is extremely advantageous, and markets are verification mechanisms. Yes, you need to have enough liquidity to get sufficient signal — there is a lot of noise in this data — but that is exactly what Meta ads are: arguably the most liquid market in the world, with trillions of ads driving conversions or not. Any model that plugs directly into that signal is going to get better sooner.

Grok 4.5

From Bloomberg :

SpaceXAI has unveiled a new artificial intelligence model built in partnership with AI coding startup Cursor that’s meant to be more adept at finance, legal and coding tasks, in a bid by Elon Musk’s firm to gain ground on rivals like Anthropic PBC and OpenAI. The software, called Grok 4.5, marks the first joint AI model developed by the two companies and comes just weeks after SpaceX formally agreed to acquire Cursor in a deal that values the startup at $60 billion.

Grok 4.5 seems to be pretty decent; it’s also quite cheap relative to its performance; this is Cursor Field CTO David Pan on X :

X Post

The benchmark on the left is Cursor’s own benchmark, so take the performance with the appropriate grain of salt, and frankly, it’s hard enough to convince people — including myself! — to even try other models once they’re used to a specific one, particularly if they use the associated harness, which is to say that Grok has a very long ways to go to actually win usage. What I’m not surprised by, however, is that the tie-up with Cursor is paying dividends. It’s a continuation of my point above: Cursor had and has a lot of usage and captured a ton of traces around code in particular, and it was always a good bet that that data would be exceptionally valuable.

What is worth noting is that this might also be another argument that OpenAI was ultimately harmed by the widespread consumer adoption of ChatGPT, at least absent a compelling advertising business: it’s not just that consumers were a distraction that didn’t subscribe enough even as they used a lot of GPUs, it’s that most consumer AI interactions aren’t particularly useful data for a feedback mechanism. This is in part due to the nature of chatbots — how do you know if the code you generated ran or not? — but also due to the fact that most people aren’t coding. They’re asking about recipes or life or who knows what else, many of which are, if not unanswerable, at least unverifiable.

Alex Karp on CNBC

Last week Palantir CEO Alex Karp delivered quite the interview on CNBC , criticizing the leading model companies in particular. The video is a ride, and worth a watch, but there was one point he came back to again and again in an interview nominally about Palantir’s deal to bring Nvidia’s open source Nemotron model to the U.S. government ( excerpt lightly edited for clarity ):

If you want to know how this came together from my perspective, there’s a lot of technical issues, the choice of who controls the models, who controls the weights, who controls the value of your business. But, you know, we’re sitting on critical infrastructure across America…and our clients are just [so] unhappy with the frontier labs…It’s like there’s just a level of discomfort and loss of trust…

The basic view among enterprises in this country is I’m going to chillax and waste my time with tokens. I’m going to get no value and they’re going to get my IP…They’re like, why would they get access to my data if they’re going to steal my alpha? Why wouldn’t I control the weights? That’s where you get this partnership. What aligns me with Nvidia and I think is what the most technical customers want, which is control over their compute, their models, their data stack and their alpha they want to know they own the means of production and it is not being transferred to someone else. They’re not interested in some fake deploy co that someone is deploying, and tokens that transfers the alpha to a third party.

Again later on:

We need to rebuild trust and that trust is going to happen where everyone gets to ask and answer basic questions. Who owns the data? Where is it cached? Are the prompts secure? Is this being transferred to you?…What is the true cost? Not just what you’re paying. The true cost is not just what you make minus what you lose, meaning the value of your business. But we can get the the frontier application to be exactly the same, as a frontier model, without the risk of transferring the alpha of your business to a model. By the way, you could do this with a frontier model closed model too, but then the clients have to be able to ask and answer very basic questions. Are you keeping the data? Are you going to enter our business?

That’s my role, but I’m telling you in this country at every single enterprise I deal with. These people are livid. They’re like, I am paying for tokens that create no value. These people are stealing the weights and alpha of my business…and I can’t safely give it to an enterprise in this country without being certain that the alpha in the business could transfer to this model tomorrow, i.e. now I’ve got no business, no job.

*You sound pretty angry.*

This is the voice of American business that is being channeled through me, and I’m telling you it is absolutely a problem for this country.

What Karp is driving at is the flip-side of the points I am making above (and, I would add, is the same argument Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella made in a recent Stratechery Interview ): the challenge for enterprises when it comes to using the frontier models is not simply that tokens are expensive, but that they are potentially giving valuable data to the labs who, in the long run, have an economic imperative to move up the stack and own the customer directly.

This was already a concern, but I think the most underrated aspect of the Fable release was Anthropic changing the terms of service such that they would retain all data, even from enterprise customers — for safety reasons, of course. I wrote in Anthropic’s Safety Superpower :

The models — not even Mythos — are not yet at this point. What they need, beyond more compute, is more and better data. Model improvements increasingly come from reinforcement learning; some of this can be generated synthetically, but the most powerful lever for a frontier lab is real world use.

This, I think, is a major reason why both OpenAI and Anthropic offer their heavily subsidized subscription plans. SemiAnalysis recently estimated that a $200 plan gets you $8,000 worth of Claude tokens and $14,000 worth of Codex tokens. Of course both are fighting for user and developer mindshare, but they’re also fighting to have access to actual usage data to make their models better.

Anthropic upped the ante in a major way with Fable, announcing that they would retain the data for all usage for 30 days, even for their enterprise plans that previously promised zero data retention. The company said they would not train on this data, but they didn’t put in any sort of safeguards to guarantee they wouldn’t do so in the future (like storing the data with a third party). If this policy change (whenever Fable is restored) doesn’t lead to a significant loss of customers, I suspect it’s only a matter of time until they start using the data: it’s simply too valuable to their end goals.

Note also the virtuous cycle with moving up into user touchpoints: the more workflows that are done directly with Claude or Codex, the more data each company gets to feed back into their training, which makes their products that much more capable and useful, expanding the number of workflows they can serve, expanding their access to data.

To take this full circle, this is another reason to be a bit bullish about Meta: they operate in markets where it is a given that Meta gets and acts on all of the data; they don’t need to fight enterprise data policies. Anthropic, meanwhile, appears to be making a bet that they can be better enough that they can get the data they need anyways (and that said data will drive that virtuous cycle where their offering improves that much more rapidly); they might cash it in.

text:
Apple is suing AI for stealing trade secrets; there is one guilty employee, but this mostly feels like lashing out.

Apple Sues OpenAI, Apple’s Real Problem

Monday, July 13, 2026

On last week’s episode of Sharp Tech , Andrew and I discussed Meta’s messaging problem, the Xbox reset, and why I’ve always been bearish on American soccer.

I am here on Monday with an Update: I couldn’t resist weighing in on the Apple-OpenAI lawsuit ASAP. I’ll be back two more times this week.

On to the Update:

Apple Sues OpenAI

From the Wall Street Journal :

Apple sued OpenAI and one of its top executives Friday alleging the AI company stole trade secrets as part of its effort to develop competing devices. The federal suit filed in the Northern District of California accuses OpenAI’s chief hardware officer, Tang Tan, and Chang Liu, a member of its technical staff, of taking Apple’s confidential information through various methods. Both are former Apple employees who went to work for OpenAI.

The lawsuit shows how the relationship between the two companies has rapidly deteriorated since 2024, when they signed a deal to have OpenAI’s ChatGPT work with Apple’s Siri chatbot. Apple’s new Siri AI, announced in June, is powered by Google’s Gemini technology. Tan is leading OpenAI’s efforts to develop its own devices, a crucial strategic effort so that the company can reach consumers directly, rather than via other companies’ devices such as Apple’s iPhone…

Apple said in its suit that it lacks visibility into what OpenAI has done with its information but alleged that “at every level, from members of its Technical Staff to its Chief Hardware Officer, and in coordination with business partners, OpenAI has been stealing Apple’s trade secrets and confidential information.” A spokesperson for OpenAI said, “We have no interest in other companies’ trade secrets. We remain focused on building innovative technology that empowers people everywhere.” Tan and Liu couldn’t immediately be reached for comment.

You can read Apple’s filing here , and almost everything you need to know is actually on the first page, in the first four paragraphs.

* Paragraph 1 is a succinct introduction to the case: “This case is about Apple’s former employees stealing Apple’s trade secrets for the benefit of OpenAI. Apple brings this suit to put a stop to it.”
* Paragraph 2 recounts how Apple has spent a lot of time and money building products that delight customers.
* Paragraph 3 basically says that everything they do is a trade secret.
* Paragraph 4 introduces one Chang Liu, and spends the next page-and-a-half recounting his crimes.

Liu is almost certainly guilty, and an idiot to boot. Apple has lots of details about Liu’s behavior, including downloading “dozens” of proprietary Apple hardware-related files and encouraging another Apple employee to do the same, because he did it on his Apple-issued laptop, and furthermore, logged onto Apple’s servers for weeks after he had already left the company.

A couple of quick points here:

* A few weeks ago there was a bit of a hubbub about Meta capturing keystrokes from employees in order to train AI. What confused me was people’s surprise that a company had this level of access to company-issued hardware in the first place. Moreover, while that access may very well be theoretical for a lot of companies, at Apple it has always been a well-known fact — going at least as far back as when I was an intern there 16 years ago — that the company could and would go through everything if you ever crossed them.
* Apple’s security, as depicted in this case, is shockingly poor! First, the company lost track of the fact that Liu didn’t return one of his laptops, or disable it remotely. Second, due to what Apple claimed was a bug, Liu continued to have access to the company’s internal servers for weeks.

Regardless, Liu appears to be clearly guilty. I don’t think, however, that Liu is the point. What he is, from Apple’s perspective, is a fishing license. The company said as much towards the end of the introduction:

This is the tip of the iceberg. Apple lacks visibility into what’s been happening behind closed doors at OpenAI, where such misconduct is normalized and exemplified by leadership. This much is clear, however: at every level, from members of its Technical Staff to its Chief Hardware Officer, and in coordination with business partners, OpenAI has been stealing Apple’s trade secrets and confidential information. As a natural result, OpenAI’s nascent hardware business now rests on the shakiest of foundations, rotten to its core by its illegal reliance on misappropriated trade secrets.

What follows are multiple appeals for discovery. Apple is actually only sure that Liu stole trade secrets; they want to use that proof — derived from their own laptop — to get access to everything OpenAI is doing.

Apple’s Real Problem

The other named defendant in this case is Tang Tan, the former Vice President of Product Design for iPhone and Apple Watch, and almost every allegation Apple makes against him could easily be restated far more benignly: of course interviews touch on what employees have worked on — how would you know if you wanted to hire them otherwise? — and when it comes to the supplier allegation, Patrick McGee wrote an entire book about how Chinese suppliers take what Apple taught them and apply it to other products for other companies. I don’t think any of what is in the lawsuit is Tan’s — or OpenAI’s — real crime, at least in Apple’s eyes.

First, I think that Apple feels betrayed not just by Tan, but also Jony Ive. Start with the fact that Ive framed his partnership with OpenAI as an attempt to undo the harms he thought were caused by the smartphone, not exactly a ringing endorsement of the company that made him famous and rich. Apple can’t bring itself to attack Ive directly, which leaves Tan to bear the brunt of Apple’s fury.

Second, Tan is the point person for the four hundred people that Apple says that OpenAI has hired away from the smartphone maker. That is no crime, of course, although one gets the sense Apple sure thinks it is. From the lawsuit:

Despite Apple’s rigorous security measures and practices, Apple’s trade secrets have been compromised through the deliberate misconduct by those previously entrusted with them. Apple’s former engineers and executives — recruited, directed and rewarded by OpenAI — along with OpenAI itself and its business cohorts, have been stealing Apple’s most sensitive information for a would-be competitor. With over four hundred former Apple employees now working at OpenAI, it is not surprising that certain OpenAI personnel have knowledge of Apple’s confidential and proprietary information, which they are obligated to keep confidential. But OpenAI has resorted to exploiting this confidential information, using it to extract still more from Apple’s current employees and trusted partners, and to structure its interview processes to try to solicit additional confidential Apple information—all while taking steps to conceal its actions. That OpenAI now employs people who were once entrusted with Apple’s trade secrets does not entitle OpenAI to use that information to jumpstart its hardware efforts.

That last sentence gets at one of the cruxes of the case: Apple’s trade secret claims in this case are impossibly broad; should this ever go to trial, narrowly defining what is and is not a trade secret will be a major point of contention. As it stands Apple is basically saying that any Apple employee at OpenAI is a walking trade secret, and, well, that’s why OpenAI hired them! From where else would OpenAI hire the personnel necessary to build a consumer electronics company?

That leads to a further point: Apple hasn’t really had competition for its best hardware and operations people until now. Yes, Meta had their headsets, and Google their phones, but from what I understand, there has never before been a mass exodus from Apple for a competitor like has happened in this case, and I don’t think Apple likes that very much! And Tan is the one leading the charge.

Third, just as Tan is the face of Apple betrayal, OpenAI is the face of AI generally, and it’s hard to escape the sense that Apple just really hates AI — and why shouldn’t they? Go back to 2022 and Apple had it all figured out: they had a lock on the premium end of the smartphone market, which they continued to slowly expand, even as they had figured out how to earn Services revenue from every iPhone user basically forever. Business was good!

AI has ruined all of that. Suddenly Apple had to make existential decisions about whether or not to compete in the model game, then they totally embarrassed themselves with the 2024 new Siri introduction, had their most prominent blogger declare that Something Is Rotten in the State of Cupertino , had to completely overhaul their software and services teams, lost their position as kings of the supply chain and most favored customer of TSMC, to the point where they had to enact an emergency mid-cycle price raise, and then, worst of all, have to actually wrestle with the possibility that AI is such a paradigm shift that it actually might threaten the iPhone. And then, on top of all that, they lose 400 of their best employees — recruited by the lead hardware engineer for the iPhone, in partnership with their most famous executive outside of Steve Jobs — and have to know that all 400 of those employees are getting hit up by their former colleagues looking for a job as well!

The AI era has sucked for Apple. Even if they aren’t necessarily doomed, and even if the relaunched new Siri ends up working out, their position is still more fragile than it was, and everything about life is worse. Given that, how sweet it must feel to suddenly have a smoking gun in the form of a seriously dumb employee blatantly lifting documents, and to use it as a cudgel to exact revenge on the company that represents everything that is making your life miserable!

This perspective does make one wonder if that phrase “rotten to its core” was projection in the end. AI is changing the world, and Apple’s contribution is to deliver two year-old technology differentiated by exclusive access to data it won’t share. It certainly has no interest in delivering on a new AI-driven paradigm that endangers its iPhone franchise in any way; any of its employees who wish to do exactly that, meanwhile, are being told loud and clear that Apple doesn’t just think it owns your laptop, but also your mind and knowledge. I think it mostly stinks — but then again, rotten things usually do.

text:
OpenAI has refashioned Codex as the new ChatGPT; is the company abandoning the chat category they pioneered?

The OpenAI Super App, ChatGPT = Codex, Whither Chat

Tuesday, July 14, 2026

I got a fun email from former Apple executive, Nest founder, and one-time Stratechery Interview subject Tony Fadell in response to yesterday’s Update about Apple suing OpenAI ( published with permission ):

Good article as always…This is Apple’s typical tactic to scare Apple employees — either former or current. I heard this lawsuit was driven by the Apple board.

Steve threatened to file a lawsuit against Nest for poaching 80-100 Apple employees. He called me, screamed for a while with lots of accusations. Then I said, “Steve, it’s Apple’s job to retain its talent, not mine.” He stopped his rant and then we went on to talk about our families and vacation plans. We kept hiring…

This sounds about right — and in terms of the Steve Jobs angle, John Gruber made a compelling case on Dithering that this lawsuit may very well have been driven by John Ternus channeling his inner Jobs.

On to the Update:

The OpenAI Super App

From Reuters :

OpenAI showcased a new AI agent on Thursday meant to help white-collar workers access the power of coding tools without the sticker shock. The agent, called ChatGPT Work, combines OpenAI’s popular chatbot with its AI coding tool, Codex, to create documents, presentations and websites, the company said. The service is powered by OpenAI’s most advanced AI model, GPT-5.6, which also debuted on Thursday. That model’s launch was delayed last month at the U.S. government’s request over national security fears.

ChatGPT Work is a direct answer to Anthropic’s Claude Cowork, an agent it launched in January that is capable of planning and executing multi-step tasks autonomously. The launch reflects intensifying competition to build and sell AI tools for professional use, as technology companies seek to capitalize on rising demand for autonomous agents that can complete complex tasks with minimal human input. Anthropic and OpenAI — both of which are preparing for possible public offerings soon — are fighting for enterprise business, which is more lucrative than selling products to consumers. Both ChatGPT Work and Claude Cowork are designed for non-coders who want to tap into the abilities of AI coding tools, which are often more capable than standard chatbots, but require specialized knowledge.

OpenAI officials emphasized that its new offerings would be both cheaper and more broadly available than its rivals’ products. The company launched three different sizes of its 5.6 model.

This was one of the most shocking product Updates I’ve ever experienced — although your experience may have differed! I’m focused in this Update primarily on the Mac app experience, and if you only ever had the Mac app installed, well, you got an updated app that was pretty much the same excellent native app you were used to, but now with access to 5.6 (it’s unclear if it’s Sol, the most advanced model, Terra, the mid-sized model, or Luna, the smallest and fastest model; the model picker only specifies reasoning level).

However, if you had Codex installed — OpenAI’s developer-focused app — then you had a much different experience. Upon updating, Codex renamed itself ChatGPT (with an option to keep the Codex icon), while the old ChatGPT app renamed itself ChatGPT Classic. That appears to be the only supported way to get ChatGPT Classic if you didn’t already have the old ChatGPT installed, because if you download ChatGPT from the OpenAI website it’s the new ChatGPT, which is a rebranded Codex (as the app bundle plainly states).

The shock doesn’t stop there, because ChatGPT — the new Codex-based app — isn’t really a chat app at all, at least at first glance. There is a dropdown menu that lets you choose between ChatGPT Work and Codex…and not chat. There is a chat option in the sidebar, which opens up a floating chat pane on the right side of the window, as if you were on an e-commerce site with an eager LLM looking for a prompt injection. It feels like an afterthought, for an app that has chat in its name.

ChatGPT = Codex

The reaction to the update has been extremely negative, particularly amongst the old Apple crowd. Gruber wrote on Daring Fireball :

The old ChatGPT app was focused. That’s the app that still ships for mobile (which includes iPad, which tells you whether OpenAI thinks iPad is a real computer or a big iPhone), and is, for some Mac users, left installed on their systems as “ChatGPT Classic”. The new app is an incredibly confusing sloppy mess. At a glance it looks like a polished app. But the UI is just slop. It has the veneer of a polished app without actually being organized or structured or labeled in ways that add clarity and coherence. It’s playing dress-up as a big-boy app. My understanding from people adjacent to OpenAI is that the company’s senior executives are singularly consumed with FOMO obsession regarding Anthropic, and the only real clout within the company belongs to the AI researchers. Not product designers or app craftspeople. What the researchers say goes, and with this update, we can see their level of taste in app design.

M.G. Siegler wrote on Spyglass :

It took me a while to figure out what was going on with ‘ChatGPT Work’ – and that was after I watched the unveiling video . I knew this was a new aspect of ChatGPT, but I assumed the “old” aspect would remain as the default here. You know, chat. Having written a post entitled “Chat is dead” specifically about OpenAI moving away from the chat paradigm for ChatGPT, I also probably should have realized this! But I just didn’t think OpenAI would make this transition so jarring.

When I see the new ChatGPT app launch into ‘ChatGPT Work’, I instinctively assume it’s an enterprise version of the app. Instead, OpenAI clearly means for ‘ChatGPT Work’ to evoke ‘Claude Cowork’, you know the agentic set of Claude tools, but this is insanely clunky branding. As much as people may know Claude Cowork, probably infinitely more think of Microsoft’s enterprise suite of productivity tools when they see ‘Work’. Or they think of the English language itself. And ‘ChatGPT Work’ makes it sound like it’s ChatGPT to use at work. Like as in your office. As in not for home. Not for personal use.

I’m a bit more sympathetic to OpenAI on one specific vector: Codex, i.e. the new ChatGPT, is one of the most incredible apps I have ever used. I’ve written about my vibe coding adventures , which have only accelerated, particularly as I have leaned into a model where I run Codex on the Mac Mini in my server rack and access it from anywhere and everywhere, including my work laptop, a MacBook Air I have upstairs, or my phone. This usage model very much feels like a glimpse into the future: the device at hand actually doesn’t matter, as long as it gives me access to my AI.

Another realization I have had is the extent to which Linux and LLMs go hand-in-hand: one of the frustrations of a Mac Mini in the rack is the number of times you have to interact with the GUI thanks to some random warning or permission that macOS will throw up; meanwhile, Docker doesn’t run natively, which means hosting basic apps requires a virtualization layer that is prone to weird failures, and things like SMB connections are flakey. Linux, meanwhile, not only handles all of these things natively and seamlessly, and not only is it designed to be used headlessly via the command line, it’s actually made dramatically more powerful by virtue of being controlled by an LLM, which makes sense: a pure text interface is a perfect match for a large language model, which suddenly gives you dramatically more control and capability than a GUI ever could (Codex is only available on Mac and Windows, but my apps are deployed on Linux).

All that noted, the most surprising experience I had was when I was setting something up with my Synology. Synologys are network-attached storage devices with their own proprietary flavor of Linux that is very GUI-centric; they generally try to steer you away from using the command line interface. To that end, when Codex wanted to make a change, it simply opened up the GUI in its in-app browser, asked me to log in, and started mousing around! It was pretty surreal — and it worked perfectly, albeit much more slowly than a command-line interface.

In short, I can understand the sentiments Stephanie Palazzolo reported on in The Information early last month :

Nearly 18 months later, OpenAI leaders—including Thibault Sottiaux, who oversaw the new team — came to a stark realization: The company’s Codex coding tool works better for many tasks than its flagship AI service, ChatGPT. For instance, Codex is better than ChatGPT at completing long-running, multistep tasks and at using external tools and writing code to complete tasks such as editing complicated spreadsheets, Sottiaux said in an interview.

The result is that OpenAI is now casting Codex as a tool that can do much more than coding and that a wide range of people other than developers can use. The company’s release on Tuesday of a research report on how Codex “is becoming a productivity tool for everyone” spotlighted that shift. Codex, OpenAI said, is “helping people across professions automate routine work, move faster and eliminate the bottlenecks of modern knowledge work.”

Also on Tuesday, OpenAI said that a previously announced combination of ChatGPT, Codex and its browser, Atlas, into a single desktop “superapp” would be launched in the coming weeks. In combining the apps, OpenAI hopes to focus its efforts on its most successful products, OpenAI’s leaders have said, which lately means Codex.

Codex is incredibly capable in a way that ChatGPT simply isn’t. They’re not really in the same category. It’s like comparing the calculator app to Excel: both do math, but the power and possibilities aren’t even remotely in the same ballpark. How many people, however, have any idea what they are missing out on?

Whither Chat

Just last week I wrote in passing about the problem with chat in an increasingly agentic world:

What is worth noting is that this might also be another argument that OpenAI was ultimately harmed by the widespread consumer adoption of ChatGPT, at least absent a compelling advertising business: it’s not just that consumers were a distraction that didn’t subscribe enough even as they used a lot of GPUs, it’s that most consumer AI interactions aren’t particularly useful data for a feedback mechanism. This is in part due to the nature of chatbots — how do you know if the code you generated ran or not? — but also due to the fact that most people aren’t coding. They’re asking about recipes or life or who knows what else, many of which are, if not unanswerable, at least unverifiable.

I guess this sentiment means that while this app launch was shocking, it shouldn’t be surprising? It really does feel, as Siegler noted, that OpenAI is killing chat. Siegler wrote in response to that The Information article, again on Spyglass :

To reiterate, that’s a current OpenAI exec speaking on-the-record about these changes. And his comments also suggest a move beyond the chatbot but also that the company believes we may yet enter a world of “ one AI to rule them all ” – something I’ve explored more recently in thinking about if the AI world might play out in a similar manner to the old “bring your own device” strategy in enterprise. Is your personal AI going to be so ingrained in your life that it’s also just most convenient to use it as your work AI?

This puts that chat window in the bottom right corner in a different context. Gruber is dismayed — for very understandable reasons! — that the new ChatGPT is abandoning the focus of the old app. That focus, however, behooved an app that was one among many: you opened it up for one specific purpose, and that was to talk to ChatGPT, and you used other apps for other things. This new app, however, is one that is best experienced full screen, with a built-in browser and everything, and a chat window in the corner. It is, for all intents and purposes, a self-contained operating system, but the primitives aren’t your processor and the platform isn’t for apps: the offering is intelligence undergirding an audacious offer to do your work for you.

I do see the vision. ChatGPT, traditionally understood, is threatened in a world of Google shoving Gemini everywhere, Meta manifesting Muse, and Apple launching a Siri that actually works for the things people used a focused chat app for; Codex, meanwhile, is the sort of product that Apple will never launch, Meta will never gain user permission to launch, and Google seems incapable of launching. OpenAI appears to have decided to go all in, trading in their massive head start in terms of a chatbot user base for the opportunity to forcibly introduce AI’s tremendous capabilities to people who probably had no idea.

I’m also not sure if it’s going to work. Codex is incredible and it’s also really complicated and a bit intimidating. It’s also about work — being productive — which is something I’m not sure most people are particularly interested in, especially in their free time. ChatGPT v1 may have made OpenAI the accidental consumer tech company ; this release seems like a deliberate rejection of that opportunity.

That, though, leaves one very big question mark: if ChatGPT is going to be about work and getting stuff done, then why is OpenAI moving full steam ahead with their advertising product? Advertising is a consumer business model, but this doesn’t feel like a consumer app, at least to the extent you think that consumers are more interested in entertainment and lean-back experiences than they are in agents. Perhaps the answer is that advertising is a mobile story, where the ChatGPT app remains much more of a pure chatbot; maybe the answer is that OpenAI still isn’t quite sure what they want to be.

Regardless, Codex ChatGPT really is an incredible app: using it has made me feel like a kid in the 90s all over again, delightfully discovering technology for the first time, imagining what might be possible, and maybe that’s enough. What is more valuable: 1 billion consumers typing questions and not paying, or a fraction of those engaging ever more deeply such that they can’t help but pay for more? I guess we’re going to find out.

text:
IBM announced preliminary results that spooked the software market generally; this is a story, however, specifically about IBM and its mainframe franchise.

IBM Misses, IBM’s Mainframe Moat, IBM’s Many AI Problems

Wednesday, July 15, 2026

Summer is in full effect, which doesn’t just mean the summer schedule continues (i.e. no Stratechery Interview), but also NBA Summer League. Andrew and new Greatest of All Talk co-host Adam Mares discuss all of the new rookies and everything else happening in the NBA in this week’s episode .

On to the Update:

IBM Misses

From Bloomberg :

International Business Machines Corp. shares slid the most in at least 58 years after the company reported preliminary second-quarter sales that fell short of expectations, attributing the miss to customers shifting their spending to chips and servers amid AI-fueled shortages. Preliminary second-quarter revenue totaled $17.2 billion, IBM said Tuesday in a statement, below analysts’ estimates of $17.9 billion. Sales from IBM’s infrastructure division, which includes mainframe computers, were especially hard hit, dropping 7%. The company said it’s still reviewing its books and final results, set to post next week, may be slightly different.

The shares plunged 25% to $217.07, the biggest single-day loss since at least Jan. 3, 1968, the earliest date for which Bloomberg has pricing data on the stock. IBM’s announcement initially weighed on other software companies, with stocks including ServiceNow Inc. and Workday Inc. slipping before making up some of the loss later in the trading day.

Software companies continue to, as Steven Tyler once sang, live on the edge: if one company reports something that reminds investors about software terminal risk in the age of AI, everyone plummets, deserved or not. And, in this case, I’m not entirely sure it was deserved; what happened to IBM was much more interesting, because hardware is always more interesting than software.

This filing from IBM was preliminary, which means there wasn’t an earnings call, just a letter from CEO Arvind Krishna to investors . Here’s the key paragraph:

When we discussed our expectations with you in April, we noted that we would be wrapping on the launch of z17 in the second quarter. Given this was the strongest start to a mainframe program in our history, we expected Infrastructure revenue to decline low-single digits for the year, beginning this quarter. What played out was worse than our expectations, driven by a shortfall in our Z performance and the associated software stack, primarily in Transaction Processing. In the last few weeks of June, we saw clients shift their quarterly capex spend toward servers, storage, and memory purchases to secure supply-constrained infrastructure ahead of expected price increases. This dynamic impacted client buying patterns. While we anticipated some supply chain related impact in our expectations, we did not anticipate the magnitude of the capex reprioritization. In addition, clients were distracted with rapidly-evolving, industry-wide cybersecurity concerns in the quarter.

This is a story that has very little to do with the ServiceNows and Workdays of the world, at least in the way that the market seemed to interpret it. Those companies — like all SaaS companies — sell products that are operational expenses for their customers, i.e. opex, not capex. That’s part of the entire premise of SaaS: you don’t need to make large up-front investments in your own software development and the hardware to run it on; you just pay a seat license every month.

The business Krishna is talking about is different: the z17 is IBM’s latest mainframe computer, and it costs real money to buy and install in the customer’s data center. That money is capex, not opex: you spend it up-front so that you can have the machine to use on an ongoing basis. What Krishna is saying is that some number of customers chose, at least last quarter, to allocate their budgeted capex numbers to non-mainframe servers, storage, and memory, crowding out IBM’s mainframe. And, to be clear, that’s a very plausible story — and it’s one that doesn’t have anything to do with crowding out of software licensing, which falls into the opex budget (a crowd-out could happen here as well, to be clear; it’s just more bureaucratically challenging than shifting capex budgets).

At the same time, there is a software story, as Krishna’s quote notes. Specifically, customers also pay IBM for the software that runs on those mainframes on an ongoing basis, which is opex. That opex, though, is very different from traditional SaaS: first, it’s intimately tied to hardware, and second, given that this hardware is used for Transaction Processing — think a massive retailer processing purchases, or an airline processing reservations — the pricing is much more akin to a usage-based model than it is a per-seat licensing model. That’s where the lack of upgrades stings: new systems create the capacity and contractual occasion for customers to add workloads and increase software consumption, and that expected expansion did not happen.

That noted, there is something that is curious about Krishna’s claims. Go back to IBM’s Q3 2025 earnings call and CFO Jim Kavanaugh’s prepared remarks:

Transaction Processing revenue declined by 3%, reflecting another quarter of z17 outperformance as clients continue to prioritize hardware spend on our latest IBM Z system. While this dynamic impacts near-term revenue, we’re encouraged by a healthy pipeline that positions us well for future demand.

Krishna expanded on this point in the question-and-answer section of the call:

Jim touched on Transaction Processing or mainframe software. We have seen this happen multiple times. In the first couple of quarters of a new cycle, TP tends to come down because people are very much focused on getting their hardware capacity. As that hardware capacity gets deployed, then the TP revenue begins to come up, along with some of the ELA cycle dynamics that are there, and we begin to see that. So I expect to see TP grow, not quite in double digits to be clear, but let’s call it low single digits, for sure, into next year.

So which is it? A year ago, when z17 sales were strong, IBM blamed those strong sales for lower-than-expected Transaction Processing software revenue. Now, when z17 sales missed, IBM is also blaming that miss for lower-than-expected Transaction Processing software revenue. Given that IBM stuck with the first narrative in the intervening two quarters — Transaction Processing grew, which IBM credited to those z17 sales — it sure seems to me that it’s this quarter that is the anomaly.

IBM’s Mainframe Moat

One thing to notice about all of this discussion is the extent to which IBM manages to make money coming and going. SaaS companies may be an operational expense, but at least you don’t have to also pay for the servers the SaaS applications run on! With IBM, that’s exactly how it works: you pay capex for the hardware and opex to IBM for the software that runs on it. It’s an amazing business!

It’s also a business basically no one opts into, or has opted into for years. Any new company is going to build their infrastructure in the cloud; if they actually have a need for their own hardware, then they will buy the hardware and run Linux on it and write their own applications. It’s an opex versus capex trade-off; going with an IBM mainframe is choosing the worst of both worlds.

In other words, who IBM is selling to is existing customers, and those customers are trapped. Most of them have been IBM customers for decades. Again, think banks, airlines, etc.: these are entities that drove the first wave of IT , wiping out entire backrooms of bookkeepers in the process. They have gained the advantages of technology the longest of anyone; the price they pay is that their transactions are so numerous and complex that they can’t afford to move them, which leaves them at the mercy of IBM taking their pound of flesh.

At the same time, a move from mainframes can be done; United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby told me in a Stratechery Interview :

*SK:* We’re trying to do it all, because it all ties together. One of the big enablers was, that we started after I got here, we spent several hundred million dollars just getting off of our legacy mainframe systems, several hundred million rewriting code.

*Is that the key? That is the key enabler?*

*SK:* That was a key unlock. You can’t do what we do unless you do that first, it was a key unlock.

*So, just for the nerds, what was the system that you were running on before?*

*SK:* Oh, we were on, it was called SHARES, but it’s a Fortran-based system that was written in the ’60s.

*And so, what are you on now? Are you just on a regular cloud environment now?*

*SK:* We’re on our own stuff. Yeah, it’s all cloud and it’s our own stuff, but we spent hundreds of millions. It’s not done. In fact, the last cutover’s coming next year for the last piece.

That upgrade was successful , but Kirby may have overstated things: SHARES was historically run on Unisys mainframes operated by EDS and later HP, and the company still has job listings for IBM mainframe developers . That noted, the job requirements are clear:

Partner with modernization and cloud teams to support mainframe-to-cloud migration initiatives, including application inventory, dependency analysis, data extraction, and coexistence strategies with Java/Spring Boot APIs and Oracle data stores.

And:

Contribute to system documentation, operational readiness, and decommissioning planning, supporting the transition from on-premises mainframe systems toward a modernized Azure-based cloud platform.

Now I’m not saying that IBM missed their numbers because of United; what I am saying is that:

* It is possible to move legacy businesses away from mainframes.
* Moving off a mainframe can eliminate IBM’s combined hardware-and-software tax and lower long-term marginal costs, although the migration itself may be extraordinarily expensive.
* United’s business has benefited significantly from its moves, because it enabled the airline to have the best tech stack in the industry, increasing loyalty amongst flyers like yours truly.

Still, who wants to actually do all of that work? It’s amazing United made that investment, but most companies will probably just pay IBM forever, because they don’t have the developers or budget to do the drudgerous work entailed in porting those mainframe applications to the cloud, which is a prerequisite for actually building new things.

But what if developers didn’t need to do it?

IBM’s Many AI Problems

IBM’s short-term AI problem is exactly what happened this last quarter: mainframe customers repurposed spend that would have gone to upgrading their hardware to other hardware purchases, most likely to support their AI initiatives.

It’s the long-term problem, however, that is much more pernicious: of all the things that AI is well-suited for, porting code has to be near the top of the list. There isn’t any creativity or design involved, and you literally have a working example to compare output against. And what is the single most attractive code to port in terms of not just economics but also enabling innovation in your business? It’s the mainframe code; you can stop double-paying IBM on one side, and actually build on top of a modern platform on the other.

This, finally, gets at what I suspect started to happen to IBM this quarter, above-and-beyond the AI crowd-out: no, I don’t think that IBM customers suddenly ported their workloads off of mainframes. What happened is that IBM customers just became aware that it was possible to do so with AI. The way that translates for IBM’s business is twofold:

* First, if it’s now possible or becoming possible to move away from mainframes because of AI, then you don’t necessarily need to do it now, but you also probably don’t want to invest in a new mainframe. Best to limp along on what you have until you decide if a move away is feasible.
* Second, if it’s now possible or becoming possible to move away from mainframes because of AI, then it starts making sense to shift incremental usage somewhere other than mainframes; it certainly doesn’t make sense to re-up with IBM for bigger deals for more usage.

The optimistic outcome for IBM is that its customers ultimately decide that the risk of porting their most essential applications is not worth it, and they resume mainframe purchases and expand their software contracts. The pessimistic take is that they decide the opposite — and the longer they wait to decide without making any purchases, the better the AI will become!

It’s not all doom-and-gloom for IBM. Its consulting business grew, for example, thanks to companies looking for help in incorporating AI into their business. The company also framed Mythos as a positive in terms of driving their cybersecurity business. And, it should be noted, the company’s other hardware businesses benefited from that capex crowd-out. Still, I think the extremely high margin mainframe business is in trouble. Customers suddenly see a way out, and even if they stick around for now, it certainly behooves them to not pour more money into a product that once seemed inescapable.
